title: Dem bucks party over alleged Alaska vote-siphoning effort: 'Neither party should be doing it'
description: Iowa's Rob Sand slams his own party's alleged vote siphoning in Alaska's Senate race, calling it "manipulating the political system" amid legal chaos.
content: Elections Disputes Dem bucks party over alleged Alaska vote-siphoning effort: 'Neither party should be doing it' The Justice Department has intervened due to concerns over ballot confusion between two candidates by the same name By Alec Schemmel Fox News Published October 26, 2026 4:39pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video Iowa gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand weighs in on Alaska Senate ballot controversy Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand discusses the dispute involving two Alaska Senate candidates who share the name Dan Sullivan during an exclusive interview with Fox News. NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! Iowa Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand is criticizing an alleged effort by Democrats to "siphon" votes from a Republican senator, calling the tactic "manipulating the political system" as the controversy consumes Alaska's bruising Senate race. Sand was asked by Fox News about allegations that Democrats have boosted unaffiliated Alaska Senate candidate Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., whose name closely resembles that of incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, in an effort to draw votes away from the senator. "Both parties are doing it and neither party should be doing it," Sand told Fox News in an exclusive interview Sunday. "To me, it's manipulating the political system and it's not a good thing to do." TOP ELECTION SCHEMES ROILING KEY MIDTERM RACES AS BOTH PARTIES ACCUSE RIVALS OF TRICKERY Democratic Party candidate for Iowa governor, Rob Sand. (Rob Sand For Iowa) The unusual candidacy has become the center of an escalating legal and political fight in Alaska, where the Justice Department has intervened, arguing that the similarity between the candidates' names could confuse voters. On the ballot, the Republican incumbent appears as "Dan S. Sullivan," identified as a Republican and the incumbent, while his unaffiliated challenger appears as "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr." Republicans argue the similarity could cause some voters intending to support the senator to instead select his unaffiliated challenger, accusing Democratic operatives of helping elevate Daniel J. Sullivan to "siphon" votes from the GOP incumbent. Democrats have blasted the Trump administration's intervention, while Daniel J. Sullivan has denied that he is a Democratic plant. TRUMP SAYS 'WE ARE LOOKING INTO' OTHER DAN SULLIVAN ON ALASKA BALLOT, WARNS ABOUT GOVERNOR'S RACE Dan J. Sullivan, who has filed to run for U.S. Senate in Alaska, poses for a photo in Petersburg, Alaska, on June 26, 2026. (Katie Holmlund/Associated Press) Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the Trump administration’s lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s Senate results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses to his Democratic opponent, Mary Peltola. The administration says the lawsuit is intended to address the possible voter confusion, but Peltola called the case "flagrant corruption," while Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has called it "an outrage." MANCHIN CALLS SCHUMER 'CRAZY' FOR TRYING TO OUST GOP SENATOR IN CRUCIAL SENATE SHOWDOWN Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images) (Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images) ((Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images) (Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)) "This is an outrage," Schumer said on social media about the suit. "It shows they know they’re going to lose. We will fight tooth and nail. And we will win." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Peltola has argued that voters can distinguish between the two candidates and her campaign has asked a federal judge to dismiss the Justice Department's case. title: ESPN fumbles the Holy War by forcing Utah and BYU into a dreaded early-morning kickoff for fans
description: BYU and Utah fans face a 10 a.m. local kickoff for their rivalry game, and the Big 12 "Holy War" deserved a late night college football slot.
content: OutKick ESPN fumbles the Holy War by forcing Utah and BYU into a dreaded early-morning kickoff for fans ESPN scheduled the Big 12 rivalry with major college football playoff ramifications in the earliest window on November 7th By Trey Wallace OutKick Published October 26, 2026 4:33pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video No. 2 BYU Cougars vs UCF Knights Highlights | FOX College Football Check out the best moments from the Week 8 matchup between the No. 2 BYU Cougars and the UCF Knights! The annual 'Holy War' between Utah and BYU deserves better. Once we get to this part of the season, television networks have to obviously start picking what they think are the most opportune times to broadcast some of the most important games they have under contract. But, that doesn’t mean companies need to sacrifice and give into the pressure of opposing conference games in order to get the better rating. And yes, I understand ESPN has the television rights to SEC and Big 12 football, so decisions like this are not easy for the programming department. This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom. LINCOLN RILEY'S TENURE SHOULD END WITH LOSS AGAINST OHIO STATE'S BACKUP QB, WITH A $70 MILLION BUYOUT Though, making Utah and BYU play at 10 a.m. local time feels criminal in this case, given the ramifications around this Big 12 game that has major CFP implications. A general view of Rice-Eccles Stadium before the Utah Utes and Cal Poly Mustangs game on Sept. 6, 2025, in Salt Lake City, Utah. (Chris Gardner/Getty Images) If you haven’t seen the news yet, here is how ESPN decided what was best for the November 7th slate of games that are filled with must-see showdowns. MORE QUESTIONS THAN ANSWERS: ARCH MANNING LIKES THE DISRESPECT, BIG 12'S DISASTER AND A CFP RACE IN DISARRAY BYU vs. Utah: 12 p.m ET on ABC/ESPN Texas vs. Missouri: 12 p.m. ET on ABC/ESPN Alabama vs. LSU: 3:30 p.m. ET on ABC Kentucky vs. Tennessee: 6:15 p.m. ET on ESPN Georgia vs. Ole Miss: 7:30 p.m ET on ABC And, NBC will broadcast the Miami vs. Notre Dame showdown at 7:30 pm ET, while Oregon will face Ohio State at 3:30 p.m. ET on CBS. Head coach Pete Golding of the Ole Miss Rebels reacts in the fourth quarter against the Texas Longhorns at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin, Texas, on Oct. 24, 2026. (Getty Images) College football fans deserved a night-game showdown in Utah So, that left the important Big 12 game between the Cougars and Utes as the odd-teams out of this television equation that will see a plethora of top-25 showdowns take place on the same day. Look, I get that ESPN was put into a spot, but this could have easily been handled by the network putting the anticipated 'Holy War' in the 9:30 pm ET time slot after Kentucky faced-off with Tennessee on ESPN. It should also be noted that the Big 12 essentially gets the 3rd round pick on these weekends, and BYU just lost to UCF this past Saturday. But, make it a 10:00 p.m. ET kickoff on the network, which is essentially what took place this past weekend when Houston played Utah in Salt Lake City. Bear Bachmeier #47 of the BYU Cougars runs the ball in the first half against the UCF Knights at Acrisure Bounce House on Oct. 24, 2026, in Orlando, Fla. (Getty Images) CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP We should be awarding the fans in college football with a better situation than having them walk into the stadium at 8-9 a.m local time for a highly-anticipated rivalry game with so much on the line. This almost feels criminal to make both fanbases wake up this early for a top-25 showdown with CFP ramifications. Cougars vs. Utes should’ve been played after the SEC slate For this, ESPN should have put this game in the late window, even if they were sacrificing some of the ratings that were undoubtably coming their way. Did the network honestly think a large portion of the college football base would not stay up for a late kickoff that came after Notre Dame played Miami, or Georgia faced Ole Miss in primetime? I also understand the conundrum ESPN was in regarding this kickoff time, but both Utah and BYU deserved better. This one is a loss, no matter how the networks come out of this I'd imagine those within the Big 12 office in Texas are fuming at this decision, and rightfully so. title: Brazilian election sends US progressives into online fever as key irregularity stokes result uncertainty
description: Lula's Brazil election victory sparked celebration from U.S. progressives like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, but a last-minute voting extension drew sharp criticism.
content: Politics Brazilian election sends US progressives into online fever as key irregularity stokes result uncertainty Progressives hailed Lula's fourth term while critics questioned a Supreme Court voting extension granted before polls closed By Leo Briceno Fox News Published October 26, 2026 4:31pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video Conservative movement gains ground in Brazil Heritage Foundation distinguished fellow Daniel McCarthy discusses Brazil’s rightward shift and the changing political landscape across Latin America on ‘Kudlow.’ NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's victory securing a fourth term spurred a social media firestorm Monday morning as progressives in the United States celebrated his win from afar. "Yesterday, Brazil showed the world that the will of the people is stronger than the authoritarians who try to suppress it," Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., said in a post to X. "Congratulations, President [Lula] and congratulations Brazil." Progressives have framed Lula’s victory as a transnational repudiation of what they regard as the core politics of the Trump administration and its allies. But questions about the election remain after one of Brazil's Supreme Court justices granted a last-minute extension of the country's polling hours, prompting Lula's opponent to question the legitimacy of the outcome. In the waning hours of the election, Lula requested a two-hour extension of voting hours from the country’s Supreme Court, citing delayed public transportation services. Less than half an hour before the polls were scheduled to close, Supreme Court Justice Christiano Zanin granted the extension nationwide, prompting an outcry from Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula’s opponent. CONSERVATIVE WAVE HITS ROADBLOCK IN BRAZIL AS LULA HOLDS OFF BOLSONARO CHALLENGE Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez, D-N.Y., pictured alongside a parade behind Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva who just won a fourth term on Sunday evening. (Adam Gray - Pool/Getty Images; Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images) "What happened today was not normal. It was something frankly unacceptable. A Supreme Court justice, for the first time in history — a former lawyer of Lula’s — issues an order at the request of a former partner of his and changes the rules of the game in the middle of the game," Bolsonaro said in a statement. Notably, Bolsonaro's campaign also asked for an extension, citing heavy rain. Election experts in the country, speaking with local media, said the inclement weather and polling extension could provide grounds for a legal challenge to the election. "There is the possibility of requesting the annulment of the election. The deluge that fell in Santa Catarina and Paraná caused harm. The lack of buses and the restriction of public transportation in strategic cities, such as Salvador and São Paulo, harmed the right to vote," Guilherme Gonçalves, an attorney and member of the Brazilian Academy of Electoral and Political Law, told Brazilian outlet GZH. Another expert, while casting doubt on whether a legal challenge would ultimately succeed, said uncertainty over the election would continue. "It is difficult for it to succeed, but the point is that the [Supreme Court] contributed to the instability of the electoral process, which is serious," Guilherme Barcelos, an attorney with a doctorate in constitutional law and specialization in electoral law, told GZH. "The election does not end today. That is the point." In the meantime, several Republican figures back in the U.S. blasted the outcome. Martin De Luca, an attorney representing some of President Donald Trump’s media groups, accused Lula of benefiting from his political connections to the Supreme Court. "Yesterday Brazil showed the world that if you are losing an election and you need to turn it around, you can call on your former lawyer turned judge to give you a lift and you’ll still be congratulated by all who share the cause," De Luca wrote. Donald Trump Jr. echoed De Luca's criticism in a reply to his post. "If a conservative government in Brazil did this, everyone in the mainstream press in America would lose their minds, but I guess they’re just choosing to be silent because it’s all for the cause," Trump Jr. said. BLANCHE WON'T RULE OUT DOJ BLOCKING ELECTION CERTIFICATION IN 'DOOMSDAY' SCENARIO "Brazil did not have an election today. They had their country stolen from them by a criminal band of corrupt hacks who belong in jail," Joey Mannarino, the co-founder of the Overton Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank, wrote. During his campaign, Bolsonaro built momentum on promises to increase public safety by expanding prison capacity and drastically cut the size of government through a 25% reduction in government ministries — policies that many Democrats viewed as mirroring efforts by the Trump administration. By contrast, Lula has advocated for anti-poverty programs, minimum-wage increases and expanded assistance for low-income families. The platform drew praise from progressive groups including the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). "It is with tremendous pride that the Democratic Socialists of America congratulate President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin … and the coalition of progressive and leftists parties on their victory and re-election in Brazil’s second round of presidential elections this past Sunday," the group wrote in a press release. TRUMP'S WAR ON DRUG CARTELS COULD GAIN POWERFUL NEW ALLY AFTER PIVOTAL ELECTION New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference at the site where a man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during an operation in the Bronx, on October 8, 2026, in New York City. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images) "We commend the wide range of forces that joined together … to defend Brazilian democracy and secure this victory." Other prominent progressives also celebrated Lula’s victory as a triumph for policies aligned with their own. "Lula has stood up for Brazilian workers and democracy — and will continue to do so in the next four years," Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., wrote in a post to X. title: Man found dead on Disneyland property near entrance to 'Happiest Place on Earth'
description: A 65-year-old man was found dead on a Disneyland sidewalk near the south entrance in Anaheim, with police saying the death appeared from natural causes.
content: California Man found dead on Disneyland property near entrance to 'Happiest Place on Earth' Anaheim police say the 65-year-old was known to the department's homeless liaison officers through prior outreach contacts By Greg Wehner Fox News Published October 26, 2026 4:22pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video Disneyland guest hospitalized after leaving ride ahead of final plunge A 13-year-old Disneyland guest exited a ride vehicle on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure before the attraction’s final drop, was taken to a hospital for evaluation and later released. (This video contains AI-assisted content.) NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! A 65-year-old man was found dead over the weekend on Disneyland property in Anaheim, California, casting a grim scene near an entrance to the resort famously billed as the "Happiest Place on Earth." Anaheim police responded shortly before 1:45 p.m. Sunday to a report of an unconscious man near the resort's south entrance off Katella Avenue, Sgt. Eric Anderson told Fox News Digital on Monday. Officers found the man unconscious on a sidewalk between the resort hotels and a park entrance, where he was pronounced dead at the scene. Police found no signs of trauma or foul play, and his death appeared to be from natural causes, Anderson said. DISNEY WORLD GUEST WITH HEART CONDITION DIES OF CARDIAC EMERGENCY AFTER ICONIC RIDE The sidewalk where the man was found is on Disneyland property rather than public land. The south entrance is separate from Disneyland's main entrance and was established in an area near resort hotels to provide guests staying nearby easier access to the park. The incident happened around 6 p.m. Sunday on Tiana's Bayou Adventure in Disneyland. (David McNew/Getty Images) The man's identity has not been released, though Anderson said any identification would likely come from the coroner's office. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Anderson said the Anaheim Police Department's homeless liaison officers regularly make contact with people experiencing homelessness in the area, checking on their well-being, offering assistance and letting them know when they may be violating the law. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS Disneyland Resort in Anaheim, California is cracking down with a new Guest Code of Conduct targeting ride disruptions tied to guest behavior. (Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register/Getty Images) CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB The now deceased 65-year-old had previously come into contact with those officers and was known to them before Sunday's incident. SEND US A TIP Those previous interactions were part of the department's outreach to the homeless population and were not related to arrests or other criminal activity, Anderson explained. GOT A TIP? After the man was found, officers remained at the scene while they waited for personnel from the coroner's office to arrive and remove his body. The coroner's office will also be responsible for determining the cause of death. DISNEY SCARE UNFOLDS AFTER TEEN EXITS LOG RIDE MOMENTS BEFORE 50-FOOT PLUNGE The 65-year-old had previously come into contact with those officers and was known to them before Sunday's incident, Anaheim police said. (Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images) LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST A beer can was found near the man, though investigators did not know whether it had any connection to his condition or death, Anderson said. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL Photos and video from the scene showed police tape stretched across the sidewalk beneath a large Disneyland Resort entrance sign, while a black privacy screen shielded the area from view as authorities investigated. title: ROBERT F KENNEDY JR, DR. MEHMET OZ: 250 hospitals join the fight for healthier food
description: Over 250 hospitals joined the Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge to cut processed food and added sugar from patient meals under Trump's health agenda.
content: Opinion ROBERT F KENNEDY JR, DR MEHMET OZ: 250 hospitals join the fight for healthier food Hospitals should be places where every aspect of the patient experience supports health and healing. The food hospitals serve on a patient’s tray should support that goal By Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. , Dr. Mehmet Oz Fox News Published October 26, 2026 4:00pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video Chef Andre Rush teams up with RFK Jr. for MAHA cooking show Former White House chef Andre Rush joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss teaming up with RFK Jr. on 'The Real Food Show' to promote healthy eating. NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! When Americans enter a hospital, they expect to receive care that helps them heal. They trust their doctors, nurses, and other healthcare professionals to provide the best possible treatments and give them the greatest chance of recovery. Yet too often, the food our nation’s hospitals serve contradicts that mission. Patients recovering from surgery, living with chronic diseases, or managing serious medical conditions may be served meals in hospitals meals featuring highly processed foods, refined carbohydrates, added sugars, and other ingredients that do little to support their recovery. RFK JR HAILS FIRST US HOSPITAL TO PROMISE HEALTHIER MEALS: 'WE HAVE A TEMPLATE' It’s a contradiction that should concern every American. And it’s one we’re determined to change. Today, we announce that 250 hospitals across the United States have joined the Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge, a nationwide initiative the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) launched to improve the nutritional quality of meals hospitals serve to patients and staff. Video AOC SAYS MAHA ADVOCATES' FIGHT 'ISN'T PARTISAN' AS SHE BLASTS HEALTHCARE SYSTEM FOR FUELING 'A TON OF ANXIETY' These commitments reflect a growing recognition among America’s healthcare leaders that food is an essential part of good medicine, and that hospitals should demonstrate that through the meals they serve. Under President Trump’s leadership, the Make America Healthy Again movement is fundamentally rethinking the role of nutrition in American healthcare. But transforming American healthcare requires more than changing federal policies; it requires changing the environments in which Americans receive care. Hospitals can help change those environments. They care for our most vulnerable citizens, educate millions of patients and families, and earn their communities’ trust. Nutrition is central to each of these responsibilities. For patients recovering from surgery, fighting infections, or managing chronic illnesses, proper nutrition can support wound healing, preserve muscle mass, strengthen immune function, and improve recovery. Malnutrition, by contrast, correlates with longer hospital stays, more complications, and greater healthcare costs. THIS AMOUNT OF DELI MEAT ASSOCIATED WITH HIGHER DEMENTIA RISK IN COMPELLING NEW REVIEW Video Hospitals also have an opportunity to teach patients habits that can improve their health long after discharge. Consider a patient who enters the hospital for complications of Type 2 diabetes. That patient may receive excellent medical treatment and counseling about the importance of healthy eating. But if the meals the hospital serves during their stay contradict that advice, what message are we sending? A hospital meal should reinforce the care plan, not undermine it. There are approximately 6,100 hospitals in the United States, collectively accounting for more than 35 million hospital admissions each year. The broader American healthcare foodservice market represents nearly $20 billion in annual economic activity. That’s extraordinary purchasing power. Hospitals are among the largest customers of major foodservice management companies, food distributors, and manufacturers. Their purchasing decisions influence which products suppliers develop, how suppliers price those products, and what becomes available to other institutions. Imagine what could happen if hospitals across America began sending a consistent message to their suppliers: We want more real food. We want healthier proteins, fruits, vegetables, and minimally processed ingredients. We want fewer products with added sugars and unnecessary additives. The food industry would have a powerful incentive to respond. As demand grows, suppliers can expand production, improve distribution networks, and invest in healthier product offerings. Larger purchasing volumes and more predictable demand can also create economies of scale, potentially reducing costs and making nutritious food more affordable. Other institutions could also benefit. Video The same foodservice companies supplying hospitals often serve schools, universities, workplaces, and other institutions. Improvements in their product offerings and supply chains could help make healthier food more accessible throughout American society. Hospitals could improve their patients’ health and help transform the nation’s food system. With more than 250 hospitals now participating, we’re beginning to demonstrate what health care institutions can accomplish together. We recognize that hospitals face real operational challenges. Hospital supply chains are complex, and patients have diverse medical and nutritional needs. That’s why the Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge is voluntary and collaborative. We are not interested in Washington dictating hospital menus or second-guessing the clinical judgment of physicians and registered dietitians. Hospitals must retain the flexibility to meet patients’ individual nutritional requirements, including those who need specialized therapeutic diets or medical nutrition support. Our goal is to get hospitals across the country to improve the nutritional quality of their meals together. We are grateful for the partnership of the American Hospital Association and the many healthcare systems that have joined this effort. Their leadership demonstrates that change does not always require new mandates, complicated regulations, or additional administrative burdens. Sometimes, it begins with a shared commitment. Hospitals should be places where every aspect of the patient experience supports health and healing. The food hospitals serve on a patient’s tray should support that goal. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Two hundred and fifty hospitals have already committed to serving healthier food. Now, we’re calling on the rest of America’s hospitals to join them. Mehmet Oz, M.D., M.B.A., is the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is the 26th Secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. title: American tourist falls 1,000 feet to her death while chasing perfect mountain photo
description: An American tourist from Miami, Florida, reportedly left a marked trail in the Dolomites, Italy, to take a photo before she fell 1,000 feet to her tragic death.
content: Travel American tourist falls 1,000 feet to her death while chasing perfect mountain photo Alpine rescue teams and air ambulance responded after witnesses called emergency services By Jessica Mekles Fox News Published October 26, 2026 4:00pm EDT | Updated October 26, 2026 4:06pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video Shoulder-to-shoulder crowds choke narrow walkways along Italy’s Amalfi Coast Viral video from Positano shows tourists packed onto a tight cliffside path with little room to move, drawing backlash online as experts say tour groups, day-trippers and social media are fueling overwhelming crowds. NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! A family vacation in northern Italy ended in tragedy when a 36-year-old American tourist fell down a steep mountain face in the Dolomites, Italy. Michelle Alejandra Rubio Leiva, a marketing and business development professional from the Miami area, died Oct. 17 after stepping off a marked trail, local news outlets reported. Rubio Leiva was hiking near Forcella Pordoi, an alpine pass with an altitude of roughly 9,000 feet, when she allegedly left the designated path to find a vantage point for a photograph, Italian national newspaper Corriere Della Sera said. THOUSANDS SWARM STUNNING MOUNTAIN ESCAPE AS SELFIE TOURISM BACKLASH ERUPTS ONLINE She lost her footing and fell an estimated 1,000 feet down the slope in view of her sister, the outlet said. An American woman "lost her life late this morning [Oct. 17] after falling for approximately 300 meters in the Forcella Pordoi area, at an altitude of about 2,750 meters," the Trentino Alpine and Speleological Rescue, a volunteer rescue organization, told Fox News Digital in a statement, which was translated. "The hiker was on vacation with her family when, at an exposed point, she slipped, plunging into the void below," the translated statement continued. A 36-year-old American tourist, pictured at right, fell down a steep mountain face in the Dolomites, Italy, shown at left, and died on Oct. 17. (iStock; Jam Press) The hiking group had been close to the upper cable-car station and originally planned to visit the Maria refuge on Sass Pordoi, local news outlet Il Dolomiti noted. Witnesses called the emergency number, the Trentino Alpine and Speleological Rescue said. While Italian media cited her attempt to take a picture, the official alpine rescue logs noted only that she slipped at an exposed point on the mountain. The woman lost her footing and fell an estimated 1, 000 feet down the slope. The 112 control center dispatched the Alta Val di Fassa team of the Trentino Alpine and Speleological Rescue Service, alongside an air ambulance, according to the Record. A mountain rescuer already in the vicinity went to the scene to provide the helicopter crew with exact coordinates, the rescue team's statement said. Medical personnel were lowered onto the mountainside by 12:30 p. m., where a doctor pronounced Rubio Leiva dead at the scene, according to Fox San Antonio. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Her family members were airlifted to the nearby town of Canazei, Il Dolomiti said. Her body was retrieved by helicopter and handed over to local authorities, News.com.au said. The Brigham Young University graduate worked as a manager for Rubio Contesse Advisors in Florida, according to Corriere della Sera, a major Italian newspaper. The Dolomites have been in the news in recent months for the massive crowds that show up and stretch through shuttle lines. (Carlo Zanella) In recent months, the Dolomites have come under scrutiny for the massive crowds stretching through shuttle lines as visitors wait to reach Tre Cime di Lavaredo, one of the most iconic destinations. Viral videos have led to outrage online, with many commenters arguing that visitors were more interested in taking photos than enjoying the mountains, Fox News Digital previously reported. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Tre Cime di Lavaredo draws visitors from around the world with its trio of mountain peaks. The UNESCO-protected mountains are subject to the Enrosadira phenomenon, in which sunrise and sunset turn the rock walls a vibrant pink and orange, according to The Dolomites — UNESCO World Heritage Centre page. title: Data brokers don't just collect facts. They guess about you
description: Data brokers assign labels predicting your health, finances and religion based on browsing and purchases, then sell those profiles to businesses.
content: Privacy Data brokers don't just collect facts. They guess about you Data brokers use personal information to predict health, finances and vulnerabilities, guesses that could put you at risk By Kurt Knutsson, CyberGuy Report Fox News Published October 26, 2026 4:00pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video Surveillance pricing: How personal data could impact what you pay Kurt ‘CyberGuy’ Knutsson explains how algorithms track browsing history and location to estimate what shoppers are willing to spend on ‘Fox & Friends.’ NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! They know where you live. They may know your phone number, your relatives' names and roughly what your house is worth. By now, most people have at least a vague sense that data brokers collect personal information. What many don't realize is what happens next. Data brokers also analyze that information. They use algorithms, compare records from different sources and sort people into categories that predict their interests, circumstances and behavior. Those predictions can involve your health, finances, religious beliefs and potential vulnerabilities. WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES Data brokers analyze personal information to identify patterns and predict your finances, health and behavior. (Neil Godwin/Future via Getty Images) Some may be wrong. Others could reveal sensitive details you never intended to share. And depending on the company and the type of information involved, those profiles may be sold or shared with businesses you have never heard of. Here's a closer look at the labels data brokers assign to you, how they come up with them and what you can do to protect your personal information. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. Here's what data brokers' labels actually look like Data brokers do far more than maintain databases of addresses and phone numbers. Some build detailed profiles designed to help advertisers identify specific audiences. The Federal Trade Commission documented this practice years ago. Its investigation found that brokers combined information from multiple sources to infer sensitive characteristics, including income, religion, political views and health conditions. Acxiom, a major data company, developed a segmentation system called PersonicX that grouped households into lifestyle categories. One documented historical category was called "Rural Everlasting." According to the FTC, it described older adults with relatively low income and educational attainment. Other categories included "Urban Scramble" and "Mobile Mixers." These were classifications built from data, not personal descriptions written by the people involved. The FTC also documented how companies used location information to create even more specific advertising audiences. For example, InMarket offered audience categories such as "Christian church goers," "parents of preschoolers," and "wealthy and not healthy." The FTC subsequently restricted InMarket's use and sale of sensitive location data. Then there was Oracle's BlueKai advertising business, which helped advertisers use extensive consumer data for targeting. Oracle shut down its advertising products in September 2024. Still, its history illustrates how sophisticated this industry became. The important point is that a label doesn't have to be accurate to influence how a company views you. Want to see how much of your personal information may already be exposed? Get a free scan to find out what data brokers may have on you at CyberGuy.com. The categories data brokers can put you in Some of these classifications sound harmless. Others are surprisingly personal. Here are examples of the information brokers have historically inferred or used to create consumer segments. Health-related labels Data broker research and enforcement cases have documented categories involving: Diabetes and related health interests Pregnancy High cholesterol Health and wellness behavior Financial status combined with health-related assumptions A major concern is that these classifications can originate outside the medical system. HIPAA protects health information handled by covered healthcare organizations and their business associates. However, health-related information independently gathered or inferred by other businesses may fall outside HIPAA's protections. For example, searching for information about diabetes doesn't mean you have diabetes. You could be researching the condition for a family member. Yet advertising systems may still use that activity as one of several signals when building a profile. Other federal and state privacy laws may apply, but they don't necessarily provide the same protections as HIPAA. AMAZON ABOUT YOU MAY KNOW YOU A LITTLE TOO WELL Your online activity can help data brokers build detailed profiles, even when you're simply browsing the internet. (Sara Diggins/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images) Financial labels Data companies have also offered categories based on estimated income, spending behavior and financial circumstances. These can include people classified as affluent, price-sensitive or likely to respond to certain financial offers. One particularly troubling example comes from the Justice Department's case against Epsilon Data Management. According to federal prosecutors, Epsilon used sophisticated modeling to identify consumers likely to respond to solicitations. The company sold information about more than 30 million Americans to operators of fraudulent schemes, including fake sweepstakes promotions. Epsilon agreed to pay $150 million as part of its deferred prosecution agreement. This is a documented example of consumer data being used to help fraudsters identify potential victims. Religious and political labels Data brokers have also inferred people's religious interests and political leanings. These predictions may draw on information such as location patterns, purchases, public records and other available data. For example, the FTC documented the use of a "Christian church goers" advertising segment. A person visiting a church doesn't necessarily belong to that faith. Similarly, someone researching a political candidate doesn't automatically support that candidate. Nevertheless, profiling systems can use these signals to group people into audiences. Life-stage labels Another category focuses on what may be happening in your personal life. Data companies have developed segments involving parents with young children, empty nesters and households at different stages of life. These classifications can help businesses decide what products or services to advertise. However, they can also reveal potential pressure points. Someone approaching retirement may receive different financial offers than a young parent. A household believed to be managing health expenses may attract another type of marketing. And when those assumptions are wrong, the resulting profile may still influence what someone sees. How data brokers make guesses about you Consider what you've done online recently. Maybe you searched for joint pain relief. Perhaps you compared retirement plans or looked up treatment options for a relative. Individually, these activities might reveal very little. However, companies can combine information from websites, apps, purchase histories, public records and commercial databases. Then predictive models look for patterns. For example, a company may consider your age range, estimated income and browsing activity when deciding whether you fit a particular advertising category. These classifications are often called modeled attributes or inferences. They represent predictions rather than verified personal facts. And here's the problem: a company buying access to an audience segment may use the prediction without knowing how accurately it describes each person. How scammers use personal data to make attacks more convincing Basic information helps a scammer contact you. More detailed personal information can help make the approach believable. For example, someone who knows your name and address could send a convincing-looking financial notice. Now suppose that same person also has information suggesting you're approaching retirement or researching medical expenses. A criminal could use those clues to tailor a fraudulent Medicare offer, investment pitch or fake medical service. This doesn't mean every scammer buys sophisticated consumer profiles. However, the Justice Department's case against Epsilon Data Management shows how targeted consumer information can end up in the hands of fraudsters. The company sold consumer data to operators of fraudulent schemes, helping them identify people more likely to respond. Meanwhile, the FBI reported that Americans age 60 and older lost approximately $7.7 billion to internet crime in 2025, up from $4.9 billion in 2024. While those losses weren't all connected to data brokers, the documented sale of targeted consumer lists shows how personal information can help criminals identify potential victims and make their scams more convincing. Can you see what data brokers have predicted about you? Finding every profile attached to your name can be difficult. Unlike a credit report, there isn't one centralized system where you can review all the marketing predictions companies have generated about you. However, some state privacy laws give residents rights to access, correct or delete personal information, including certain inferences. California provides one important example. Under the California Consumer Privacy Act, eligible residents can request information held by covered businesses, subject to legal exceptions. California also launched its Delete Request and Opt-out Platform, known as DROP at privacy.ca.gov/DROP/, in January 2026. It allows eligible California residents to submit one deletion request covering registered data brokers. Those companies began processing requests in August 2026. Matching records, including inferences, generally must be deleted unless an exception applies. Other states have different privacy protections, so your options depend on where you live. IS YOUR PERSONAL DATA CHANGING WHAT YOU PAY ONLINE? Scammers can use personal information to create targeted attacks that appear more convincing and trustworthy. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images) How to reduce what data brokers know about you You may not be able to eliminate every prediction about yourself. However, you can take practical steps to reduce how much personal information remains available. Here's where to start: Search for your personal information. Look up your name, phone number and home address on people-search websites. Submit removal requests. Use the opt-out processes offered by data brokers and people-search services. Review your privacy rights. Check whether your state allows you to request access, correction, deletion or an opt-out from data sales. Limit unnecessary sharing. Review the information you provide to apps, shopping websites and online services. Check your family members' exposure. Relatives' names, addresses and phone numbers can appear together in people-search databases. Consider an automated removal service. Ongoing removal requests can help address information that reappears over time. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. Reducing publicly accessible personal information can make it harder for unfamiliar businesses and scammers to build detailed profiles. However, removal services cannot guarantee that every existing inference will disappear or prevent companies from collecting new information. Kurt's key takeaways I've warned you before about data brokers collecting your personal information, but I find the predictions they make about us even more troubling. Think about it. You could search for a medical condition on behalf of someone you love and end up in a category suggesting you have that condition yourself. Someone buying access to that profile may have no idea the assumption is wrong. And when personal information gets into the wrong hands, it can help scammers make their pitches sound much more convincing. What concerns me is how little most of us know about the profiles being built around our names. You may never see every label a company assigns to you, but you can start reducing the information available to build those profiles. I recommend checking what appears when you search for yourself and taking advantage of the privacy protections available in your state. A reputable data removal service can also help by automatically sending removal requests to data brokers and continuing to check when your information reappears. You won't disappear from the internet, but you can make it harder for strangers to assemble a detailed profile of your life. What would concern you more, a data broker accurately predicting something deeply personal about you or selling a completely false prediction as if it were fact? title: Sophie Cunningham's cowboy hat message has fans talking, Holly Rowe's WNBA Finals plan & Is Texas' field gray?
description: Sophie Cunningham's cowboy hat at the F1 race in Austin fired up patriots and outraged critics who called the flag-waving moment anything but safe.
content: OutKick Sports Sophie Cunningham's cowboy hat message has fans talking, Holly Rowe's WNBA Finals plan & Is Texas' field gray? The WNBA star waved the flag at the Austin GP, prompting strong reactions on both sides of the political aisle By Zach Dean OutKick Published October 26, 2026 3:33pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video President Trump Shouts Out Sophie Cunningham | Don't @ Me w/ Dan Dakich "Good for Donald Trump, good for Sophie Cunningham. She wants her brand. That's why she came to Indianapolis to hook on to the brand that is Caitlin Clark. And she, well, she got a presidential endorsement. That's pretty damn good." 'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news, and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com. Well, we're here, folks. The final week of October. It's an exciting time, right? Halloween in five days. The always enjoyable "Sports Equinox" tonight with all four major sports in action at the same time. Five if you want to count the WNBA. That's up to you, though. It's a fun time to be alive right now. That's my point. October is the best month of the year, and this is our final push until things get really hectic. I'd urge everyone to enjoy this week. Everything shifts gears in seven days. We've got an election next Tuesday. Yuck. That'll be miserable. More importantly (to me, at least), this is the final week until the holidays begin. And by that, I mean at midnight Saturday, everything shifts to Christmas. The commercials. The music. The department stores. It'll happen in the blink of an eye. You're gonna go to bed Saturday dreaming of Michael Myers, and wake up to insufferable Mariah Carey jamming her song down our throats. VOLS FANS SET NOISE RECORD AND TERRIFY ALABAMA'S KALEN DEBOER, TIFF ANN'S HALLOWEEN COSTUME & DANICA STUMPS! And there is NOTHING we can do to stop it. Nothing. So enjoy this week. I surely will. Let's roll. Welcome to a Monday Nightcaps — the one where Sophie Cunningham's cowboy hat at yesterday's F1 race fired up all the PATRIOTS across this great country. Sophie never misses. What else? I've got ESPN's Holly Rowe with an incredible idea for the WNBA Finals, I've got a legit question about Texas' field color on TV, and was Dan Campbell's decision to go for it on fourth down yesterday as insane as everyone thinks? I don't think so, and Dan's explanation after the game might sway you, too. It's a thinker! OK, grab you a pumpkin for National Pumpkin Day, and settle in for a Monday 'Cap! Sophie Cunningham walks with an FIA official on her way to wave the checkered flag and enrage some lefties. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images) Sophie popped up at F1 this weekend and didn't skip a beat We still haven't gotten our pumpkins yet down here, but that'll be coming in the next few days. We can't just carve pumpkins and let them sit on our porch all month in Florida. They'd be rotten before breakfast on Day 3. As for my earlier rant on the upcoming holiday season ... Don't get me wrong, I love the holidays. I love Christmas (although Christmas Eve is the better holiday). I love the whole season. I just think it starts way to soon after Halloween. The radio stations all play Christmas music on Nov. 1. That's insane. Every single commercial has Santa in it all of a sudden. We go from Pumpkin Spice to Peppermint Mocha at every single coffee shop in America. There needs to be a two-week buffer, in my opinion. We wait all year for "fall," and then we're so quick to stuff it all back in the attic on Nov. 1 and jump right into winter. And don't even get me started on the disrespect towards Thanksgiving. That's a battle I've been fighting for years now. Anyway, the holiday season is always welcome here ... I just think it doesn't need to start on Nov. 1. Now, let's get this week started by welcoming Sophie Cunningham back to class! No need to have a two-week buffer for Sophie! Sophie Cunningham waves teh checkered flag to end the Formula 1 United States Grand Prix. (Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images) Get a load of this idea! "Yee MF Haw!" What a hat. What a message to send to the libs who absolutely lost their MINDS yesterday because big, bad Sophie Cunningham waved the flag at the F1 race in Austin. And yes, they completely lost their minds. Shocking, I know. Especially for such a level-headed group! Yet again the US races proving that F1 is still not a safe space for the LGBTQIA+ community with Sophie Cunningham waving the flag and Ted Cruz giving out trophies. Goodness, these people are just the best. They're the gift that "keeps on giving the whole year!" Wait. That's a Christmas movie quote! I just broke my own rule. Not yet! Respect Halloween. OK, let's get back on track and stay in the WNBA with ESPN's Holly Rowe, who has an excellent idea for where Game 6 should be held later this week: Dan's roll of the dice & a Texas-sized question Problem solving…. Hear me out. Game 6 in Atlanta at Mercedes-Benz? Could we pack that out ATL???? @WNBA. I nearly spit out of my Maxwell House when I read that tweet this morning. I thought it was a fake account. I thought it was satire. It was not. Quick, show of hands: Who thinks a WNBA game could sell out Mercedes-Benz Stadium, which holds 72,000 people? Anyone? Anyone? Bueller?! Come on. I know there's a lot of debate right now about attendance and ratings for these WNBA Finals. I don't care about either, because, frankly, I'm tired of talking about it. But if anyone here thinks a WNBA (!!!) game could sell out a 72,000 stadium, you're probably also setting aside room in your bank accounts for the $5,000 dividend checks from Trump. Ain't happening. I'm not sure the Atlanta Hawks could sell that stadium out, much less the Dream. Folks, Atlanta couldn't fill up Truist Park last month for the Braves' first two playoff games! And Holly thinks 72,000 people are showing up to watch the Dream? Wild take. It's so wild, I almost respect it. Almost. OK, let's rapid-fire this Monday class into a big HALLOWEEN week. First up? You know who had the Sunday Scaries yesterday? Lions fans. Take a look: Dan Campbell took A LOT of heat for that decision yesterday, and I was baffled at first, too. But I gotta say ... I get it. I agree with it! "I knew we'd get the ball back if it didn't work out," Campbell said after the game. He's right. Think about it. If Detroit punts the ball, Green Bay could very well march down the field, drain the rest of the clock, and kick a field goal to win the game. There's a good chance the Lions never see the ball again. It happens all the time. By going for it, you either A) get it and the drive continues, or B) don't get it, but give them a short enough field that you're pretty much guaranteed to get the ball back with a chance to win/tie. Detroit's defense is terrible. The offense is excellent. Dan rolled the dice and decided he'd rather have his offense end the game with the ball, one way or the other. Chess, not checkers! Finally, on the way out ... I've been thinking about this for years now, and it really came to a head this past Saturday ... Why is the turf at Texas' home stadium so gray for night games on TV? It's baffled me for decades now. So, here's the thing ... I know I dumped on the "alt-casts" last week, but I actually watched the second half of the Texas-Ole Miss game in the alternate "SkyCast" view Saturday night because a reader recommended it. I didn't hate it. Didn't love it, but it wasn't awful. I'd imagine coaches eat it up. Anyway, the field looked pretty normal in that broadcast. It was relatively green. I didn't notice it nearly as much as the regular broadcast. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Texas Longhorns quarterback Arch Manning runs for a touchdown during an SEC football game against Ole Miss on Oct. 24, 2026, at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin, Texas. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) So, is this an ABC/ESPN camera issue? Is the field actually gray? I'm so confused. I know we have Longhorn fans in class. Please, let me know. And then, go have a big final week of October. What's the deal with Texas' field? Zach.Dean@OutKick.com. Zach Dean is a writer for OutKick. title: Colorado pro-life sidewalk counselor battles state 'bubble law' she says curtails First Amendment
description: Pro-life sidewalk counselor Wendy Faustin tells Fox News Digital that Colorado's "bubble law" could land her in jail for offering abortion alternatives.
content: Abortion Colorado pro-life sidewalk counselor battles state 'bubble law' she says curtails First Amendment Sidewalk counselor goes to court against state restriction barring approaching people outside abortion clinics By Rachel del Guidice Fox News Published October 26, 2026 3:07pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video Colorado pro-life counselor warns she could face jail for approaching women outside abortion clinics Wendy Faustin and attorney Roger Byron speak exclusively with Fox News Digital about Colorado's abortion clinic "bubble law" and their First Amendment concerns. NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! A Colorado woman who offers abortion alternatives outside clinics is battling a state law that prohibits her from approaching someone too closely, warning the rule has turned what she considers a compassionate conversation into a legal risk. Wendy Faustin, a pro-life sidewalk counselor challenging Colorado's so-called "bubble law," told Fox News Digital the restrictions prevent her from quietly offering women information about pregnancy resource centers, adoption agencies and other alternatives to abortion. "If you're within 100 feet of the entrance to an abortion clinic, I can't approach someone within 8 feet to give them any alternative information," Faustin said. Last July, a federal judge rejected her challenge to the Colorado law. Her case is currently on appeal at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit. CHRISTIAN WOMAN PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO NEW 'ORWELLIAN' CHARGES FOR STANDING AND SILENT PRAYER Wendy Faustin is a pro-life advocate and sidewalk counselor. (Zoom screenshot) Colorado state law and a Denver municipal ordinance prohibit individuals from knowingly approaching within eight feet of another person without their consent to distribute literature or engage in protest, education or counseling within 100 feet of a health care facility entrance, including abortion clinics. Violations are classified as a petty offense, which carries with it a fine or even a possible short jail sentence. The U.S. Supreme Court upheld Colorado's 1993 law in its 2000 decision in Hill v. Colorado, ruling that the restrictions did not violate the First Amendment. The restriction, she said, forces her to speak from a distance about an intensely personal subject, potentially allowing others to overhear conversations she would prefer to keep private. "I would rather be able to just walk up to somebody, offer them alternative information, places where they can get help," she said. PRO-LIFE GROUP SAYS MAIL-ORDER ABORTION PILLS VIOLATE FEDERAL LAW, URGES TRUMP ADMIN TO TAKE ACTION Pro-life advocate Wendy Faustin is fighting a Colorado law that prohibits individuals from knowingly approaching within eight feet of another person without their consent to distribute literature or engage in protest, education or counseling within 100 feet of a health care facility entrance, including abortion clinics. (First Liberty ) "I believe that every woman who is facing this decision deserves to have all the possible information that she might need," Faustin said. "Sometimes she's feeling kind of backed into a corner by circumstances or maybe by other people, and she may not be aware that there can be help somewhere for her through a crisis pregnancy center, an adoption agency, and so that's all the information that I give is offering her information where she can get help and also information about the development of her baby." Her attorney, Roger Byron, senior counsel for First Liberty Institute, argued the dispute extends far beyond abortion and raises fundamental questions about the First Amendment. DOJ WEIGHS CIVIL RIGHTS PROBE INTO FORT WORTH POLICE OVER ALLEGED FIRST AMENDMENT VIOLATIONS A pro-life demonstrator holds a crucifix while praying outside the Planned Parenthood building during the National Men's March to Abolish Abortion and Rally for Personhood in Boston, Massachusetts, on Nov. 1, 2025. (Joseph Prezioso/AFP via Getty Images) "These laws literally make it a crime for Wendy to approach within 8 feet of a woman," Byron told Fox News Digital, describing restrictions he says would not survive constitutional scrutiny if applied to other forms of protest. "These laws would be struck down immediately if they restricted anti-war protesters or union workers on strike outside of their employer's facility," Byron said. "However, because they restrict pro-life sidewalk counselors, they do not. This decision, Hill versus Colorado from the Supreme Court and the statutes that it protects, make sidewalk counselors, because of their pro-life message, second-class citizens. It literally creates two First Amendments. An oppressive one for pro-life sidewalk counselors, and the real one, the good one for everybody else." TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS A woman hands a pamphlet to a person outside a facility that provides abortions. (Josh Ritchie for The Washington Post via Getty Images) "What's at stake is the free speech rights of anyone whose message is something other than what the government wants it to be," he said. Byron said the ruling at the Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit will determine what happens next. "I suspect either way, this case is going to end up in front of the U.S. Supreme Court," Byron said. title: WNBA Finals Game 6, a potential title-clincher, will be held in the afternoon on Thursday
description: Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream face a midday Thursday Game 6 after scheduling conflicts with the Hawks forced the WNBA Finals to an odd time.
content: OutKick Sports WNBA Finals Game 6, a potential title-clincher, will be held in the afternoon on Thursday The WNBA announced Game 6 between the Dream and Valkyries, which can be a title winner for one team, will be at 12:30 pm ET. By Scott Thompson OutKick Published October 26, 2026 3:06pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video The WNBA Can’t Find a Place to Play Its Championship | Don't @ Me w/ Dan Dakich "The Atlanta Dream have run into another arena scheduling conflict and may be forced to play Game 6 in the Gateway Center. The Gateway Center hosts about as many as my house." Game 6 of the WNBA Finals finally has a place to play, as State Farm Arena will be the site for the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries to continue their best-of-seven series. There is one big problem: the game, a potential clincher for the team that wins Game 5 on Monday night, will be held at 12:30 p.m. ET. An afternoon game for a league finals series is interesting in and of itself, but for the 2026 WNBA season to potentially end in the afternoon on a weekday is less than ideal. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese looks on during the first half of Game 3 of the WNBA Finals against the Golden State Valkyries on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, in Atlanta. (AP Photo/Brynn Anderson) The NBA’s Atlanta Hawks are scheduled to host the Cleveland Cavaliers at 8 p.m. ET now, agreeing to move their start time one hour from its originally-scheduled 7 p.m. tip-off that night in the second half of a back-to-back at State Farm Arena. That’s what caused the scheduling snafu, with Game 6 of the WNBA Finals originally set for 8 p.m. ET on Thursday. ANGEL REESE BLOCKS SOCIAL MEDIA INFLUENCER'S 'MARRIAGE PROPOSAL' AFTER WNBA FINALS GAME So, it appears the WNBA, wanting the much-larger State Farm Arena in terms of capacity (17,000) compared to the Dream's usual Gateway Center Arena home court (3,500), might not have had a choice of where to stage Game 6. The game will still air on USA Network and stream on Peacock. The Dream have been drawing sold-out crowds through these Finals, and as a result, the league has had to maneuver to ensure the most seats are filled in larger arenas. The Golden State Valkyries celebrate during Game 1 of the 2026 WNBA Finals against the Atlanta Dream on Oct. 17, 2026, at Chase Center in San Francisco, Calif. (NBAE via Getty Images) Game 3 was moved from Oct. 22 to Oct. 21 to avoid a concert conflict. Meanwhile, Game 4 was pushed to an afternoon tip-off, though it was this past Saturday to accommodate the Hawks’ home opener against the Houston Rockets that night. A weekend can be justified, but for a weekday to be an afternoon tip-off is mind-boggling even given the circumstances. The Athletic reported the Hawks could’ve moved their Thursday night game to Friday, however that would have created a Friday-Saturday back-to-back for both NBA teams. And the rescheduled matchup would’ve been on opening night of NBA Cup group play. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Then, there was the option of the Dream playing at their normal home in College Park, though thousands of fans wouldn’t be able to enter the arena due to the lack of seats. There were other Georgia-area arenas to think about, though, including Georgia Tech’s McCamish Pavilion and the Georgia State Convention Center, per CBS Sports. Angel Reese, who’s enjoyed a strong Finals performance thus far, did state her wish to stay at State Farm Arena if it could work. (NBAE via Getty Images) "The fan support here has been amazing, and we appreciate the love and support," she said after the Game 4 loss to the Valkyries, which tied the series at two. title: Omar’s menacing message hidden in seemingly innocent tweet exposed: 'Crushed the enemy'
description: Ilhan Omar's lakeside video featured a Somali hip-hop song with lyrics about enemies scattering, posted days after HSI agents raided her D.C. home.
content: Politics Somali rap promising to 'scatter' enemies underscores Omar's serene lakeside video Lyrics boast 'no enemy dares threaten me' as Omar faces a criminal investigation into potential immigration fraud By Peter D'Abrosca Fox News Published October 26, 2026 2:50pm EDT | Updated October 26, 2026 3:51pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video Trump suggests House could refuse to seat Ilhan Omar if she wins reelection Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on President Donald Trump's demand that Rep. Ilhan Omar resign from Congress over disputed claims about her legal status, name and eligibility to serve. NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., posted a serene lakeside video Friday set to a Somali hip-hop song whose lyrics boast of enemies scattering and being "crushed," days after federal agents searched her Washington home as part of a criminal investigation. "Less scrolling, more strolling. Enjoying our beautiful Minnesota lakes," the embattled congresswoman wrote on X in a post made at the end of last week. She attached a video of herself and her husband, Tim Mynett, walking on a dock over a lake with vibrant fall foliage in the background. The pair posed, smiled and appeared to chat as they serenely strolled across the dock, looking fondly at each other as the lawmaker running for reelection held a coffee. It ended with a montage of images from their walk. But a loud Somali hip-hop song accompanying the video told a much different story. Rep. Ilhan Omar arrives to Karmel Mall of Somalia to attend Friday prayers at Karmel Masjid in Minneapolis. Minn., Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital) ILHAN OMAR DOUBLES DOWN ON ‘REAL NAME’ WHEN CONFRONTED AT MALL OF SOMALIA "Let me reveal who I really am. No enemy dares threaten me, wherever I step, they scatter," the lyrics to the song say in Somali, according to a translation obtained by Fox News Digital. "They flee and stay far away. I have always been the source of their distress." The song, "Nimaan Ciilayba Icaaya," is by Ilkacase Qays, whose real name is Muse Abdikadir. His website describes him as a "U.S. based Somali singer, rapper and activist." The duet-style track features Somali singer Hodan Abdirahman. A cultural analysis of the song says it is "a powerful example of Somali lyrical poetry built around pride, bravery, personal dignity and unwavering trust in Allah." "A fool’s words carry no weight," the lyrics say. "Those I have angered now insult me. If the just one had felt anger on my behalf, would he not have crushed the enemy underfoot? With the strength the almighty has given me, If I draw on it late in the afternoon, by evening, I will have taught you a lesson." Rep. Ilhan Omar speaks during the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor (DFL) Party Convention in Rochester, Minn., May 30, 2026. (Alex Kormann/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images) FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION The analysis describes the artist as using "exaggerated imagery to ridicule his opponents, portraying them as people who would lose sleep, suffer humiliation, and even seek supernatural assistance out of desperation." "You go without sleep, overcome with anguish, weeping in spite," the lyrics continued. "You howl like a demon through the night, because you cannot match me! Swallow your anger and choke on it if the just one had felt anger on my behalf." Omar, who sources say is actually named Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, reemerged in Minnesota on Friday. It came after nearly two weeks out of the public eye following an Oct. 12, 2026, raid on her Washington, D.C., home, conducted by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents. Members of the media followed her intently as she cast an early ballot alongside state Attorney General Keith Ellison at a polling place in Minneapolis on Friday. The pair then appeared at the Karmel Mall of Somalia in Minneapolis, where they enjoyed lunch among members of the Somali community and posed for photographs. HOMAN SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD BE STRIPPED OF NATURALIZATION, DEPORTED IF IMMIGRATION FRAUD IS PROVEN Later in the day, Omar posted the video to X. It is unclear when it was filmed. The Somali-born Minnesota lawmaker restricted who can respond directly to her social media post, with the only publicly facing comment being from ousted former U.S. House "Squad" member Cori Bush, who wrote: "We love this." Video Omar is being investigated for potential fraud related to immigration paperwork filled out by her or her father when she was becoming a United States citizen. HSI is the main investigatory agency for the Department of Homeland Security. During the raid, Omar's passport and cellphone were confiscated by federal agents. Her sister, Sahra Noor, was interviewed by federal investigators in the wake of the raid. Federal agents have also obtained Omar's DNA, Fox News reported. title: Haley Stevens ripped by fellow Dems for refusing to explicitly back El-Sayed: 'Stay the f--- off television'
description: Abdul El-Sayed's former primary rival Haley Stevens dodged a direct endorsement on CNN's "State of the Union," sparking progressive backlash online.
content: Politics Haley Stevens ripped by fellow Dems for refusing to explicitly back El-Sayed: 'Stay the f--- off television' The former Michigan Senate primary candidate said she's 'on the team' but stopped short of naming El-Sayed directly By Elizabeth Elkind Fox News Published October 26, 2026 2:45pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video Black Michigan voters open up on El-Sayed vs. Rogers Lawrence Jones hosts a panel with voters Naura Evans and Rev. Dr. Charles Williams II to analyze the impact of dueling Michigan rallies held by President Donald Trump and Barack Obama. The guests discuss recent polling data showing how Black Michigan voters view candidate Abdul El-Sayed compared to Mike Rogers. The discussion highlights divisions and shifting political alignments within key voter demographics ahead of the midterm elections. NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! Abdul El-Sayed's former Democratic rival is getting hammered by fellow left-wingers online for failing to explicitly endorse him during a weekend television appearance. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., who unsuccessfully ran for the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan, told CNN's "State of the Union" that she broadly supports her state party's ticket for the coming midterm elections. "Look, I'm on the Democratic ticket. I can't say that I agree with everything that's gone on," Stevens answered. "I'm looking to be on the team to support my next governor, Jocelyn Benson, and frankly, these great Democrats who are working their tails off, who are going to make Hakeem Jeffries the first Black Speaker of the House." BERNIE SANDERS CLAIMS SOME DEMOCRATS MAY WANT THEIR OWN SENATE NOMINEE TO LOSE Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan, right, and former Wayne County Health Department Director Abdul El-Sayed faced off in the state's Democratic Senate primary. (Evan Cobb for The Washington Post via Getty Images; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images) When pressed about El-Sayed specifically, she said, "Well, look, I would just say, if you had asked me if I'm still on the team, I'm on the team." But that was not enough for progressives, who promptly accused Stevens of undermining her fellow Democrat. "Ridiculous. For all the folks still pretending El-Sayed’s race is the same as [Roy Cooper’s] or [Mary Peltola’s], do they have former Dem rivals refusing to fully endorse them on national TV? ‘Blue no matter who’ was a hypocritical centrist lie and this hypocrisy may hurt Dems in 2028," Mehdi Hasan wrote on X, referring to Democrat Senate races in North Carolina and Alaska. Leah Greenberg, who leads the progressive activist group Indivisible, wrote, "It is late October and people are voting every day, if you cannot give a full-throated endorsement to the Democratic nominee who could be the key vote in flipping the Senate, then stay the f--- off television." MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT WHO LOST SENATE PRIMARY TO ABDUL EL-SAYED TAKES AIM AT BERNIE SANDERS OVER ISRAEL STANCE Former congressional candidate Kyle Blomquist accused Stevens of "practically fawning over Mike Rogers" and said "her only real ideological commitment is to zionism." Progressive commentator Emma Vigeland wrote on X, "There are financial and institutional incentives to remain on the side of genocide. Stevens is sabotaging El-Sayed on national TV, one week before the midterm, to protect her pocketbook and career over democracy." More moderate and establishment-friendly Democrats pushed back on some of the criticism. Strategist Lis Smith responded to Hasan, "People—Democrats, Republicans, Independents—clamoring to support the Peltolas and Coopers is actually a validation of their candidate quality! It’s good to have candidates people want to associate with and that should be a factor when assessing candidate quality!" Then-Democratic Senate candidate Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan, left, and retiring Sen. Gary Peters, take questions at a news conference, on August 2, 2026, in Madison Heights, Mich. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News) El-Sayed edged Stevens out by just 1% in the Michigan primary earlier this year, after fellow Democrat Mallory McMorrow dropped out of the race. El-Sayed won 48.5% of the vote compared to Stevens' 47.5%, with McMorrow netting 4%. Stevens was notably the establishment-backed pick with support from top Democrats like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. El-Sayed is backed by "Squad" Democrats like Reps. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. title: Obama judge rules Trump DOJ illegally fired James Comey's daughter, rejects sweeping Article II claim
description: The Trump Justice Department fired Maurene Comey without cause, but a federal judge ruled it violated the Civil Service Reform Act and ordered backpay.
content: Federal Courts Obama judge rules Trump DOJ illegally fired James Comey's daughter, rejects sweeping Article II claim The Obama-appointed judge rejected the administration's Article II claim and ordered Maurene Comey reinstated with backpay By Charles Creitz Fox News Published October 26, 2026 2:41pm EDT Comments Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video There could be something more 'nefarious' behind Comey's '86 47' stunt: Gregg Jarrett Fox News legal analyst Gregg Jarrett evaluates the federal indictment of former FBI Director James Comey for an alleged threatening social media post on ‘Hannity.’ NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! An Obama-appointed New York federal judge ruled Monday that the Trump Justice Department unlawfully fired former FBI Director James Comey's daughter Maurene, rejecting the administration's sweeping claim of executive authority and warning that its argument threatened the nation's constitutional balance of power. The Justice Department acknowledged in court filings that Comey's firing was not for-cause and was not based on her performance, but argued that the attorney general had the authority to remove her under Article II of the Constitution. "Defendants’ argument that [Constitution] Article II bars Congress from regulating the removal of AUSAs (assistant U.S. attorneys) flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent," Judge Jesse Furman wrote, adding that accepting the administration's argument would "unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation's constitutional system." TRUMP’S FIRING POWER FACES TWIN SUPREME COURT TESTS, BUT ONE AGENCY MAY GET SPECIAL TREATMENT Former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey and her father, former FBI Director James Comey, are seen in this split image. Comey, a longtime U.S. prosecutor for the Justice Department, sued the Trump administration Monday, Sept. 15, over her abrupt firing earlier this year. (Getty Images) A DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital the department disagreed with the decision and will appeal it in "due course." Furman ordered Comey retroactively reinstated and awarded back pay through Dec. 20, 2025, when she accepted another job. While federal law gives the attorney general authority to fire assistant U.S. attorneys, Furman ruled that Congress placed limits on that power through the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA), which generally requires cause for termination and procedural protections for government workers. OBAMA JUDGE HALTS TRUMP FIRING BID AS DECADES-OLD LEGAL AUTHORITY TEES UP POSSIBLE MAJOR REVERSAL Patrice Failor (L), wife of former FBI director James Comey, is embraced by her daughter Maurene Comey as they arrive at the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia's Bryan Courthouse on October 8, 2025, in Alexandria, Virginia. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images) The judge found that Comey's firing violated those requirements, noting that the government conceded her removal was not based on misconduct or poor performance and that she received neither advance notice nor an opportunity to respond. Comey had served about a decade in the prominent Southern District of New York, where she worked on some of the office’s biggest cases, including the prosecution of Ghislaine Maxwell – associate and rumored partner of Jeffrey Epstein — as well as the sex trafficking trial of rapper Sean "P. Diddy" Combs. Furman also recently rebuked the Trump administration during its efforts to deport pro-Palestinian Columbia University student activist Mahmoud Khalil, leading the federal government to argue for a change of venue to New Jersey. The judge, nominated in 2011, previously served as a federal prosecutor in the same Manhattan U.S. attorney's office where both Comeys worked during their careers. Furman's brother, Jason, served in the Obama administration as chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers. James Comey served as the top prosecutor at SDNY early in the George W. Bush administration, where he investigated President Bill Clinton’s controversial pardon of financier Marc Rich as well as interior designer Martha Stewart. The younger Comey was the second in her family to be fired under Trump, after the president terminated her father as FBI director in 2017 during the Russia collusion investigation. The elder Comey later came under fire for posting a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to form the sentiment "86 47" – with critics saying "86" was a reference to killing something, such as in restaurant lingo, and "47" referred to Trump, the 47th president. Maurene Comey’s attorneys said in a statement to The Associated Press that their victory was "hard-earned" for both their client and all civil servants. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Prosecutor Maurene Comey, arrived at federal court for the Sean "Diddy" Combs trial on Wednesday, May 21, 2025, in Manhattan. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital) CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "As the court correctly held, to accept the government’s argument about unlimited executive power ‘would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation’s constitutional system.’ This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law," they said.
