description: Former Golden State Warriors star DeMarcus Cousins slammed GM Mike Dunleavy Jr. for failing to build a strong roster around Steph Curry.
content: NBA Ex-Warriors star calls for GM Mike Dunleavy’s job over Steph Curry roster failure By Grant Young Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:36 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Four-time NBA All-Star DeMarcus Cousins doesn’t think the Warriors’ issues will improve any time soon, given his harsh comments during an appearance on FanDuel TV’s “Run It Back” show on Monday. 3 DeMarcus Cousins of the Golden State Warriors reacts against the Toronto Raptors in the second half during Game Six of the 2019 NBA Finals at ORACLE Arena in Oakland, California, Thursday, June 13, 2019. Why this guy still has a job, I’ll never know,” he added. 3 Golden State Warriors General Manager Mike Dunleavy speaks at a press conference during media day at Chase Center in San Francisco, California, on Monday, September 28, 2026. title: Jake Bauers may have out-priced his own Brewers desires
description: Bauers, who’s listed with career earnings estimated at $4.6 million on Baseball-Reference, can cash in now.
content: Jon Heyman Jake Bauers may have out-priced his own Brewers desires By Jon Heyman Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:33 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source Milwaukee Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers holds the NLCS MVP trophy after Game 4 of baseball's National League Championship Series between the Milwaukee Brewers and the Los Angeles Dodgers, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026, in Los Angeles. title: Europe’s leaders still refuse to face the far-left’s assault on civilization
description: Can France’s Emmanuel Macron and other European leaders admit that the violence sweeping their nations has nothing to do with any legitimate grievance? It’s not students seeking better schools or moms decrying the high cost of groceries, as media reports keep…
content: Opinion editorial Europe’s leaders still refuse to face the far-left’s assault on civilization By Post Editorial Board Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:32 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source French police officers in riot gear facing off with protesters in Paris on Oct. 24, 2026. James Breeden for NY Post Can France’s Emmanuel Macron and other European leaders admit that the violence sweeping their nations has nothing to do with any legitimate grievance? It’s not students seeking better schools or moms decrying the high cost of groceries, as media reports keep gaslighting: It’s the far left, allied with Islamists, out to bully their neighbors into submission. The rioters aim to burn it all down, spread chaos, destroy the civilized world’s very foundations. Pretending these are “cost of living” protests offers the goons a false legitimacy. Sure, the riots, which began in France and have echoed in numerous other European nations now (Italy, Spain, Greece, Portugal, Albania and Belgium), follow on far smaller protests about schools and then living-cost grievances. More From Post Editorial Board Ilhan Omar hurls the ‘genocide’ charge at Israel — but it belongs much closer to home Fast Takes: Ilhan Omar’s dad’s dubious past, Trump’s sensible appeal and more New York voters need more genuine general-election choices — or democracy is doomed But the far left, joined by unassimilated migrants, turned those demonstrations into rioting, looting, arson and attacks on police. Not to mention statue-smashing and attacks on synagogues. “Down with the state, the police and the fascists,” shouted Saturday’s marchers in France. Some government officials admit organized radical leftist groups are enflaming the violence; a French intelligence assessment reportedly cited Antifa and other far-left groups as key instigators. See Also Democrats scheme to turn the US into France — riots and all Far-left politicians, above all presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, cheer on the madness while insincerely tut-tutting at the violence and pretending socialism is the cure rather the disease. Yes, Macron has blamed “ultra-left groups” for the turmoil, but he also promises billions more for in public funding for schools, as if that’s the real issue. And when a gunman Friday opened fire on people of North African descent, killing one, he damned it as “the first time there has been a terrorist act aimed at killing our compatriots and our children for the color of their skin” or religion — outrageously ignoring decades of deadly antisemitic and anti-Christian attacks, as well as mass Islamist terror such as the 2015 Bataclan slaughter. Disgraceful, especially when so many rioters carry Palestinian flags. The rioting — a black-bloc assault on the Colosseum! — should be a wakeup call, prompting Macron & Co. to rally the sensible center against the anarchists, crypto-communists and Islamists. Stand up for civilization, or the assault will redouble. title: Government officials alarmed by Anthropic’s delay in reporting ‘rogue agent’ Georgia vote hack
description: Both the incident and Anthropic’s handling of it are raising alarm bells, just days before the midterm elections.
content: Tech exclusive details Anthropic’s delay in reporting ‘rogue agent’ Georgia vote hack alarms government officials By Lydia Moynihan Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:32 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source Administration officials say Anthropic dragged its feet in disclosing its AI’s “alarming” attack involving Georgia’s election data. While the company reported the incident to White House officials in October, sources told The Post the breach by a “rogue” AI bot happened months earlier — around the same time other Anthropic AI agents had made unsanctioned attempts to fill out non-immigrant visa applications at the State Department in August. Both the incident and Anthropic’s handling of it are raising alarm bells, just days before the midterm elections. 4 Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei has called for the government to aggressively regulate artificial intelligence or “pace the frontier.” AFP via Getty Images Anthropic says its Claude Large Language Model was working on a statistics project when it bypassed a paywall and retrieved aggregate counts, but not individual voter records from a Georgia state website. Georgia officials have made clear the state’s voter-registration system was not accessed or compromised. However, some administration sources are skeptical of that explanation, describing the incident as an attack by a rogue agent from an unreleased model. Explore More Microsoft announces buyouts for 60K employees — quarter of workforce — as part of AI transformation Ex-Yahoo CEO under fire for bragging about birthday message to daughter — written by AI: ‘Who would do this?’ Workers at OpenAI, Anthropic made to ditch company logos as it makes them targets for spies, seduction That has, in turn, raised concerns about Anthropic’s oversight of its systems and whether it has proper safeguards in place — as well as what prompt sparked the rogue agent to hack into an election website. One source noted the idea that Anthropic was merely working on a statistics assignment doesn’t fully explain its AI’s actions — and noted how odd it was for an agent to seek election-related data which could potentially be shared with bad actors or used for campaign purposes. Anthropic, which has just filed to take the company public, did not respond to requests for comment from The Post, but told Axios it had implemented measures to prevent similar actions. 4 Administration officials say Anthropic dragged its feet in disclosing what they describe as an alarming attack involving Georgia’s election data, sources told The Post. Getty Images In a blog post, the company wrote: “We have chosen not to name the organizations involved in the examples below to avoid exposing vulnerabilities in their systems, and at their request.” This latest security breach comes amid debate about whether the government should be cracking down more aggressively on AI companies and what responsibility frontier labs should implement to keep track of their agents. Some in the tech world have openly called for increased regulation — including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. He has asked for the government to “pace the frontier” innovation. Others, like former AI Czar David Sacks, have said tech companies need to act responsibly and police themselves, slowing down their development if they cannot guarantee safety. 4 This latest security breach comes amid a debate about whether the government should be cracking down more aggressively on these companies and what responsibility frontier labs have to keep track of their agents. REUTERS “If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible,” Sacks wrote in a post on X last month. This isn’t the first instance of an Anthropic agent taking unauthorized action. Anthropic agents submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police earlier this year, and in July its bots also escaped their ‘sandbox’ and got onto the open internet, where they accessed the site Hugging Face. The Georgia incident has also raised concerns about whether states have sufficiently secured all of their systems amid rapidly improving technology. 4 Amodei, flanked by President Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA). Trump has warned about China stealing US voting data. REUTERS This also comes after President Trump expressed concern that China has accessed US data. . In a primetime speech earlier this year he claimed the country’s Communist Party had stolen the voter registration of 220 million Americans. “Over a period of years, starting during the 2020 election cycle, the People’s Republic of China carried out what is believed to be the largest compromise of election data in history, resulting in China’s illicit acquisition of 220 million US voter files,” Trump said in an address from the White House in July. “The intelligence even shows that China assigned a data exploitation unit specifically to this new project.” Filed under Anthropic artificial intelligence 10/26/26 Read Next Apple addresses reports of cracked screens on $2K iPhone D... title: Matthew Schaefer’s increased Islanders workload isn’t as cut and dry as it seems
description: Despite the stated desire from coach Pete DeBoer to be careful with Matthew Schaefer’s workload, the 19-year-old’s minutes are up by over 90 seconds per game from last season.
content: NHL New York Islanders Matthew Schaefer’s increased Islanders workload isn’t as cut and dry as it seems By Ethan Sears Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:29 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Despite the stated desire from coach Pete DeBoer to be careful with Matthew Schaefer’s workload, the 19-year-old’s minutes are up by over 90 seconds per game from last season, enough that he’s now fourth in the league at an eye-popping 26:13 per night. That, however, is not an issue for either Schaefer or the Islanders, albeit for different reasons. For Schaefer’s part, he simply likes playing, feels his body is fine and is never going to ask for fewer minutes. And for the Islanders’ part, DeBoer pointed at the breakdown of those minutes — namely, taking Schaefer off the penalty kill this season — as the team’s way of managing him, rather than the raw number. “I think 26 minutes isn’t necessarily all the same type of minutes,” DeBoer said after the Islanders practiced on Monday at Bridgestone Arena. “If you’re defending all night, if you’re killing penalties, those are different minutes [than] power play and offensive situations, things like that.” New York Islanders defenseman Matthew Schaefer (48) shoots the puck against the Dallas Stars during the first period of an NHL hockey game at American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Through Schaefer’s first year and change in the NHL, there’s been little reason to suspect that his workload has had a massive effect on his day-to-day output. He’s yet to experience an extended slump in the NHL, and doesn’t tend to fade late in games, even when the Islanders lean on him heavily. Explore More Three-goals-a-night formula comes with issues for low-scoring Islanders Islanders see how far they have to go with key deficiency exposed in eye-opening loss to Stars The Barry Trotz formula longtime Islanders see in Pete Deboer’s success To the extent there’s a worry, it’s less about the here and now and more that the mileage Schaefer accumulates as a teenager could affect him in the future. “Obviously sometimes [DeBoer] will check in and be like, make sure you’re resting the body, taking the option you need and things like that,” Schaefer told The Post. “At the end of the day, I think he knows I love to be out there. I’m still young, so try to burn some energy out there. It’s fun.” On the ice from Long Island Sign up for Inside the Islanders by Ethan Sears, a weekly Sports+ exclusive. Thank you Enter your email address Please provide a valid email. By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy. Enjoy this Post Sports+ exclusive newsletter! Check out more newsletters The Islanders moved Matias Maccelli (lower body) and Calum Ritchie (lower body) to injured reserve, clearing two roster spots with which they called up Kashawn Aitcheson and Pierre Engvall as paper transactions. Neither Aitcheson nor Engvall are expected to play or even to join the team, but adding their cap hits allows the Islanders to get closer to the salary cap ceiling and maximize their long-term injury pool, if and when Alexander Romanov is added to LTIR. Paper transactions in the opposite direction — that is, sending a player down on paper to maximize cap accrual — has been legislated out of the NHL, but doing so with a call-up is still allowed. Matias Maccelli (63) of the New York Islanders battles against Auston Matthews (34) of the Toronto Maple Leafs during the first period in their NHL game at Scotiabank Arena in Toronto, Canada, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. NHLI via Getty Images Moving to IR doesn’t affect the time frame for Maccelli or Ritchie, as both have already missed the required seven days. title: I’m a naturalized citizen — Ilhan Omar must play by the same rules I did
description: There must be consequences for breaking the law — yes, even immigration law. We shouldn’t have to pretend otherwise to protect Ilhan Omar.
content: Karol Markowicz Opinion I’m a naturalized citizen — Ilhan Omar must play by the same rules I did By Karol Markowicz Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:27 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source A supporter of Rep. Ilhan Omar holds a "Stand with Ilhan" poster at a rally in Minneapolis on Oct. 12, 2026 after Homeland Security agents raided her Washington, DC, home. REUTERS/Tim Evans Once again, Republicans are acting to enforce immigration laws — and Democrats are aghast. How dare the Department of Homeland Security investigate the possibly shady way that Ilhan Omar became a US citizen? The probe should “outrage all Americans,” former President Barack Obama proclaimed, while House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called it “deeply disturbing.” There’s nothing outrageous or disturbing about it. A federal magistrate judge in the US District Court for DC saw sufficient evidence to approve a search warrant for Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home — President Trump isn’t waving a magic wand and making the Minnesota Democrat disappear. REUTERS After all, a federal magistrate judge in the US District Court for the District of Columbia saw sufficient evidence to approve a search warrant for Omar’s home — President Donald Trump isn’t waving a magic wand and making the Minnesota Democrat disappear. More From Karol Markowicz I was a Trump skeptic — but his second-term wins made me a believer Seniors’ demands for ‘grandparents’ rights’ could spell big political headaches Kim Kardashian targets youth sports with ‘Team Moms’ — but here’s what she’s missing The New York Times editorial board rushed to Omar’s defense. “End the Ilhan Omar investigation,” it demanded. “If her naturalization can be revisited, that means no naturalized citizen is safe.” Well, no: That means that no naturalized citizen who lied to get into the country is safe. I’m a naturalized citizen. I’m not worried. There must be consequences for breaking the law — yes, even immigration law. Most naturalized citizens don’t do that. We shouldn’t have to pretend they do to protect Ilhan Omar. So much of the Democratic rhetoric surrounding immigration is intended to skirt this vital distinction. See Also Miranda Devine: Dems know Ilhan Omar is in deep trouble — that’s why they had Obama parachute in Democrats like Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico promise voters they don’t want open borders, and take offense when it’s implied that they do. But El-Sayed has called for abolishing the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency — that is, the people who enforce our immigration laws — and has said, “I believe we owe it to the world to open our doors.” Both candidates support pathways to citizenship for people who violated our laws to enter our country. Strange: That’s not the case for other crimes. We don’t let a thief hang on to the flat-screen TV because he got it all the way home. It’s recently dawned on some Democrats that failing to enforce laws leads to more law-breaking. Bluest-of-the-blue cities like San Francisco are implementing far-out policies like actually arresting criminals and putting them in jail. As District Attorney Brooke Jenkins told The Post in April, “Those who break our laws and commit crimes are not only identified and arrested, but also prosecuted.” Imagine that! What if we tried that with immigration? It’s an idea so crazy it just might work. Get opinions and commentary from our columnists Subscribe to our daily Post Opinion newsletter! Thanks for signing up! Enter your email address Please provide a valid email. By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy. Never miss a story. Check out more newsletters But Democrats insist on putting immigration law in its own separate category. Check out how the Times described illegal immigrants in a story last week: “Someone [who] comes here and follows all the rules, except the ones about how to enter the country.” “Except” is doing quite a lot of heavy lifting here. “He followed all the rules of obtaining a new TV, except for the paying-for-it part.” The report itself is about a police officer who finds it depressing to enforce immigration law. We frequently hear the sad stories of people who broke immigration law and made it to the United States, but were then kicked out because of their illegal status. See Also I’m a legal immigrant — don’t you dare lump me in with border-jumpers We never seem to hear the equally sad stories of people who patiently waited their turn to come here but never made it, because others had cut the line in front of them. They, too, had dreams and ambitions of making a better life for their families — their only mistake was abiding by the laws of the country they wished to join. Or consider last weekend’s teary “60 Minutes” segment about Moussa Diawara, who ignored a final order of removal and was deported after living in the United States for 25 years. Diawara’s children and wife got plenty of screen time to tell us how much they miss him. Unmentioned in their interviews, as DHS General Counsel James Percival later pointed out, is that Diawara entered the US by claiming that he feared for his life in Mali because he’s gay. The wife and two children would seem to make that tale unlikely. For too long, we’ve been rewarding the line-cutters, the rule-breakers, the law-mockers. We have to stop it. To survive, any country must have secure borders and immigration laws that aren’t scoffed at. Ilhan Omar does a lot of scoffing. Questions have long swirled around Omar’s immigration process and citizenship status. Numerous sources have charged she wed her own brother to help him get a green card — a persistent rumor she’s lamely sought to deflect (asked last week whether she was related to her ex, Omar responded, “Not that I know of”). There’s substantial evidence that she’s lying about her age — in a way that could cancel the citizenship she says she gained via her late father’s status — and the federal court filings indicate that “Omar” isn’t her true surname. Omar’s naturalization shouldn’t protect her if she broke the law to win it — and the Trump administration is right to make sure it doesn’t. Karol Markowicz is the host of the “Karol Markowicz Show” and “Normally” podcasts. title: Paper straws worse for the environment than plastic ones, says study
description: Paper straws can actually be worse for the environment, according to studies.
content: Lifestyle Paper straws worse for the environment than plastic ones: study By Faran Krentcil Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:22 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source This scientific study might be the last straw. A damning study out of South Korea has revealed that paper straws might actually be worse for the planet than plastic ones, especially when their life cycle is traced from the factory floor to the landfill. The findings suck the air out of some long-winded environmental protests, which claimed for a decade that plastic straws were on par with toxic fumes or forest fires — and fought to make iced lattes nearly impossible to drink through a soggy, wilted tube of cardboard. 3 Plastic straws may have a marginal effect on the environment compared with paper ones, according to a South Korean study. sonyachny – stock.adobe.com The research comes from South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment, which analyzed four types of straws — paper, plastic, biodegradable plastic, and sugarcane-based — across 16 environmental categories. Explore More New ‘prestige porn’ makes sex the ultimate luxury — and hot older women the main characters Dictionary.com’s Word of the Year is one of the most viral — and controversial — terms to date My friend is reselling the expensive birthday gifts I give her son Traditional plastic straws showed the lowest environmental footprint in 10 of the 16 categories, including human toxicity, particulate matter, and overall climate change impact. Meanwhile, paper straws were found to generate over six times more carcinogens than standard plastic, along with double the impact on environmental acidification. As for “Bio-PE” straws — the kind made from renewable sources like sugarcane — they produced 16 times the carcinogenic impact of standard plastic straws, along with six times the acidification damage (the metric scientists use to measure changes in ocean and soil pH levels). 3 Paper straws were found to be difficult to recycle, with a higher chance of upsetting the ocean ecosystem. Tetiana Ivanova – stock.adobe.com But aren’t paper straws better anyway because they can be recycled? Not exactly. The study found that because paper straws are so small, they routinely slip through sorting equipment at recycling facilities, meaning almost none actually get recycled. Furthermore, their water-resistant coatings and industrial glues prevent them from breaking down easily, demanding more energy during processing and leaving open the possibility that microplastics could end up in the recycled pulp anyway. Confronted with the findings, South Korean lawmaker Kim Wi-sang criticized domestic environmental groups and his own government for prioritizing feel-good narratives over hard science. 3 Reusable straws are an ideal alternative, if possible. Matija – stock.adobe.com “The government must acknowledge the failure of its greenwashing policy, which fixated on ineffective substitute materials,” he said. The public seems to agree. According to a government survey of 1,001 South Korean citizens, 87.5% dislike paper straws. So what’s the solution? If possible, invest in a set of reusable straws made from durable materials like stainless steel or silicone, which are dishwasher-safe and easy to rinse out in the sink. Or you could simply sip your drink using nature’s original straw: your mouth. title: New York’s 2026 governor race: Letters to the Editor — Oct. 27, 2026
description: NY Post readers discuss Nassau Exec Bruce Blakeman’s challenge to Gov. Hochul in New York’s 2026 gubernatorial race.
content: Opinion letters to the editor New York’s 2026 governor race: Letters to the Editor — Oct. 27, 2026 By Post readers Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:20 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman speaks to members of the media during his campaign event in New York's Chinatown, in New York, New York, Oct. 23, 2026. OLGA FEDOROVA/EPA/Shutterstock The Issue: Nassau Exec Bruce Blakeman’s challenge to Gov. Hochul in New York’s 2026 gubernatorial race. My prayer for New Yorkers is that they can look past their partisan leanings and simply vote for the best governor (“A needed Blake from Kat’s mess,” Michael Goodwin, Oct. 25). New York is true-blue state, but if enough residents can’t vote for change in the form of Bruce Blakeman, then my capacity for any pity will be replaced by the cold reality that “people deserve exactly what they voted for.” Amy Hendel Manhattan Now 81, I’ve been a registered Democrat since I was able to vote. However, I find myself agreeing with everything Saritha Komatireddy and Bruce Blakeman have said about how they would run New York. Explore More Blue states like New York might dash Democrats’ Blue Wave dreams Ilhan Omar hurls the ‘genocide’ charge at Israel — but it belongs much closer to home Dreadful Elon Musk hit-piece documentary only serves to fuel Dems’ frenzy against him before midterms Their solutions are both fair and feasible. I have such confidence in their capability of solving whatever problems come up. So I am going to vote for them, and hope my prayers come true. Lois Grossman Woodmere I don’t understand how people can vote for Kathy Hochul. Everyone complains about affordability and crime. Of course, she likes to blame President Trump, but the fact remains that she is the governor of New York. She can’t even get the public to pay their bus and subway fares. But she did build a billionaire’s new football stadium as soon as she became governor. How can anyone trust her to run the state? Robert Leavy Middle Village I was happy to see The Post come out early to endorse Blakeman for governor. Goodwin points out all that is wrong with New York under Hochul. Blakeman needs to keep repeating Ronald Reagan’s question: “Are you better off now than you were four years ago?” Sadly, many people can’t answer that question honestly, instead blindly following their political beliefs. Those who fail to learn from history are doomed to repeat it. Wake up, New York! Bo Madden Jupiter, Fla. Not one resident in upstate Elmira should vote for Hochul (“Penn Frack Boom Is NY’s Bust,” Oct. 23). Because of her desperation to secure the Green Party’s votes, she won’t allow fracking, and this once-prosperous town is being smothered by unemployment and crime. All New Yorkers can thank former Gov. Andrew Cuomo for “gifting” Hochul to us. Nicholas Maffei Yonkers The Issue: Two ex-FBI officials charged with allegedly lying about their roles in the Hunter Biden laptop probe. Surprise, surprise! FBI agents covered up the Hunter Biden laptop scandal as Russian misinformation (“Agents Turned A Blind FB-Eye,” Oct. 24). I’m relatively certain the two agents named in the coverup weren’t acting alone and making decisions without orders from the top. I wonder who that could be. Does the name James Comey ring a bell? Bill Lewis Danbury, Conn. Get opinions and commentary from our columnists Subscribe to our daily Post Opinion newsletter! Thanks for signing up! Enter your email address Please provide a valid email. By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy. Never miss a story. Check out more newsletters It’s about time those who were responsible for investigating the laptop are held accountable. The American public deserves better. It doesn’t matter what political party it is; a crime is a crime. Now it’s time to expose the mainstream media for their complicity in the coverup. Dan Gardner Staten Island The recent news of retired FBI Agents Floris and Benavides being charged with lying to Congress shouldn’t surprise anyone. The sad part is, the former senior officials who orchestrated the entire cover-up on behalf of the Democrats and Joe Biden used Floris and Benavides as pawns and won’t be held accountable. title: Federal election monitors swarm California to face off with Democrat watchers as voting war turns toxic
description: Federal officials and Democratic groups will descend upon California in the coming days to monitor the state’s elections amid an intensifying partisan feud over voting. The Department of Justice plans to deploy 1,000 election monitors across the country, incl…
content: Politics Federal election monitors swarm California to face off with Democrat watchers as voting war turns toxic By Annie Gaus Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:20 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make California Post a Preferred Source Federal officials and Democratic groups will descend upon California in the coming days to monitor the state’s elections amid an intensifying partisan feud over voting. The Department of Justice plans to deploy 1,000 election monitors across the country, including in California, for “routine election monitoring the department has done for decades,” per a spokesperson, as partisan and third-party groups ready volunteer armies to keep watch on polling places. “We will have around 1,000 monitors in counties throughout the United States, but we will not share the full list until Election Day. Every monitor will merely observe and report any potential violations of federal law to the Department, which will be reviewed after Election Day,” the DOJ spokesperson said. CHRIS TORRES/EPA/Shutterstock A collection of watchdog groups and political volunteers are also planning to deploy poll watchers in what could amount to unprecedented scrutiny on the midterm elections. Among those are the Democratic National Committee and Republican National Committee, both of which are helping to train poll monitors, according to Associated Press. But “we’ve never had to deal with the president of the United States saying that he may seize ballots, put ICE agents outside polling locations and other kinds of very clear direct threats to the voting process.” 7 HSI LA books Omar Alexander Muñoz, 72, a Belizean national charged with voter fraud. Carlin Stiehl for CA Post The California Democratic Party’s Voter Protection Team is recruiting poll watchers and volunteer attorneys to monitor the Nov. 3 election, according to its website. State Democratic parties have roughly 10,000 volunteers to observe polling places and report potentially concerning actions by federal agents, per AP. 7 Rob Bonta, Attorney General of California,. REUTERS Likewise, the The Republican National Committee said it plans to deploy “election integrity deputy state directors” in 22 states, among them Arizona, Michigan, Georgia and North Carolina. It’s hired 22,000 poll workers and is recruiting poll watchers for competitive districts, according to Ally Triolo, the RNC’s election integrity communications director. 7 The potentially unprecedented election monitoring push comes amid a legal battle between California and federal officials over claims of voter fraud. CHRIS TORRES/EPA/Shutterstock Common cause, a Washington DC-based pro-democracy group, is among the nonprofit watchdog groups planning to send volunteers to polling places, including in California. “At voting locations across the state, our volunteers will check for language and disability access, assist any voters who are encountering problems, and monitor to help ensure that voter harassment and disenfranchisement do not occur,” Common Cause wrote in a post about the California volunteer effort. Common Cause has roughly 16,000 more volunteers to watch voting precincts, Suzanne Almeida, vice president of states for the group, told Associated Press. A broader coalition involving 300 other groups has trained tens of thousands more, she said. 7 People watch on monitors as workers process ballots at the Orange County Registrar of Voters in Santa Ana, California, Tuesday, Nov. 12, 2024. A camera above each work station allows the public to see what the ballot processor is seeing, as a large voter turnout and the ballot verification process add to the time it takes to get a final tally. MediaNews Group via Getty Images Dem-aligned nonprofits Indivisible and MoveOn are activating their networks for the midterm elections, AP reported. Smaller groups of volunteers, including roughly 100 organized by Senate Democrats and hundreds more from Dem-allied group Save America, which is training clergy members, veterans, teachers and other, are also planning a presence on Election Day. The potentially unprecedented election monitoring push comes amid a legal battle between California and federal officials over claims of voter fraud. The Justice Department sued California this months seeking to block 20,000 ballots it claims were sent to noncitizens ahead of the midterm elections. 7 California Secretary of State Shirley Weber. Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Federal agents arrested and charged California residents for allegedly registering to vote illegally or casting illegal ballots. More than two-dozen suspects arrested in a statewide bust last week have been charged. California officials, including Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Attorney General Rob Bonta have strongly pushed back on allegations of widespread voter fraud in the state, with Bonta calling any cases of noncitizen voting “one-offs” that don’t reflect a systemic problem. At a rare Sunday hearing, a 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals panel appeared skeptical of the DOJ’s request to set aside thousands of ballots in California. The court indicated it will issue a decision quickly. title: The rise and fall of CrossFit’s cult-like founder: Cocaine, $200k phone bills and private jet fast food detours
description: A new book reveals the sex, drugs and excessive spending that went along with the intense workouts.
content: Fitness Cocaine, affairs, $200K phone bills and private jet fast food detours: The rise and fall of CrossFit’s cult-like founder By Eric Spitznagel Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:19 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source In the late 2010s, Greg Glassman’s private plane was less than an hour from Denver when he decided he couldn’t wait that long for Chick-fil-A. The CrossFit founder instructed his pilot to land in Grand Junction and arranged for two chauffeured Chevy Suburbans to meet him and his entourage at the airport. According to Jeffrey Cain, then the company’s CEO, they drove to the fast-food restaurant, picked up their order and returned to the plane to finish the flight. Cain put the cost of the detour at more than $5,000. “That anecdote is entirely typical of Glassman and his spending habits,” said Calum Marsh, whose new book, “The Glass Box: The Shocking True Story of How CrossFit Broke the Rules, Made Millions, and Changed Fitness Forever” (HarperOne, out Oct. 27), recounts the excursion. “If he got a sudden hankering for fast food mid-trip, they’d land the plane and get some.” 10 A new book charts the rapid rise of CrossFit and its cult-like founder. Getty Images Marsh tracks Glassman’s journey from a broke California trainer to the owner of a fitness company that generated an estimated $100 million in annual revenue by 2015. But the edgy charisma that helped Glassman, now 70, build a well-muscled empire was ultimately his downfall. When Glassman arrived in Santa Cruz in 1995, he was a college gymnast-turned-college dropout who didn’t own a car or a house. He shared a room with his young son in a friend’s house and started training local police officers. Explore More A game-changing new treatment just arrived for one of the deadliest cancers — here’s why doctors are so excited Skip the dental drill — a simple liquid could stop cavities from progressing: study My nonverbal autistic son began speaking at 8 after taking wonder drug — here’s what he said His workouts could seem alarming to anyone accustomed to doing just a few curls and heading for the showers. Glassman mixed demanding weightlifting with gymnastics, sending clients outside to do lunges across the parking lot and sometimes leaving them vomiting into a trash can. He also timed them, turning exercise into a competition. Clients could watch their scores improve, or discover that someone they thought they could easily beat was considerably fitter. “It is our observation that men will die for points,” Glassman later wrote. Keeping score, he explained, could “motivate unprecedented output.” Lauren Jenai, a young hairdresser who wanted to lose weight, became a client that summer. She was so impressed by the results that she quit her job and community college to help him train people, although she wasn’t entirely sure what to make of her new boss. “This guy is either the biggest f–king con man in history,” she told a friend, “or he’s onto something pretty f–king spectacular.” The two began dating and married in 1998, wearing Hawaiian shirts and leis at a backyard ceremony. Their growing following and loud, aggressive workouts didn’t make them popular with gym owners, so in, 2001, they opened their own gym dedicated to what they called CrossFit. 10 “I was fortunate enough to receive a lot of financial records, internal documents, emails, and other documentation from that period that outlined some of the extreme spending and the lack of oversight for the finances at CrossFit,” author Calum Marsh told The Post. Jenai handled much of the financial administration while Glassman developed the workouts and talked about the possibilities. Money remained tight enough that clients helped finance equipment purchases. Glassman recalled sleeping on a futon with Jenai while his son had the bedroom and a friend slept in the kitchen. “I was fundamentally broke at forty-five,” he told Marsh. “I was always worrying about money.” Posting daily workouts online changed the size of their audience. People who had never met Glassman began following his program, comparing scores in the comments and asking how they could teach it themselves. Soon, weekends certifying trainers in the CrossFit method were packed. Newly trained muscleheads wanted gyms of their own, and Glassman let them license the CrossFit name for a modest annual fee while retaining control of their businesses. 10 Greg Glassman was a college dropout when he started CrossFit. His uniquely intense workouts went viral. CrossFit/YouTube By 2005, according to Marsh, there were more than 50 CrossFit gyms across 21 states and several countries. Two years later, the first CrossFit Games was held on a California ranch. But, as CrossFit expanded, the couple’s marriage began to unravel. Jenai was spending years pregnant or caring for their children while Glassman traveled to seminars and affiliates. At one point, she told Marsh, he announced, “This next year I’m going to have a lot more sex, either with you or without you.” She said they had never discussed an open relationship. In 2009, while Jenai was pregnant with twins, Glassman began a relationship with the wife of a CrossFit gym owner, Marsh reports. He hired the woman as his personal assistant and reportedly persuaded the couple to move a few houses away from his Arizona home. 10 The first CrossFit cames were held in California in 2007. In 2010, Reebok signed a ten-year licensing and sponsorship agreement that would put its name on the Games and produce CrossFit-branded footwear and clothing. ZUMAPRESS.com Affairs were so common within the organization that Jenai had T-shirts made with a warning. “If you sleep with one of my trainers,” they read, “I’m going to tell your wife.” Several former employees told Marsh they were uncomfortable with Glassman’s affairs and how openly he conducted them. “It was baked into the culture from the beginning,” the author told The Post. “It made some women uncomfortable.” Meanwhile, corporate sponsors were discovering CrossFit’s appeal. In 2010, Reebok signed a ten-year licensing and sponsorship agreement that would put its name on the Games and produce CrossFit-branded footwear and clothing. During negotiations, Reebok executives tried to demonstrate their commitment to Glassman’s dietary advice by avoiding bread and alcohol at dinner. They arrived to find him eating dinner rolls and drinking tequila, Marsh writes. 10 The edgy charisma that helped Glassman, now 70, build a well-muscled empire was ultimately his downfall. ZUMAPRESS.com The entertaining could leave even his companions struggling to keep up. Former executive Brian Mulvaney recalled a Fourth of July stop at the Four Seasons in Scottsdale in the early 2010s, when an all-night party left him furious before a business meeting the following day. Glassman proposed a remedy. They would buy cocaine, then get Bloody Marys at the airport lounge before continuing their trip, Mulvaney recounts. “It ended up being a great day,” he told Marsh. By 2012, the breakdown of Glassman and Jenai’s marriage had become a battle over CrossFit’s ownership. Jenai wanted to sell her half to investment firm Anthos Capital, while Glassman was determined to keep an outside investor from becoming his equal partner. He ultimately secured financing to buy her out that year, leaving him the company’s sole owner. Their divorce was finalized in 2013, Jenai later said. 10 Lauren Jenai helped Glassman launch CrossFit. The two married in 1998 and divorced in 2012. ljg771/Instagram With control secured, “his whims really took over,” Marsh told The Post. The man who once worried about paying rent was traveling with an entourage — including “overpaid yes men,” some without precise job titles or clearly defined responsibilities, according to the author. They expected first-class flights and rooms at the Four Seasons. When Cain became CEO in 2016, he began examining what that generosity cost. One item that caught his attention was a Verizon bill approaching $200,000 a month. CrossFit was paying for several hundred phones and service plans, including those belonging to employees’ relatives and people who didn’t work for the company, Cain told Marsh. He recalled Glassman buying iPhones for attractive women he met and adding them to the company plan. “I was fortunate enough to receive a lot of financial records, internal documents, emails, and other documentation from that period that outlined some of the extreme spending and the lack of oversight for the finances at CrossFit,” Marsh told The Post. “The Verizon bill was just one line item amid a wide array of unreasonable expenditures.” Cain canceled the phone contracts, Marsh said. He also repeatedly warned Glassman that the company couldn’t keep spending this way. 10 At its peak in 2018, there were more than 15,000 CrossFit affiliates worldwide. SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Some expenses would be reined in temporarily, according to Marsh. But “it would always balloon again soon.” CrossFit was also paying for nearly a thousand gym memberships, according to Cain’s account. He said Glassman would meet women and arrange a full year of membership at their local affiliate. Glassman defended the practice as helping the recipients and supporting local gyms. “When you look at the money we were making, it didn’t seem like a waste,” he told Marsh. The business was still enormous, with more than 15,000 affiliates worldwide at its 2018 peak. Glassman rejected the suggestion that his spending should be treated as a corporate scandal. Reporters questioning his parties, he told Marsh, acted as though he had taken money from a publicly traded company. “But the till was mine,” he said. “I owned 100 percent of the company.” 10 The company now advertises more than 9,000 affiliated gyms across over 150 countries. ZUMAPRESS.com That ownership did not protect him from the revolt that followed his comments in June 2020. As protests spread after the police killing of George Floyd, Glassman responded to a health institute’s statement about racism with the tweet “It’s FLOYD-19.” Reebok announced it would end its partnership, and gym owners pledged to abandon the CrossFit name. Glassman apologized and stepped down as CEO on June 9. Later that month, workers publicly accused him of sexual harassment and demeaning treatment of women. Marsh recounts allegations that Glassman made vulgar comments about female employees and tried to photograph their breasts. Glassman called the accounts of his crude comments “complete made-up bulls**t” in interviews with Marsh. He also denied pressuring women to sleep with him, saying, “I’m just not that guy.” Marsh says Glassman participated extensively in the book, speaking with him for more than 15 hours and answering subsequent questions by text and email. Glassman did not respond to The Post’s request for comment. 10 Glassman sold CrossFit in 2020 for a reported $200 million. The Washington Post via Getty Images His resignation initially left him as CrossFit’s owner, but later in 2020 he sold the company to entrepreneur Eric Roza and investment firm Berkshire Partners. Marsh puts the deal at $200 million. “I was sixty-four years old and I had little kids,” Glassman told Marsh. “I saw a $200 million buyout.” In 2024, Glassman and former journalist Emily Kaplan launched MetFix, a nutrition and fitness venture. CrossFit, meanwhile, has continued without him, though its network is smaller. The company now advertises more than 9,000 affiliated gyms across over 150 countries, down from its peak of more than 15,000. Former chief operating officer Bruce Edwards was brought back on as CEO in May. Its influence extends well beyond the gyms still paying to use its name. Marsh argues that CrossFit helped make mixed workouts and competing against a clock familiar enough to support a new generation of fitness businesses. 10 Participants pull weights in a HYROX competition at the Fibo 2025 fitness trade fair in Cologne, North Rhine-Westphalia, Thursday, April 10, 2025. dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images Among them is the extreme Hyrox, whose races combine eight one-kilometer runs with eight exercise stations. Participants push weighted sleds and perform lunges, competing on a standardized course that allows them to compare results across events. “[It’s] basically a single CrossFit workout scaled as a mass participation event,” Marsh writes. In one form or another, he notes, “CrossFit the methodology will almost inevitably continue.” Filed under books crossfit fitness weightlifting 10/26/26 Read Next The surprising number of daily steps that could sharpen yo... title: Ex-49er Matthew Judon’s 2 baby mamas change tune on ‘Master’ claim and bizarre relationship arrangement
description: Former San Francisco 49ers player Matthew Judon's baby mamas clarified their living dynamic and calling Judon "Master" in a video.
content: Sports Entertainment Ex-49er Matthew Judon’s 2 baby mamas change tune on ‘Master’ claim and bizarre relationship arrangement By Grant Young Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:17 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make California Post a Preferred Source Two of former San Francisco 49ers defender Matthew Judon’s baby mamas are living together with him. The two women, named Lex and Arabia, made an Instagram video explaining this on Sunday. They also called the four-time Pro Bowler (who was released by San Francisco earlier this month) their “Master” in the video, which raised eyebrows. 3 San Francisco 49ers’ Matthew Judon warms up before an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara, Calif., Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. This is not a throuple, where Matthew has two girlfriends. Matthew very much has one girlfriend, and that’s Lex. title: Mahmoud Khalil headed back to Columbia for book tour, outraging Jewish alumni: ‘Appalled’
description: The anti-Israel rabble-rouser is speaking at the Ivy League about his newly released memoir.
content: Metro Mahmoud Khalil headed back to Columbia for book tour, outraging Jewish alumni: ‘Appalled’ By Carl Campanile and Alex Oliveira Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:15 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source Anti-Israel rabble-rouser and former Columbia student Mahmoud Khalil is returning to campus after being freed from ICE custody — sparking outrage from Jewish groups. Khalil is appearing on the Ivy League’s campus Tuesday evening to promote his new memoir, “No Land to Stand On,” which documents the 104 days he spent in a federal lockup when he was arrested after participating in the Manhattan school’s explosive 2024 anti-Israel protests. “A revelatory and powerful testament of protest, courage, and imprisonment in America’s deportation regime,” says a flyer for the event, which is hosted by Columbia’s Center for Palestine Studies and the Simon and June Li Center for Global Journalism. Mahmoud Khalil leads a chant at a protest on the Columbia University campus, Friday, October 13, 2023, in New York. Getty Images It’s not the first time the 31-year-old has returned to campus since his arrest — he notably returned a day after he was freed from custody in June 2025 — but campus Jewish groups were nevertheless outraged that a school group had invited him back again. “We are appalled that, after the enormous reputational damage Khalil’s behavior inflicted on the University, the Journalism school would stoop to inviting him back to campus,” said Columbia University Jewish Alumni Association president Ari Shrage. Explore More United flight forced to turn around midair after crew member spotted horrifying text on passenger’s phone New details emerge after United ‘hijacking’ threat — as 25-year-old suspect’s chilling messages are revealed Historic 80-ton boulder comes crashing down after more than a century at US attraction “At a time when Columbia should be working to restore public trust and rebuild its reputation, this decision suggests that the University has learned nothing,” he told The Post. That reputational damage was no small detail — Khalil served as a negotiator for the virulent anti-Israel demonstrators who took over the campus from 2023-2024, and tried to convince the school to divest all its investments from Israel. Mahmoud Khalil after his detention by US federal immigration agents in 2025. via REUTERS Those protests resulted in the Trump administration yanking $400 million in funding from the school for failing to protect students from antisemitism, before Columbia backed down and ceded to the president’s demands to help prevent similar demonstrations in the future. Khalil — a Syrian-born permanent US resident, who was studying at Columbia and married to a US citizen — became the face of those movements after he was arrested by the Trump administration, which alleged he’d lied on his green card application. But he was released after a New Jersey federal judge ruled he’d been unfairly retaliated against by the Trump administration, only for a Louisiana judge to then order his deportation citing alleged green card application omissions. Khalil has since sued the US government, arguing various rights — including free speech — were violated by the arrest. Columbia said it was merely supporting such rights by allowing Khalil to speak on campus — insisting the school does not necessarily endorse his views. “Columbia supports the right of faculty members to organize academic events. An invitation to speak does not signify University endorsement of a speaker’s views,” a school spokesperson said in a statement. “We remain committed to rigorous debate, inquiry, and respectful dialogue across differing perspectives.” Filed under columbia university israel Mahmoud Khalil protests 10/26/26 Read Next California half marathon descends into chaos as dozens of ... title: J.J. McCarthy’s resurgence took root long before joining Giants — with plenty of room to grow
description: It’s J.J. McCarthy who has perhaps the greatest chance to alter the trajectory of his career after being shipped to the Giants for a fifth-round pick less than a month ago.
content: NFL New York Giants J.J. McCarthy’s resurgence took root long before joining Giants — with plenty of room to grow By Dan Martin Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:14 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source Perhaps the only thing more unlikely than the Giants being in first place in the NFC East heading into their bye week is how they got there. John Harbaugh was expected to make a difference in his first year at MetLife Stadium, but not like this. Access the Giants like never before Get texts from Paul Schwartz with all the latest Giants news and insights, exclusive to Sports+ subscribers. tRY IT NOW Not with Devin Singletary, an afterthought for much of the season, ending Sunday’s win in Houston with a 30-yard touchdown run. Not with Jameis Winston — thrust into the starting role when Jaxson Dart was lost for the year with a knee injury in the second week of the season — now back in a backup role and still rushing for a score against the Texans. And certainly not with J.J. McCarthy leading the way as the team’s new quarterback after his career appeared to be going nowhere in Minnesota, which drafted McCarthy 10th overall in 2024. But here are the Giants, at 4-2-1 and with a clear path to a division title. Explore More Giants sticking with Dominic Zvada after ugly kicking performance John Harbaugh has rescued the dysfunctional Giants — now comes the interesting part Giants’ John Harbaugh declares himself ‘day-to-day’ after getting tackled by Devin Singletary: ‘I just felt so weak’ It’s McCarthy who has perhaps the greatest chance to alter the trajectory of his career after being shipped to the Giants for a fifth-round pick less than a month ago. He responded by throwing for 243 yards in less than a quarter when he replaced Winston late in their loss to the Saints, then followed with a career-best 252 yards against the Texans in the same stadium where he led Michigan to a national title in 2024. 3 J.J. McCarthy (18) of the New York Giants reacts after a game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium in Houston, Texas, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Getty Images “It’s one of those things where you think you’re starting over, but no, you’re starting from experience,’’ McCarthy said of righting himself with the Giants. He is still only 23 and started just 10 games with the Vikings last season before falling to third on their depth chart behind Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz to start this season. But he arrived at MetLife Stadium seemingly built for the offense the Giants hoped to run before Dart got hurt. Go behind the scenes with Big Blue Sign up for Inside the Giants by Paul Schwartz, a weekly Sports+ exclusive. Thank you Enter your email address Please provide a valid email. By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy. Enjoy this Post Sports+ exclusive newsletter! Check out more newsletters In their first game of the season against Dallas, Dart and the rest of the offense looked virtually unstoppable. Dart and McCarthy are not the same player, but they do possess similar attributes and were drafted in the first round just a year apart. McCarthy was selected four spots behind Malik Nabers and there was no shot anyone would have predicted the pair would be connecting on passes together. But Nabers has been a huge reason why McCarthy has been so successful so quickly with his new team. In less than five quarters together, Nabers has caught 11 passes for 206 yards from McCarthy. 3 Minnesota Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell greets quarterback J.J. McCarthy (9) during warmups prior to a game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Nabers, of course, is rounding into form after missing most of last season with a torn ACL. He’s surpassed 100 yards receiving in each of the past four games. And as much as any team enjoys a bye week, it should be especially beneficial to the Giants, as it will give McCarthy more time to work with his new teammates before they return to action Nov. 8 in Philadelphia. Despite his struggles with the Vikings, McCarthy said Sunday he began feeling more comfortable in the league in a Week 14 win over Washington. Coming off three straight losses in which he threw six interceptions and just two touchdowns, McCarthy — after missing a week in the concussion protocol — carved up the Commanders on 16-for-23 passing for 163 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. He then won his final three starts, though he missed another with a hand injury. 3 New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy, center, looks to pass during the first half of an NFL football game against the Houston Texans in Houston, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Gerald Herbert “Just being able to really start feeling like the defense is slowing down and understanding concepts, intent of plays, understanding the situation,’’ McCarthy said. “There’s a lot of things that go into playing NFL quarterback and it takes a little bit to figure those things out. I really feel like I was on an upward trajectory after that game. I continue to just refine my craft and get better every day.’’ He looks to have gotten a solid foundation in Matt Nagy’s offense already, which is why Harbaugh was confident in going with McCarthy against Houston. For the Giants to continue to build on their success, McCarthy will have to prove he can keep growing as a quarterback. The early returns, though, are promising — and another example, according to Harbaugh, of a player taking advantage of another opportunity. “It’s understanding if things aren’t working out for you, that’s not the final say,’’ Harbaugh said Monday. “You have the final say on everything, ultimately.” Filed under j.j. mccarthy john harbaugh New York Giants 10/26/26 Read Next Raiders coach gives update on starting QB as Kirk Cousins ... title: Israeli PM Netanyahu and challenger Gadi Eisenkot have very different views on how to end the Iran war
description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot remained split on the best way to handle Iran — as Israeli polls are set to open in hours to decide the country's next leader.
content: World News Israeli PM Netanyahu and challenger Gadi Eisenkot have very different views on how to end the Iran war By Ronny Reyes Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:11 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot have offered vastly different ideas on how to end the Iran war — as polls are set to open in hours to decide the country’s next leader. Eisenkot has said he believes economic pressure is currently the best way to defeat Iran, and backs strikes on the Islamic Republic’s nuclear program, but not a return to all-out war. 4 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to Israeli Air Force pilots and ground crews during a visit to Tel Nof Air Base in Tel Nof, Israel, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. Zuma / SplashNews.com Netanyahu, meanwhile, has remained adamant that Israel must wipe out the current regime in Tehran to secure the safety of the Jewish state — going as far as to post an AI-generated image of a nuclear bomb destroying Tel Aviv on Sunday to get his point across. The prime minister has also reportedly pushed for joint US-Israel strikes on Iran prior to the elections, but Washington has refused to do so yet as President Trump weighs his options, according to CNN. “Netanyahu really wanted and tried to convince Trump for a joint attack in Iran before the elections, and Trump did not give a green light,” one Israeli source told the outlet. Netanyahu’s office slammed the report as “fake news,” but the prime minister has been accused of trying to restart the war in hopes of postponing the elections as he faces a tight race against Eisenkot’s opposition coalition. 4 Netanyahu pushes for all-out war and regime change in Tehran, while Eisenkot favors economic pressure and targeted strikes on nuclear facilities. X/@netanyahu Explore More Polls open in Israel for country’s first election since October 7 attacks Mahmoud Khalil headed back to Columbia for book tour, outraging Jewish alumni: ‘Appalled’ Israelis in war-ravaged border communities rebuke Netanyahu as country heads to polls: ‘We need ‘hope’ Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, believes regime change in Iran is “not an achievable goal,” and he has called for a balance of military strikes and diplomacy to end the war. He has long criticized the prime minister’s approach to war as poorly planned, with Israel facing three fronts in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran earlier this year. 4 Gadi Eisenkot, Israel’s former military chief of staff and leader of the Yashar party, addresses supporters at the party’s final campaign rally before the legislative election in Tel Aviv, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. AFP via Getty Images The former IDF chief said he supports Trump’s policy of “peace through strength,” telling The Post over the weekend that Iran must not be allowed to become “another North Korea.” Despite favoring war in the past, Eisenkot now says Trump’s economic pressure has a better chance of giving the ruling mullahs “a sense of defeat” than a renewed military campaign. While Eisenkot backs renewed strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities, he appears less hawkish than Netanyahu — who has repeatedly called for all-out war to resume and for the Islamic republic’s citizens to overthrow the government. “We have another two years of Trump to finish the work in Iran,” Netanyahu wrote on X. 4 Israeli emergency responders inspect a site hit by a missile fired from Iran south of Tel Aviv on Saturday, June 14, 2025. AFP via Getty Images “Future generations will not forgive us if we miss the historic window of opportunity that allows us to try and complete the most critical mission facing our generation.” Netanyahu maintains that his ties with Trump and the US are the best protection Israel has, with Trump endorsing the prime minister last week. Eisenkot has repeatedly stated that Israel must focus on a future without relying on the US, claiming that Netanyahu is unable to defy Trump and act independently. title: California half marathon descends into chaos as dozens of runners return to find their cars vanished
description: Instead of relaxing and refueling after finishing the 21 kilometer race, a crowd of exhausted runners found themselves waiting in line at the Western Towing impound yard to get their cars back.
content: California News California half marathon descends into chaos as dozens of runners return to find their cars vanished By Sheetal Banchariya Published Oct. 26, 2026, 6:10 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make California Post a Preferred Source A celebratory cross-border marathon ended in frustration for dozens of participants after their vehicles were towed during Sunday’s San Diego-Tijuana Binational Half Marathon. Instead of relaxing and refueling after finishing the 13.1 mile-race, which started in San Ysidro and crossed into Tijuana, exhausted runners found themselves waiting in line at the Western Towing impound yard to get their cars back. Many runners said they followed parking directions posted directly on the event’s official website, which assured participants that nearby mall parking was safe. title: Tot accidentally shoots and kills sister, 4, with teen sibling’s gun: authorities
description: A 16-year-old – who was also identified as Jurnee’s sibling – was taken into custody after the tragedy and charged with possession of a firearm, local outlets reported.
content: US News Older brother, 6, accidentally shoots and kills sister, 4, with teen sibling’s gun: authorities By David DeTurris Published Oct. 26, 2026, 5:57 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source A little Wisconsin girl was horrifically killed by her older brother after he accidentally blasted her with her teenage sibling’s gun Saturday morning — that reportedly left one responding officer “crying.” Jurnee Scales Walker, 4, was playing with her 6-year-old brother in Milwaukee, when the tot somehow got his hands on the gun around 9 a.m., authorities told the Milwaukee Sentinel Journal. 3 Jurnee Scales Walker, 4, was fatally shot by her 6-year-old brother in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, around 9 a.m., authorities told the Milwaukee Sentinel Journal. WISN 12 News The sibling then shot little Jurnee, Milwaukee police said. Emergencies services rushed to the 2700 block of North 53rd Street and pronounced Jurnee dead at the scene, according to authorities. 3 “The one officer came out, and he was crying, and that’s when I knew something was sad,” neighbor Rodney Mckinney told WTMJ. A 16-year-old – who was also identified as Jurnee’s sibling – was taken into custody after the tragedy and charged with possession of a firearm, local outlets reported. 3 A 16-year-old – who was also identified as Jurnee’s sibling – was taken into custody, local outlets reported. WISN 12 News The teen was charged in Milwaukee’s juvenile court system on Monday, as authorities said they’re looking into how he came to acquire the gun. Jurnee’s heartbroken cousin, Amya Burton-Lewis, said there was “nobody like” the “sweet” four-year-old, who was playing cops and robbers when the siblings got ahold of the gun. “I hate that this is how everybody has to know Jurnee,” Burton-Lewis told WTMJ. She also told the local TV station that the gun was securely stored before the shooting, and that she didn’t know how the child got access to it. As a result, local police are asking gun owners to be especially diligent in storing their firearms and keeping them out of the reach of children. title: I traded glitzy LA for California’s forgotten heartland — and found my American dream
description: Coming back to the Central Valley has provided me with something I didn’t expect: comfort. It brings more breathing room, open space and a quieter day-to-day life.
content: Opinion I traded glitzy LA for California’s forgotten heartland — and found my American dream By Sydnie Hamby Published Oct. 26, 2026, 5:57 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make California Post a Preferred Source I was born in California’s Central Valley and, after leaving for Los Angeles, never thought I would return. Just look at me now. I’m back in the valley, and I love it. My four year old, however, has to adjust. “Why does it smell like that?” my son asked from the back seat, as he held his nose. Sign up for the California Morning Report newsletter The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now. Thanks for signing up! Enter your email address Please provide a valid email. By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy. Never miss a story Check out more newsletters We were driving into the Central Valley, where my husband and I grew up and where we were now returning for good. It was a fertilizer day, a smell that has become strangely nostalgic to me. We promised he’d get used to it. As one of California’s most misunderstood areas, the Central Valley stretches 20,000 square miles from Shasta County to just south of Bakersfield. Often left out of the state’s cultural conversations, it’s more than a stop for gas on the way to San Francisco. Many Californians, especially with young families, have fled urban areas, or the state altogether, for various reasons. Before packing up for Nevada, Texas or Arizona, the Central Valley deserves another look. Many Californians, especially with young families, have fled urban areas, or the state altogether, for various reasons. Sydnie Hamby With metro housing shortages, traffic congestion and the high cost of living, the Central Valley shouldn’t just be seen as a fallback option; it should be celebrated as a place worth choosing for those seeking a different pace of life. After years in LA, and in other sought-after regions in California, I ultimately found myself back where I started. Growing up, I couldn’t wait to leave. There was never a question of whether I was going, only where. When it came time to decide, I couldn’t resist the glitziest place of all — Los Angeles. As someone used to cornfields, backroads and tractor-caused traffic jams, it was a culture shock. I eventually fell in love with being surrounded by perpetual dreamers like myself. The fabulous weather, restaurants, arts and culture and endless forms of adventure were hard to beat, as was the ability to order takeout at any hour. So even though I’ve returned to the Central Valley, I’ve borrowed something from LA: the city’s ambitious “anything is possible” attitude rubbed off on me. And in the Central Valley, anything is truly possible. Just look at its agriculture. At its core, California is an agricultural workhorse. As the top farming state in the US, it accounts for over 75% of the nation’s fruit and nut production. I live in the heart of the valley affectionately called the “breadbasket.” It’s the kind of place where the produce is so local that your neighbor may be the farmer. (For me, my best friend is the almond farmer.) The Central Valley is the kind of place where the produce is so local that your neighbor may be the farmer. Sydnie Hamby My hometown feels like vintage Americana: tree-lined streets, an old-fashioned downtown with quaint shops, bakeries and antique stores. On autumnal Friday evenings, we can faintly hear the nearby high school’s football game announcer and marching band from our backyard. There is something charmingly wholesome about this kind of life: I can roll the windows down, drive the backroads and reconnect to myself, anytime. Last week, while my husband was traveling for work, I thought I missed our trash pickup day. My older neighbor realized he was gone and moved the cans for me before the trucks came at daybreak. That would have never happened in LA. In addition to a strong sense of community, my children will grow up with both sets of grandparents nearby. Our folks attend every soccer game and school event, and are present for the small, everyday moments that will make up our children’s earliest memories. Being centrally located also means being a few hours’ drive from some of California’s greatest natural wonders: Yosemite, Big Sur, Carmel-by-the-Sea, Lake Tahoe, Santa Cruz, the Sierra Nevada mountains and more. Proximity to iconic spots aside, the region’s affordability (relative to the Bay Area and LA) can make the housing dream more attainable. In 2026, the median home price in the Los Angeles metro area reached $860,000, while Stanislaus County’s sits at $489,240. According to the California Association of Realtors, a third of Stanislaus County households can afford a median-priced home, versus 17% in the Los Angeles metro area. Coming back to the Central Valley has provided me with something I didn’t expect: comfort. It brings more breathing room, open space and a quieter day-to-day life. It’s not for everyone, and it has drawbacks. Some are minor inconveniences, like fewer entertainment options, not to mention the intense heat — a major inconvenience, so my husband argues. Some limitations are not so minor, such as fewer job opportunities (especially in tech, AI and other specialized industries), lower wages, Bay Area commutes and limited airport access. But like complementary pieces to a puzzle, LA and the Central Valley fill each other’s gaps and trade-offs. If you’re craving small-town charm, tight-knit communities and a lower cost of living, the Central Valley may host your new California dream. I know one day our children will fondly remember growing up here — despite the days when the air smelled of fertilizer. Sydnie Hamby is a wellness writer, IVF advocate and mom of two living in California’s Central Valley. title: Lakers’ preseason weakness has carried over despite 3-0 start
description: A preseason weakness has carried into the regular season for the Lakers.
content: NBA Lakers’ preseason weakness has carried over despite 3-0 start By Khobi Price Published Oct. 26, 2026, 5:55 p.m. ET See more of our coverage in your search results. Make California Post a Preferred Source SALT LAKE CITY — The statistic that Austin Reaves was told after the Lakers’ comeback win over the Jazz was so astounding that the star guard was taken aback. “Jesus Christ,” Reaves said. “I didn’t know it was that bad.” The stat that drew that reaction: The Jazz grabbed 21 more rebounds than the Lakers on Sunday at Delta Center. 4 The Jazz dominated the Lakers on the glass on Sunday. NBAE via Getty Images Explore More Pat McAfee vows not to return to University of Utah: ‘I was very uncomfortable’ Saquon Barkley suffers new injury in disastrous Eagles return Giants reveal rookie kicker’s fate after ugly performance The hosts grabbed six more defensive rebounds (32-26), but the real advantage came on the offensive glass. The Jazz nabbed 15 more offensive rebounds (20-5) than the Lakers, leading to a 34-11 advantage in second-chance points. Ace Bailey had more offensive rebounds (six) than the Lakers did as a team. 4 The Lakers’ struggles with securing defensive rebounds have been present all month. NBAE via Getty Images Luka Doncic, who was Bailey’s primary defender, took blame for the Jazz wing’s early domination on the boards, with the former Rutgers star grabbing five offensive rebounds in the first quarter. “We just didn’t box out sometimes,” Doncic said. “I think Ace Bailey got like three offensive rebounds on me so that was my bad point. But the struggles on the glass against the Jazz weren’t isolated to Sunday. 4 Walker Kessler hasn’t been impactful enough on the defensive glass. Getty Images The Lakers have been a putrid defensive rebounding team since the moment this group first stepped on a court together. It was a significant preseason talking point. They gave up 13 offensive rebounds in their preseason-opening win over the Kings on Oct. 5 en route to ranking 23rd in defensive rebounding rate among all NBA teams during the preseason. And they’ve been even worse to start the regular season, ranking second-to-last in defensive rebounding. There was a hope that Walker Kessler, who played in just two of the five preseason games, would be a difference-maker on the glass. That hasn’t been the case so far, with the Lakers struggling on the defensive boards regardless of who’s on the floor. 4 The Lakers need to be more consistent with boxing out. NBAE via Getty Images “Box out,” coach JJ Redick responded when asked how the Lakers can improve. Reaves echoed Redick. “It’s as simple as box out, but I’ve tried to box out a couple times and the ball just goes over my head and I can’t grab it,” he said. “I guess I need to learn to jump higher. I don’t know.” Whatever the solution is, the Lakers need to find it. Sign up for the California Morning Report newsletter The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now. Thanks for signing up! Enter your email address Please provide a valid email. By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy. Never miss a story Check out more newsletters Hot shooting has carried them to a 3-0 start, but they can’t expect to turn into the championship-caliber team they’re setting out to be if they’re being doubled up in second-chance points on a nightly basis. Opponents are averaging 23 second-chance points compared to the Lakers’ 11.3 so far, The Lakers were focused on cleaning up their turnover struggles entering the weekend. And they did that, at least for one game, by only recording 10 giveaways against the Jazz But they still have another weakness to address. And if they don’t fix it, it’s only a matter of time until it comes back to bite them in a more significant way.
