title: I'm one of a growing number of Gen Z birdwatchers - it helps my mental health
description: Caitlin Andrew hated birdwatching as a child but found a passion for it in her 20s.
content: I'm one of a growing number of Gen Z birdwatchers - it helps my mental health Image source, Nina Torrance/BBC Alba Image caption, Glasgow-based Caitlin Andrew found a passion for birdwatching in her early 20s BySteven McKenzie BBC Scotland Published 26 October 2026 Updated 4 hours ago "I would be such a grump," says Caitlin Andrew, recalling her teenage self on walks with her parents. "They are both into birdwatching and they would stop and listen and look at things. "We had some really nice walks and experiences, but I just didn't have an interest in them at the time. I do feel quite bad about it now." Three years ago, during a difficult period in her life, Caitlin discovered birds offered an unexpected escape from her troubles. She joined the growing number of young people flocking to birdwatching. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland More stories from Scotland "I was 24 and living in Glasgow as a student," says Caitlin, who grew up in Midlothian. "I had poor mental health and was feeling a bit low, and finding it quite difficult to connect to the world around me." Around that time, Caitlin joined her family for a holiday on Islay. The southern-most island of the Inner Hebrides is renowned for its wild birds, with more than 120 species to spot during the spring and autumn migrations, external. "When we were there we did a lot of birdwatching," says Caitlin. "And as you can imagine there are incredible things to see - choughs and white-tailed eagles." Caitlin says, rather than feeling grumpy, she found a sense of peace and calm watching birds. "Just taking time to look and listen and take in everything you are connected to the environment you are in." Her parents were delighted when she asked for a pair of binoculars for her birthday. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Gannets are one of Caitlin's favourite birds But making her first forays into birdwatching, Caitlin felt no-one else shared her passion for birds. "I did feel a little bit embarrassed to say I was doing it," she says. "It is a stereotype, isn't it? It's associated with older people with a sedate life and picking it up in retirement - all things which I don't think are negative at all. "But among my peers I was certainly the only person doing it properly in any kind of capacity." Image source, Nina Torrance/BBC Alba Image caption, Caitlin enjoys how different birds give pointers to changes in the seasons Caitlin, who is a Gaelic speaker, found she was far from alone as a young female birdwatcher when she made a BBC Alba documentary about her hobby. She came across an Inverness chapter of the Feminist Bird Club - a group founded in New York in 2016 to help make the interest inclusive and safe. Caitlin also met female professionals and volunteers involved in bird conservation. She says: "In the birdwatching community, everyone is so friendly and happy to tell you they have something interesting in their scope or have seen something interesting." Research carried out for the RSPB suggests there are more than four million birdwatchers in Britain, up from 2.7 million eight years ago. The number of Gen Z enthusiasts - people aged 16 to 29 - rose from an estimated 61,000 in 2018 to 724,000 today, according to the study. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Crested tits are another of Caitlin's favourites to spot Caitlin's favourite birds include crested tits, which in the UK are found in native pine forests in parts of the Highlands, Moray and Aberdeenshire, external. "I love seeing crested tits in the Cairngorms. They are rare, so its a special thing to see them," she says. Gannets are another favourite. "I'm always happy to see a gannet. They are big and so powerful. They're like dinosaurs." Caitlin enjoys how different birds signal changes in the year. "When you start to hear a chiffchaff in maybe March or April you know spring is coming, and that is really exciting," she says. "And then when coming into winter there are redwings and fieldfares. "It feels like these creatures are giving you pointers that things are changing, and it's lovely to connect to that." She adds: "Life can be so turbulent. Things go and down and you never know what's coming - the political nonsense and all the rest of it. "And these little animals, they are just all about finding food, raising babies, fledging their young and then doing it all again - they're just trying to survive. "It does make your problems feel very small." title: Chris Mason: The Budget is imminent as tricky things pile up for Burnham
description: From Brexit debates to North Sea oil, there is plenty getting the cabinet, the Labour Party and the country talking.
content: Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days Image source, Getty Images Image caption, There are several issues on the horizon for the prime minister By Chris Mason Political editor Published 26 October 2026 This feels like the week where the rubber hits the road for the prime minister's new government. It is now 100 days since Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street from Buckingham Palace and began to assemble his cabinet. Three months later, Labour MPs are more chipper, the party's poll ratings have notched up and the tone and style of government feels very different from when Sir Keir Starmer was in charge. Coming next, though, there are a whole series of crunchy decisions and trade offs – economic and political – some of which are inevitable and some of which Burnham has decided to lean into. First up, the Budget You would be forgiven for only just clocking there is a Budget this week. There are three reasons for this year's feeling like a comparatively low key affair: it is happening a month earlier than a year ago, squeezing the space available for briefings, leaks and speculation. It is considerably smaller in big picture terms – in other words the scale of tax rises – so limiting the noisy talk in advance about who might get clobbered. And the new chancellor John Healey and his team have sought to make a virtue out of not saying very much beforehand. But woe betide suggesting to anyone involved in assembling this Budget that it is a steady-as-she-goes, nothing-to-see-here thing. Every Budget is a big deal, goes the argument run past me by some. They don't all have to be visible from space in the way some recent ones have been – think Kwasi Kwarteng in one direction followed by Jeremy Hunt in the other four years ago, or Rachel Reeves in the last two years. Cost of living support for some, help for entrepreneurs, more financial clout for mayors in England and an economy now recuperating will be themes for Healey on Wednesday. You will be the judge of this Budget's scale – its value, or the lack of it to you – before long. Next, Brexit – and our relationship with the EU In recent years, many but not all politicians have approached the issue of Brexit like you or I might approach an electric fence. Avoid getting too close and, if needs must, climb over it gingerly. Burnham has no such reservations: he has repeatedly said in the last few weeks, let's talk about Brexit. He reckons the current deal between the UK and European Union isn't good enough. Over the weekend he went further, suggesting he wanted an "honest discussion" about freedom of movement. Countries in the EU's single market have to sign up to freedom of movement, which lets people live and work in all the countries that are part of it. Given how big a deal immigration was for many in the EU referendum in 2016, even reopening the question of freedom of movement feels like a big deal. On Monday morning, the prime minister appeared to add more detail, suggesting freedom of movement would only return in the UK having been sanctioned in a referendum. Later, though, his team wouldn't repeat that, instead emphasising that Burnham wants to start a broad based conversation – without at this point committing to any possible outcome. Some of his MPs felt this was a self-inflicted tangle he could have done without. Others see merit in Burnham's penchant for narrating his thoughts and possible direction publicly, thereby using his position to seek to dominate the political debate. While the Labour Party's centre of gravity tilts towards a collective instinct that a closer relationship with the EU would be preferable to the status quo, there are differences of emphasis and indeed outright disagreements about how much closer and when would be wise. Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds Published 1 day ago Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm Published 2 days ago No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion Published 18 hours ago Some Labour MPs representing seats in the north of England and Midlands, which backed Brexit, are privately nervous about anything coming across as too enthusiastic an embrace of Brussels. A nod to that scepticism appeared to come publicly from Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood who noted that a call for an honest discussion is "not the same as settled policy". She added: "The prime minister has also observed that there were very significant issues with freedom of movement when we were within the EU. An honest debate means actually being honest about all of the aspects of that debate and not cherry-picking." Next month, there will be a UK-EU Summit in Brussels, which was due to happen in the summer but was postponed when Sir Keir Starmer resigned. We can expect both sides to talk up tweaks to the current deal and the government to also, in time, set out options for what the long term relationship might look like. On the detail, there are divisions from the cabinet and down. The key thing will be what the party decides to include or not in its next general election manifesto. The question of North Sea oil Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved drilling in the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen. This is principally a gas field and Fahnbulleh grounded her justification in providing the UK with greater energy security, at a time of war in Ukraine and in the Middle East. The gas, she said, could be tapped into and serve British homes and businesses pretty much straight away, with the tax revenue put into an "energy wealth fund", with the aim being to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects. But what about the Rosebank field, 80 miles north west of the Shetland islands, with its focus on oil? Labour figures in and outside government acknowledge this is a much, much harder sell to plenty in their own party and beyond. Some, who want to see the project go ahead, fear that the energy secretary is not likely to be convinced that it should. It is in that context that we should see allies of the chancellor pointedly making it known that he is in favour of it. His public language was quite telling on the day Jackdaw was approved, when he was talking about the Energy Wealth Fund: "It means the extra tax revenues that come from North Sea oil and gas can be directed into developing more clean energy projects for the future." Note his reference to oil. Fahnbulleh said that Rosebank was "a different proposition" to Jackdaw. Can those who worry, in particular, about the emissions from a new oil field, be won over by an argument grounded in this being a geopolitically pragmatic and environmentally credible part of transition to cleaner fuels? Some Labour MPs hope so, but they know it's a tall order to persuade some, including some in government – which could, if it was approved, raise the question of ministerial resignations. Let's see. There is more: benefits, immigration, defence Expected before long, the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn's review into young people and work – and with it a set of suggestions to try to cut the number of young people not in work, education or training and, in time, to try to cut the benefits bill too. Plenty of Labour MPs acknowledge these are nettles that need grabbing, but how many may flinch when presented with the sharper edges of what might be proposed? Meanwhile, we await where the government eventually ends up on how long migrants should have to wait to claim permanent residence in the UK. And then, beyond what is set out in the Budget, how ministers will find the money to spend 3% of national income on defence by the end of the decade – and with what trade offs to make that happen. There will be plenty to observe in the second 100 days of Burnham's government and beyond. What is the Budget and what could be in it? title: Family's anger at delays to review of stab death case
description: The family of a Fife man who died from a stab wound to the chest have long challenged the original police ruling.
content: Family's anger at delays to review of stab death case Image source, Margaret Graham Image caption, Colin Marr, 23, died from a single blow from a kitchen knife in 2007 after a row with his fiancée ByAndrew Picken BBC Scotland Published 26 October 2026 Updated 5 hours ago The family of a Fife man who died from a stab wound to the chest have hit out at delays to a review of the case by prosecutors. Colin Marr, 23, died from a single blow from a kitchen knife in 2007 after a row with his fiancée. His family have long challenged the original police ruling that it was suicide and a Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (COPFS) forensic and pathology review which started in 2023 has still not finished. COPFS said its inquiries were nearing completion in what it described as a complex investigation. The 2007 police investigation concluded Colin had killed himself at his flat in Lochgelly after an argument with his fiancée Candice Bonar about his alleged infidelity. Marr's family believe there has been a miscarriage of justice while Bonar has always maintained her innocence. Image source, Margaret Graham Image caption, Colin, pictured here as a teenager and as a baby with mum Margaret, grew up in Fife New lines of inquiry into the death were first identified in 2021 and then the forensic and pathology review was launched in May 2023. Later that year the review was widened after a key 2012 forensic report about the stab wound was withdrawn. Stuart Graham, Colin's stepfather, said the family had received many promises of updates and next actions but nothing had been forthcoming. He said: "We will soon be coming up for five years since we were promised a detailed revision and we get nothing. "Our perspective and concern is that COPFS are attempting to push this into the long grass and hope that media concern is lost. "Is it because the issues they face point at the failings of their office and this is what is being protected?" Graham, who handed over a cache of new material about the case to Police Scotland in 2021, added: "As always we will keep pushing. We believe they already have enough evidence to proceed." The unusual death of Colin Marr Published 26 March 2021 Forensic review ordered in unusual stab death case Published 3 May 2023 Crown Office to make new inquiries into stab death Published 19 May 2021 The forensic and pathology aspects of the original investigation into Colin's death have in the past been challenged by independent experts. Leading pathologist Dr Nat Cary has previously said it was "both possible and plausible" that Colin's injury was "inflicted by a third party", and he questioned previous police reports on the location of the stab wound. Colin's fiancée Ms Bonar has been interviewed three times by the police and voluntarily appeared in person at the 2011 fatal accident inquiry (FAI) into his death. At the inquiry Sheriff Alastair Dunlop said he could not decide if the death was suicide or homicide. Speaking after the FAI, Ms Bonar said: "My name is cleared. I have always been honest and declared my innocence throughout this heart-breaking nightmare. "What Colin did, he did to himself and that's the truth." 'Complex investigation' Both COPFS and Fife Police, now part of Police Scotland, have previously produced reports that were critical of the original investigation into Colin's death and issued apologies to his family. The Police Investigations and Review Commissioner has also upheld 12 complaints over the force's handling of the case. A spokesperson for the COPFS said: "We recognise how frustrating delays can be for those grieving the loss of a loved one and will continue to keep the family updated on significant developments in this complex investigation. "Our inquiries are nearing completion. "Once finalised, all of the evidence will be reviewed by an independent senior prosecutor who has had no previous involvement in the case." title: New weather warnings as third storm set to hit Scotland
description: The country is braced for the third storm in as many days as communities continue to clean up after the weekend.
content: New weather warning as third storm hits Scotland Image caption, High, gusting winds blew a caravan over on a shoreside road in Aberdeen Published 26 October 2026 Updated 49 minutes ago A new weather warning is in place as a third storm in a matter of days hits Scotland. It comes as thousands of homes across the country remain without power in the aftermath of Storm Boelo. A yellow wind warning, external, covering most of the country as well as parts of northern England and Northern Ireland, came into effect at 03:00 and runs until 21:00 on Tuesday. The latest weather system is unlikely to be as widely disruptive as Storm Boelo - or Storm Austen which came before it - and has not been named. The next name on the storm list for the 2026/2027 season is Chloe. Storm Boelo brought heavy flooding and wind gusts in some areas of up to 85mph (137km/h) on Monday. In pictures: Storm Boelo leaves a trail of destruction across Scotland Published 1 day ago Tributes paid to man killed by falling tree in Storm Boelo Published 17 hours ago Thousands still without power after Storm Boelo batters Scotland Published 17 hours ago The Met Office said gusts of up to 65mph (105km/h) would hit coastal communities in the south-west on Monday evening and into the morning. Forecasters added strong winds would be accompanied by heavy rain at certain points. A person was reportedly swept out to sea in Largs on Monday night, after large waves struck the Ayrshire coast. The coastguard, police, fire service and RNLI lifeboats were involved in an extensive search, which has now been halted. No-one was found. A 60-year-old man died after being struck by a falling tree at Mid Kelton, near Castle Douglas, in Dumfries and Galloway on Sunday. On Monday evening, Scottish and Southern Energy Networks (SSEN), which covers the north of Scotland, said work was ongoing to reconnect the supplies of about 8,600 homes that remained without power. Meanwhile, Scottish Power Energy Networks (Spen) said all but a "very small number" of its 50,000 customers who lost power in Ayrshire and Dumfries and Galloway would have it restored by 02:00 on Tuesday. Almost 100,000 homes had power restored in both areas across the weekend. Rail and ferry disruption Image source, Getty Images ScotRail , externalsaid the "vast majority" of its services were running as normal. However, it warned that speed restrictions would be in place on several routes until 16:00 on Tuesday due to heavy rainfall. They are: Glasgow Queen Street – Oban/Mallaig Inverness – Kyle of Lochalsh Glasgow Queen Street/Edinburgh Waverley – Inverness Aberdeen – Inverness Glasgow Central – Largs Glasgow Queen Street – Helensburgh Central Ayr – Stranraer Inverness – Wick/Thurso West coast ferry operator CalMac, external said many its services remained liable to disruption or cancellation at short notice and urged travellers to check its website for updates. Passengers on NorthLink Ferries, external were advised that there was the "possibility of disruption" to services until Thursday because of the weather. Image source, John Paul Lusk/Leven Films Image caption, Dumbarton Golf Club was almost completely under water after the River Leven burst its banks on Sunday School closures All schools and nurseries in the Western Isles will be shut until Wednesday at the earliest. Ellon Academy will remain closed on Tuesday after being shut on Monday as a result of damage caused by the storm. Banchory Academy is also closed due to an issue with the school building. It is expected to reopen on Wednesday. It comes after more than a dozen primary schools in Aberdeenshire and Rothiemay Primary School, in Moray, were closed on Monday due to a lack of power. Thirty primary schools and six secondary schools across the Highlands were also subject to full or partial closures, external. Lockerbie Campus - including Lockerbie Academy, learning centre, primary school and nursery - in Dumfries and Galloway is closed due to heating failure, while schools in St John's Town of Dalry have not opened as a result of roof damage. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, The aftermath of Storm Boelo across Scotland The Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa) said it had put an amber risk of flooding in place for the northern and Western Isles and Caithness and Sutherland. Sepa said areas of the southwest and Argyll, including the Solway Firth and Firth of Clyde, would experience volatile conditions, with large waves and strong winds. They said flooding of low-lying land was likely. Highland Council said flood gates on the mile-long Caol and Lochyside flood protection scheme, near Fort William, had been closed following a warning from Sepa. In Orkney, Police Scotland have closed the Churchill Barriers causeways which connect the mainland to the islands of South Ronaldsay, Burray, Lamb Holm and Glimps Holm. The main road through the village of St Mary's Holm has also been closed due to flooding caused by high winds and high tide. Police Scotland said a high risk of disruption remained with poor weather conditions expected on Tuesday. Police Scotland Assistant Chief Constable Mark Sutherland said that, although the amber weather warning was no longer in place, disruption was "likely well beyond that due to further poor weather, fallen trees and other damage caused by the storm". Social Justice and Housing Secretary Shirley-Anne Somerville told BBC Scotland News there were "challenges ahead" due to the prolonged nature of the conditions. She urged councils to review their readiness, adding authorities were working to ensure that "everything that can be done is being done". Somerville also said that everyone can play a part by getting "households as resilient as we can, as well as looking after neighbours and friends". title: More than third of deaths of ex-prisoners on probation drug related, says report
description: Politicians are being urged to tackle "systematic failures" in the criminal justice system.
content: More than third of deaths of ex-prisoners on probation drug related, says report Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The report's author Dr Robert Jones says there is a lack of debate about finding a solution to the problem of drug-related deaths ByMark Palmer Wales politics assistant editor Published 26 October 2026 Updated 1 hour ago More than a third of deaths of former prisoners on probation in Wales in a year were drug related, according to a new report. This was higher than across England and Wales combined, where just over a fifth of total deaths were drug related. The Wales Governance Centre at Cardiff University published the report and urged politicians to tackle "systematic failures" in the criminal justice system. Report author Dr Robert Jones called on the UK and Welsh governments to find a solution to the "tragic" situation. The Welsh government said it was working to reduce "harms caused by substance misuse", while the UK government said it was spending £3.4m to support prison leavers to overcome addiction. According to the report, 37% of all deaths among prison leavers supervised by probation in Wales in 2024-25 were drug related. The number of drug poisonings where the intent was "undetermined" in Wales accounted for 19 of the 52 who died. Jones said this was "substantially higher" than the proportion across England and Wales as a whole, where deaths in this same category accounted for just over a fifth (21%) of the total - 131 out of 620. Criminal justice in Wales is controlled by Westminster. The Plaid Cymru Welsh government, and the previous Labour administration in Cardiff before it, argue it should be devolved. Speaking to BBC Wales, Jones said the research looked at UK government data including Freedom of Information requests. He said: "The added shock value to this is that these data point towards some systematic failures with incredibly tragic circumstances and consequences. "Yet there isn't really a particular debate or discussion ongoing at the moment about these deaths, and indeed their causes, and how we might actually find a solution to them." Jones said many areas of social policy, including "responsibility for tackling substance use, housing, education and local government" were devolved to the Welsh government. "So what tends to happen is that criminal justice matters can often fall between the gaps between debates in the Senedd and debates in Westminster," he added. Jones said the report raised "important questions about the current devolution settlement and whether the Welsh government has the powers and levers necessary to address the underlying causes of many of the challenges facing Wales". He added: "Only by confronting the realities highlighted throughout this report can politicians and policymakers hope to overcome the many challenges facing communities across Wales." Image source, Matthew Horwood/Getty Images Image caption, The Welsh government has called for control of prisons and other parts of the criminal justice system to be devolved David Bennett, from Wallich, Wales's largest homelessness charity, claimed most drug-related deaths "are preventable if we treat drug use as a health, not criminal justice, issue". "Housing, health and justice need a joined-up approach," he said. He said the charity supported "conversations to devolve justice and policing" and said without "co-ordinated" support prison leavers were "being set up to fail". "The war on drugs hasn't worked," he added. The report also says homelessness among former prisoners in Wales is continuing to rise. The number of people leaving prison, supervised by Welsh probation services, who were recorded as rough sleeping on the day of their release rose by 24% in 2025-26. In total, 695 prison leavers managed by Welsh probation services were rough sleeping on the day of their release. Other findings include that more than a third (39%) of all custodial sentences given to women in Wales in 2025 were for offences related to thefts from shops. Meanwhile, people from black ethnic groups in Wales remained the most overrepresented ethnic group in the prison population in 2025. There were 58 black people from Wales in prison for every 10,000 of the population, compared with 15 white people per 10,000 of the population. A spokesperson for the Welsh government said: "Every drug-related death is a tragedy. "We are working closely with health boards, local authorities, Public Health Wales and other key partners to reduce the harms caused by substance misuse, focusing on early intervention, prevention, treatment and recovery support." They added that the findings "strengthen the case for the full devolution of justice to Wales". "Bringing responsibility for justice into line" with devolved services "would enable a more effective and joined-up approach to improving outcomes, reducing reoffending and building safer communities across Wales", the spokesperson added. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "We inherited prisons in crisis but we're acting on all fronts, including by reducing the number of women in custody through investment in community services and cutting the flow of drugs into prisons. "In Wales we invest more than £3.4m into services which work across prisons, probation and courts to help support prison leavers overcome their addiction." They added that prisoners at risk of becoming homeless can be offered temporary accommodation by the prison and probation service. Chair of the Welsh Affairs Committee at Westminster, Ruth Jones, said: "It is devastating to hear that more than a third of all deaths among prison leavers in Wales were due to drug poisoning, and that the number of homeless prison leavers in Wales has increased. "The data underscores the findings of our inquiry that reported earlier this year: the prison and probation system is struggling with increasingly complex demand, which has serious implications for rehabilitation outcomes." She added: "Improving Wales-specific justice data is something my committee has consistently pressed the UK government on, and in light of several of Dr Jones' data requests to the Ministry of Justice not receiving a response, it is clear that there is still work to be done here." Additional reporting by David Deans. title: Lancashire consider Anderson farewell amid fan unrest
description: Lancashire will look into organising a farewell for bowler James Anderson amid fan unrest over his departure from the club.
content: Lancashire consider Anderson farewell amid fan unrest Image source, Getty Images Image caption, James Anderson has taken more wickets than any other pace bowler in Test cricket ByMatthew Henry BBC Sport Journalist Published 26 October 2026 Lancashire will look into organising a farewell for bowler James Anderson amid fan unrest over his departure from the club. It was announced last week the 44-year-old, England's all-time leading wicket-taker, has been released by the county he first represented in 2001. The topic dominated a tense meeting between the club hierarchy and members at Old Trafford on Monday evening, with many members angered by the decision. Some raised their upset at the fact the end-of-season decision had denied fans the chance to thank Anderson for his service to the county and celebrate his career. The club, represented by new chief executive Richard Kenyon and incoming director of cricket Paul Farbrace, agreed to look into a solution. Farbrace joined the meeting via video from his holiday in the United States and is understood to have taken ownership of the decision when taking questions from members. The former England assistant coach, who left his role in charge of Sussex before joining the Red Rose county, reiterated his explanation from Lancashire's public statement on Sunday - that he wants to build a squad capable of winning the County Championship within the next four years and does not believe Anderson, who turns 45 next year, will play a part in that. One attendee among about 200 members at the meeting told BBC Sport the atmosphere in the room remained mixed. Other members suggested Farbrace had gone some way to calming the unrest. Anderson was Lancashire's captain in the County Championship last season and while the county finished second bottom in Division Two, continuing a poor run of results in recent years, he remained one of their best performers. He took 50 wickets and was named their Championship player of the year. A number of counties have expressed an interest in signing the veteran for next season. Anderson first played List A cricket in 2000 as a 17-year-old for the Lancashire Cricket Board against Suffolk. He made his professional debut for Lancashire a year later and was in the England team by the end of 2002. In addition to his 911 international wickets - an England record and a record for all pace bowlers - Anderson claimed 443 first-class scalps for Lancashire, along with 83 in List A cricket and a further 50 in T20s. When his England career was abruptly ended in 2024, Anderson opted to continue playing with Lancashire in 2025. At the time, he said he felt he could play for three more years. In his first public comment since the decision on Sunday, he expressed his sadness at the situation but stopped short of retiring. title: Kane ends England's 25-year Ballon d'Or wait - how he bucked the trend
description: Harry Kane becomes the first English player to win the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001 after being crowned the world's best player at a ceremony in London.
content: Kane ends England's 25-year Ballon d'Or wait - how he bucked the trend Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Harry Kane broke Bayern Munich's goalscoring record for a season in his third campaign at the club ByEmlyn Begley BBC Sport journalist Published 26 October 2026 Harry Kane has become the first English player to win the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001 after being crowned the world's best player at a ceremony in London. The 33-year-old Bayern Munich striker is the fifth Englishman to win in total, with Stanley Matthews (1956), Bobby Charlton (1966) and Kevin Keegan (1978 and 1979) the others. Denis Law of Scotland (1964) and Northern Ireland's George Best (1968) are the other winners from the United Kingdom. Real Madrid and France forward Kylian Mbappe finished second, while Barcelona and Spain attacker Lamine Yamal completed the top three. "Not many people would have thought it, and maybe even I wouldn't have thought I'd be this far," Kane told Dazn. "I had to go through many ups and downs, especially early in my career. I was never the person that people thought was going to be the superstar like some of the guys now. "I had to bide my time and work hard, a lot of times it was me against my own mind and I had to come through it, I had to show self-belief, determination. "I think that grounded me even when I did make it at the highest level to keep improving and keep getting better." England manager Thomas Tuchel said he was "delighted" to see Kane win the award as he hailed the forward's success as a "huge honour". Prince William, meanwhile, said the former Tottenham Hotspur player was a "brilliant captain" and "remarkable player". Kane scored 61 goals in 51 club matches last season, the most a Bayern player has ever struck in one campaign. Including England matches, it was 73 goals - plus eight assists - in 65 matches. Only one player at a club in Europe's top five leagues has ever scored more goals in a season. But he wins it despite not lifting either of football's biggest prizes last season, having lost in both the World Cup and Champions League semi-finals. Remarkably the Three Lions captain becomes the first Bayern player to win the Ballon d'Or since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge in 1981. To celebrate Kane's success, the Wembley arches were lit up in gold on Monday night. BBC Sport looks at why Kane won it and how unusual it is to do so without securing one of those major trophies. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, 'Anything is possible' - Kane wins Ballon d'Or England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender Published 6 October Putellas wins record-equalling third Ballon d'Or Published 12 hours ago Quiz: Kane and who else? Name every men's Ballon d'Or winner Published 2 hours ago Kane's record-breaking 2025-26 season To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Kane explains how his game has evolved In terms of trophies, Kane may have 'only' lifted the German double last season. But that more than doubled his career trophy total - having also won the Bundesliga the season before. But in terms of individual output Kane - whose previous best Ballon d'Or finish was 10th - was unmatched last season. His 61 goals in all competitions for Bayern was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five leagues managed. In fact it was the most anyone has recorded since Cristiano Ronaldo also notched 61 for Real Madrid 11 years ago. He was the Bundesliga's top scorer with 36 goals - 17 clear of anyone else. In the Champions League he scored 14 for the beaten semi-finalists. In the German Cup he scored 10 goals, including a hat-trick in the 3-0 win over Stuttgart in the final, and he also netted once in the German Super Cup. No player has ever scored so many goals in a season for Bayern, a club who have had legendary goalscorers like Gerd Muller, Rummenigge and more recently Robert Lewandowski in their ranks. Kane's 12 goals for England last season - including six at the World Cup - take him up to a total of 73. Only one player in history from Europe's top leagues has scored more in a season, Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12. Next on the list are Muller (72 in 1972-73), Cristiano Ronaldo (66 in both 2011-12 and 2014-15), former Brazil striker Ronaldo (66 in 1996-97), Erling Haaland (64 in 2022-23) and Luis Suarez (64 in 2015-16). Former England striker Alan Shearer recently told BBC Sport: "The winner of the Ballon d'Or should be Harry Kane. "His numbers for the last 12 to 18 months have been absolutely sensational for Bayern and for England. For that reason, he should get it." Another ex-Three Lions player Danny Murphy added: "His goalscoring has been relentless, brilliant. He's had one of the best seasons of his career and it'll be a great reward for him if he gets the trophy. "He's been brilliant at Bayern Munich since he's been there, adapted really well and he's been the best centre forward in the world for the last 12 months." How rare is winning Ballon d'Or without a top trophy? The Ballon d'Or was only available to European players from its formation in 1956 until 1995 when it was opened up to everyone. Since then in four of the seven World Cup years, the Ballon d'Or has been awarded to a world champion - including Messi in 2023 (as the 2022 World Cup was in the winter). However, that was the first time since 2006 it had happened, with Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo and Luka Modric all winning since then despite not winning the World Cup that year. This is only the fifth time in the past 20 years that the Ballon d'Or has not gone to a player who has won either the World Cup, the Champions League or a European Championship/Copa America - with Kane joining Messi (three times) and Ronaldo. Lamine Yamal, who won the World Cup with Spain, had been one of the favourites but lost out to Kane. Last year, winning the Champions League helped PSG and France's Ousmane Dembele to the crown. Could Kane make it two in a row? Kane may have just won the Ballon d'Or but some are already wondering if he is in a good place to retain it next year. The striker has scored 10 goals in his opening 12 games for Bayern this season. Throw in six goals in four Nations League games for England and that is a total of 16 in 16 matches so far. Bayern are unbeaten in the Bundesliga and Champions League this season. If they were to win a Treble - and Kane keeps scoring at about a goal a game - it would be tough to look past him, especially in a season with no World Cup, European Championship or Copa America. The last player other than Messi or Ronaldo to win it two years in a row was Marco van Basten in 1988 and 1989. However, Lamine Yamal will be hoping to make it to the top, having now finished second and third over the past two years. He has started the season in electric form, with 10 goals and 10 assists in 13 games for Barcelona in La Liga and the Champions League. And Barca are currently favourites to win the Champions League, which could ultimately end up being a deciding factor. He would be the youngest player to win the Ballon d'Or - aged 20 - if he does lift it next year. Real Madrid's Mbappe will also fancy his chances of winning for the first time, with 14 goals in 13 appearances for club and country. The youngest winner remains Brazilian Ronaldo, who was 21 when he won in 1997. Arsenal, who have never had a Ballon d'Or winner, and Paris St-Germain are two of the other frontrunners to win the Champions League. title: Putellas wins record-equalling third Ballon d'Or
description: Barcelona and Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas wins the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time.
content: Putellas wins record-equalling third Ballon d'Or Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Alexia Putellas won four trophies with Barcelona last season and 38 over the course of 14 years ByAlex Brotherton BBC Sport journalist Published 26 October 2026 Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas has won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time, keeping the prize in Spanish hands for a sixth consecutive year. Putellas, 32, captained Barcelona to Champions League glory as part of a quadruple in 2025-26, before joining Women's Super League (WSL) side London City Lionesses in July. She joins Spain team-mate Aitana Bonmati on three Ballon d'Or Feminin crowns - her former Barcelona colleague won the award in 2023, 2024 and 2025 after Putellas did so in 2021 and 2022. The past six Ballons d'Or have been won by the Spanish pair, with Norway's Ada Hegerberg (2018) and Megan Rapinoe of the United States (2019) the only non-Spaniards to claim the prize. Putellas' latest victory caps a remarkable return to the pinnacle of world football after suffering a career-threatening anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in 2022. "All the boys and girls around the world - if you love football and if you want to play football, play football. It doesn't matter if you're a boy or if you're a girl," Putellas said. "Doesn't matter where you come from. Don't listen if someone tells you, you can't do it. Believe in yourself." She collected the most votes from an international panel of journalists across Fifa's top-50 ranked countries, with Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor coming second and Manchester City forward Khadija Shaw third. Meanwhile, England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or, becoming the first English player to do so since Michael Owen in 2001. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Putellas wins Ballon d'Or for third time The numbers don't lie While Barcelona are always overwhelming favourites to win the three competitions on offer in Spain, Putellas' performances last season showed that she is still among the world's elite. Nicknamed 'La Reina' - meaning the queen - Putellas scored 21 goals and provided 13 assists in all competitions, ranking her third and second respectively among players across Europe's top five leagues. Seven of those goals came in the Women's Champions League as Barcelona claimed a fourth continental title in six seasons. Only Pernille Harder (eight), Alessia Russo (nine) and Ewa Pajor (11) scored more, all of whom are strikers by trade. But Putellas' contributions to Barcelona's attacking play went far beyond scoring goals herself. In Liga F - which Barcelona won for a seventh consecutive season - she finished joint-sixth for assists (seven) and fourth for open-play chances created (40). Across Europe's top five leagues, only Claudia Pina (199), Vicky Lopez (183) and Georgia Stanway (168) recorded more sequence involvements ending in an open-play shot than Putellas (151). In all competitions, she created more chances (89, 19 of which were big chances) and completed more passes ending in the final third (965) than any other player in Liga F, the Champions League, Copa de la Reina and Supercopa de Espana. Only Bayern Munich's Klara Buhl created as many chances as Putellas in the Champions League last season (36), the most by a player in a single edition of the competition since Caroline Graham Hansen in 2021-22 (38). From watching Iniesta to winning it all Putellas was born and grew up in the Catalan municipality of Mollet del Valles, about 12 miles north-east of Barcelona. She began playing football in the street, and soon became a Barcelona fan and a regular attendee at Camp Nou. With matches always on the TV at home, former Spain and Barcelona star Andres Iniesta and Brazilian duo Rivaldo and Ronaldinho quickly became her idols. After attending a summer football camp run by Xavi and playing for local side CE Sabadell, Putellas spent a year at La Masia, Barcelona's famous youth academy. Spells at Espanyol and Levante followed the disbandment of her girls team, before she eventually returned to Barca in 2012. Cue the start of a 14-year career with her childhood club during which she won 38 trophies, including 10 league titles and four European cups. But after winning the Ballon d'Or for the first time in 2021, one of the toughest moments of Putellas' career came when she suffered an ACL injury on the eve of Euro 2022, ruling her out of the tournament. Though she retained the Ballon d'Or later that year, it took a while for her to return to her best level. Playing only a bit-part role in Spain's triumphant 2023 World Cup campaign would have stung. After scoring in the 2024 Champions League final and improving further the following season, in 2025-26 she shouldered much of Barcelona's creative burden as Aitana Bonmati missed five months through injury and ended the season a quadruple winner. If that was not enough, the midfielder scored twice in a 4-0 thrashing of England in June that secured Spain's place at the 2027 World Cup at the Lionesses' expense. With her contract at Barcelona expiring and keen for a fresh challenge, Putellas made the decision to leave her childhood club. She, and her fans, were distraught. She had several offers from England, Mexico and the United States, but joined the ambitious project of US billionaire Michelle Kang at London City Lionesses in July. "I'm just always looking forward to better things and that's why I'm here too, because I always need to be moving as a person and a player," Putellas told BBC's Women's Football Weekly podcast in August. With three goals and one assist in seven WSL games for her new club, it is clear Putellas is still deserving of her nickname. title: Healey vows cheaper marmalade and gherkins in pre-Budget package of 'everyday fixes'
description: The chancellor will axe tariffs on some staples as part of plans to give households "breathing space".
content: Chancellor to cut tariffs on some food and freeze fuel duty to give families 'breathing space' Image source, Getty Images ByArchie Mitchell and Dearbail Jordan, Business reporters Published 26 October 2026 Updated 50 minutes ago Making higher tax-free mileage rates permanent and the removal of import taxes on some food items are among the measures being announced ahead of Wednesday's Budget. The BBC understands the government will also freeze fuel duty again in the Budget, while the Times reports, external it may also slow the pace of pay increases for younger workers on the minimum wage. The series of small announcements is part of Chancellor John Healey's pledge to give families what he is calling "breathing space" with the cost of living. The government is also planning to end the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments. Speaking ahead of his first Budget, Healey said that the ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine had "hit families here at home through higher everyday costs". "We can't control global events, but we can act where we can make a difference," he added. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds defended the government's plan to remove tariffs from 100 food items, which it calculates could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June. "We're not going to say it is everything," he told the BBC, but taken alongside the changes implemented in the summer on goods such as pasta, fruit juice and tuna, he said it would save around £500m a year. Other measures the government announced include: Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the period And rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes to make sending parcels easier The government will also freeze fuel duty again in the Budget, the BBC understands. The 5p duty discount is also set to continue. That discount was first introduced in 2022, and was due to last 12 months, but has been extended ever since. Minimum wage rise Healey will announce the new National Minimum Wage for 18 to 20-year-olds on Wednesday as well as the National Living Wage for those aged 21 and over. Labour had promised in its manifesto it would remove "discriminatory age bands so all adults are entitled to the same minimum wage". The business secretary would not comment on the new pay rates but appeared to confirm the pace of rises would slow for people on the National Minimum Wage. Reynolds told the BBC: "The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies but we were always clear it could happen over time. "Of course, you want not just good wages but good work, " he added. "It is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account." The Times has reported that the National Minimum Wage is likely to rise by 3.9% from £10.85 an hour to around £11.27. It is far below the 26% increase the Labour government has put in place since returning to power in 2024. Even after the reported rise, the rate remains below the National Living Wage which is currently £12.71 an hour. It is set to rise by 3.9% to £13.20, the Times said. Andrea Egan, general secretary of the union Unison, said it was "deeply unfair" to keep paying different rates for the same job. "Twenty year-old care workers, teaching assistants and security guards do the same work as their older colleagues," she said. "They don't pay less in the supermarket or at the petrol pump. They must be paid equally." 'I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40.' What do you want from the Budget? Published 5 hours ago What is the Budget and what could be in it? Published 59 minutes ago Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds Published 1 day ago The list of products the government is removing tariffs on includes: Baked beans Garlic Gherkins Chocolate-coated wafers and waffles Boiled sweets Toffees, caramels and similar sweets Citrus jams, marmalades and pastes Throat pastilles and cough drops Plant-based drinks including soya, nut, cereal or seed Kerosene Fertilisers The government said removing tariffs on fertiliser aimed to help farmers, while changes to import levies on kerosene is targetted at households that rely on heating oil. The Treasury said it would publish on Wednesday a full list of the products that will have tariffs removed. A tariff is an import duty paid by domestic businesses buying products from overseas. Asked why the government was making it cheaper to buy goods from abroad rather than cutting business costs for UK firms, Reynolds said: "Where you can make a reduction in the cost of importing goods into the UK, when you think you can balance that with your domestic economic interests, that's a decision we will take." But Balwinder Dhoot, director of sustainability and growth at the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said: "It's more expensive to make food and drink here in the UK than in many of our close neighbours, as businesses face such high energy costs." The Conservatives said the government's "everyday fixes" had already been wiped out by higher borrowing costs, taxes and inflation. Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham's plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises." Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here. Related topics John Healey

title: Dundee councillors approve £21m RAAC repair scheme
description: Almost 1,000 homes in the city contain the defective concrete - the highest number in Scotland.
content: Dundee councillors approve £21m Raac repair scheme Image caption, Craigie Drive is one of five areas affected by Raac in Dundee Published 26 October 2026 Councillors have approved a £21m repair scheme for Raac-affected homes in Dundee. Work will be carried out on council-owned properties and in buildings where the local authority retains an interest. The council has agreed to write to both the UK and Scottish governments seeking financial support and a dedicated funding mechanism for homeowners. Almost 1,000 homes in the city contain the defective concrete - the highest number in Scotland. The material was used in flat roofing, floors and walls between the 1950s and 1990s. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) said Raac was now beyond its lifespan and could "collapse with little or no notice". More stories from Tayside and Central Listen to news from Tayside and Central on BBC Sounds Raac stands for reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete. It is a cheaper alternative to standard concrete, is quicker to produce and easier to install. It is aerated - or "bubbly" - like an Aero chocolate bar. But it is less durable than other types of concrete and has a lifespan of about 30 years. Its structural behaviour differs significantly from traditional reinforced concrete. It is susceptible to structural failure when exposed to moisture as the bubbles can allow water to enter the material. Raac is often coated with another material, such as bitumen on roofing panels. But this material can also degrade. title: Busted's James Bourne says 'hero' brother saved his life with kidney donation
description: The guitarist says doctors had given him "a few years left to live", but is now recovering well.
content: Busted's James Bourne says 'hero' brother saved his life with kidney donation Image source, Press Association Image caption, James Bourne: "I can't believe how much better I'm starting to feel already." ByIan Youngs Culture reporter Published 26 October 2026 Busted star James Bourne has said his brother "saved my life" by donating a kidney, after doctors had given him "a few years left to live". The guitarist, 43, dropped out of an arena tour featuring his band and fellow punk-pop favourites McFly in September 2025, just a day before it began. He blamed health problems and was replaced by his younger brother Chris. James later said he needed major surgery to "extend my life", and has now thanked his "hero" Chris and said they are both recovering from their transplant operations. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Bourne with his Busted bandmates Charlie Simpson and Matt Willis in 2023 "Wow, what the hell happened?" James wrote on Monday. "One minute you're heading out on tour, the next thing you know you're on the bench and out of the game. "My condition was serious and the doctors told me I had a few years left to live. "I'm happy to share now that my youngest brother, Chris, who stepped in for me on tour last year, has saved my life yet again. This time quite literally by donating me one of his kidneys." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Chris Bourne went on tour with Busted after his brother was forced to drop out James continued: "I can't believe how much better I'm starting to feel already. "I'm still going to need some time, but I wanted you to know that we're both recovering from surgery just fine. My brother is a hero." Chris posted his own message on X saying simply: "We did it brother." Bourne has not given any more details of his condition. Image source, Press Association Image caption, Busted had eight top 10 hits in the UK between 2002 and 2004 The guitarist, vocalist and songwriter shot to fame with Charlie Simpson and Matt Willis in Busted in the early 2000s, and the trio had hits including What I Go To School For, Year 3000 and Crashed the Wedding. They scored four number one singles in the UK before splitting up in 2005. In 2013, Bourne and Willis teamed up with McFly to make McBusted, before Simpson rejoined Busted for a full reunion in 2015. Bourne has written songs for McFly and 5 Seconds of Summer, and also fronted his own band, Son of Dork. He recently released the music from his stage musical Murder at the Gates. title: Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time
description: Comey's lawyers say the case stems from alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in 2016.
content: Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: "I'm still innocent" - James Comey responds to new charges BySareen Habeshian Published 26 October 2026 Updated 22 minutes ago Federal prosecutors have taken steps to charge ex-Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director James Comey with leaking national defence information, according to a court filing. It marks the third time the justice department has moved to bring criminal charges against Comey, a longtime critic of President Donald Trump. Few details are provided about the two counts in the three-page filing, but Comey's lawyers said in separate court papers that the case stemmed from an alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in October 2016, while he was head of the FBI. Comey denied any wrongdoing in a video posted on Substack on Monday, calling the charges an "appalling abuse". "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the department of justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said in the clip. "Nothing's changed with me - I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary." Comey was charged in Washington DC through a criminal information, which is a formal written charging document filed directly by a prosecutor. This is different to a criminal indictment, which must be approved by a grand jury, a group of citizens sworn in to review if evidence is strong enough to prosecute. Comey's lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that two different teams of prosecutors had investigated the alleged disclosure to the New York Times a decade ago during the first Trump administration. "Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said. The attorney said the court filing "purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit". His legal team has filed a motion to dismiss the charges. Former federal prosecutor Glenn Kirschner told the BBC that the case may have exceeded the 10-year statute of limitations, giving the motion to dismiss the charges "a very good chance of being granted". Kirschner said it seemed like the charges against Comey were a "revenge-fuelled attempt by Donald Trump to have his Department of Justice find something that might stick". Jessica Levinson, law professor at Loyola University in Los Angeles, said that because the charges were still under seal, the details about what federal prosecutors are alleging were slim. "We do have some examples of the Trump administration and the department of justice going after a variety of people who are his political enemies; we have very different outcomes in some of these cases, though," she told the BBC World Service's Newsday programme. While other cases involving Comey have not moved forward, cases brought against other Trump adversaries have moved forward, Levinson noted. Image source, Getty Images Comey was fired by Trump during his first term, after the former FBI director opened an investigation into claims of Russian meddling in the US 2016 presidential election. Since then, Trump has repeatedly called for his prosecution, and these charges are the administration's third attempt to do so. Comey was first indicted by a federal grand jury in September 2025 on charges that he had lied to Congress during testimony and obstructed a congressional proceeding. He pleaded not guilty the following month before the case was dismissed in November. In April 2026, Comey surrendered to authorities to face charges alleging that an image he briefly shared on social media posed a threat to Trump's life. The case stemmed from a 2025 Instagram post by Comey, which contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47". "Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump, the 47th president. Comey denies any wrongdoing, saying he did not know what the numbers meant, and accusing the prosecution of political motivation. That case is ongoing. The latest charges against Comey were made public the same day a federal judge ruled the justice department illegally fired his daughter, Maurene Comey. Maurene Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father and because of her perceived political affiliations. The judge ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay. title: Manhunt for suspect with 'altered appearance'
description: Erdem Mustafa, 35, was shot dead in Hertford Road, Enfield, last Monday.
content: Manhunt for suspect with 'altered appearance' Image source, Metropolitan Police Image caption, Police believe the two images show Abreham Woldegiworgis ByWinnie Agbonlahor Reporting fromLondon Published 26 October 2026 Police are hunting a man who they say "significantly altered his appearance" since being captured on CCTV at the time of a fatal pub shooting in north London. Erdem Mustafa, 35, was shot dead in Hertford Road, Enfield, last Monday. Metropolitan Police want to trace Abreham Woldegiworgis, 35, who they believe is the person captured in CCTV footage wearing a grey beanie and a bright orange wig. Scotland Yard released "before" and "after" images of him on Monday in an appeal for information. The force said both images show the same person with and without a beard. Image source, Met Police Image caption, Police believe Abreham Woldegiworgis is the person captured in CCTV footage wearing a grey beanie and a bright orange wig at the time of the shooting Scotland Yard said the man they want to speak to has since "significantly altered his appearance" from the CCTV footage. People have been urged not to approach him. A 23-year-old man was arrested on Monday on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and remains in police custody. Ch Insp Allam Bhangoo said: "We remain committed to securing justice for Erdem as our thoughts remain with his loved ones at this unimaginably hard time. "While I am pleased my team have made an arrest, our work continues at pace to investigate the full circumstances around Erdem's murder. "We are now releasing the details and images of a man we urgently need to speak to in connection with the incident. "We are carrying out a number of inquiries to trace him but are also asking for the public's help. "If you recognise him or have any information on his whereabouts please come forward. "We are still appealing for anyone with wider information about the shooting, including any CCTV, doorbell, dashcam or mobile phone footage, to also contact us." title: Four games, no wins - Ulster aim for URC turnaround
description: Head coach Richie Murphy says Ulster are "small margins" away from a first victory in the United Rugby Championship after a winless start in the league.
content: Four games, no wins - Ulster aim for URC turnaround Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Ulster boss Richie Murphy is without his nine-strong Ireland cohort in Cape Town ByAndy Gray BBC Sport NI Journalist Published 26 October 2026 On the face of it, Ulster are without a victory in their four United Rugby Championship outings this season. But head coach Richie Murphy is not ready to hit the panic button. Despite a winless start, the Irish province are just one point outside the play-off places despite a struggle for results. An opening defeat by Edinburgh was followed by two thrilling draws against Glasgow and Munster, and then a loss to the Bulls in the first of a South African double-header. There has been a constant theme throughout: Ulster have allowed the opposition to build an early - and often significant - lead. On each occasion they have fought back, but have yet to seal a comeback with victory. Murphy admits his side have been "digging a bit of a hole" in each of their four matches this season. "Obviously, we're not quite getting the results that we wanted, but we're in every game," said Murphy, whose side defeated Zebre in their Challenge Cup opener. "We're playing against top-class opposition and we're fighting for everything we can get." "It's really important that we don't throw the baby out with the bathwater. We will stick to our process and stick to what we believe in, and that's what we're trying to do." McNabney keen to show Ireland coaches 'what I'm all about' Published 1 day ago Murphy praises Ulster for 'sticking in the fight' Published 2 days ago 'We strive for consistency' Despite admitting the opening results have left him with "mixed emotions", Murphy feels his side "can compete with the best teams in the league". "We're not a million miles away from winning opportunities to win every one of those matches," he added. "We're just trying to double down on the areas that we need to improve. If you ask me what areas are they, it's a little bit of everything. "If we could be a little bit better at the breakdown, or if our pass quality could be a little bit better. All these tiny little aspects of the game add up to wins." If Ulster are to pick up an elusive first URC victory of the season, Murphy knows that consistency is going to be key - starting against the Stormers in Cape Town on Saturday (12:45 GMT). "In each of the games that we've played, we've played some very high-class rugby in both attack and defence, but we haven't been consistent," he said. "The thing that we strive for is consistency and if our execution can very slightly improve, it's amazing what that will do to the results. "We'll stick to the process, believe in what we're trying to do and we believe that the results will come." 'A different headache' While Ulster have been soaking up the heat in South Africa - a stark contrast to the current weather back home - Murphy knows his side are about to face a storm of a different kind on Saturday. The Stormers will likely have their Springbok stars available - such as Siya Kolisi, back row Evan Roos and fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu - which is not a luxury Murphy will have. In fact, Ulster head to Cape Town without nine of their key players after they were called up for Ireland duty ahead of November's Nations Championship fixtures. Backs Stuart McCloskey, Jacob Stockdale, Robert Baloucoune, Nathan Doak and Jamie Benson have been included along with forwards Tom O'Toole, Tom Stewart, James McNabney and Nick Timoney. The experience of hooker Rob Herring and centre James Hume should help to fill the void despite their lack of minutes through injury, and returning wing Zac Ward will offer plenty of try-scoring prowess. Murphy admits it "causes a different headache for us" having so many players unavailable. "We didn't know the amount of players we were going to lose and nine is probably more than we were expecting. "But at the same time, we're delighted for those players to get the opportunity to go and represent Ireland." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, James McNabney (left) and Jamie Benson (with the ball) have been called into Andy Farrell's Ireland squad Of the nine players called up for Ireland's Nations Championship games in November, Benson and McNabney have been called up for the first time. Murphy said Benson, a versatile Irish-qualified former England Under-20 international, has been "excellent" since joining from Harlequins in the summer. The 24-year-old has featured in both centre positions and fly-half for Ulster, and can also play at full-back. "He has shown good signs of leadership in our group as well and his attitude has been so good in relation to playing in three different positions "That versatility is really good for any squad and Ireland are obviously recognising that as well." Back row McNabney, who Farrell described as "some specimen", has been included after recovering from a year on the sidelines with an ACL injury. "He's finding his feet in a little bit, but you can see the attributes that he has," said Murphy. "It's great to have those guys in there, but it obviously puts pressure on our squad." Related topics Rugby Union Irish Rugby Ulster Ireland Rugby Union Northern Ireland Sport

title: Oscar-winning producer says BBC gave her £400,000 payout after she raised antisemitism concerns
description: The BBC says it did not uphold any of the allegations of antisemitism but accepted there were "shortcomings" in how it treated Lucie Kon.
content: Oscar-winning producer says BBC gave her £400,000 payout after she raised antisemitism concerns Image source, Getty Images ByEmma Saunders Culture reporter Published 26 October 2026 An Oscar-winning executive producer claims she received a £400,000 payout from the BBC after alleging she faced antisemitic remarks from colleagues at the corporation. Lucie Kon, who worked as a commissioning editor overseeing several documentaries, including Mr Nobody Against Putin, told The Telegraph, external that BBC colleagues said Zionists like her were "evil" following the 7 October attacks. Kon's post was made redundant as part of a BBC restructure. She said the payment she received was for redundancy back pay and settlement for personal injury caused by the process. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Lucie Kon (far left) with fellow members of the the Mr Nobody Against Putin team, who won the best documentary at this year's Baftas The BBC says it did not uphold any of the allegations of antisemitism but accepted there were "shortcomings" in how it treated Kon, which had a "personal impact" on her. The corporation did not specify what the shortcomings were. Kon says she raised a number of concerns about how she was treated following the Hamas-led 7 October attacks. "I became a problem," she told BBC News. "I really did feel like I had Jew stamped on my forehead. I became a problem. And anytime I tried to mention anything, it was like, 'Oh God, there she goes again.' "I became a proper pain. They didn't know what else to do with me." Kon also claimed she was told by a colleague that "if you want to call Hamas terrorists then you have to call Israel terrorists, too". She helped lead a group representing Jewish staff in the corporation and raised issues with the then-director general, Tim Davie. Kon told The Telegraph that her religion had not been an issue during her many years working for the BBC until the October 7 attacks. She later told LBC that the BBC was "not institutionally antisemitic". The BBC said it was grateful that Kon acknowledged the BBC is not institutionally antisemitic, adding that she was a "valued member of staff with many years of dedicated service" to the corporation. Related topics BBC

title: Will the public change its mind about Meghan?
description: This complicated - and developing - story could prove to be a turning point for Meghan.
content: Will the public change its mind about Meghan? Image source, Reuters By Sean Coughlan Royal correspondent Published 26 October 2026 The allegations of sexual abuse against Thomas Markle have put his daughter Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, under an uncomfortable spotlight. She has been dealing with this potential news time-bomb out of sight for seven years, while appearing to share so much about her life in TV series and interviews. Thomas Markle has strongly rejected the claims as "lies" which are being used to destroy his reputation. But could this complicated story prove to be a turning point for Meghan, who has had a complicated and often hostile relationship with the UK public? What has emerged so far means re-thinking some of the criticism she's faced. Image source, ITV/ Shutterstock Image caption, Thomas Markle has strongly denied the allegations against him Meghan, who recently moved back to the UK with Prince Harry and their children, has frequently been accused of cutting off those once close to her. Her treatment of her father was seen as a prime example. "She ditched her family, ditched her dad, ditched most of her old friends, split Harry from William," wrote one commentator in 2020. "Get on a plane and go see the poor man before it's too late," she was told on social media about her father. All of that might need to be viewed in a different and more sympathetic light. By 2019, Meghan had received disturbing allegations about Thomas Markle, in a letter from her father's first wife, Roslyn Loveless. She says it is why she kept her distance and also why she didn't bring her children to him, including when she moved to the United States with her family. That letter was shared with Meghan by the police, at a time when she was classified as a working royal. It's not clear who else knew about the letter, including Palace officials, but it must have been a sensitive matter for her. And according to the Sussexes' spokesman, Meghan believed an investigation into the allegations was going ahead, presumably at a time when she was on official trips and having to put on a brave face. Letter making claims about Meghan's father written by his first wife, BBC understands Published 1 day ago Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims Published 2 days ago Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018 Published 3 days ago There was also criticism levelled at Meghan in December 2025 when her father was in hospital in the Philippines, undergoing the amputation of his leg. "I don't want to die estranged from Meghan. I want to meet my grandkids. It might be nice to meet her husband too," Markle told the Mail on Sunday at the time. There was a media storm about whether Meghan was going to reach out to her father, culminating in a letter being delivered from her to her father, which at the time was assumed to be well-wishes. But that whole episode now looks different with the benefit of hindsight. That letter was a much more fraught affair. It revealed that Meghan knew about the allegations against her father. We now understand that Meghan was telling him he would never see his grandchildren. Thomas Markle has strongly denied all the allegations against him, saying they are "sick lies" which are trying to destroy his reputation. His daughter Samantha Markle has also rejected the claims, saying the stories are "fake news" and "clickbait". "There will be no legal action against my dad with no evidence in so many flimsy stories and my dad never had access to any such content and was in the hospital most of the time that he was there," she wrote on X on Sunday. Samantha also challenges the credibility of the letter written by her mother, Roslyn Loveless, which was shared with Meghan in 2019 and contained details of allegations of sexual abuse against Thomas Markle. Image caption, Thomas Markle in a photo with his daughter Meghan When you look through photos of Meghan at events over the last seven years, you wonder what was going on behind the familiar smile. Those years have seen Netflix films, a tell-all memoir by Prince Harry, cookery series, podcasts and TV interviews. But a hidden narrative has been running in the background. Meghan's supporters have pointed to other factors in how she has been treated, with racism and sexism part of that toxic mix. But maybe there was also a sense of not knowing the authentic person behind the polished Brand Meghan. On Instagram, she has curated her life to look idyllic, but perhaps she'll get a more generous hearing now that her back story is as messy and imperfect as everyone else's. It could still be an uphill struggle to become more popular, beyond her own vocal, core group of supporters. A survey from YouGov earlier this month found 22% of people had a positive view of Meghan, compared with 49% who dislike her. That suggests there is still some way to go before Meghan fully wins the trust of the public. Fascination, yes. But affection, not always. For the British public, Californian Meghan hasn't always translated well. But perhaps this complex, still developing story - and the light it sheds on previous years - might mean there's a more rounded view of her in the future.
