title: Macklemore begins Free Palestine tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
description: Proceeds from the tour, which begins in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians, he says.
content: Macklemore begins Free Palestine tour after Ed Sheeran fallout Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Macklemore has pledged to donate the proceeds from his tour to organisations supporting Palestinians ByGabija Gataveckaite, Dublin correspondent and Barry O'Connor, BBC News NI Published 26 October 2026 Updated 27 October 2026 00:11 GMT Macklemore has begun his Free Palestine tour in Dublin after Ed Sheeran's controversial decision to drop the rapper from his tour last month. The American star played to a crowd of up to 13,000 at the city's 3Arena, having promised "many incredible surprise guests" on the bill for the sold-out show. The artist, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, announced the tour days after being dropped from Sheeran's Loop Tour after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage. He was criticised by Jewish groups after saying "free Palestine" at two concerts and making political speeches, including referring to the death toll from Israel's military action in Gaza as a genocide - a claim that Israel rejects. Sheeran later said that the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoter, not by himself. Among the acts who performed at Macklemore's Dublin show were singer-songwriter Hozier, rap trio Kneecap and folk band Beoga, who had also performed on Sheeran's tour. Macklemore has said that proceeds from his Free Palestine tour will go to organisations supporting Palestinians. He will perform in Paris on Thursday and in London on Friday. The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage. During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 70,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law. 'This is the hottest ticket' Tickets for the Dublin show sold out and dozens of concertgoers were queueing at the venue hours before its doors were opened. Some were dressed in Palestinian jerseys, others had tied Palestinian and Irish flags to themselves, and many were wearing keffiyeh scarves, a symbol of Palestinian identity. Vendors outside the arena sold Palestinian bucket hats and flags, as well as hats and flags with the Kneecap logo. Image caption, Nicola McCollough and her daughter Lily Rose Murphy say they are big fans of Macklemore Nicola McCollough travelled with her daughter Lily Rose Murphy from Belfast for Lily Rose's first ever concert. They both said they were happy Macklemore spoke out in support of Gaza. "More people need to, if you have the platform, do it because not everybody has that kind of stage," said Nicola. "I would speak about anything if I'm supportive of it," said Lily Rose. Image caption, Gillian Duffy and her son Joshua were among those in the queue for the gig Gillian Duffy travelled from Cork with her son Joshua. She said that if Macklemore had "put on 10 shows in Dublin, all 10 would have been filled". "This is the hottest ticket because people want to be here, they really, really want to show their support," she said. "You're going to hear [the chant] 'Free, free Palestine' all over Dublin tonight." Jess O'Riordan, who also travelled from Cork, said it was "absolutely appalling" when Macklemore was "kicked off" Sheeran's tour. "I wish we had more people out there that would use their platform the way he does," she added. Why was Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour? The controversy began when Macklemore, performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in New Jersey in early September, said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine." The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University in the US. The lyrics are critical of Israel's military actions in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack. After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out. He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza. Sheeran said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group. His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity with Macklemore, and fans to express frustration. Sheeran then addressed the controversy during the start of a gig in Philadelphia. He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue". He described the 7 October 2023 attacks as "horrific" and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate". title: Trump's media bans 'deprive the public', press freedom groups argue
description: The plaintiffs allege they are no longer able to do their work without reliable access to information delivered by the White House press.
content: Trump's media bans 'deprive the public', press freedom groups argue Image source, Getty Images Image caption, In court filings, the six plaintiffs allege they are no longer able to do their work without access to information delivered by the White House press ByKayla Epstein, National Reporter and Bernd Debusmann, White House Reporter Published 26 October 2026 Press freedom groups are suing the Trump administration over its efforts to block mainstream US news outlets from covering the White House, according to court filings. The six plaintiffs, which include scholars, advocates and journalists, argue media bans issued by the White House violate the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which protects the press and freedom of speech. Their lawsuit comes after CNN, Politico and MSNOW brought a separate legal challenge over the White House's attempts to revoke or restrict their press access. The Knight First Amendment Institute and Yale Law School's Media and Information Access Clinic filed the legal case on the plaintiffs' behalf. The six plaintiffs have asked a New York federal court to declare that the White House's selective media bans violate the First Amendment, and to block the administration from continuing to enforce them. In court filings, the plaintiffs allege they are no longer able to do their work without access to information delivered by the White House press. The White House policy, they argue, "deprives the public" of reporting, and forces journalists who cover Donald Trump "to account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked". Such a ban has a "distorting effect" on coverage from the White House, the court filing argues. The BBC has asked the White House for comment. The lawsuit did not ask a judge to award financial damages, only to require the defendants to cover their legal fees if they win. Since Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, the White House has engaged in a standoff with many longstanding US media outlets, which the president has frequently accused of publishing "fake news". Last month, it banned reporters from CNN, Politico and MSNOW from the White House, leading several other media organisations to temporarily suspend their pooled coverage of the president in protest. The affected news outlets sued, arguing the White House was illegally discriminating against them because of the content of their coverage. A federal judge later ordered the White House to restore the credentials of the impacted journalists while their lawsuit plays out. The reporters later said they were allowed back into the White House complex. Major US outlets suspend shared Trump coverage in protest at media ban Published 22 September What is the White House pool and why is it in a row with Trump? Published 22 September Media outlets banned by Trump resume White House coverage after judge's order Published 25 September The White House has, however, continued to selectively bar journalists, which news organisations in the US argue violates their press freedom protections. CNN, for instance, has threatened to take further legal action in court as its reporters continue to be denied access aboard Air Force One. And last week, the White House banned a correspondent from the Independent from covering the president's trip to the state of Iowa, after Trump berated the reporter from the UK news outlet during a news conference. In his second term, Trump has also moved to bring conservative bloggers, influencers and other "new media" figures into the press room, arguing it is necessary to provide diverse perspectives in White House coverage. In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool - the small group of journalists that has access to the president on any given day - which for more than a century had been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association. The same month, the White House moved to bar Associated Press journalists from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because the outlet used the term "Gulf of Mexico" rather than "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing. Trump last week confirmed he was considering moving the entire press corps from the White House grounds following reports he was contemplating the reconstruction of a swimming pool that sits underneath the James S Brady briefing room. "I am thinking about moving the press, and putting them in a different location," he wrote on Truth Social. "I will use that location for very badly needed space." Related topics White House Press freedom Donald Trump Media

title: Trump administration illegally fired James Comey's daughter, judge rules
description: Maurene Comey believes she was let go from her job as a federal prosecutor because her father is the former FBI director.
content: Trump administration illegally fired James Comey's daughter, judge rules Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Maurene Comey has worked on a number of high-profile legal cases ByMadeline Halpert Published 26 October 2026 The US justice department illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) director James Comey, a federal judge has ruled. Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father, a critic of US President Donald Trump, and because of her perceived political affiliations. Judge Jesse Furman ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay. A spokesperson for the justice department said in a statement that it disagreed with the decision and "will appeal in due course". In his ruling, Judge Furman said Comey's dismissal violated the US Constitution as well as her right to a fair legal process. He said the US attorney general can fire federal prosecutors but only "in a particular manner and only for certain reasons". Furman noted that in Comey's role, "she was assigned some of the country's highest profile cases and consistently received the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike". Comey has worked on cases against the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, and hip-hop mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs, who was convicted on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends last year. Furman ordered that Comey be given back pay from July until December 2025, when she accepted a new job. In a statement, Comey's lawyers said: "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law." Comey had previously said the only reason she was told about her firing was that it "came from Washington". A complaint filed by her lawyers in September 2025 stated that they believed Comey had been fired "solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both". The justice department said in court filings that the decision was made by former Attorney General Pam Bondi. The Trump administration has twice brought charges against James Comey, including for allegedly lying to Congress, but that case was dismissed by a judge who said the prosecutor who brought the case was unlawfully appointed. Earlier this year, the justice department charged Comey with knowingly and wilfully making a threat to take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm, on the president. He has denied any wrongdoing. The case stems from a 2025 Instagram post shared by Comey that contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47". "Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump. Related topics Donald Trump United States James Comey More on this story Comey surrenders over charge of threatening Trump's life in Instagram post Published 29 April Prosecutor in Diddy and Epstein cases fired by US justice department Published 17 July 2025

title: 'Maxxing' selected as Dictionary.com word of the year
description: The term "maxxing" is used as an adjective, adverb, noun and verb by many in Gen Z and Gen Alpha to describe an emphasis in optimisation.
content: 'Maxxing' selected as Dictionary.com word of the year Image source, Reuters ByAna Faguy and Nardine Saad Published 26 October 2026 Americans have gone all in on "maxxing", making it the 2026 Word of the Year for Dictionary.com. Short for maximising, the term "can be used on its own or added to the end of any word to convey you're doing something to the fullest or optimizing it as much as possible", Dictionary.com said in a statement. It's a major departure from two years ago, when the site, after analysing US social media trends, news stories, and search data, chose demure as word of the year. Last year's was "67". "Maxxing is the linguistic manifestation of a culture increasingly preoccupied with getting the most out of everything," said Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group. Digital media used "maxxing" nearly 19 times more in August 2026 compared to the 2025 monthly average, Dictionary.com found. The site also considered affordability, data centre, odyssey, and the shortened form of uncle, "unc", as potential words of the year. On social media, many people in Generation Z and younger - those under 30 - post extensively about their maxxing efforts to achieve all sorts of perfection. Influencers focused on fitness and wellness post about "proteinmaxxing" and "fibermaxxing". Those giving their full attention to improving sleep habits say they are "sleepmaxxing". The influencer Clavicular has gained thousands of followers as he chronicles his extreme "looksmaxxing" - working to meet a set of prescribed criteria for attractiveness, with particular importance given to jawlines, eyes and physique. "Whatever we're doing, we want to push it further," Johnson said. "But its expanding uses also reveal how people are responding to that impulse. Some embrace it. Some exaggerate it for laughs. Others subvert it entirely to describe stepping back from the relentless pursuit of more." People were playing with the term - and idea - for decades before Clavicular started posting videos. In the opening song for the 1990s television show The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, for example, Will Smith raps: "Chillin' out, maxin', relaxin' all cool." "Unfortunately, by the time the dictionary gets a hold of it, that probably means that it's reached critical mass," says teacher Lauren Cella. Cella, a content creator known for her viral Gen Z history lessons, says she and her students have been using "maxxing" for some time as a suffix. "They're actually, in their own way, reinventing grammar, which I think is super cool," she says. Maxxing gives the students permission to "optimise to meet a goal" or do something others might think of as "cringe", and allows them to own it, she says. "It's a fun, harmless way that kids are expressing themselves and sharing different goals that they have," she says. Linguist Vanessa Croft, who teaches English, says the internet and digital media make language move at "warp speed", even faster than radio, film or television ever did. As swiftly as new terms are added to the lexicon, they can just as quickly fall out of favour. "By the time millennials and Gen X or Gen Y start using the terms, Gen Z and Gen Alpha aren't using those terms anymore," she says. While she and her secondary-school aged students are still "maxxing" too, they are now using it "almost ironically", she says. Related topics Language Culture United States Social media

title: Heavenly Creatures killer Pauline Parker dies in Orkney, aged 88
description: The death of the convicted murderer in Orkney at the age of 88 brings to an end a 70-year story that inspired an acclaimed film.
content: Heavenly Creatures killer Pauline Parker dies in Orkney, aged 88 Image caption, Peter Jackson's 1994 film of the events starred Melanie Lynskey (left) as Pauline Parker and Kate Winslet as Juliet Hulme By Pauline McLean Scotland arts correspondent Published 26 October 2026 To her neighbours and friends, Hilary Nathan was a quiet, religious woman who ran a riding stable in the small Orcadian island of Burray. But her death in an island care home last week at the age of 88 closes a chapter on an extraordinary life that began 70 years ago on the other side of the world with a sensational murder trial. As a 16-year-old and under her birth name of Pauline Parker, she was convicted alongside her schoolfriend Juliet Hulme of the murder of her mother Honora Parker. The case shocked New Zealand – and the rest of the world. The court heard the girls had become inseparable at Christchurch Girls' High School. Fearing that they'd be separated following the divorce of Juliet's parents and a planned move to South Africa, they plotted to kill Mrs Parker, who they believed stood in their way. They lured her to a park and bludgeoned her to death with a brick inside a stocking. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Pauline Parker (middle) and Juliet Hulme (right) were tried together in Christchurch By the time filmmaker Sir Peter Jackson was born in 1961, both girls had served five years in prison, been released, given new identities, and left New Zealand for good. "It was known for its tabloid sensational aspect. I know a lot of English tabloids flew to Christchurch, New Zealand, to cover the case of the 'evil schoolgirl killers'," he told the BBC's Late Show in 1995. "Repeating that stuff would have been easy, but that's not what we wanted to do. We wanted to understand more about Pauline Parker and Juliet Hulme, and what made them become friends." His film Heavenly Creatures starred Kate Winslet as Hulme and Melanie Lynskey as Parker. It showed how their intense friendship spilled over into a strange shared fantasy life which culminated in the brutal murder. The defence argued insanity, but both girls were found guilty of murder and only avoided the death penalty because of their age. In 1960, having served five years in separate prisons, they were given new identities and moved away from New Zealand. The court ordered that they should never meet again, and yet they lived part of their lives about 80 miles (129km) apart. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Parker was just 16 when she was tried for her mother's murder When the film came out in 1995, Juliet was living in Portmahomack in Rosshire, where she'd become a crime writer living under her new name, Anne Perry. She told the Late Show that she didn't plan to see the film. "It would be too harrowing," she said. "What was close to the truth would be distressing and what was far from the truth would be even more distressing." "It's a bit like being stripped naked in the High Street for everyone to come and look and pick and poke. I'd rather put my clothes on and go back home, thank you." During filming, Kate Winslet said she had no idea where the two women were, and after Anne Perry's identity was revealed, the actress expressed the hope that Pauline Parker would be able to retain her anonymity. "These are two women who, for the last 40 years, have had to overcome so much in order to get on with their lives and just survive," she said. "I hope she is never found." But Parker was found - by lawyer and true-crime author Peter Graham, who had written a book about the case called So Brilliantly Clever, its title taken from her diary, which was used as evidence in court. She, like Juliet, had come to the UK, where she had settled in a small village in rural Kent and opened a riding school. By 2004, now known as Hilary Nathan, she had moved to Orkney, running another stable when her identity was discovered. A friend recalled her locking herself in her house for a week when people discovered her past and resolving to leave the island and start again. The friend said that although the community hadn't known about her past, they appreciated what she did for the children she taught at the riding school, often for free. Their support convinced her to stay, living a simple and quiet life until her death in a care home in St Margaret's Hope a week ago. For both women, religion and small tight-knit communities provided a haven. According to an interview her sister gave to the New Zealand Women's Weekly, Nathan was a devout Catholic who led a reclusive life. Perry was a Mormon, enjoying the support of her own community when reporters began to arrive after Heavenly Creatures was released. She said: "The media descended on Portmahomack. I was horrified, especially since my mother lived in the village. It's not just the people the film is about, it's all the people around them. I felt it might ruin my family." Although her books were hugely successful in America, she never really found the fame she merited here in the UK, partly because of her reticence to do any promotion. Prime Suspect creator Lynda La Plante expressed interest in a TV version of Perry's books, but the author vetoed the plan for the same reason. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Juliet Hulme became a successful crime author under the name Anne Perry In 2001, I visited Perry in Portmahomack for a rare interview for Newsnight Scotland. At that stage, she was a glamorous author, with a back catalogue which had sold 15 million copies around the world. "I think after 51 years, you can let it go," she told me. "It's not who I am now. It's not who I have been for decades." We didn't talk about the murder directly, but you don't have to look far in her books for insight into what happened and how her life had turned out. Her detective, the Victorian policeman William Monk, suffers from amnesia, and sometimes wonders exactly who he is. "Monk sees himself as just himself but because of his memory loss, he has to deal with the fact that he may be someone else. That comes from my own sense that other people view me as a monster," she admitted. "Of course it affects what I write. I have far more compassion and understanding for people who do wrong things than I'd ever have if I hadn't been in that position. "The questions of right and wrong and compassion and forgiveness concern me in a way they wouldn't have, had I not had the life I had." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Anne Perry became a successful crime writer Anne Perry died in Los Angeles in 2023 at the age of 84. Hilary Nathan's death last week brings their strange story to a close. How they reinvented themselves out of the world's harshest headlines, and found redemption in the smallest of Scottish communities. "I would say if you had something which harrowed you, or caused you to feel shame, you should never give up," Anne told me. "There's more forgiveness, understanding and help out there than you might think." More on this story Murderer-turned-novelist Anne Perry dies aged 84 Published 13 April 2023

title: Bristol sign Auvaa following Saracens sacking
description: Bristol Bears have signed 21-year-old Samoan forward Totoa Auvaa, two weeks after he was sacked by Saracens.
content: Bristol sign Auvaa following Saracens sacking Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Totoa Auvaa made one appearance for Saracens in the Prem Cup this season ByAndrew Raeburn BBC Sport England Published 26 October 2026 Bristol Bears have signed Samoan forward Totoa Auvaa, two weeks after he was sacked by Saracens. Auvaa, 21, was involved in a nightclub altercation with England cricketers Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson in June. He was let go by Sarries following another incident in St Albans, which police are investigating. "His agent reached out to me to see if I would be willing to help him and give him a second chance," Bristol's director of rugby Pat Lam said. "I've always believed that young people deserve the opportunity to learn from those experiences, grow and become better people." Lam, himself a former Samoan international, told Bristol's website, external he believed the club could help provide support to Auvaa and was the right place for him to develop on and off the field. "Totoa is a big, physical young man with enormous potential, who unfortunately has made some mistakes since arriving from a small village in Samoa to the massive city of London. "Having spent time with Totoa, I feel confident that we can provide him with the mentorship, guidance, support and structure to give him the best possible opportunity to succeed, not just as a rugby player, but as a person - someone his parents and family all the way back in Samoa will be proud of." Two punch-ups, two red cards, no chances left - Saracens sack Auvaa Published 13 October Saracens sack academy player Auvaa after latest incident Published 12 October Auvaa's disciplinary issues have not been restricted to late-night altercations. While on loan at Championship club Ampthill last season, he was sent off twice for violent conduct - once, punching an opposition player in the face in the aftermath of conceding a try, and, in another match, kicking someone in the head at the bottom of a ruck. Auvaa's youth, recent arrival in England and the stress of supporting his father through illness back home in Samoa were put forward in mitigation. When he was involved in the nightclub incident with Atkinson and Stokes, in which a member of England's security staff was left bloodied after being struck by Auvaa, Saracens said they would stand by him. However, after the incident in St Albans, the club said, external his conduct had fallen "short of the standards expected of everyone who represents Saracens, both on and off the pitch" and he was sacked. A statement issued by Hertfordshire Police on the incident said: "Police are investigating an altercation which occurred between 0215 and 0220 on Sunday [11 October] in St Peter's Street, St Albans. "It is alleged a man aged in his twenties was approached by another man who then punched him to the face. Enquiries are ongoing at this time." Auvaa made one appearance for Saracens, playing 20 minutes of a Prem Rugby Cup match in September. Related topics Rugby Union Bristol Saracens

title: Pope's South American trip to go ahead as planned after lung cancer surgery
description: The Pope underwent surgery in to remove a tumour on the lower part of his right lung and is gradually resuming his duties.
content: Pope's South American trip to go ahead as planned after lung cancer surgery Image source, EPA ByGabriela Pomeroy Published 26 October 2026 The Vatican has confirmed that Pope Leo will go on his South American tour as planned, following his surgery for lung cancer. He was diagnosed with lung cancer and underwent successful surgery in Rome on 13 October to remove a tumour on the lower part of his right lung. The 71-year-old is scheduled to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on 6-17 November, the Vatican said, adding that the he was looking forward to it "with great joy and enthusiasm". The Pope will follow the same programme as planned, visiting 10 cities on the tour. "I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," Pope Leo said. The Pope's trip will begin in Uruguay on 8 November, where he will visit the capital Montevideo, as well as other key cities. He will then travel to Argentina from November 11-17, visiting a number of places including the capital Buenos Aires. After that he will spend six days in Peru, where roughly 76% of the population are Catholic, and will include stops in Lima, Chiclayo, Cuzco and Pucallpa. Peru's Cardinal Castillo, the Archbishop of Lima, has said the trip would involve young people, women who help run community kitchens and members of the country's indigenous communities, according to Vatican News. The archbishop highlighted the Pope's close ties with the people of Chiclayo, where he lived for several years. The Pope has Peruvian citizenship. The Catholic Church sent him to Peru as a missionary in 1985, when he was 30 years old. He joined the Augustinian mission in Chulucanas, in the Peruvian department of Piura, and the following year, joined the mission in the city of Trujillo. For almost three decades, he worked between the US and Peru. Image source, Reuters Image caption, The Pope leaving Gemelli Hospital following his lung surgery on 17 October Leo announced the news of his lung operation himself to the world on 11 October during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung. He reassured pilgrims that the growth was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage" but that his doctors had advised him to have it removed. The surgery lasted for 90 minutes, and he was discharged from Rome's Gemelli hospital on 17 October. The Pope's surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said he was in an "absolutely satisfactory clinical condition", and said there were "no clinical reasons" why the trip should not go ahead. Tests showed the cancer was "localised". Since his operation, the pope has been resting and gradually resuming his work. He has been "adjusting his daily schedule in consultation with his doctors to prioritise his recovery while continuing to fulfill the responsibilities of his ministry," the Vatican said. Leo was "deeply grateful for the prayers and affection he has received from throughout the world," the Vatican said. The Vatican said Friday that Leo would cancel a planned trip to Assisi on October 27th, on the recommendation of his doctors. Related topics Pope Leo XIV More on this story Pope Leo XIV thanks wellwishers in first event after cancer surgery Published 18 October Pope discharged from hospital days after lung cancer surgery Published 17 October

title: Donovan backed for big future on signing new Celtic deal
description: Manager Martin O'Neill is sure Colby Donovan is destined for "very big future" as the Celtic full-back extends his contract until 2031.
content: Donovan backed for big future on signing new Celtic deal Image source, SNS Image caption, Donovan has stepped up to replace the injured Alistair Johnston at Celtic Published 26 October 2026 Manager Martin O'Neill is sure Colby Donovan is destined for "very big future" as the Celtic full-back extended his contract until 2031. The 20-year-old has made 15 starts for the Scottish champions this season, having made his debut in August last year. He was called up to the Scotland squad for the first time in September although he did not feature in any of the four Nations League matches under new boss Sebastien Pocognoli. "He has come in when we needed him, given everything for our cause," O'Neill told club media, going on to praise the defender's "tremendous attitude". O'Neill added: "I know the love Colby has for the club and I know what signing this deal means to him and his family. "I am sure that he will continue to progress and enjoy a very big future in the game, and I am so pleased that he sees his long-term future at Celtic." Donovan made 27 appearances last season and has been O'Neill's preferred deputy for the injured Alistair Johnston. "I've loved every single minute," said Donovan, "But it doesn't stop now. I'm just going to keep kicking on. "You've got to have that belief as a young player coming through here at Celtic. You see all the signings that they bring in. "When I was a kid, I knew I could come through and do it." title: Star Trek actor Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov, dies aged 90
description: He played the eager Russian crewman in the original Star Trek series and later appeared in Babylon 5.
content: Star Trek actor Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov, dies aged 90 Image source, CBS via Getty Images Image caption, Walter Koenig as Pavel Chekov on board the USS Enterprise during an episode of Star Trek from 1968 ByPaul Glynn Culture reporter Published 26 October 2026 Walter Koenig, who played the spirited Russian crewman Pavel Chekov in the original Star Trek TV series, has died aged 90. The US actor was a mainstay on the show as the eager and earnest navigator of the Starship Enterprise, from season two in 1967 until it ended in 1969, later reprising his role in the six original cast movies from 1979 through to 1991. In the mid-late 1990s, Koenig portrayed a very different character, the ruthless Psi Corps telepath Alfred Bester, in another sci-fi space series, Babylon 5. His Star Trek co-star George Takei led the tributes, external on social media on Monday, writing: "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend." Representatives for Koenig said in a statement given to the BBC: "Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world." They confirmed he had died "of old age at home in North Hollywood" on Sunday night, "surrounded by his daughter and niece". Koenig's Chekov added heart and humour to the adventures of the crew, led by William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk. Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu, added: "Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course." Image source, CBS via Getty Images Image caption, William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk speaking into his communicator with James Doohan as Montgomery "Scotty" Scott and Walter Koenig as Pavel Chekov (right) in an episode of Star Trek from 1968 Born in Chicago and raised in Manhattan, Koenig was the son of Soviet Jewish immigrants whose family had lived in Lithuania. He studied at the famous Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre in New York, alongside the likes of James Caan, Christopher Lloyd and Dabney Coleman. His big break came as the capable young Chekov, who would often joke that everything was invented in Russia. The character was introduced to appeal to younger audiences, with his Beatles/Monkees-style mop-top haircut. But Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry's studio also publicised the role as a response to criticism in Pravda, the main newspaper of the Soviet Communist Party, about the lack of a Russian character. This was a claim Koenig later denied. The American show, which aired during the Cold War and Space Race between the US and Soviet Union, imagined a future in which nations worked together to explore the galaxy, and Chekov's Russian heritage fitted that ideal. Koenig once said that the character's purpose on the NBC show was to "set out the bones of the plot and let McCoy, Spock and Kirk fill it in", according to the Hollywood Reporter., external He was arguably more integral to the movies, being nominated by the Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror for his work on The Wrath of Khan (1982) and The Voyage Home (1986). Koenig's seventh Star Trek film appearance was a brief one in Generations (1994) - mainly a Next Generation film - and he later voiced President Anton Chekov in the modern series Star Trek: Picard in 2023. He also wrote an episode of the original show's animated series spin-off, in 1973, titled The Infinite Vulcan. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Actor Walter Koenig speaking during The Original Series panel at the 18th annual Official Star Trek Convention in Las Vegas in 2019 A published author, Koenig's other on-screen credits included Columbo and Futurama. Earlier this year, his performance in the short film Mr Fleischmann saw him collect the Platinum Award for best actor at the 2026 Independent Shorts Awards, in recognition of his craft and career. He married Judy Levitt, who appeared with him in three Star Trek movies and Michael Straczynski's futuristic space opera Babylon 5, in 1965. And they were together until her death in 2022. The family suffered a personal tragedy in 2010, when their son Andrew, who played Richard "Boner" Stabone on the ABC sitcom Growing Pains, died by suicide aged 41. Koenig is survived by their daughter, the actress and screenwriter Danielle Koenig, who worked on the animated series Star vs. the Forces of Evil. Related topics Acting Film Television Star Trek

title: Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of 10 Downing Street
description: The building has been described as a "gloomy, mice-infested, bomb-curtained rabbit warren".
content: Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of 10 Downing Street Image source, Future Publishing/Getty Images Image caption, Andy Burnham has not formed a view on the suitability of Downing Street as a workplace, it is understood ByJack Fenwick Political correspondent Published 26 October 2026 Sir Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of Downing Street because of concerns about its suitability as a workplace, senior figures from his administration have said. Ministers and officials from successive governments have privately complained that Number 10's rabbit warren-like layout can lead to a lack of collaboration among those working there. James Lyons, who served as Sir Keir's director of communications, said over the weekend that "moving out was something that was discussed" during his time in post. Two other senior figures confirmed that discussions were had about moving staff into an open plan space in another government department. One source said a space inside the Foreign Office building, a short distance from Downing Street, had been identified. Both stressed that discussions did not go beyond an early phase and it's not known whether Sir Keir himself was consulted. There's no suggestion that the prime minister would have stopped living in Downing Street if the plan had gone forward. 10 Downing Street is more than 300 years old and is an amalgamation of three houses, which comprises more than 100 rooms. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Downing Street's White Room is one of many in the building The building was given to Robert Walpole, widely regarded as the UK's first prime minister, by King George II in 1732. Lord Walker, the boss of supermarket Iceland and a former adviser to Sir Keir, told the Financial Times on Friday that Number 10 was no longer "fit for purpose". He said: "I think we should turn it into residences, or a museum. It's a national treasure. It's amazing. But it's ridiculous. "It's just a Stuart-era building, not fit for purpose. It has tiny, tiny meeting rooms, all on different levels. There are hazards." Lyons, who led Sir Keir's communications operation from October 2024 to September 2025, posted on LinkedIn that "Lord Walker is 100% right". He added that staff were "deeply envious" of other departments and described Number 10 as a "gloomy, mice-infested, bomb-curtained rabbit warren". Lyons added: "Moving out was something that was discussed when I was in 10 Downing Street." Image source, AFP/Getty Images Image caption, Downing Street's famous staircase is lined with portraits of former prime ministers. Pictured are former PM David Cameron and British astronaut Major Tim Peake One source said "there were chats at senior staff level about moving to an open plan office in FCDO" (Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office). They said they didn't believe the idea went far, but said "the reason for discussion was serious" and added that the alternative plan was "about staff being open plan and able to collaborate". Sir Keir became increasingly frustrated at Whitehall's ability to deliver change during his time as prime minister. He was accused of picking a fight with civil servants when he said "too many people in Whitehall are comfortable in the tepid bath of managed decline". Darren Jones, who served as Sir Keir's chief secretary, told MPs last week that he "tried to abolish the Cabinet Office three times but failed". Image source, Getty Images Image caption, One of Downing Street's ornate rooms was used to stage government press conferences during the early days of the Covid pandemic He proposed replacing it with a new department that would "abolish those barriers and walls and make them just one integrated team, focusing on the same things and really supporting each other to move it forward". In his first days after succeeding Sir Keir, Andy Burnham created the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet. The move was seen as an attempt to ensure that things happen when metaphorical levers of power are pulled. It comprises Number 10, Number 10 North and other key parts of the Cabinet Office and is led by the UK's most senior civil servant, Dame Antonia Romeo. The government says the new office will "ensure the centre of government is focused on our top strategic priorities". Those around Burnham say he is yet to form a view about the adequacy of Number 10 as a workplace. Correction: This story has been amended to make clear King George II offered Number 10 Downing Street to Robert Walpole in 1732, not King George III as an earlier version stated. Related topics UK government Andy Burnham

title: Kane prematurely announced as Ballon d'Or winner - but he wasn't only one
description: Harry Kane's dream of winning the Ballon d'Or seemed as if it had come true on Monday when the organisers released an article claiming he had won the award.
content: Kane prematurely announced as Ballon d'Or winner - but he wasn't only one Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Harry Kane has become the first Englishman since 2001 to win the Ballon d'Or ByKeifer MacDonald BBC Sport journalist Published 26 October 2026 Harry Kane was crowned winner of the men's Ballon d'Or on Monday night, but a few hours earlier that confirmation appeared to have been announced prematurely. At 17:15 GMT, an article from the award's official website titled 'Harry Kane wins the 2026 Ballon d'Or' began to circulate online. The widespread sharing of the article caused confusion online, with some wondering whether France Football - the organisers of the award - had fallen short at the final hurdle of keeping the winner, who was voted for by journalists at the end of September, under wraps. That was until further digging on the Ballon d'Or website revealed that some of the other favourites to win the award - including Barcelona's Lamine Yamal, Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe - also had similar pieces penned and published about them. When asked about the articles by BBC Sport, a Ballon d'Or spokesperson said: "Some profiles of nominees prepared by BallonDor.com were inadvertently published online. "These articles had been prepared for all nominees and should in no way be considered as an indication of the final results or rankings." By 17:40, the articles about Kane and Mbappe had been removed from the website. Similar articles were also written about London City Lionesses star Alexia Putellas and Barcelona's Ewa Pajor. Putellas went on to be officially confirmed as the winner of the women's Ballon d'Or. That premature announcement may have sparked some excitement in Kane that this could be his year, but he only had to wait a little longer to find out for sure. title: Political battle intensifies within Labour over Rosebank oil field
description: Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra is urging the energy secretary to approve the controversial plans.
content: Political battle intensifies within Labour over Rosebank oil field Image source, PA Media Image caption, Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor John Healey visited the St Fergus Gas Terminal on Wednesday ByParis Gourtsoyannis Westminster correspondent, BBC Scotland Published 26 October 2026 Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra is wading into the political battle which is intensifying over the Rosebank oil field. He is making a direct appeal to Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to approve the plans to allow production to begin in the North Atlantic. Environmentalists have long campaigned against the proposals for drilling in the UK's largest untapped oil field, 80 miles north-west of Shetland. That the debate is now taking place within the Labour Party is a sign of the UK's recent journey on the politics of energy. When Labour came to power in 2024, it was with a manifesto pledge not to allow any new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea. Image caption, Rosebank is the UK's largest untapped oil field A legal challenge thrust the future of the Jackdaw and Rosebank developments into the hands of the then-Energy Secretary, Ed Miliband. At that point, senior offshore industry figures didn't hold out much hope of getting the go-ahead, given Miliband's deep commitment to renewable energy and his close political ties to Prime Minister Keir Starmer. All that was before the outbreak of the war between the US, Israel and Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz and made an ongoing cost of living crisis even worse. A new government under Andy Burnham entered 10 Downing Street with greater political freedom on the issue - and a new energy secretary to make the decisions. Strictly speaking, Jackdaw and Rosebank aren't applications for new drilling licences, just the adjudication of existing ones. But in political terms, the change of tone within Labour has been clear. What had been an article of faith on energy has become something much more flexible. It's a shift that's also plain to see within the SNP, with the Scottish government that once favoured a presumption against new oil and gas drilling now issuing a careful welcome to the Jackdaw announcement. Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh announced that production could begin on the Jackdaw gas field. She said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, the project would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy. Image source, EPA Image caption, Campaigners have called for the Rosebank plans to be rejected Environmentalists said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security. The UK government has always insisted that these decisions are part of a quasi-judicial process, judged on strict environmental criteria, not politics. But as attention turns to Rosebank, the politics are seeping in. Within hours of Jackdaw being granted approval, a briefing campaign began suggesting that Fahnbulleh was "minded" to reject Rosebank. Now, in the week of the Budget, reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval. The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank Neither cabinet minister has given their view publicly, of course. Fahnbulleh has insisted that the decision is "a regulatory process not a policy process," adding: "It sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because in the end only I can make it." Even though she isn't looking for advice, the Scottish Labour leader is willing to offer it. Marra is in Westminster meeting both Healey and Fahnbulleh in the run-up to the Budget on Wednesday. Marra believes that on jobs and investment, the case for Rosebank is clear. Image source, PA Media Image caption, Michael Marra will be meeting both the chancellor and the energy secretary "I supported Jackdaw and Rosebank because I think they're really crucial for the Scottish economy, for employment, and for the public finances as well," he told me. "We need to make sure that we're a country that people feel they can invest in. "You've seen what's happened with Jackdaw in recent days - a real boost to the morale and the investment climate in the north east of Scotland." He's also arguing for increased levies on banks in the Budget, to contribute towards the cost of help on the cost of living. That second request looks set to be granted - which is likely why Marra feels able to make it publicly. On Rosebank, we still can't say for sure how things will go. But the fact this debate is even being had is itself a symbol of our new energy reality. Related topics Scotland North Sea oil and gas Oil & Gas industry Climate More on this story Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm Published 2 days ago I will make final decision on Rosebank oil field, energy secretary insists Published 4 days ago Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences Published 5 days ago

title: Renfrew flooded after council failed to activate barriers during Storm Boelo
description: Renfrewshire Council said "predicted tide levels" for the storm did not meet the threshold needed to use the flood barriers.
content: Renfrew flooded after council failed to activate barriers during Storm Boelo Image caption, Renfrewshire Council said the threshold for using the barriers had not been met ByJonathan Geddes BBC Scotland Published 26 October 2026 A crucial part of a flood defence system that cost millions of pounds to install in Renfrew was not activated by a council ahead of Storm Boelo, despite an amber weather warning. Renfrewshire Council said "predicted tide levels and available forecast data" for the storm did not meet the threshold needed to use flood barriers. Water from the River Clyde burst through on Saturday night and swamped shops and homes in the area, causing serious damage to local businesses. The North Renfrew Flood Prevention Scheme cost about £10m to install. When it was launched in 2016, officials declared it would provide protection against any extreme flooding events. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland More stories from Scotland The flood prevention scheme includes both a three-metre high embankment and an underground pumping station. However, while the pumping station was in use, the council said its data - which included predicted tide levels for the Clyde - did not reach a required threshold for using the barriers. It said water levels on Saturday then rose far higher than had been predicted. Locals described being being knee deep in the water as it surged through. Image caption, Maureen Gray described water as gushing into local shops Maureen Gray works in the Ferry Nice Food takeaway on Ferry Road, a business owned by her daughter. The flooding on Saturday caused the shop's electrical equipment to go out, their fridges to break, and stock to be lost. It will now be shut for days. She said: "The damage is devastating. It was very sudden, within 15 to 20 minutes we were knee deep in the water. The banks broke and it was gushing in. "It's absolutely terrible the barriers weren't used. We've never actually seen them used before and all that money was spent on it. No-one knows yet what happened. "We know this is a flood area, but we expect help from the council." She added local businesses were now "rallying together" to help each other, but insurance would not cover them due to them being in a flood area. Gray said some of the businesses had also requested sandbags ahead of the storm hitting but the council had not provided them. In 2016, the embankment was described as providing a barrier against direct flooding from the Clyde. It runs westward for 0.62 miles (1km) from Ferry Road. The pumping station was intended to ensure tidal surges on the Clyde did not cause the Mill Burn to overflow and flood local properties. It was in operation over the weekend. The flood barriers were being tested and raised when BBC Scotland News was in the area earlier on Monday. Image caption, Tarun Wadhwa said he had never seen flooding as bad as during Storm Boelo Tarun Wadhwa, who runs the Green Gates Indian Restaurant in Renfrew, was checking the restaurant after closure when he saw the water coming in and rising rapidly. He said: "It was a disaster. I have never seen the water like that before. "This will be a big loss for me financially." He hopes to have the restaurant open again by Tuesday or Wednesday. A Renfrewshire Council spokesperson said: "The available forecast data and information for the severe weather at the weekend, which included the predicted tide levels for the Clyde, did not meet the currently set threshold for activating the flood barriers in Renfrew. "Unfortunately, the water levels which affected various locations on the estuary, raised significantly above predicted levels resulting in some local flooding. "We will review the arrangements in place to ensure these procedures reflect the impacts of a changing climate environment." Tens of thousands of homes across Scotland remain without power after the storm struck, with wind gusts in some areas of up to 85mph (137km/h). title: Coronation Street star returns to cobbles after 11 years
description: The Welsh actor is back as Owen Armstrong and looking forward to a "cracking" storyline.
content: Coronation Street star returns to cobbles after 11 years Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Ian Puleston-Davies has enjoyed a career in film and television and on the stage for more than 40 years ByJames McCarthy BBC Wales Published 26 October 2026 Coronation Street star Ian Puleston-Davies is returning to the soap opera more than a decade after he left. The 67-year-old will reprise his role as Owen Armstrong almost 11 years after the character left Weatherfield, following the collapse of his business and breakdown of his relationship with Anna Windass. The no-nonsense builder's return will see him move in with daughter Izzy and grandson Jake, and making it clear he blames Anna Windass' son, Gary Windass, for his family's misfortune. Puleston-Davies, from Flint, in Flintshire, said: "I can't wait to pick up where I left off 10 years ago. "It's brilliant to be back and to get stuck into a cracking storyline. Owen's back and he's still angry." Puleston-Davies will start filming Owen's return next week and will be back on screen on the cobbles in January. Since leaving Coronation Street, Puleston-Davies has starred in dramas Pennyworth, Tin Star and After The Flood. Coronation Street producer Kate Brooks said she was "thrilled" Puleston-Davies was back. "He wreaks havoc on the street, and his relationship with Gary is severely put to the test," she said. title: Edinburgh's Christmas ice rink axed after almost 30 years
description: The winter attraction will not be in the city this year after concerns over city centre access and funding.
content: Edinburgh's Christmas ice rink axed after almost 30 years Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The ice rink originally stood in Princes Street Gardens Published 26 October 2026 Edinburgh's Christmas ice rink has been axed after nearly 30 years, organisers have confirmed. The winter attraction, that has been on George Street in recent years, will not be present during the festive programme between 14 November and 27 January. The ice rink has been a feature of the city centre celebrations over the last three decades. It was once in Princes Street Gardens before moving to St Andrew Square and then George Street. Edinburgh's Christmas said the decision was made during the summer, due to uncertainty while part of Princes Street was still closed due to a fire that tore through the former Debenham's department store. The seven-week festival is organised by arts company, Unique Assembly Ltd, who produce Edinburgh's Hogmanay and Edinburgh's Christmas celebrations on behalf of the City of Edinburgh Council. An spokesperson for the company said, "An ice rink requires a great deal of advance planning, with the ice rink supplier, design of structures and site arrangements committed months ahead. "Those decisions had to be made over the summer, at a time when key parts of the city centre were closed and there was real uncertainty about when Princes Street would reopen and what the knock-on effects would be." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The rink was later moved to St Andrew Square The spokesperson also said significant costs and no opportunity for funding support led to the decision. "We know how much people have enjoyed skating as part of Edinburgh's Christmas celebrations, and we hope the rink will return as we start the planning process for future years," they added. The Christmas fair in Edinburgh, which has been a mainstay of the festive season in the city since 1999, will still have many of the usual features such as the traditional Christmas Markets, live outdoor events, and fairground rides. title: Lewis conquers self-doubt to hunt more Wales caps
description: Dragons prop Dillon Lewis is hoping for more Wales caps in the Nations Championship after a successful return from the international wilderness.
content: Lewis conquers self-doubt to hunt more Wales caps Image source, Huw Evans Picture Agency Image caption, Dillon Lewis played for Wales at the 2019 and 2023 World Cups ByChris Kirwan BBC Sport Wales Published 26 October 2026 Tight-head prop Dillon Lewis is braced for his next challenge in the Nations Championship after conquering self-doubt to impress for Wales last summer. The Dragons front-row forward has joined up with Steve Tandy's squad for the four November Tests. Lewis has retained his spot after grasping a chance in the summer when he started against the Barbarians, Fiji, Argentina and South Africa. He now has 60 caps, but the former Cardiff and Harlequins man returned from the international wilderness with some anxiety. "There was a lot of doubt going into it because I hadn't been in a squad for two years," said the 30-year-old. "I'd had a few injuries since my last call-up, so there were a lot of question marks – are you still good enough to be at that level? "I got thrown straight in with four starts, so hopefully they liked what they saw." 'I'm no yes-man' - new WRU chair to review region cut Published 1 day ago Wales deputy helps Ospreys make themselves at home Published 2 days ago Lewis made nine appearances for Dragons last season after suffering a torn calf in his fourth game for the club. His form when helping Filo Tiatia's side make the semi-finals of the Challenge Cup earned a return to Test rugby. "It was amazing to be back there and was something that I didn't think would happen, purely because of the length of my injury," Lewis added. "I had a small window to come back to play. I wasn't sure if I had done enough but I was over the moon." Lewis grasped his opportunity in the summer while Tomas Francis was rested and Archie Griffin had toe surgery. The Sale and Bath props have returned, meaning the Dragons man has a tough battle for action in the four November Tests. "There is some good competition and both of those tight-heads have been going well over the bridge," admitted Lewis. Image source, Huw Evans Picture Agency Image caption, Dillon Lewis played 29 times for Harlequins over two seasons Lewis won his 50th cap for Wales against France in 2023 and played in the past two World Cups. He credits Dragons for helping him reignite his Test career to chase selection for a third tournament in Australia next year. "It wasn't the start to my Dragons career that I wanted, with a lengthy spell on the sidelines, but I did enjoy the environment here," said Lewis. "Filo and the coaches give players the freedom to express themselves within the structure of the game model. "My recall was testament to what was being build here and an environment that allowed me to be comfortable. I am loving my rugby again." Wales have started preparations for their 7 November opener against Japan in Cardiff, which is followed by home Tests against New Zealand and Australia. Tandy's squad then play another fixture against a southern hemisphere rival at Nations Championship finals weekend at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium. Related topics Rugby Union Welsh Rugby Wales Rugby Union Dragons

title: Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising details
description: Anthropic’s IPO prospectus is 355 pages and full of never before disclosed company information.
content: Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know Image source, EPA Image caption, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has become a key figure in the current AI era. ByKali Hays Technology reporter Published 26 October 2026 Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic just released the required paperwork ahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market. The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by. Anthropic also detailed some of the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology. Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing. 1. Armageddon is an occupational hazard Every public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong. Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole. "Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said. It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies. But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models". One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology. 2. The company is haemorrhaging cash Anthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing. The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance. Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether. The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even. Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added. Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment. "As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added. 3. But luckily it has plenty of cash on hand Despite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about. At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day. Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined. Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants. The leasing of data centres alone is costing the company $321.4bn so far this year. Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth. Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said. 4. Anthropic relies on a few big customers Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers. A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10mn in the past year. An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract". The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue. Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted. Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year. Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time". The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed. 5. AI promises 'extraordinary' benefits to the world For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good. "Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said. That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity." "We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission. " Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice and making more efficient power grids and batteries. Decades of scientific progress could be condensed into years, accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy. Anthropic said AI could provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities. "Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said. Related topics Stock markets Artificial intelligence

title: BBC Women's Football Weekly

title: McDowell becomes latest major champion to exit LIV
description: Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell becomes the latest major champion to exit LIV Golf.
content: Former US Open winner McDowell confirms LIV exit Image source, Getty Images Image caption, McDowell joined LIV when the breakaway tour launched in 2022 ByMatt Gault BBC Sport NI senior journalist Published 26 October 2026 Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell has become the latest major champion to confirm his departure from LIV Golf. The 2010 US Open winner, 47, announced on Monday he has "decided not to pursue" LIV 2.0, the new version of the breakaway tour which is due to start in 2027. Major winners Jon Rahm and Louis Oosthuizen have also confirmed their departures, while McDowell's fellow countryman Tom McKibbin said he was exiting LIV to return to the DP World Tour last week. England's Tyrrell Hatton and Ian Poulter have also left the competition. Saudi's Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing from LIV in April - having pumped in more than $5bn (£3.8bn) - leading to the league filing for bankruptcy protection in the United States last month. It has secured a possible $300m (£224m) in financing from BC Partners Credit to try to move forward with 'LIV 2.0', but only a handful of players have so far committed. Former world number four McDowell joined LIV when it launched as a lucrative Saudi Arabia-backed project in 2022. The 11-time DP World Tour winner's best finish on LIV was a tie for second in Virginia in June 2025. "I've decided not to pursue LIV 2.0," said four-time Ryder Cup player McDowell. "I'm grateful for the opportunity I've had over the last four years and want to thank everyone who has been part of that journey. "I look forward to the next chapter in my career." Earlier this year, McDowell told BBC Sport NI he had held "really positive" talks about returning to the DP World Tour next season, adding he was "lucky to have that option". Poulter & Hatton leave LIV as exodus continues Published 3 days ago Rahm sacrifices £75m to secure exit from LIV Golf Published 16 October Former Open champion Oosthuizen quits LIV Golf Published 5 days ago LIV pushes on by appointing new senior adviser By Laura Scott Sports news correspondent Meanwhile, LIV has announced the appointment of former Taylor Made and Adidas executive Mark King as senior adviser. King said: "Having spent much of my career in golf, I believe there is a tremendous opportunity for LIV Golf to establish itself as a competitive and enduring force in the game." In the same announcement, the league said it "remains laser focused on advancing its conversations with players regarding their participation" in LIV 2.0. A deadline for player sign-ups had been set for Sunday, although BBC Sport understands there is a degree of flexibility to enable ongoing discussions with players. The lawyer representing LIV told a bankruptcy court hearing earlier this month it needed to sign a "sufficient number of players to have a bona fide golf league", and would know by the end of October whether it could proceed with LIV 2.0 or move to winding down the breakaway league. League sources told BBC Sport that LIV 2.0 is generating "inbound interest from established, elite professionals and emerging talent across global professional golf". Related topics Golf Northern Ireland Sport

title: Celtic & Rangers wait for stadium closures ruling
description: Rangers and Celtic submit appeals against a ruling that they must play their next home Scottish Cup ties behind closed doors following scenes of disorder in last season's competition.
content: Celtic & Rangers wait for stadium closures ruling Image source, SNS Image caption, Fans from both sides made it on to the pitch at Ibrox in March ByKheredine Idessane BBC Sport Scotland Senior Reporter Published 26 October 2026 Rangers and Celtic are waiting for a Scottish FA appellate tribunal to rule on their respective appeals against an order that they must play their next home Scottish Cup ties behind closed doors. The Glasgow clubs presented their cases on Monday and the tribunal will now undertake a period of deliberation before announcing whether the sanctions stand. The stadium closure penalty was announced in late August following the disorder at the end of last season's quarter-final tie at Ibrox, which Celtic won after a penalty shoot-out. The clubs are also challenging fines of £100,000 after their fans clashed on the Ibrox pitch. Supporters threw fireworks and other missiles and police officers were injured, while 43 arrests had been made by 25 August. Both clubs were warned that they could be forced play a second home match without supporters in the event of further unacceptable conduct. An independent review published in July concluded the incident "came within a very small margin of becoming a violent mass confrontation". The report, led by Mark Blackbourne, identified failings by both clubs and criticised the SFA for not taking a tougher approach to crowd disorder. An agreement was reached in September to have no away fans at any of the Old Firm derbies in this season's SPFL competitions. Related topics Football Scottish Football Celtic Rangers Scottish Cup

title: Welsh football sets out new aims - and says it needs more money
description: The Football Association of Wales (FAW) has called for greater funding for Welsh football after setting out ambitious targets for the next decade.
content: FAW sets ambitious 10-year plan but seeks more money Image source, FAW Image caption, FAW chief executive Noel Mooney wants to double the number of women and girls playing football in Wales by 2035 ByChris Wathan BBC Sport Wales Published 26 October 2026 The Football Association of Wales (FAW) has called for greater funding for Welsh football after setting out ambitious targets for the next decade. Wales' governing body says it wants more players, more pitches and more qualifications for major tournaments over the next ten years. The FAW's aims have been outlined in a new strategic plan that includes seeing the men's national side return to the top 20 of Fifa's world rankings. Their plan – Llunio Cymru – sets out a number of measures of success between now and 2036, all based on growing participation and helping the national sides "perform on the world stage". A key goal includes ensuring "quality" facilities are in place "within 15 minutes of every community" with a target of 100 new or upgraded pitches by 2030. But chief executive Noel Mooney admits the association will seek greater Welsh government support to develop new facilities, as it aims to increase the number of registered players in Wales by 30%. "We need a lot more support," said Mooney. "We're very clear on the growth of the female game that we need facilities for that. We've spent more than £30m over the last four years building pitches all across the country but we've a long, long way to go. "Thankfully, our resources are increasing - which is good - but we really need more support from Welsh government and from the 22 local authorities to deliver this." FAW posts loss for 2025 despite record revenue Published 16 April Welsh football bosses reveal cost to improve facilities Published 29 June FAW CEO Noel Mooney on Bellamy, FIFA and the grassroots game Club academies key to world ranking plans Key targets for the elite game include qualifying for every other major tournament and reaching the knockout stages of the co-hosted Euro 2028 and 2035 Women's World Cup. The FAW wants 80% of men's and women's national team players to be regular starters in the world's top five leagues, with the men's squad currently at 65%. One plan to achieve that is the introduction of two elite category club academies in the country, having admitted there has been a drop-off in talent produced for the men's national side following Swansea City's loss of category one status. Now the FAW said it will work with clubs to lend resources and staff and boost chances of new talent emerging – with an aim of producing two players per team every year. In the meantime, the FAW said it has developed data tracking of dual-qualified players and continue work on the national academies for the women's game. But the aims are underpinned by a long-term focus to grow the number of people playing the game. Funding and facilities vital Image source, Huw Evans Picture Agency Image caption, The FAW wants to reach the knockout stages of the 2035 Women's World Cup The FAW last set out targets in 2021. Qualification for the 2022 men's World Cup and the 2025 women's Euros were two key goals ticked. They also hit goals for increasing the number of people playing the sport, with the registered players count rising from 80,0000 to 120,0000. The FAW now want that number to grow to 160,000, including doubling the number of registered women and girls to 40,0000. They believe increasing playing numbers will help the top level while also boosting the nation's health – with the need for more facilities key. Projects in the 100 most deprived and diverse communities will be a priority, as well as a 50% increase in priority pitch access for women and girls. A specific strategy for the women and girls' game will be launched next month, and it will include doubling the money invested. Delivering the facilities needed by local authority areas would cost an estimated £150m, according to a recent review. Mooney says increased revenues from Fifa after the 2026 World Cup, and the planned windfall from staging Euro 2028, has helped the FAW nudge towards revenues of £50m. But he hopes the forthcoming Welsh government budget – the first since Plaid Cymru's election success earlier this year – will bring increased investment in capital projects. The FAW has secured UK government funding for some of its plans, but Mooney believes the Welsh government must now do more, describing the current £13m in capital expenditure as "a scratch on the surface of what we need to get to". "We've got confidence. We've had a lot of discussions with the new government and they've given us all of the signals that we're going in the right direction," he added. Mooney says football's place in preventative health was key, and noted that allocating greater resources was "a no-brainer". Other key aims include ensuring every match above under-12 level has a qualified, neutral referee, halving teenage drop-out rates, increasing the number of qualified coaches by a third and lifting average Cymru Premier attendances above 1,000.
