title: Trump faces backlash after invoking 9/11 in verbal assault on El-Sayed
description: The Democrat himself has hit back, as has Senator Bernie Sanders and a key Trump supporter from 2024.
content: Trump faces backlash after invoking 9/11 in verbal assault on El-Sayed To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: Moment Trump accuses El-Sayed of being a "jihadist" ByJames FitzGerald Published 26 October 2026 US President Donald Trump is facing a backlash after invoking 9/11 as part of a verbal assault on Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Michigan. Speaking at a rally in the state on Sunday, Trump accused El-Sayed of being "a jihadist". He introduced as a guest speaker the father of a passenger who fought back against the 9/11 hijackers. Trump also suggested that El-Sayed would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate". Critics condemned Trump's attack as Islamophobic. El-Sayed himself responded to Trump's decision to refer to him by his middle name, Mohamed, saying during a rally of his own: "I'll be Senator Mohamed to you, bro." To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: The BBC's Sarah Smith asks Democrat El-Sayed about tight Michigan Senate race He also said: "They think that by pointing at my name and my faith, that somehow you're going to ignore the fact that you can't afford your gas or your groceries, can't see a doctor." Appearing alongside him, Senator Bernie Sanders said: "The reason they are using Islamophobia against Abdul is because they have nothing to say about the real issues." El-Sayed is taking on Republican candidate Mike Rogers on 3 November. The race is expected to be one of the closest in the midterm elections, and is proving to be particularly bitter. The seat is considered to be one of just a handful that could decide the balance of power in Congress. It is currently held by the Democrats. El-Sayed, a former public health official who was born in the US to Egyptian parents, will be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate if he wins the seat. He has previously dismissed the various attacks made against him by both Trump and Rogers and denied any connection to extremist groups. Michigan Senate debate spotlights increase in anti-Muslim rhetoric as midterms race heats up Published 9 October Rapper Nicki Minaj joins Trump onstage at Michigan rally Published 1 day ago During his remarks on Sunday, Trump said: "If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas." Trump made a variety of allegations against El-Sayed and his family members, including that he was a member of the Muslim Brotherhood. He introduced as a guest speaker the father of Todd Beamer, a man from Michigan who was part of a group of passengers who fought back against the hijackers of United Airlines Flight 93, before the plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. "Michigan needs to stand up and fight, just like Todd did, to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol," Trump said. Claims centre on proscribed Muslim Brotherhood El-Sayed's opponents have sought to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist organisation that was founded in Egypt. Trump designated certain chapters of it as Foreign Terrorist Organisations earlier this year. Some of the scrutiny of the affiliations of El-Sayed and his family members relates to their writings from more than a decade ago. A social media post, external in 2012 by El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, appeared to refer to the movement, saying "my family has long been MB". El-Sayed's team have previously distanced him from other comments by Abdelhadi. Critics have also pointed to an opinion piece El-Sayed wrote in Huffington Post in 2011, external about pro-democracy protesters in Egypt. In it, he acknowledged concerns that "supporting democracy in Egypt might allow the country to fall to the hands of the Muslim Brotherhood". A year later he also allegedly signed an open letter by Egyptian Americans. In it, the group urged Mohamed Morsi, Egypt's first democratically elected president and a leader of the Muslim Brotherhood, to "purge the media and police" following the toppling of the authoritarian regime in the Arab Spring. This letter has not been discussed by El-Sayed. El-Sayed has previously denied any connection to the Muslim Brotherhood and has stressed his loyalty to the United States. Asked recently at a town hall event whether he would disavow the organisation, he responded: "Absolutely." Also in 2012, El-Sayed's current opponent Rogers, who was then a US representative and chairing the House Intelligence Committee, appeared to call for cautious engagement with the Muslim Brotherhood, telling Reuters, external: "Do I think there are moderate Muslim Brotherhood individuals we are going to have to reach out to and talk to? Yes but we are going to have to watch it carefully." HA Hellyer, senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) and an expert on Egypt, says the row has more to do with Islamophobia on the political right in the US than with the Trump administration's actual position on the Muslim Brotherhood. "If the accusation is to be taken sincerely, then [Trump] should surely have a problem with engaging with any government that has engaged positively with the Brotherhood or with groups that are even more to the right of the Brotherhood," Hellyer told the BBC. "He clearly has not done that." To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers clash in US Senate debate. 'Crossing a red line' Among the others who condemned Trump's attacks were one of his key supporters ahead of the 2024 presidential election. "The president's statements are out of line," Bishara Bahbah told the Associated Press. "They are crossing a red line. They are racist." Bahbah was the founder of Arab Americans for Trump, a group believed to have been important in helping the president connect with a wider range of voters two years ago. The group later changed its name, removing the reference to Trump. Trump clinched the White House in 2024 after victories in Michigan, which has a prominent population of Arab Americans, and a number of other swing states. Asked about accusations of Islamophobia, White House spokesman Davis Ingle said: "Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed wants to massively raise taxes, advocates for defunding the police, and wants to destroy the Michigan auto industry by banning gasoline powered vehicles. "President Trump will continue to call out complete and total extremists like El-Sayed without apology." Additional reporting by Jake Horton and Tom Bateman GUIDE: What are the US midterms? title: Army officer killed by reversing Warrior with faulty alarm - inquest
description: Second Lt Max George, 26, died during a training exercise on Salisbury Plain, an inquest is told.
content: Army officer killed by reversing Warrior with faulty alarm - inquest Image source, MOD Image caption, Second Lt Max George had exited the armoured vehicle when he was struck, an inquest heard ByKirsten Robertson, Wiltshire and Scott Ellis, Reporting fromSwindon and Wiltshire Coroners' Court Published 26 October 2026 An Army officer died when a Warrior armoured vehicle with a broken safety alarm was reversed into him, an inquest has been told. Second Lt Max George, 26, of Durham, died at the scene of a training exercise on Salisbury Plain, Wiltshire, on 21 June 2022. The ongoing inquest at Wiltshire and Swindon Coroner's Court heard an alarm, which was designed to alert the driver when the Warrior's rear doors were open, had been faulty since 2018. Lt Col Graham Watson, who led a service inquiry into the incident, said the driver of the Warrior "would have almost certainly stopped" if the alarm had sounded. More from Wiltshire Much-loved community pub on track to reopen Published 1 day ago Frustration as months of roadworks begin Published 1 day ago Theatres at risk and fighting back across the West Published 1 day ago Members of 5 Rifles got up at 05:00 BST on the day of the incident and left their barracks at 07:00, the inquest heard. They were undertaking an exercise called Combat Spirit, which formed the final part of four courses to qualify for Armoured Infantry. The inquest heard two groups of soldiers had converged on a target and 2nd Lt George was ordered to leave the Warrior through a rear door and take command on the ground. "[Second] Lt George exited the vehicle and was seen momentarily struggling either with a day sack or trying to free a radio antenna, which may have snagged," Col Watson said. "He then went to grab his weapon, which was still inside the vehicle and, simultaneously, the student commander commanded the gunner to reverse." Second Lt George's exit from the Warrior created a "clunking noise", which may have led the commander to assume he was safely off the vehicle and had shut the doors, Col Watson added. Image caption, The inquest took place at Wiltshire and Swindon Coroner's Court The armoured vehicle was stationary for between 38 and 43 seconds after the collision, the inquest heard, as soldiers shouted "wait" and horns sounded. A stop call was sent at 10:25, which halted the exercise. A built-in alarm system, which would have sounded a noise and shown a light to indicate the rear doors were open, did not work as a wire was broken, the inquest was told. Col Watson said: "The built-in alarm would have alarmed because the rear doors were open, and had that gone off the driver would have almost certainly stopped." Alarms had been installed on Warriors after two fatal incidents in the 1990s. Col Watson said several faults with the armoured vehicles were known about, but he told the inquest that these had not meant the vehicle should have been taken out of service. The inquest also heard the FV-511model involved in the incident was not ordinarily used for disembarking troops and close combat. "The student commander had done the majority of his training on the FV-510, which is the platoon variant of the vehicle," Col Watson said. "In general, the crew and service personnel within 5 Rifles were not that familiar with the FV-511 and its differences with the FV-510." 'A hole in our lives' A pen portrait was read out by 2nd Lt George's mother, Vivienne, during the hearing. She described her son as "modest and great fun" and said he would "quietly" fundraise through events like the Great North Run and Royal British Legion street collections. Second Lt George had won the Queen's Medal for best cadet when he passed out from the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, the inquest was told. He had also attended Durham School, earned a first in politics with Russian at Newcastle University and obtained a Distinction in his Masters in Eastern European and Eurasian Studies with Russian at the University of Glasgow. His mother continued: "Max had effortless leadership qualities and his potential was enormous," she said. "His loss has left a hole in our lives, he was the very best of all of us." The inquest continues. Get in touch Tell us which stories we should cover in Wiltshire Contact form Contact form Follow BBC Wiltshire on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. title: England-Republic of Ireland U15 World Cup game ends over alleged racism
description: The Under-15 World Cup Group C match between England and Republic of Ireland is abandoned after England allege an opposition player made a racist comment.
content: England-Republic of Ireland U15 World Cup game ends over alleged racism Image source, DAZN Image caption, England players gathered at the side of the pitch after the alleged incident By Laura Scott Sports News Correspondent Published 26 October 2026 England walked off the pitch during a match at the Under-15 World Cup after an allegation of racism by a Republic of Ireland player, which resulted in the game being abandoned. Following an altercation between players from both sides, shortly before the end of the match in Azerbaijan on Monday, an England player approached his bench and made a complaint to coaching staff. Match footage then showed England staff members relaying the complaint to the referee, alleging a racist slur had been said, and calling their players off. The Republic of Ireland were leading 4-1 at the time of the incident. World governing body Fifa told BBC Sport it is investigating and gathering reports. "Fifa is aware of an incident at the U-15 World Cup and Festival match between England and the Republic of Ireland," a spokesperson said. "The match was abandoned by the referee following England's refusal to continue. "The official reports are being gathered, and the matter will be referred to the independent disciplinary committee, who will decide in due course." The Football Association (FA) told BBC Sport it is awaiting more information and was in touch with Fifa, adding the wellbeing of players is a priority. The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) has also been contacted for comment. The aftermath of the incident The alleged incident happened in the final minute of the Group C match in Baku. Immediately following the allegation, England head coach Matt Thorpe was seen on the match coverage on DAZN asking for the referee to come over, before calling his players off the pitch. After an initial report from Thorpe, the referee told England's coaching staff, "I cannot hear". One of Thorpe's assistant coaches can then be heard telling the referee "we are reporting racism", before adding "we do not want to play". When another official came over, talking about what would happen after the match, the assistant told him: "No, our players do not want to play". He was later heard saying that a player was "upset". Heated words were then exchanged between each set of coaching staff, with both saying they were trying to protect their players. This is the first time the U15 World Cup and Festival has been played, and involves 189 countries and territories. Matches are played in an eight-a-side format, on smaller pitches, with 20-minute halves. Later on Monday, England beat Zimbabwe 2-0, while the Republic of Ireland were 4-1 winners over Cambodia. title: More than 60 Christians killed in Ethiopia 'massacre', church official says
description: One resident, whose 75-year-old father was killed, described it as an ambush, saying they were surrounded.
content: More than 60 Christians killed in Ethiopia 'massacre', church official says Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Attacks against Christians have been increasing recently, according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church ByOndiro Oganga Published 26 October 2026 More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks on Christians in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the country's Orthodox Church. One resident, whose 75-year-old father was killed, described it as an ambush. "We were completely unprepared and had no prior knowledge. They surrounded us from all four directions," he told BBC Amharic. The regional government said that it would take action against those responsible. A local official blamed the attacks on a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has not commented but has denied carrying out previous such attacks. A statement from the Holy Synod of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church said that 20 houses were burnt to the ground in the attacks. It did not say who was responsible. Eyewitness told BBC Amharic that five of those killed were children. A church official described the attacks on three areas in the Shirka district as a "massacre", saying security forces arrived at the scene but were unable to stop the assault. Many residents have now fled the area. Condemning the violence, the Orthodox Church said attacks against Christians had been increasing recently, and that "such actions undermine the country's values of mutual respect and peaceful coexistence". In a statement posted on Facebook, the Orthodox Church said it had repeatedly raised concerns about insecurity with authorities at different levels of government, but that "so far there has been no solution". The Ethiopian Human Rights Council, a non-governmental organisation, said in a report released in July 2026 that 458 people had been killed in attacks in that area over the previous four years. But this is one of the most deadly attacks in that period. The report said armed groups had repeatedly targeted local communities, particularly followers of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, in what it described as religiously motivated attacks. The government has previously blamed the OLA for the attacks, with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed saying violence targeting civilians and religious institutions was part of a plan to destabilise the country. The group, which says it is fighting for greater rights for the Oromo people, denies these allegations. Previous reports have also documented attacks against Muslims in the area. Residents who spoke to the BBC on various occasions have described the violence as both ethnic and religious in nature. About two-thirds of Ethiopians are Christians, mostly Orthodox, while one third are Muslim. title: Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global
description: The next fortnight sees two elections on different continents. The outcomes will shape geopolitics and the global economy, writes James Landale
content: Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global Published26 October 2026 Image source, Getty By James Landale Diplomatic correspondent, Reporting fromJerusalem In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world. By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other. Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress. A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global. For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined. The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region. And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy. Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls. Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has highlighted his alliance with US President Donald Trump - including in this Likud party election billboard in Tel Aviv Marc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC. But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. The massive aerial attack, which began in February, destroyed many military targets and killed much of Iran's leadership. But it failed to overthrow the regime which hit back hard across the Gulf and seized control of the Strait of Hormuz and the energy that flowed through it. The Iran question The sheer fact of the elections has already shaped decision-making. Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the campaign to talk up the possibility of launching a fresh attack on Iran. He has made new claims – without providing evidence – about Iran's nuclear threat, insisting again the Islamic regime must be overthrown. His aim: to shore up his reputation as a security leader, which took such a battering after the deadly 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel. US President Donald Trump has added to the speculation of renewed attacks on Iran by endorsing Netanyahu's re-election campaign, saying both men should "soon finish the job" in Iran. Yet for all the sabre-rattling, there have also been contradictory reports that Trump intervened to restrain Netanyahu from attacking Iran before polling day, fearing a fresh spike in energy prices would remind US voters of his unpopular war. Image source, REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst Image caption, President Trump has been campaigning on behalf of Republican congressional candidates, including in Michigan on Sunday, where there's a tight Senate race So might an attack on Iran, then, be delayed until after the elections? Israel's media is full of speculation Netanyahu could try to engineer his survival by attacking Iran as caretaker prime minister after the election. He would argue, so the theory goes, for a government of national unity – involving him – rather than a coalition between opposition parties. Netanyahu has long been seen as a great survivor of Israeli politics. If he were to lose power, he would face an official inquiry into his actions before the October 7 attacks and renewed legal proceedings involving allegations of corruption. So real is this speculation that Netanyahu's rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has already ruled out joining any unity government. Like all mainstream Israeli politicians, Eisenkot sees Iran as an existential threat to Israel and supports military action against the Islamic regime. But he has explicitly warned against escalating the war for political purposes. 'Legacy mode' Certainly, Trump may be more willing to attack Iran after the midterms if he is unconstrained electorally and hoping to extract himself from the war with one more push. Some analysts believe Iran is so economically weak from the war and economic sanctions that a fresh round of military strikes might encourage Iranians to overthrow the regime. Others see this as yet more wishful thinking. It is a strategy that has repeatedly failed, but still has currency in Washington. "After the midterms, he will be in legacy mode," one well-placed Western diplomat told me. "He will want to show agency on anything that is not the quagmire at home." In Israel there is a broad consensus across most parties about the threat from and the need to constrain Iran. But if voters elect a new government, they might have a prime minister with less political and personal investment in fresh attacks. In those circumstances, Trump has suggested his thinking may change, too. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi [a nickname for Netanyahu], America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote on social media. Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, Netanyahu has used this year's election campaign to talk up the possibility of a fresh attack on Iran Little wonder policymakers in Tehran have been following US opinion polls as closely as any analyst inside the Washington beltway. The risk, of course, is that any post-electoral strikes would plunge the Middle East into fresh chaos if Iran were to retaliate hard. Publicly and privately, Iranian officials have threatened to hit airports, pipelines, undersea cables, energy facilities, desalination plants as well as US bases and warships. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, wrote in the Financial Times that new attacks would put "civilian lives and the wellbeing of all regional states and the global economy at great risk". It's the economy The two elections again intertwine around the global economy. Affordability and cost of living have dominated campaigning for the midterms, issues made worse by Trump's war that raised prices as Iran choked the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz. The economy is also an election issue in Israel, where voters face high costs and low wages. But here, too, the war plays its part with soaring defence spending putting even more pressure on the public finances. Trump has sought to appease voters ahead of the midterms. He has lifted sanctions on Russia, hoping in vain that by importing diesel from Moscow, prices might fall significantly. He has been taking a tough line with Ukraine, calling on its leadership to make concessions in the hope – also so far in vain – of claiming a foreign policy victory. But Republican ire at his controversial strategy is growing. Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a frequent critic of Trump, told CBS News: "If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid [favour] for Vladimir Putin." Image source, Chris Torres / EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, Early voting has already started in many US states for next month's midterms One consequence of the Iran war – along with Israel's military operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank – is that traditional bipartisan support in the US has fractured. Abdul El-Sayed, the left-wing Democratic candidate for the Senate in Michigan, campaigns on cutting military aid to Israel. "An ally that takes your money, to push you into wars you shouldn't be fighting, is not an ally," he told ABC News. The US and Israel initially attacked Iran to destroy its ballistic missiles, degrade its nuclear capability, weaken its support for proxy militias and even oust the entire regime. Since then its war aims have changed to reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Brad Lander, a Democratic congressional candidate in New York who also sits on the left of his party, chose even to travel to the West Bank only days before polling. He helped Palestinians harvest olives and was briefly detained by Israeli forces, all grist to his social media electoral mill. In the history of US politics, this is not normal. Even Netanyahu is warning that Israel may in future have to survive without a US security blanket. Image source, Abir Sultan Credit / EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, The leader of Israel's Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, has ruled out joining a unity government after the elections Of course, if Israel's prime minister were to lose, his departure would end a scratchy bromance that has seen Trump blow hot and cold. Last week the president called his Israeli counterpart a "great warrior prime minister". During the summer, he said Netanyahu was "effing crazy". A new Israeli leader would have to forge a new relationship with an outgoing US president, a very different dynamic. If the Democrats were to win greater control in Congress, that might place some check on blanket US support for Israel. Congress has traditional powers that it can use to restrain military spending. It could also cut military aid to Israel. But as president, Trump would retain significant executive power – and a veto – to continue prosecuting the conflict as he saw fit. The decision by Israel and the US to go to war with Iran earlier this year transformed the global economy and international geopolitics. The choices voters in both nations make in coming days may shape where the world goes next. Top image credit: Getty. title: Tributes paid to man killed by falling tree in Storm Boelo
description: Richard Baines was the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Gardens near Stranraer.
content: Tributes paid to man killed by falling tree in Storm Boelo Image source, RBGE Image caption, Richard Baines worked at Logan Botanic Garden near Stranraer ByNichola Rutherford , Reporting fromCastle Douglas and Lori Carnochan, BBC Scotland, Reporting fromLogan Botanic Garden Published 26 October 2026 Tributes have been paid to a man who died after being hit by a falling tree in Dumfries and Galloway. Richard Baines, 60, the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden near Stranraer, died during Storm Boelo on Sunday morning. It is understood that he was walking near his home in Mid Kelton, just outside Castle Douglas, when the accident happened. David Knott, director of horticulture at the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh, said they were "desperately sad, devastated" by the news. "He had a warmth, a genuine sense of humour, he always made time for individuals and that's one of the tributes that has been said many times this morning," Knott told BBC Scotland News. "He always found time for his colleagues. And he was always very supportive in providing opportunities for the next generation of horticulturalists. He was a very genuine and warm human being." Logan Botanic Garden is home to a range of exotic plants as it benefits from the warming influence of the Gulf Stream. It is one of four Scottish gardens run by the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh. Knott said Baines came up with the description of Logan as "Scotland's most exotic garden" and worked hard to promote both the garden and the south-west of Scotland. Image source, RBGE Image caption, Baines described Logan as "Scotland's most exotic garden" Knott said his colleague would be remembered for his "passion and enthusiasm for plants" and for significantly expanding the plant collection at Logan. During his tenure, he was primarily responsible for significant developments including the first public conservatory to be powered by green energy in the UK. Baines also participated and led fieldwork in China, the Canary Islands and Vietnam, from where seven plant species new to science were catalogued. "Richard's contribution as an enthusiastic plantsman and curator at Logan and to the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh's wider work and culture has been immeasurable, and he will be deeply missed by many," Knott said. Image caption, The accident happened at Mid Kelton, near Castle Douglas, in Dumfries and Galloway Dumfries and Galloway MSP Finlay Carson also paid tribute to Baines, a former school friend. "Richard was a remarkable gentleman and a good friend to many, always ready with a warm smile, a kind word and an infectious enthusiasm for life," he said. The Scottish Conservative MSP said that Baines' work at Logan Botanic Garden had earned him national recognition. "His expertise, commitment and achievements brought credit not only to his profession but to Galloway as well," he added. Baines died as Storm Boelo swept across Scotland, causing flooding, travel disruption and power cuts over the weekend and into Monday. The wind picked up on Saturday and an amber warning was in place from Saturday night. The Scottish garden helping Vietnam's plant life Published 6 October 2023 Rare tree offspring given lifeline at Scottish botanic garden Published 17 September Galloway Mountain Rescue Team (GMRT) said they had responded to "one of the most gruelling callouts our team had faced in recent history" on Saturday. They were called to Curleywee in the Minigaff Hills to help a runner who was injured while taking part in the OMM mountain challenge. In a post on Facebook, external, they said 10 members of their team pushed through "torrential rain, severe wind and unforgiving boggy ground" to reach the casualty. A coastguard helicopter had to turn back due to the deteriorating weather. The team said they had to carry the casualty off the hill, with the help of members of the OMM safety team, before handing the runner to the Scottish Ambulance Service. OMM has faced some criticism on social media for allowing the run to go ahead in the poor weather. A spokesperson said the course was closed and all competitors accounted for before the amber wind warning took effect at 21:00 on Saturday. "The event team continually assessed the mountain weather forecast in the build-up to and throughout the event, with competitor safety guiding every decision," they added. The spokesperson said they were grateful for the "understanding and support" shown as the event was adapted to the forecast conditions. They said they would be making as a donation to GMRT, as is usual practice at OMM events whether or not a callout takes place. Related topics Severe weather Castle Douglas Mid Kelton Stranraer

title: 'Cutting doubles would destroy careers & dreams' - angry players urge ATP rethink
description: More than 150 doubles players - including Wimbledon champions and tennis legends - urge the ATP to rethink "drastic" cuts which they believe could kill the format.
content: Angry players urge ATP rethink over doubles cuts Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Finland's Harri Heliovaara (left) and Britain's Henry Patten - the world number ones and reigning Wimbledon champions - have signed the open letter By Jonathan Jurejko BBC Sport tennis news reporter Published 26 October 2026 More than 150 men's doubles players - including British world number one Henry Patten and the legendary Bryan brothers - have urged the ATP Tour to rethink "drastic" changes which they believe could kill the format. In a show of collective action, the players have written an open letter to the men's governing body as they fight proposals which would cut draw sizes and reduce prize money from 2028. "We're at risk of losing a discipline of tennis which is historic - but has a big future," Dutch player Sem Verbeek, one of the architects of the letter, told BBC Sport. "These proposals would destroy careers, livelihoods and dreams." The ATP proposed halving the doubles draws at its flagship Masters 1000 events to 16 teams, with smaller tournaments reduced to eight teams. The percentage of prize money devoted to doubles could fall from 20% to 10% - with the difference redistributed to singles players. 'You're taking our jobs' - doubles players angry at proposed cuts Published 3 July On Monday, a group of 137 current players, 28 legends and 20 national federations signed a letter which they hope will pressure the ATP into rethinking the proposals. The tour's board - comprised of chairman Andrea Gaudenzi, four tournament representatives and four player representatives - will vote on the plans at next month's ATP Finals in Turin. The doubles reform is part of a wider review by the ATP, which it says is designed to "strengthen" the tour from 2028. The ATP aims to create "a more sustainable long-term model", insisting it wants to "maintain the important role" of doubles. "Commercial success matters. Fairness, player welfare and the long-term health of tennis matter just as much," the players' letter says. "Let us grow tennis together, without leaving doubles players behind." Why is doubles under threat? The proposals provoked an angry response from the men's doubles cohort when they were revealed in July. British pair Lloyd Glasspool and Julian Cash, who won Wimbledon in 2025 and became world number ones, accused the ATP of trying to "kill part of the sport". Others within tennis believe reform is needed. They suggest a 20% share of the prize money for doubles is disproportionate to the interest shown by fans. The doubles players argue the ATP should do more to promote their discipline and attract greater audiences, pointing out it is the format played by most club members and therefore more relatable. The ATP says the proposals are based on data-led analysis centred on costs, revenue and viewership. With fewer singles players now competing in doubles, it believes the current size of the standalone doubles events puts severe strain on tournaments. "We support progress. We also understand the need to grow the sport, strengthen tournaments and increase commercial value," the players' letter says. "Still, the proposed reforms go much too far." Might the dispute lead to legal action? Reigning Wimbledon champion Patten recently told BBC Sport the players were facing "an uphill battle", but remained "optimistic" the tour would consider counter-proposals. Since Wimbledon there have been several meetings between both sides, including recently at the Shanghai Masters. The players still believe there is little appetite for negotiation from the ATP. But ATP sources insist a compromise is likely to be found. At this stage the players are "squarely focused" on "meaningful discussion and collaborative innovation", says Verbeek. Mike and Bob Bryan - the identical twins considered the greatest doubles pair of all-time - said they would support the group considering legal action to protect their discipline. In 2005, the American brothers led players in a lawsuit against the ATP, when it planned radical changes to doubles. "The tour's in the healthiest financial state it's ever been - in our opinion it should be creating more opportunities," Bob Bryan told BBC Sport in an interview at Wimbledon in July. Mike Bryan added: "These proposed changes are anti-competitive. That's the stance we had to take in 2005. We still believe in doubles and we believe in the players fighting for this." title: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting
description: Two bishops in images that show them praying with Trump have said they believed the meeting was private.
content: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting Image source, x.com/MargoMartin47 Image caption, A screengrab of a clip from the 22 October meeting at the White House. ByBernd Debusmann Jr White House reporter Published 26 October 2026 Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were released and prompted many to ask if they were making a political statement. Photos and video of the 22 October meeting show a group of bishops standing around Trump at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, one of those pictured, said he had believed the meeting was private and not "a political photo opportunity". Trump and Pope Leo XIV have a contentious relationship, and some US bishops have criticised the White House's immigration stance. Trump won the support of 55% of Catholic voters in 2024, a Pew study found. In a statement posted online, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, said the meeting was arranged by officials with the White House Faith Office to discuss issues including immigration, visas for international clergy and the "exploitation of vulnerable poor persons". "In no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," Joensen said. "I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes," he added. A video of the meeting was released by Margo Martin, a special assistant to the president and communications adviser who frequently shares behind-the-scenes images of Trump on social media. Archbishop Grob said that after 90 minutes of meetings with officials, the religious leaders were ushered into the Oval Office to pray with Trump. Grob said images of the meeting later caused concern among some of his congregants. "I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he wrote. "I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family have been harmed by the president's policies," he added. Grob said none of the participants in the meeting gave permission for the public distribution or posting of video or photos of the event. When contacted for comment by the BBC, the White House did not directly address questions regarding the meeting or subsequent comments by the two bishops. "There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it," White House Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement. According to Pew Research Center, which analyses religion in the US, opinions of Trump's performance have slipped among all major religious groups. In a survey this month, 30% of all US Catholics said they approved of his job performance, compared to 47% when he returned to the White House in 2025. That could have an effect on the 3 November midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress. More Catholics in the survey, 42%, said they preferred the Democrats running in their local House of Representatives races, where slightly less, 39% favoured Republicans. During his second term, Trump has had a tense relationship with the head of the Catholic church, Pope Leo, as he has moved aggressively to remove people believed to be in the US illegally. Nine days before the Oval Office meeting with the bishops took place, Bishop Brendon Cahill and Walter Kim, the president of the National Association of Evangelicals, issued a statement urging "Christian compassion and wisdom in the immigration debate". They said the immigration clampdown has led to the "sowing of fear, the fracturing of families, the deprivation of due process, and the vilification of our neighbors." The US Conference of Catholic Bishops also recently condemned the Trump administration's plans to livestream a military execution, which were later scrapped. Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are Catholics who have visited the Vatican during Trump's second term. A Midwestern member of the bishops' conference, Robert Barron of Minnesota, agreed to serve on the president's Religious Liberty Commission last year, as did former New York Archbishop Timothy Dolan. title: Police arrest teenager after shooting that injured 12, including children, in Florida
description: The incident happened on Saturday night, close to an American football stadium where a game had just been played.
content: Police arrest teenager after shooting that injured 12, including children, in Florida Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The incident happened close to Florida A&M University's Bragg Memorial Stadium (file image) ByMadeline Halpert Published 26 October 2026 Police have arrested a teenager in connection with a shooting on Saturday that injured 12 people in Florida. The incident took place at 20:00 local time (01:00 Sunday GMT), close to an American football stadium in the city of Tallahassee where a university game had recently been played. Eleven people were injured by gunfire, local police said, while another hurt their ankle while fleeing the scene. Six of the victims were children. Anthony Rivers III, 15, has been charged with 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent. Police said the shooting followed an altercation between people who knew each other and that additional arrests were possible. None of the victims appear to have been the intended targets, they said in a statement. "What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families," Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said. "We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family impacted by this tragedy." Police said on Sunday that six people were in hospital, including one person who was in a critical condition. Five people had been released. Revell told a press conference on Sunday that police had had to carry victims in their arms to get them to emergency responders because of the crowds from the football game. title: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp chat helped turn Brazil election around
description:
As polls pointed to defeat, millions joined a 'Lula's Army' channel 
that is credited with helping transform online enthusiasm into real-world mobilisation.
content: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn Brazil election around Image source, Reuters Image caption, Lula's supporters mobilised en masse despite polls pointing to a defeat for the incumbent ByJulia Braun, Rute Pina and Luiz Fernando Toledo, BBC News Brasil, Reporting fromLondon & São Paulo Published 26 October 2026 A WhatsApp channel created to support Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's re-election campaign is being credited by allies with helping deliver one of the most unlikely comebacks in recent Brazilian politics. Brazil's left-wing president had been trailing right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro, but managed to turn the race around in just three weeks. The rise of 'Lula's Army' At a moment when many doubted Lula could reverse the result, a WhatsApp channel called Lula's Army emerged, and rapidly grew to 10.8 million followers. Led by Congressman André Janones, the operation encouraged supporters to share videos, promote hashtags and recruit new voters. Its dramatic growth between the two rounds was particularly notable because it appeared to reverse a long-standing imbalance in Brazilian politics. For years, conservatives aligned with former President Jair Bolsonaro had been widely seen as dominating online political mobilisation, especially on platforms such as WhatsApp and Telegram. Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Lula called André Janones "our General" after his major contribution paid off The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning. Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media. Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off". "Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions. On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro. The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula. In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day". Social media's role in the comeback Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult. While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation. Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback. Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground. According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights. "It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media." By contrast, Holzhacker argues that Flávio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively. Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media. "It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters." In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement. "Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says. She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration. "I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters." Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead. In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed. "We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government." title: Thousands still without power after Storm Boelo
description: Up to 5,000 homes in north-east England and Cumbria still have no power following Storm Boelo.
content: Thousands still without power after Storm Boelo Image caption, A tree crashed into the roof of an unoccupied new-build in Darlington ByJason Arunn Murugesu North East and Cumbria Published 26 October 2026 Thousands of households across Cumbria and parts of north-eastern England remain without power in the wake of Storm Boelo. Electricity North West said it was working to restore power supplies to about 3,000 homes, with the worst affected parts of Cumbria including Allerdale, Copeland and South Lakeland. Additionally Northern Powergrid said hundreds of customers were cut off in Northumberland and County Durham. On the trains, Northern said disruption was expected on its services between Carlisle and Newcastle, as well as between Lancaster and Barrow. Derek Story, from Scotby near Carlisle, said it was "disappointing" how long it was taking to get power back on as the lack of a mobile signal meant he felt a bit "isolated". Stephen Cawley, also from Scotby, said the absence of an internet connection had led his family to spend time together the old-fashioned way. "We're back to talking to each other and playing Scrabble," he said. Image caption, Many trees have toppled over in the storm, including in South Shields Westmorland and Furness Council said it responded to 90 calls over the weekend, 70 of which involved fallen or dangerous trees. In Whitehaven, the storm ripped out the power cable running along West Pier. Whitehaven Harbour Commissioners posted on Facebook: "The pier will remain closed while the cable is recovered from the water and returned to its proper position." Meanwhile a tree fell on to a completed new-build house at the Homes by Esh development at Havelock Park in Darlington. It left a huge hole in the roof of the building which was yet to be occupied. Trees also crashed into allotments near Durham, blocking a footpath leading into the Flass Vale nature reserve. Image source, Whitehaven Harbour Commissioners Image caption, Whitehaven's West Pier remains closed until further notice after the storm damaged a power cable National Rail said trains between Ashington and Newcastle would not call at Northumberland Park, while services from Newcastle to Ashington would not stop at Blyth Bebside. Electricity North West offered free welfare support to residents at Cartmel Food Shed Takeaway until 14:00 GMT, as well as at locations in Ulverston and Askam-in-Furness. Paul Killilea, of Electricity North West, said the majority of homes affected should have their power restored on Monday, but hundreds of homes could remain without power overnight. "[There is] a significant amount of work to do today," he said. The A66 reopened on Sunday evening after it was closed in both directions between the A67 near Bowes in County Durham and the A685 near Brough, Cumbria, because of strong winds - a section of road nearly 15 miles long. The Redheugh Bridge was shut on Sunday afternoon due to high winds but was later reopened. The Shields Ferry is running following its cancellation on Sunday. A yellow wind warning was issued in Cumbria, to apply from 18:00 GMT on Monday. title: Howe and Nagelsmann high on Man Utd's list if Carrick sacked
description: BBC Sport takes a look at who could replace Michael Carrick at Manchester United if the head coach was sacked.
content: Carrick arrives at training ground with future unclear Image source, Press Association Image caption, Manchester United have gone eight matches without victory under Michael Carrick By Sami Mokbel Senior football correspondent Published 26 October 2026 Updated 50 minutes ago Michael Carrick arrived at Manchester United's training ground on Tuesday morning as doubts persist over the head coach's future at Old Trafford. The 45-year-old's position is under major threat following United's poor start to the season, with work towards identifying his successor believed to be ongoing. But no decision over Carrick's future had been communicated by Tuesday morning, with the Englishman arriving before first-team training at about 10:00 GMT. It remains to be seen whether Carrick will take training, with United preparing to take on Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday (12:30 GMT). Director of football Jason Wilcox, who has been criticised by supporters over the club's transfer business in the summer, was also pictured arriving at Carrington. It is understood Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann both feature prominently on the list of candidates the club has explored to potentially replace Carrick, and that both managers are aware of United's interest. Sources have also indicated Aston Villa boss Unai Emery is admired at United, but the fact he is under contract would complicate any move for the Spaniard. Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that former Newcastle boss Howe is fully open to joining United if Carrick loses his job. Sources have told BBC Sport that Newcastle would be owed a multi-million pound compensation package should Howe join Manchester United - or any other club - following his resignation from the Magpies in the summer. Howe stepped down in July following five years at Newcastle. He had three years to run on his deal. Nagelsmann is available after leaving his job as Germany head coach after the World Cup, while Antonio Conte - who has also been linked with Juventus - is open to returning to football after leaving Napoli in May. Carrick signed a two-year deal with United at the end of last season, after guiding the club to a third-place finish in the Premier League during an interim spell in charge. Should he be dismissed, the 20-time English top-flight champions will be looking to appoint their eighth permanent manager or head coach since Sir Alex Ferguson departed the club in 2013 on the back of winning their most recent title. Here, BBC Sport takes a closer look at the contenders who could be up for the job. Why is Wilcox in line of fire from Man Utd fans? Published 20 hours ago End approaching for Carrick but Man Utd fans make clear who they blame Published 1 day ago MNC: No smiles for the cameras at Manchester United Eddie Howe Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Howe resigned as Newcastle head coach in July The Englishman has been out of work since leaving Newcastle in the summer. Howe, 48, helped the Magpies end their 56-year wait for a trophy when he led them to League Cup glory in 2025 and secured two Champions League qualifications in his five years in charge. The former Bournemouth and Burnley boss is available and would be considered. Sources have indicated Howe is open to returning to management with United specifically after leaving St James' Park in the close season. Antonio Conte Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Conte won the Premier League title in his first season at Chelsea in 2017 The Italian has been out of work since leaving Napoli in June and is interested in the job. Conte has won Serie A titles with three different clubs as manager - Juventus, Inter Milan and Napoli. The 57-year-old led Chelsea to the Premier League title in 2017 and FA Cup in 2018. During his time at Tottenham between November 2021 and March 2023 he helped them qualify for the Champions League. Julian Nagelsmann Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Nagelsmann left the Germany national team in the summer Also out of work, interested and high up on the club's list of contenders. The German left the role of manager of his country's national team after a World Cup last-32 defeat on penalties by Paraguay last summer, having lost in the quarter-finals of Euro 2024 to Spain. Nagelsmann, 39, earned his reputation as a young coach at Hoffenheim and RB Leipzig before he landed the Bayern Munich job in 2021. He led them to the Bundesliga title in 2022 but was sacked the following season amid fluctuating form. Unai Emery Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Emery guided Aston Villa to the Europa League trophy last season The Aston Villa head coach's stock is high at United given how he has steered the Midlands club to Champions League qualification twice since arriving in 2022. However, he would be difficult to prise from his current role given his contract runs until 2029. Emery, 54, has won five Europa League trophies at Sevilla, Villarreal and at his current club while he also helped Paris St-Germain to domestic honours in a two-year stint there. However, he lasted just 18 months at Arsenal before being sacked in 2019. Fabian Hurzeler Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Hurzeler has impressed so far at Brighton The Brighton manager is another who is well liked at Old Trafford, but the Seagulls would have little interest in discussing his availability. It would be a difficult deal to do financially for United as well. Hurzeler, 33, guided German club St Pauli to promotion to the Bundesliga in 2024 before he was picked up by Brighton where he is enjoying a very strong start to his third season at the club. Cesc Fabregas Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Fabregas won 110 caps with the Spanish national side The former Arsenal midfielder masterminded United's humiliating 4-1 defeat in Como on Wednesday night in a game that pushed Carrick to the brink. Fabregas, 39, is considered one of the best young coaches in Europe for his work in helping to steer Italian club Como from Serie B to the Champions League and will be wanted by many major clubs in the coming months. title: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak
description: The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa.
content: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak Image source, Handout Image caption, Henry Nowak was 18 when he was stabbed to death in Southampton in December 2025 ByHenry Moore Published 26 October 2026 Updated 4 hours ago Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak. The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused and had acted in self-defence. Digwa was jailed for life on 1 June, with a minimum term of 21 years. Following the teenager's murder, police bodycam footage of him being handcuffed as he lay dying led to intense scrutiny of the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and sparked wider debates around knife laws, race, policing and public trust. The review, which was welcomed by Nowak's family, will be led by former Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC. "We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate," Mahmood told the House of Commons on Monday. Mahmood said the review will investigate what was known about Nowak's killer and if there were missed opportunities to intervene as well as the treatment of his family in the justice system and whether they received enough support. In a statement published on Monday, the Home Office said the review will be carried out in two parts. Phase one will cover the police, health services, local authorities educational institutions and faith organisations, including if any concerns were raised relating to weapon possession and violent behavior, the statement said. It will also look to determine if there were missed opportunities to prevent Nowak's murder. Chalk told Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that would include looking at whether any reports had been made but people or organisations had held back due to a "misplaced sense of cultural sensitivity". Phase two will follow after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has concluded its investigation into the actions of police officers who attended the scene. It will consider the actions of the IOPC and "if necessary" the police, the Home Office added. The IOPC launched its own investigation into the response on the night of Nowak's death after bodycam footage showed the 18-year-old was handcuffed and left dying on the floor despite informing officers of his injuries. The investigation was launched despite a sentencing judge ruling Nowak would not have survived his injuries, however quickly he received treatment. The Nowak family described the announcement as a "significant moment in our fight for justice." "We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for," they added in a statement. "Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have." Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed the decision to launch the review. "There must be proper accountability for those who failed Henry and his family," she said. The review is due to report in five months. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: What CCTV tells us about how Henry Nowak's murder unfolded Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was a first-year accountancy and finance student at the University of Southampton when he was murdered. On the night of Nowak's muder, it was Digwa's brother who called 999, claiming Vickrum had been attacked "racially". Bodycam footage released by Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary, with the permission of Nowak's family, showed officers speaking to Digwa and others while Nowak lay on the ground. Nowak could be heard repeatedly saying that he had been stabbed and could not breathe. Violent disorder broke out in Southampton in the days following the release of the footage. After Digwa's sentencing, Nowak's father Mark called for a "full, fearless and transparent" investigation into the police response. But he also urged people not to use his son's death to "create further division, hatred or tension". title: Why is Wilcox in line of fire from Man Utd fans?
description: With Michael Carrick's position as Man Utd boss under scrutiny, focus has also turned to director of football Jason Wilcox.
content: Why is Wilcox in line of fire from Man Utd fans? Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Jason Wilcox (fourth from left) watched United's 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth alongside chief executive Omar Berrada By Simon Stone Manchester United reporter Published 26 October 2026 As the clock ticked down during Manchester United's 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday, the home fans made it clear what they thought about director of football Jason Wilcox. Singing his name along with an obscenity, the message was brutal and to the point. It was sung by a majority of the United supporters, and on more than one occasion. It came less than two weeks after United defender Lisandro Martinez had launched a blistering attack on the club's hierarchy for not strengthening the squad, with a particular message for Wilcox. "I expect more from our technical director," said Martinez. Pressure is growing on United boss Michael Carrick after eight games without a win - their worst run since 2015-16 - and two three-goal defeats in a week. But focus is turning to Wilcox too. Howe and Nagelsmann high on Man Utd's list if Carrick sacked Published 50 minutes ago End approaching for Carrick but Man Utd fans make clear who they blame Published 1 day ago Why is Wilcox under pressure? Wilcox is a former England winger who won the Premier League with Blackburn in 1994-95. He joined United in April 2024 - initially as technical director after 15 months in a similar role at Manchester City, where he had previously been in charge of the academy. At City he worked with current United chief executive Omar Berrada and also Stephen Torpey, who was appointed United's head of academy in August 2025. When he arrived, it was said by United officials that Wilcox would work across all technical areas of the club to achieve "highest standards of performance" and would be answerable to the sporting director. That changed the following December, when that sporting director - Dan Ashworth - was sacked amid a difference of opinion over who should replace Erik ten Hag as manager. Ten months on, a poor series of results and dissatisfaction with transfer business has put Wilcox in the spotlight. There are some who have sympathy with the position Wilcox finds himself in. The 55-year-old is not in charge of transfer budgets, which are set at a higher level. Wilcox was also - obviously - not responsible for the injury Manuel Ugarte sustained playing for Uruguay at the World Cup, which wrecked a plan to sell the midfielder in the summer to bolster the transfer budget. He, too, was powerless to prevent Barcelona backing out of a £26m deal to sign England forward Marcus Rashford. Both issues affected the amount United could spend in the summer - both on transfer fees and wages. Wilcox rarely speaks to the media, although in England that is not uncommon when managers do the vast majority of news conferences. However a general lack of communication means we don't know why United decided to focus exclusively on strengthening their midfield in the summer, rather than bring in competition at left-back for Luke Shaw and striking support for Benjamin Sesko. With both players injured, that looks like a major error. The general consensus is Carrick has been sold badly short, and Wilcox's job title - and the fact he is often photographed with United's new signings and quoted in official press releases - means he is being blamed. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Wilcox was pictured with £70m signing Carlos Baleba when he joined in August MNC: No smiles for the cameras at Manchester United When has he had public backing? Since arriving at United from Southampton, Wilcox has twice been given very public backing by his bosses. On the first occasion - around Ruben Amorim's recruitment as successor to Ten Hag - it was Ashworth who lost his job while Wilcox kept his. Thirteen months later, when Amorim railed publicly against interference around United's formation - identifying Wilcox as one of those responsible - the Portuguese coach went, and Wilcox remained. Minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe is yet to offer his thoughts on the present crisis engulfing Old Trafford, but the United fans delivered their verdict loud and clear during the match against Bournemouth. There are many reasons why United find themselves 16th in the Premier League and without a win in their past eight matches, but recruitment is one of the bigger ones - and for that, rightly or wrongly, Wilcox is getting the blame. Is his media silence causing a problem? Since joining United, Wilcox has given one extensive interview - to the in-house Inside United podcast in October 2025. A month before that, he spoke at the 40th anniversary gala dinner of United's past players' association. There have been a couple of instances in the past 12 months of him stopping for the briefest of chats with journalists when he walked past an area they were waiting in to speak to a United player after a game. After the defeat by Bournemouth, Carrick was asked directly if Wilcox and Berrada should speak directly to supporters. "It's not for me to say who speaks and who doesn't speak, when they speak, and how they speak," said Carrick. "I know my role here is to speak to you guys and represent the team and football club as best as I possibly can from this position." There has never been an opportunity to ask Wilcox about the parameters of his role. But with Carrick's situation as it is - his popularity intact and his status as a legendary figure at the club secure - the focus is moving to Wilcox. United fans have made it clear they want him out - but does Ratcliffe feel the same? title: Exercise helps woman recover from partying life
description: Megan Hamon says her life has turned around after struggling with excessive drinking and partying.
content: Exercise helps woman recover from partying life Image caption, Meg Hamon says she hopes her story might help others who struggle with excessive drinking and partying ByChris Craddock Jersey communities reporter Published 26 October 2026 Meg Hamon was struggling with her self-confidence after she began to rely on partying and drinking to get by. The problems began to develop during the Covid-19 pandemic and then continued until the start of this year when Hamon decided a change was needed as she was going to turn 30, she said. Since then, she had focused on exercising through activities such as gym workouts and running, as well as going to therapy to improve her wellbeing, she added. Hamon said: "Exercise has helped me massively with my confidence... If I'm ever feeling low, a good gym session will always help." 'I was struggling' Hamon felt her problems had been growing for some time before she decided to take action to make a change in her life. She said: "I think my lowest was Covid. I think that was like a struggle for everyone and I just had gone through quite a bad breakup. "I was struggling with that and I just think I'd never really processed my emotion. "I really neglected myself mentally and physically... but I just never really noticed how unhappy I was until I started to make a change." More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey Hamon said she had felt the benefits on focusing on her physical and mental wellbeing since making lifestyle changes. She said: "Even if I had just done the therapy – it would be incredible... but I think the exercise side has just helped me massively with my confidence." Hamon has been sharing her experiences on social media as well, adding : "If it inspires one person to make a change, then I think it's really important to do that as well. "If you get stuck in the same cycle... I just think you can find so many other things to do than going out and just drinking excessively." Image caption, Therapist Sally Agathangelou says younger people are more open to getting support Hamon has been going to therapist Sally Agathangelou as part of her work to improve her wellbeing. Agathangelou said: "It could be various issues, it can be drinking, it can be gambling, it can be drugs, it can be self-harm - but it's all bridges for coping." "I'm really quite proud of this generation because they are very open to therapy," she added. "I'm very, very proud of them because I can support, but it's down to them at the end of the day to make that change." Follow BBC Jersey on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. title: Woman dead and three in hospital after crash
description: The woman, a passenger in a Vauxhall Astra, was pronounced dead at the scene following the incident.
content: Woman dead and three in hospital after crash Image source, Getty Images Published 26 October 2026 A woman has died following a single-car crash in Glasgow which left three others in hospital. Kennishead Road in Thornliebank was closed for about nine hours following the incident involving a black Vauxhall Astra at about 19:25 on Sunday. Police Scotland said the woman was pronounced dead at the scene. Two other women, aged 18 and 33, and the male driver, 20, were taken to hospital for treatment. The road has since reopened and police have launched an appeal for information, external. Sgt John Houston said: "Our thoughts are with the family of the woman who has died at this difficult time." title: Olid, Cuthbert and Weir on Scottish awards shortlist
description: Manchester United head coach Eva Olid, Chelsea midfielder Erin Cuthbert and Ballon d'Or nominee Caroline Weir are among those on the shortlist for the Scottish Women's Football Awards 2026.
content: Weir 25th in Ballon d'Or and joins Olid & Cuthbert in award shortlist Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Eva Olid, Erin Cuthbert and Caroline Weir are among the Scottish football nominees Published 26 October 2026 Caroline Weir has been ranked the 25th best women footballer in the world on the day she also joined fellow Scotland midfielder Erin Cuthbert and Manchester United head coach Eva Olid on the shortlist for the Scottish Women's Football Awards 2026. It was the second year in a row that 31-year-old Weir, who left Real Madrid for Lyon this summer, has been a Ballon d'Or nominee having been ranked 30th 12 months ago. She also joins Chelsea's Cuthbert, Brann winger Lauren Davidson and striker Kathleen McGovern, who switched from Hibernian to Newcastle United, on the shortlist for Scotland international player of the year. Glasgow City's Nicole Kozlova, who was named PFA Scotland player of the season in May, is also in the running for the SWPL 1 player of the year award. The Ukraine international is up against three other strikers - Celtic's Saoirse Noonan, Rangers' Katie Wilkinson, and Georgia Timms, who left Heart of Midlothian for Ipswich Town this summer. Olid led Hearts to their first Scottish Women's Premier League title last season before moving to England's Women's Super League. The Spaniard has already been named PFA Scotland manager of the season and could make it a double as she is in the running to be SWPL coach of the year. Olid is up against Leanne Crichton, whose Rangers side finished runners-up and currently lead the 2026-27 table, Hibernian's Joelle Murray, and Jack Beesley, who led Spartans back to the top flight. The winners will be announced at Hampden Park on 28 November. Related topics Football Scottish Football Scottish Women's Football Scotland Women's Football Team

title: Russell Brand asked assistant for female fan phone numbers, court hears
description: Helen Berger said she left her job working for Brand after she became "sick of him."
content: Russell Brand asked assistant for female fan phone numbers, court hears Image source, Getty Images ByClaire Ellison, Southwark Crown Court and Emma Saunders, Culture reporter Published 26 October 2026 A former personal assistant of Russell Brand has told a court she was instructed to get phone numbers for the entertainer from female fans when she first started working with him. Helen Berger, who worked closely with Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, said the request "felt uncomfortable" and, after seeking advice, she told the TV personality that she would not do that anymore. Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of indecent assault. The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges. Brand had an "insane sexual appetite", Berger told Southwark Crown Court in a written statement on Monday. Berger left her job with Brand after she became "sick of him", she said. She added that he had sex with numerous women during the time she was his assistant. She described a work environment where Brand would ask her if he could "go and have sex now" when frustrated with a particular task. Berger added that she never "witnessed anything against the law" but that "everyone normalised and dismissed his behaviour" so it "made me think it was accepted." She told the court that "peacock" Brand found random women online to satisfy his "insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night", but sex often made him depressed. She told the court Brand used MySpace to find women for sex, and said: "At his house, women often came over and it was clear they were there for sex." She recalled once finding a female celebrity asleep in Brand's bed while he was wandering around the house half-dressed, and said of the comedian: "He was like a peacock, women would always approach him." Russell Brand's defence team says any sexual activity was consensual and accounts have been twisted in the light of a defamatory TV documentary in 2023 which made allegations of sexual abuse against the entertainer. The prosecution is due to finish on Tuesday morning.
