title: Part of Antarctica named after former BBC science correspondent
description: A stretch of water in the west of the continent is now called the Amos Channel after the ex-BBC journalist.
content: Part of Antarctica named after former BBC science correspondent Image source, MODIS Image caption, The Amos Channel sits between Rothschild Island (bottom centre) and Alexander Island, which is the larger landmass to the right ByRebecca Morelle , Science Editor and Alison Francis , Senior Science Journalist Published 26 October 2026 Part of Antarctica has been named after former BBC science correspondent Jonathan Amos. A stretch of water between Rothschild Island and Alexander Island in the west of the White Continent is now called the Amos Channel. Amos was given the honour for his "exceptional and influential role in bringing Antarctic research to the forefront of public understanding" during his 38-year career at BBC News, the naming committee said. The channel is a new feature in Antarctica that appeared when a chunk of ice that connected Rothschild and Alexander Islands disintegrated. Image source, BAS Image caption, Jonathan Amos reported on science at the BBC for many years The melting ice sheets of this remote continent are just one of many aspects of polar science that Amos reported on while at the BBC. He also covered colossal icebergs, the fate of penguin colonies and a BBC exclusive about the discovery of Ernest Shackleton's lost ship, the Endurance. "It's absolutely incredible - what an extraordinary accolade. I'm so touched that there's a little bit of Antarctica named after me," Amos said. Despite his fascination with the South Pole, he has not yet travelled to the continent. "I've written about it so often, but always from my desk - this is quite the incentive to go and visit. "Antarctica is the front line of the biggest news story on planet Earth - climate change," he added. The naming of geographical features in Antarctica follows strict rules. The Amos Channel was recommended by the UK Antarctic Place Names Committee, which looks after names for sites within the British Antarctic Territory, as well as South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. Athena Dinar, from the British Antarctic Survey, said: "Jon's passion for Antarctica and engaging journalism offers something for every reader, viewer or listener. "The naming of an Antarctic place in his honour is a fitting recognition of his outstanding contribution to the promotion of Antarctic research." Amos joined the BBC in 1986 as a local radio reporter in Cambridge. He was part of the team that launched the BBC News website in 1997, and ran the online science desk for many years. He later worked as a BBC science correspondent across TV, radio and online, before leaving the organisation in 2024. "Jon consistently highlighted the importance of Antarctic research, explaining not only what science is being done there, but why it matters for society, climate understanding and the global environment," said Fiona Fox, from the Science Media Centre. Related topics Science & Environment British Antarctic Survey Antarctic Jonathan Amos

title: Police Scotland could cut officer numbers to lowest level in 20 years
description: The Scottish Police Authority says a funding standstill could lead to an end to an end to recruitment.
content: Police Scotland could cut officer numbers to lowest level in 20 years Image source, Press Association Image caption, The warning comes against a backdrop of increased pressure on police budgets By David Cowan Scotland home affairs correspondent Published 26 October 2026 Police Scotland will have to cut officer numbers to their lowest level in 23 years if it gets a "devastating" flat cash funding settlement, an oversight body has warned. The Scottish Police Authority (SPA) says recruitment would have to stop, taking officer numbers down to 15,600 - the lowest figure since 2003-04. Police Scotland is currently in line to receive a standstill budget allocation for next year from the Scottish government, but is asking for a £110m increase to maintain current staffing levels and respond to an increasing workload. The government said it delivered record levels of funding for policing this year and is discussing next year's budget with the force. The SPA's dire predictions are contained in an uncharacteristically undiplomatic submission to the Scottish Parliament's criminal justice committee. The authority says the creation of Scotland's national police force has already resulted in savings of £2.5bn since 2013, but high levels of inflation have driven up wages and other costs. Officer numbers have fallen by more than 700 since 2022-23, and the SPA argues further reductions are not sustainable. "Policing is currently under severe strain," the authority says. "Demand has changed, increasing in both complexity and volume in some areas. Trust and confidence in policing is decreasing." The SPA says a flat cash settlement would result in an £80m budget deficit, requiring a workforce reduction of 958 officers and 302 staff. On top of that, officer numbers would have to be cut by a further 400 the following year. "Given the extreme nature of the actions required to deliver these savings, a flat cash funding scenario is not achievable in year and would devastate the service," the submission says. Forty five Scottish police officers suspended over alleged crimes against women Published 8 October Police watchdog calls for live facial recognition to tackle football disorder Published 20 August Closure of region's last road policing department a 'sad day' Published 18 September Police Scotland has told the committee its workforce has fallen from 24,000 in 2013 to just under 22,500. It has backed up its request for a funding hike with a barrage of alarming statistics. The force says 999 calls have increased by 10%, crimes involving violence against women and girls are averaging 200 a day, and domestic abuse has gone up by 10.4%. Referrals related to online child abuse rose to 2,276 in 2025 and are projected to reach 4,000 this year, with roughly a quarter requiring enforcement action. The number of registered sex offenders being managed in the community has gone up to 7,451, a 56% increase since 2015, and bail offences are up 25%. Last year, more than 230,000 callouts related to mental health accounted for 18% of the incidents dealt with by the police. Of those, 85% did not involve a crime. Image source, Press Association Image caption, Neil Gray said the government will continue to work with Police Scotland The police say the threat of state-sponsored criminal activity is "at its highest level" and civil unrest has resulted in a 19% hike in deployments to protests. The number of Police Scotland officers currently on modified duties because of health issues now stands at 1,656. Against this backdrop, the force is asking for an extra £78.8m to meet its current commitments and a further £31.8m to support an investment strategy. "Without targeted investment, we will prioritise emergency response and the highest threat, risk and harm to keep people safe," it says. "Prevention and early interventions will be limited, ultimately increasing costly reactive responses at the point of crisis. "Pressure on the policing workforce will be intensified." Justice Secretary Neil Gray said: "Our police perform a vital role keeping Scotland's communities safe, which is why we have invested record funding of more than £1.7bn for policing in 2026-27. "We will continue to work with Police Scotland and the Scottish Police Authority to understand their 2027-28 budget requirements which will feed into the Scottish government budget process." Related topics Scotland Police Scotland Scottish government

title: Owners of Elvis music rights sue Anthropic for copyright violations
description: The company is accused of using hundreds of songs by the American rock-and-roll star to train its Claude AI model.
content: Owners of Elvis music rights sue Anthropic for copyright violations Image source, Getty Images ByMax Matza Published 26 October 2026 The owners of the rights to music by Elvis Presley have sued artificial intelligence company Anthropic, claiming in court that the company violated copyright law by using Elvis music to train its AI model Claude. In a legal case filed on Friday, Authentic Brands Group - which owns the music - accused Anthropic of using 274 Elvis songs without paying for any licence. "The Elvis Plaintiffs' iconic collective catalog contains some of the most groundbreaking, revolutionary, influential, and enduring musical compositions in human history," the case states. A spokesperson for Anthropic told BBC News: "We disagree with the claims and intend to defend this case fully." Authentic Brands alleges in its legal complaint that Anthropic "has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before", according to the court filing seen by the BBC. "The Elvis Plaintiffs are deeply protective of these iconic songs." It argues that songs that were infringed include hits such as All Shook Up, Can't Help Falling in Love, A Little Less Conversation, Don't Be Cruel and Return To Sender. These songs were used to create "unlicensed derivative works", Authentic Brands says. The legal complaint asks for payments of up to $150,000 (£112,000) per infringed song, adding up to $41m. Anthropic is also being sued by the owners of other music rights. Last week, it was accused of stealing lyrics by music company Reservoir. In January, it was sued by Universal Music Group. Both cases remain ongoing. Authentic Brands' legal complaint references other legal actions, and says that Claude admitted to crossing a line. "Even after the Defendant supposedly put up 'guardrails' after being sued, in one of its latest iterations, Claude continues to infringe," it says. "When recently asked to recreate specific songs 'for a modern audience,' Claude did so and admitted: 'These renders keep landing very close to the originals: same structure, same hooks reused with light rewording, and full sets of verses/choruses/bridges.' "That's edging past 'inspired by' into reproducing the copyrighted song, even when the words are swapped out." Last year, Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5bn to settle a class action legal case filed by authors who said the company stole their work to train its AI models. The lawsuit was the largest publicly reported copyright recovery in history, according to lawyers for the authors. title: Ireland prop Furlong cited over alleged groin grab
description: Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong is cited over an alleged groin grab in Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster on Saturday.
content: Ireland prop Furlong cited over alleged groin grab Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Tadhg Furlong has been included in Ireland's squad for November's Nations Championship fixtures ByAndy Gray BBC Sport NI Journalist Published 26 October 2026 Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong has been cited over an alleged groin grab in Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster on Saturday. Munster back row Gavin Coombes raised the allegation against an unnamed Leinster player with match referee Andrew Brace in the closing stages of the first half at the Aviva Stadium, but television match official (TMO) Colin Stanley could not find any video evidence at the time. However, three-time British and Irish Lions tourist Furlong has now been cited over an act of foul play under Law 9.27, which says a "a player must not do anything that is against the spirit of good sportsmanship including but not limited to grabbing, twisting or squeezing the genitals". A statement from the URC said "arrangements for the disciplinary process are currently in progress and will be announced in due course". If found guilty of the offence, the 33-year-old would be in danger of missing Ireland's Nations Championship matches with Argentina, Fiji and South Africa in Dublin, as well as the finals weekend in London. In October 2025, South Africa front-rower Jan-Hendrik Wessels received a nine-match suspension for grabbing Josh Murphy's genitals in the Bulls' URC win over Connacht. For that incident, Wessels was handed a 12-week suspension - the shortest ban under World Rugby rules for such an offence - that was reduced by three weeks due to his "good conduct prior to and at the hearing and good record". If similar action was taken against Furlong, he would potentially miss Leinster's Investec Champions Cup Pool match with Sale, as well as the festive inter-provincial derbies with Ulster and Munster. Speaking after the 24-18 defeat at the Aviva Stadium, Munster head coach Clayton McMillan said he would "back our players 100% that if they make an allegation like that". Leinster head coach Leo Cullen said he did not see the incident, which occurred in the 37th minute when Munster were leading, but acknowledged it was a "serious matter". title: Shoppers fill Oxford Street on first traffic-free day
description: Almost 1km of the popular shopping destination is pedestrianised between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street.
content: Shoppers fill Oxford Street on first traffic-free day Image source, EPA Image caption, Some visitors welcomed the changes and looked forward to using the street at Christmas ByJess Warren London Published 26 October 2026 Part of Oxford Street has been pedestrianised, with visitors experiencing the first day that cars, taxis, buses and bicycles have been banned from some of the central London street. Almost 1km (0.62 mile) of the popular shopping destination has been pedestrianised between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street by the mayor's Oxford Street Development Corporation. The change has been welcomed by some shoppers, although questions have been raised about accessibility for disabled visitors and how the bike ban will be enforced. London's mayor Lord Sadiq Khan said it was a "momentous day for London", and the changes were the first phase in lifting the street out of "decline". Image source, EPA Image caption, Workers were installing changes to the road as Londoners began their day The roll-out was met with some confusion as many cyclists continued to pedal through the newly installed barriers, with some being shouted at by security staff to "dismount" and walk their route instead. Despite the ban on cycling and e-scooters, people were observed riding through the pedestrianised section throughout Monday morning. A Transport for London (TfL) spokesperson said riders were "obliged to follow the rules". "We are working with dockless hire companies and delivery companies to ensure this is made clear and will continue to monitor and review as required," they added. TfL said, as well as barriers and signage, it was working with e-bike hire companies to "enforce strict geo-fencing" for the pedestrianised zone, which would cut or reduce power for dockless e-bikes entering the area and require riders to walk them. Whether the number of cyclists ignoring the restrictions was a teething problem or a longer-term enforcement issue remains to be seen in the weeks and months ahead. A police officer was also seen getting to grips with the new arrangement, as he asked an Oxford Street security worker: "How do I get my car down there?" To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, A cyclist rides down the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street But as shoppers started to descend on the street, many celebrated the change. Lucia, who works nearby, said she took a detour to see the newly pedestrianised street. "It's very joyful," she said. "We are used to walking on crowded pavements, so it's really exciting to see the people using this space." "Let's see how it regenerates with time, how different types of businesses pop out, how different spaces for people to hang out appear. "I think in summer it will be lovely. Christmas will be great, it will be more enjoyable." Her views were echoed by others, and as the day went on, more people could be seen walking on the newly changed road rather than sticking to the pavement. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: Time-lapse shows Oxford Street pedestrianisation However, concerns were raised by some about accessibility, and whether the re-routed buses and new bus stops and taxi ranks, installed about 200m and 100m from the pedestrianised area respectively, would be enough to support disabled shoppers. One black cab driver who spoke to BBC London said he was worried that access to Oxford Street would "become a problem" for some of his disabled passengers. Last week, chair of Inclusion London, Adam Gabsi, said "the proof will be in the pudding". "If access to buses and taxis becomes difficult, then there'll be problems for people like me," he said, adding that although disabled Londoners were consulted on the plan, it was not co-produced by them. Sight loss charity Guide Dogs welcomed the changes, and Wheels for Wellbeing argued that accessibility needed to be properly built into the final design. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, The last bus down Oxford Street before it went traffic-free Michael Bolt, from the Marylebone Association, was among a number of locals who said they feared surrounding areas would be "ruined" as traffic was displaced on to other roads. Karen Jones, who has lived in the area for 20 years, also said she was worried what would happen to their "beautiful garden neighbourhoods". Image source, EPA Image caption, Barriers have been installed along part of Oxford Street Lord Khan said he wanted people to be "in charge" of Oxford Street, not traffic, and hoped it would become a site for "culture, leisure and tourism". "This is a street that has been known as the nation's high street for more than 100 years," he said. "Over the last couple of decades it's been in decline. "I'm not willing to stand by as shops leave this street, as jobs leave this street, and that's why I'm really proud 1km of this street is traffic free." Image source, Press Association Image caption, Mayor Lord Sadiq Khan said they will learn from the first phase and take on concerns The mayor said the area would be "safe and spacious" in the lead-up to Christmas, with more improvement works coming in the new year. "We're going to carry on testing and learning, refining the plans we have to make sure everyone gets to enjoy this street," he said. "We don't want it to be horrible, we want it to be great. "We are going to learn from this first phase to make sure the next phase takes on people's concerns." Seb Dance, London's deputy mayor for transport and deputy chair for TfL, said "people will see very quickly the benefits" of pedestrianisation. TfL previously told BBC London it expected to see "a manageable increase in traffic" on Wigmore Street, Cavendish Place, Henrietta Street, Marylebone Lane and Welbeck Street. Image source, EPA Image caption, Westminster City Council said it would monitor the effects of the scheme Tim Barnes, deputy leader of Westminster City Council, said residents had regularly raised issues with pedestrianisation of Oxford Street whenever a scheme was proposed in the past. "We just couldn't find ways that would practically work," he said. "I think we need to see a lot of how this works in practice. We will be monitoring for traffic problems or noise problems, pollution issues, and taking those back to TfL and the mayor, and charging them with the responsibility of fixing those problems if they've created them." Image source, EPA Image caption, The changes to the road mean bus route alterations and new stops The Oxford Street Development Corporation, which is leading the change, previously said it had worked with the emergency services to understand their access needs to Oxford Street, and would continue to do so as the changes unfold. It said police, ambulances and the fire service would be able to access the pedestrianised areas along "multiple access points". What is walking down the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street like? Published 23 hours ago As it happened: Stretch of Oxford Street goes pedestrian-only The project, which is estimated to cost about £150m, will see gradual changes unfold along the road, with road surfaces being raised, trees and seating installed, and traffic lights rephased. The corporation said "possible future phases are being considered and costed". Kate Boothman Meier, director of corporate affairs at New West End Company, said: "The ultimate aim is to try and pedestrianise the wider Oxford Street. That is further down the line, we have to see how this goes first." Additional reporting by James W Kelly, Gem O'Reilly, Lauren Stanley from BBC London and Tom Edwards, BBC London transport correspondent. title: US Marine indicted for murder and robbery of woman in Japan
description: Prosecutors have indicted Devin Jacob Ballard for a killing that has caused outrage in Japan, local media reports.
content: US Marine indicted for murder and robbery of woman in Japan Image source, Reuters Image caption, Devin Jacob Ballard was stationed at Futenma Air Station ByGeorge Wright Published 26 October 2026 A US Marine has been indicted on suspicion of murdering and robbing a woman in Japan earlier this month in a case that has triggered protests, Japanese media reports. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who was stationed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested on suspicion of killing Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa. Prosecutors have now indicted him for allegedly strangling Yagi with a telephone cord and then stealing her backpack and wallet on 3 October, media reports, citing the indictment document. It wasreported Ballard had denied the allegations, but Asahi Shimbun and Kyodo News cited investigators saying he has made some statements suggesting involvement. Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings. Yagi's death has caused outrage in Japan, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi describing the crime as "brutal and heinous". Earlier this month, the Marine Corps said it was "actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine" and extended condolences to the victim's family. It is the latest case involving a US serviceman in Okinawa, which hosts the highest concentration of around 55,000 US soldiers stationed in Japan. Previous criminal cases have sparked anger and protests, the largest of which took place in 1995, when tens of thousands took to the streets following the abduction, beating and rape of a 12-year-old girl. In 2024 alone, there were four sexual assault cases involving US troops in Okinawa, including that of air force member Brennon Washington, who was given five years for the rape and kidnapping of an underage girl. In 2025, US marine Lance Cpl Jamel Clayton was sentenced to seven years in prison for sexually assaulting a woman. Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said the prefecture has repeatedly demanded that the US take action to prevent such incidents, and said he sees the alleged crime as a sign of a lack of discipline. The prime minister said her government has registered a "strong" protest with the US and called for "strict disciplinary action against US military personnel and thorough measures to prevent a recurrence of such incidents". People in Japan have been voicing anger, with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo earlier this month. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice, with one user saying: "Enough is enough." title: Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?
description: BBC Sport's Ask Me Anything team explains why Cole Palmer's red card suspension will not rule him out of Chelsea's Premier League match against Manchester United.
content: Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card? Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge Published 26 October 2026 Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match. Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban. The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher. In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge. Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night. This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in. Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received. So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside. title: Fans assist Penicuik clear-up for Clyde tie - watch on BBC
description: Penicuik Athletic are sure Tuesday's Scottish Cup tie with Clyde will go ahead in front of the BBC cameras as the community rallies to clear storm debris from the pitch at Montgomery Park.
content: Fans assist Penicuik clear-up for Clyde cup tie Image source, SNS Image caption, Montgomery Park, Penicuik, on a sunny April day in 2020 Published 26 October 2026 Penicuik Athletic are sure Tuesday's Scottish Cup tie with Clyde will go ahead as the community rallies to clear storm debris from the pitch at Montgomery Park. Club president Andy Penman said around 30 volunteers have offered to begin the clear up on Monday evening. The game had been scheduled for Friday in front of the BBC cameras but was called off due to a waterlogged surface. Then came the high winds of Storm Boelo. "The ground on one side is surrounded by fairly old trees and there is a substantial amount of debris strewn across about 50% of the pitch," Penman explained. "We've had branches coming down and actually going into the surface vertically. "Underneath it all, the pitch is in fine condition. The rain that was lying on Friday has disappeared very quickly." Penicuik sit ninth in the East of Scotland Football League Premier Division, while Clyde are level on points with League Two leaders Stranraer. However, the hosts can take inspiration from a 3-0 win over Stenhousemuir at the same stage of the competition in 2019. They beat Kilwinning Rangers in the first round and East Kilbride, fourth in League One, await the winners of this game. "This is our cup final," said Penman, with a capacity 1300 tickets sold for the 19:45 GMT kick-off. "We've been up and down in the league, probably distracted the by the cup run. Now the players are just looking forward to the challenge." Related topics Football Scottish Football Scottish Cup Clyde

title: 'The storm didn't ruin our wedding, it made it'
description: Leigh and Paul Hutchinson unexpectedly had their first dance in the iconic Blackpool Tower ballroom.
content: 'The storm didn't ruin our wedding, it made it' Image source, Family handout Image caption, After the ceremony Leigh and Paul walked down the Prom in the storm ByEmma Stanley Reporting fromNorth West Published 26 October 2026 A couple whose wedding day coincided with Storm Boelo said last-minute changes caused by the weather did not ruin their day, "it made it". Leigh and Paul Hutchinson had planned to surprise their wedding guests with a glass of fizz at the top of Blackpool Tower, but high winds forced the venue to close the area. Instead, staff arranged a private bar on the upper balcony of the Tower Ballroom and later cleared the dance floor so the newlyweds could share their first dance there. "They did something really special for us," Leigh said. "It made the day so much more than we could have ever imagined." The couple met 10 years ago and decided they wanted a low-key wedding at the chapel next door to The Beach House where they met. Leigh said: "It was just going to be us. A quick wedding and a meal with family afterwards. So it spiralled to say the least." Image source, Nancy Lisa Barrett Photography Image caption, The couple had their first dance in the Tower Ballroom After the ceremony, the bride, groom and wedding guests walked down the Prom in the storm. Leigh said: "I don't know how we made it! We caused quite a stir. I think there's still a few brollies missing." Later, when one of the guests suggested it would be nice to dance in the Tower Ballroom, staff cleared the dance floor to let them. "They played the organ and we had the most magical first dance," Leigh said. "We were really overwhelmed with everyone's comments and cheers. It was incredible." Image source, Nancy Lisa Barrett Photography Image caption, Straight after the ceremony Leigh and Paul walked down the Prom in the storm Groom Paul joked that if he had known his first dance would take place on one of the most iconic dance floors in the world, "he wouldn't have turned up". "I was nervous dancing in front of 40 people, never mind hundreds I didn't know, but it made the day," he said. "It was full and there were a lot of good dancers in there too." Rob Smith, general manager of Blackpool Tower, said: "It was a special moment and one our team will never forget. "The Tower Ballroom is one of the most famous venues in the world and Leigh and Paul are now part of its history. "We wish them both all the very best for the future." title: Surrey head coach Batty quits for IPL role
description: Surrey head coach Gareth Batty steps down to join Indian Premier League side Chennai Super Kings as assistant head coach.
content: Batty leaves Surrey to join Chennai Super Kings Image source, Shutterstock Image caption, Under Gareth Batty, Surrey won the County Championship in 2022, 2023 and 2024 Published 26 October 2026 Surrey head coach Gareth Batty has stepped down to join Indian Premier League side Chennai Super Kings as an assistant coach. Batty led Surrey to three consecutive County Championship titles in his first three seasons in charge and twice guided them to T20 Finals Day. "Thank you hardly seems enough for all that Surrey has meant to me," the former England spinner told the club's website, external. "The new journey is a very exciting one for my family and I, and I'm looking forward to getting going." Batty's departure ends a 21-year association with Surrey. He had two spells as a player, the first from 1998 to 2001 after leaving Yorkshire. He then spent seven seasons at Worcestershire before returning to The Oval in 2010. Batty was club captain between 2015 and 2017, and in total played more than 350 times for Surrey, taking more than 500 wickets across all formats. Batty, who played nine Tests for England, retired in 2021 and immediately joined Surrey's coaching staff. After he was appointed head coach in 2022, Surrey became the first team in nearly 60 years to win three County Championship titles in a row. "It is difficult to put into words just how much Gareth Batty has given to Surrey County Cricket Club, both as a player and as head coach," director of cricket Alec Stewart said. "I have known and worked with Gareth for many years and throughout that time he has shown an outstanding commitment to this club. "While we are sorry to see him go, I understand that this opportunity was too good for him to pass up on and will enable him to spend more time with his family outside of the IPL season." Three of the 10 teams who will play in Division One of the County Championship next season are now without a head coach, after Glamorgan's Richard Dawson joined the England set-up and newly-promoted Durham's Ryan Campbell moved upstairs to become the club's director of cricket. Related topics Cricket County Cricket Surrey

title: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback
description: The left-wing incumbent president had lost the first round to right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.
content: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, ByIone Wells, Reporting fromBrasília and Hafsa Khalil Published 26 October 2026 Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since Brazil's return to civilian rule in 1985 to be elected after losing the first round of voting. Lula told jubilant crowds his victory was a "loss for negativity, lies", adding "long live democracy". Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled. World leaders have congratulated Lula on his re-election. Bolsonaro's rejection comes as no surprise to observers. His father did the same. But a challenge appears unlikely to succeed. Firstly, it seems to centre on the unprecedented decision by the Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting nationwide by two hours. Some Bolsonaro fans are pointing out that Zanin was once Lula's lawyer and alleging bias. But both teams had requested an extension to voting times - Lula's had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as their reason. Both knew every vote would count and did not want their side to miss out. The president of the Supreme Electoral Court Kássio Nunes Marques – appointed by Jair Bolsonaro – confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voter extension did not change the outcome of the race. The sheer gap between the two candidates' tallies - 4.4 million votes - makes the result more difficult to challenge. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Lula is making history as the first Brazilian to be elected four times The result came as a surprise after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October with 47% of votes ahead of Lula's 45%. But Lula's camp gained momentum ahead of election day, focusing on boosting voter turnout after 33 million people did not vote in round one. Sunday saw the largest drop in abstention between the two rounds of a presidential election since 1989. Bolsonaro had been poised to give a victory speech and said the result should be annulled, calling it "inexplicable". As his disconsolate supporters left the house in Brasília where their candidate had been watching the result, Lula took to the streets in São Paulo to celebrate. "This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country," the former metal worker told supporters. "It will be the one in which I listen most to the Brazilian people." After pulling off this victory, Lula faces big hurdles: a divided country, an opponent that won't recognise the result, and a hostile Congress packed full of Bolsonaro allies. Markets reacted negatively to the unexpected outcome. The Sao Paolo stock exchange opened 15% down, sparking a brief suspension before recovering slightly. Interest rate futures rose as investors scrutinised Lula's fiscal plans. Lula wins in Brazil but faces hostile Congress and divided country Published 1 day ago How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp chat helped turn Brazil election around Published 20 hours ago Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again Published 1 day ago Reacting to the result, US President Donald Trump suggested the election had been stolen. "I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," he told reporters on Monday, without providing evidence or more details. "It looked very bad to me." Other world leaders from across the political spectrum have congratulated Lula. Mexico's left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum said in a post on X: "The people of Brazil won." Peru's right-wing President Keiko Fujimori praised Brazil's "democratic day". Similar messages were shared by the presidents of Chile and Ecuador. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted that their two countries had already "flourished under our partnership". European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "democracy and multilateralism" had won. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez - also a left-wing leader - called it a "great victory". French President Emmanuel Macron said the two nations should work "in service of a more just world". South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called Lula's victory one for the "global south and progressive forces throughout the world". Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, Flávio Bolsonaro has refused to accept the result, calling for it to be annulled In a video posted on Instagram later on Monday, Flávio Bolsonaro said police had told him to hand over his passports and had been banned from leaving the country. Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. Flávio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support. Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023. His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030. But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from the US president. Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" - which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard". Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power. Related topics Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva Brazil Jair Bolsonaro

title: Alaska's Democratic Senate candidate pauses midterms campaigning after car crash
description: Mary Peltola, who suffered minor injuries, is running in one of the most closely watched races in the upcoming elections.
content: Alaska's Democratic Senate candidate pauses midterms campaigning after car crash Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Peltola is currently a member of Congress ByAna Faguy Published 26 October 2026 Mary Peltola, Alaska's Democratic Senate candidate, has paused campaigning ahead of the US midterm elections after sustaining "minor injuries" in a car crash. Peltola, 53, and her family were travelling to an event on Saturday when the vehicle they were in was hit by another driver, her campaign said in a statement. She is running in one of the most closely watched races in the elections, which take place on 3 November - one that could help decide the balance of power in government. Peltola has rescheduled campaign events "as she takes time to recover" on the advice of medical professionals, her campaign manager, Cheryl Bruce, said in a statement. "Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits," Bruce said. Peltola is trying to unseat incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan website that rates and tracks US elections, has classified the Alaska senate race as a "toss-up", meaning neither the Republicans nor the Democrats hold a decisive advantage. Trump told the justice department to file a federal lawsuit last week to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Sullivan loses, arguing that another candidate with the same name may confuse voters. The suit said the inclusion of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot could lead some to mistakenly cast their votes for the wrong candidate. Previous efforts to remove that Sullivan, a retired teacher, from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court. GUIDE: What are the US midterms? title: Racecourse fined after jockey taken to A&E in horsebox
description: Sedgefield Racecourse is fined £6,500 after failing to comply with five 'general instructions' of safety.
content: Racecourse fined after jockey taken to A&E in horsebox Image source, Getty Images Image caption, An inspection in April revealed 'significant progress' at the course Published 26 October 2026 A racecourse has been fined £6,500 after a jockey was taken to hospital in a horsebox instead of an ambulance. The incident took place in March at Sedgefield Racecourse in County Durham. A disciplinary panel of the British Horseracing Authority (BHA) found that the racecourse had failed to comply with five "general instructions" within its Rules of Racing. The injured jockey's identity was kept private but it was reported that he suffered a left clavicle and shoulder injury after a fall, and was examined by a doctor at the course. He was cleared to race again but said he was still in pain, which resulted in a doctor advising him to go to A&E. By then all the ambulance crews had left the venue, and he was taken in a horsebox with the medical staff following behind. "The 'general instructions' require proper transfer to hospital with accompaniment from qualified medical staff not, as here, being followed in a car," the BHA panel said. It also added that the jockey was in too much pain to get into the following car. The other failings at the venue included a telephone line not working and "tired worn rooms not conveying a clean clinical area". The racecourse has acknowledged the "errors and shortcomings" and an inspection took place in April which revealed "significant progress". title: Dangerous drivers jailed for mum and girl's deaths
description: Hardeep Bhachu and Jasskamal Riyat are warned of the 'irreversible' consequences of their actions.
content: Drivers who killed mum and girl while racing jailed Image source, Family handout Image caption, Justyna Hulboj, 27, and her four-year-old daughter Lena Czepczor were killed on Scott Hall Road in Leeds in January 2023 ByElizabeth Baines, Reporting fromat Leeds Crown Court and Andrew Barton, Yorkshire Published 26 October 2026 Two men who killed a mother and her four-year-old daughter as they raced their high-performance cars along a Leeds city centre road have been jailed. Justyna Hulboj, 27, and her daughter Lena Czepczor were killed when they were hit by an Audi TT RS as they walked to the girl's nursery on the A61 Scott Hall Road on 16 January 2023. At Leeds Crown Court on Monday, Hardeep Bhachu, 29, was jailed for 12 years and Jasskamal Riyat, 37, for 16 years. Sentencing the men, Judge Singh said the road was "not a race track" and told them the deaths had consequences that were "immeasurable", with an "immense" impact on those left behind. Bhachu, of Grant Row in Adel, had earlier admitted two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, while Riyat, of Buckstone Avenue in Moortown, was convicted by a jury after denying he had been racing him. The court heard the pair, who did not previously know each other, accelerated away from traffic lights on Scott Hall Road shortly before the crash. Prosecutors said Bhachu's Audi reached speeds of up to 89mph (143 km/h) in the 40mph (64 km/h) zone, before he lost control of the car, which then mounted the pavement and struck Hulboj and her daughter. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Dashcam footage shows drivers moments before fatal crash Judge Singh said the victims had "done nothing wrong" and were "simply walking to school". Addressing the defendants, he said: "A road is not a race track. A powerful car is not an invitation to test its limits on a public road. "The consequences of competitive driving at extreme speed can be, and in this case were, irreversible." He added: "Justyna and Lena should have gone to school that morning. They should have returned home. They should have continued with their lives. "Instead, their lives ended on a pavement because two drivers chose to drive in a manner which placed speed and competition above the safety of everyone around them." Image source, West Yorkshire Police Image caption, Hardeep Bhachu and Jasskamal Riyat were sentenced at Leeds Crown Court Susannah Proctor, for Bhachu, told the court that her client was a "normal person who's made a massive mistake". She said he "must live with himself in the knowledge of the devastation he has caused". And she said: "He did not intend to cause this devastation but cause it he has." Hulboj's fiancé Dominik Czepczor watched the sentencing hearing in court. A statement from him was read, which said: "My whole world collapsed in one second. "Every day I feel a huge void after their departure. "We had so many hopes and dreams and in one moment it all ended. "My dream was to have a wonderful family, and I must say that it came true for a short while, but that was taken away from me on January 16. "Unfortunately, all that remains are wonderful memories and a constant fight for the next day, which is not easy." To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Drivers who killed mum and girl while racing jailed Det Insp Paul Conroy, of West Yorkshire Police's Major Collision Enquiry Team, said: "A woman and her young daughter have died because of the actions of these men, and I know no sentence will ever feel enough to compensate for the lives that have been lost. "This sentencing hearing though does mark the end of a long criminal justice process for Justyna and Lena's family. "It is over two years since Bhachu admitted his part in this tragic incident and I know that the wait for justice has taken its toll. "My thoughts are firmly with them today." title: Campaigners call for new body to lead Mackintosh Building restoration
description: The Charles Rennie Mackintosh Society said a special-purpose organisation should lead reconstruction of the landmark.
content: Campaigners call for new body to lead Mackintosh Building restoration Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Glasgow School of Art's Mackintosh Building was devastated by two fires in 2014 and 2018 Published 26 October 2026 Responsibility for rebuilding the fire-damaged Mackintosh Building should be transferred from Glasgow School of Art (GSA) to a new independent body, campaigners have said. The Charles Rennie Mackintosh Society said a special-purpose organisation would be better placed to lead fundraising, governance and reconstruction of the landmark, which was devastated by fires in 2014 and 2018. In July, GSA said the estimated cost of a faithful restoration had soared to £265m and warned it could not proceed without significant extra financial support. The art school said it would invest insurance settlement funds in preparatory works but full reinstatement would require external partners and funding. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland More stories from Scotland The Charles Rennie Mackintosh Society is an independent heritage charity founded in 1973 to promote the work of the Scottish architect and designer. Director Matthew Williams said: "The society has plenty of common ground with The Glasgow School of Art and support their first stage of work to stabilise the building and remove the current scaffold which is holding the structure in place. "This will allow for future phases of reconstruction and the public will be able to see what currently remains. "However, as an independent critical friend to the Art School, we believe that following that first phase an external body should take on the building and get the project finished in the coming years." The proposal is set out in a report by the Charles Rennie Mackintosh Society. It said the estimated £265m cost of a full reconstruction would require significant financial support from both the Scottish and UK governments, alongside private and charitable funding. The campaign group said the building should be rebuilt as it is one of Scotland's most important architectural landmarks. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The second fire broke in June 2018 It also argued that extensive surveys, drawings, archive material and 3D scans created before the 2018 fire, mean an accurate reconstruction remains possible. The society said eight years of limited progress since then have left the future of the building unresolved and called for a new structure to drive the project forward. A Glasgow School of Art spokesperson said: "We welcome the Charles Rennie Mackintosh Society's continued engagement on the future of the Mackintosh Building and its shared ambition to see the building rebuilt. "The Society remains an important stakeholder as we continue our discussions with potential funders and partners." title: Anthropic unveils details of planned historic stock market debut
description: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
content: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing Image source, Getty Images ByRachel Clun, Business reporter, Liv McMahon, Technology reporter and Kali Hays, Technology reporter Published 26 October 2026 Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US. The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer. Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing. The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn. Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology. In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity. It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy". Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June. Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans. Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously. Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools. As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude. Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know Published 16 hours ago 'Bold but sane' In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers. Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance". "In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said. Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business". Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI. Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US. It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems. However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields. "We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said. Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's. The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity. 'Significant milestone' Matt Orton, chief market strategist at investment management firm Raymond James Investment, said investors expected to see rapid growth as well as rapid financial losses in Anthropic's finances, so Monday's filing would not come as a surprise. "Getting the details from this filing, I think will help provide the market with more visibility, because we need to know where its revenue growth is coming from," he told the BBC. Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, told Reuters that Anthropic's plans to list was "a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence". He added that the outcome of its stock market debut would be "fairly indicative of the sentiment" among investors to continue ploughing cash into AI development. Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? title: Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973
description: The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger, near the Libyan border.
content: Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Algeria recently donated four military helicopters to Niger (file photo) ByOndiro Oganga and Chris Ewokor, BBC Africa Published 26 October 2026 Algeria is to send troops to Niger in its first foreign deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war in 1973. The deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister, as the country seeks support against armed groups, some of which are linked to al-Qaeda or Islamic State. Algeria has economic interests in Niger, including a planned gas pipeline that would carry Nigerian gas through Niger to Algeria. The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger, near the Libyan border. The deployment comes as the two neighbours rebuild ties after a diplomatic rift in 2025, when Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers. Algeria's upper house of parliament held an emergency session on Sunday to vote on the proposed deployment. According to AFP news agency, 148 of the 174 senators voted in favour. It was later backed by the lower house of parliament. However, the timing and number of soldiers to be deployed have not been announced. The move would mark the first use of a 2020 constitutional provision allowing overseas military deployments and a significant shift in Algeria's long-standing policy against sending forces abroad. "We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure," Algerian senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after the vote. Algeria's state-owned energy company, Sonatrach, has also signed an agreement with Niger's petroleum ministry to explore for oil in the Kafra region. Two exploration wells are estimated to contain 168 million and 100 million barrels, respectively, Reuters reported. Relations between Algeria and Niger have not always been smooth in recent years. Algeria condemned the 2023 coup that ousted Niger's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum, and brought Gen Abdourahamane Tchiani to power. Tensions rose again in 2025 after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near its border. Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers in solidarity with Mali, a close ally which is also under military rule. Relations have since improved. Tchiani visited Algeria in February 2026, and in late August, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune sent fighter jets to Niger to help suppress a coup attempt and also donated four military helicopters. title: Smotherman beats Ireland's Power in delayed PGA Tour finish
description: Austin Smotherman claims his second PGA Tour title with a Monday play-off victory over Seamus Power at the weather-hit Bermuda Championship.
content: Smotherman beats Power in Monday finish in Bermuda Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Smotherman prevailed on the third extra hole to secure back-to-back PGA Tour wins Published 26 October 2026 Austin Smotherman claimed his second PGA Tour title with a Monday play-off victory over Seamus Power at the weather-hit Bermuda Championship. The 32-year-old American parred the third extra hole to fend off the Irishman and seal his second tournament win in as many starts after a breakthrough victory in Utah earlier this month. Smotherman and Power contested the sudden-death play-off on Monday after inclement weather forced organisers to cancel Sunday's scheduled final round. With more bad weather forecast on Monday, officials decided to scrap the final round and proceed with a play-off between the 54-hole leaders. Smotherman carded 65, 66 and 66 to reach 16 under through three rounds, with 2022 champion Power matching his 197 total with rounds of 66, 64 and 67. On the first play-off hole - the par-three 16th at Port Royal Golf Course - Power missed a 20-footer for his third PGA Tour win before getting up and down from the bunker to force a third extra hole. With the hole location having been changed, Smotherman two-putted from 15 feet for the win after Power failed to get up and down for par from the rough. "We're out here playing an incredible sport in a beautiful spot," said Smotherman. "Whatever things are going to be thrown at us, Zak [Williamson, caddie] and I were going to be on top of our game. "Yesterday I felt like we handled everything pretty well and the tour has been great at communicating what's going to happen today for us. "Once we got that news, it was nice to know what's going on. To come out on top is a cherry on top, so it's pretty awesome." While Power missed out on the trophy, the runner-up finish effectively guarantees his PGA Tour card for 2027 after playing with conditional status this year. Having entered the week 103rd in the FedEx Cup Fall standings, the 39-year-old is projected to climb to 53rd, with the top 100 earning PGA Tour cards for next year. "Had a chance this morning, wasn't able to do it, which is disappointing, but overall great week, can't complain too much," said Power. "Hit some good shots in the playoff, just didn't quite judge the wind right, but that's golf sometimes. I'll move onwards." Related topics Golf Northern Ireland Sport

title: Harrison and Jones among world player of the year nominees
description: England pair Zoe Harrison and Meg Jones are named among the nominees for the World Rugby Player of the Year award.
content: Harrison and Jones among world player of the year nominees Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Meg Jones (left) and Zoe Harrison won the Women's Rugby World Cup with England in 2025 ByElla Gibbs BBC Sport journalist Published 26 October 2026 England duo Zoe Harrison and Megan Jones are among four nominees for World Rugby Women's 15s Player of the Year award. They are nominated alongside Canada's DaLeaka Menin and New Zealand's Kaipo Olsen-Baker for the award, which recognises exceptional performances during the 2026 season. Fly-half Harrison, 28, scored 88 points from the tee for England this year while Red Roses captain Jones, 30, is nominated for a second year in a row - missing out to Canada's Sophie de Goede in 2025. The World Cup-winning pair played important roles in England claiming their eighth successive Women's Six Nations title in May, part of a 41-match unbeaten run ended by back-to-back defeats by Canada this month. The winner will be announced following this weekend's final WXV Global Series matches, with England facing the United States on Friday (21:15 GMT). Elsewhere, England's Abi Burton has been shortlisted for Women's 15s Try of the Year for her try against Australia in the WXV Global Series in September. title: Chris Brown given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack
description: The R&B star previously pleaded guilty to affray, after attacking a music producer with a glass bottle.
content: Chris Brown given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: Chris Brown greeted with cheers as he leaves court BySteven McIntosh Published 26 October 2026 US singer Chris Brown has avoided jail after striking a man twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in a London nightclub. The R&B star was given an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, over the attack at private members' club Tape in Mayfair, in the early hours of 19 February 2023. Brown's vocal coach, rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months. Both men, who had pleaded guilty to affray, were also ordered to pay £1,500 costs. Judge Tony Baumgartner said Brown's use of the glass bottle to hit the victim twice over the head "was plainly dangerous", adding that the violence of the attack was "intense". To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Met Police release annotated CCTV footage of Chris Brown's 2023 nightclub attack The sentence means Brown will not be imprisoned unless he commits another offence during the 12-month period of suspension. The court heard Brown's attack on music producer Abraham 'Abe' Diaw left the victim in need of hospital treatment for his injuries. In sentencing, Judge Baumgartner said: "The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained." CCTV footage was shown where Brown struck Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head, and then hitting his shoulder. Sentencing Brown, Judge Baumgartner said: "This was not planned violence. It was nevertheless serious violence by two people in a crowded nightclub." Image source, Julia Quenzler/Reuters Image caption, Chris Brown (left) and Omololu Akinlolu were sentenced at Southwark Crown Court on Monday The judge told Brown: "Violence of this kind in a crowded nightclub is serious, it creates an obvious risk, not only to the person against whom it is directed, but also to others nearby." He added that Brown's conduct was "particularly dangerous" and that he had to be "physically pulled away" from the attack. The judge said Brown's fame, commercial success and professional standing "do not entitle you to special treatment - the law applies equally to everyone". But judge Baumgartner also said he had noted Brown's guilty plea, compliance with bail conditions, and the impact a custodial sentence would have on Brown's children, and said the singer's "risk of further offending is low". Brown and Akinlolu pleaded guilty to a charge of affray at Southwark Crown Court in July. The singer had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied, and which were subsequently dropped. These were assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon. Following Brown and Akinlolu's guilty pleas, the CPS released a statement outlining that Brown had approached Diaw on the dance floor, hitting him over the head with a glass bottle twice, before Akinlolu then punched Diaw in the head. "They continued their assault whilst the victim attempted to flee through the club," the CPS said. "The victim was kicked while he was seated defenceless on the floor." Judge Baumgartner told the pair that while he had concluded they had both crossed the threshold to be jailed, this year's changes to sentencing laws meant that he had to put off doing so, unless there were exceptional reasons. "I have considered whether the seriousness of the offending, taken together with the need for punishment and deterrence, amounts to exceptional circumstances requiring immediate imprisonment. I have concluded, in relation to each of you, that it does not," he said. "These were serious offences deserving of custodial sentences, but the circumstances do not justify displacing the [new legal] requirement that those sentences be suspended." Image source, Press Association Image caption, Brown's vocal coach, rapper Omololu Akinlolu, also previously pleaded guilty to affray On Monday, the court was shown three pieces of CCTV footage from inside Tape nightclub on the night of the attack. The attack lasted no more than 20 seconds, but Brown could be seen hitting the victim four times with a tequila bottle, twice to the head. Prosecutor, Heidi Stonecliffe KC, described the weapon as a "heavy square-shaped tequila bottle" and said Diaw was approached by Brown at around 03:00. The footage showed that the nightclub was very small and packed at the time. The defence described Chris Brown as a "dedicated and a loving father of four children," someone who is "positive and present". The singer is described as having lived "a good and law-abiding life" since his last conviction in 2013. The events in Tape nightclub were described by the defence as a "short and deeply regretted incident". Brown's defence lawyer told the court that he apologises to all those present at the club at the time of the attack. "This is an ugly and unattractive incident," Sallie Bennett-Jenkins KC said. "It is, however, an incident which was very short-lived, lasting something more than 17 seconds but no more than 20. "It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr Brown... offers a profound apology to all those present." The court heard Akinlolu "genuinely believed" that Brown was "under attack" when he joined the attack, punching Diaw. Brown was described as being like a "brother" to Akinlolu, his lawyer Laurie-Anne Power KC told the court. She added: "He genuinely believed him to be under attack and became involved, and thereafter accepts his initial involvement very quickly evolved into the events he has pleaded guilty to." Diaw was taken to St Mary's Hospital in London after the attack. Ms Stonecliffe KC said he was discharged with "pain relief and a diagnosis of head injury and superficial injury of the knee". An MRI scan taken in early March showed a "high grade injury to a ligament on the inner side of the left knee", the court heard. Defending Brown, Ms Bennett-Jenkins KC said there was a "relatively low level of force" and disputed how significant the injuries were. The defence argued that the attack left no fractures or broken skin and there was an absence of serious injuries. Diaw, the victim, was "not supportive of the prosecution" and "withdrew" his support some time after the incident, the court heard. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Chris Brown is one of R&B's most successful singers, with hits including Yeah 3x and Forever Brown and Akinlolu stood up and faced one another and clasped hands after the judge concluded his sentencing remarks before walking out of the glass dock. There were loud cheers outside the court as Chris Brown left the building as he appeared to stop to sign an autograph. After the sentencing, Brown shared a video from inside his car on his Instagram story, showing him looking out the window before turning to the camera and giving a thumbs-up. Affray is an offence under the Public Order Act and a person is deemed guilty in law if they use or threaten "unlawful violence towards another" with their behaviour, leading someone to fear for their personal safety. Brown, 37, is considered one of the biggest stars in R&B, with a string of hit songs including Turn Up The Music, Ayo, Freaky Friday, Run It, Forever, Yeah 3x and Don't Wake Me Up. title: Excitement grows for new ACOTAR book
description: Dozens will be gathering at Wolverhampton Arts Centre to celebrate the series' newest release.
content: Excitement grows for new ACOTAR book Image source, Holly Fellows Image caption, Fan Holly Fellows from Redditch has organised a party to celebrate the release tonight ByRachael Lewis, West Midlands and Sarah Julian, BBC Radio WM Published 26 October 2026 Fans of the book series A Court of Thorns and Roses are planning parties and taking days off work, ahead of a new edition being released at 00:01 GMT on Tuesday. Dozens will be gathering at Wolverhampton Arts Centre on Monday night, to celebrate the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony. "It's the escapism, it's a way for people to escape from every day life. So many people, especially young women, see themselves in these characters and there are so many really strong messages about empowerment and finding strength," party organiser Holly Fellows, from Redditch, said. The fantasy series, written by American author, Sarah J. Maas, is popular with readers across the world. To pass the time until the book goes on sale fans will take part in arts and crafts projects. "Waterstones Wolverhampton will be bringing the books, and bang on midnight everyone will receive their book and we will spend some quiet time reading," Fellows said. "I've booked the day off work [tomorrow]. I'll be undisturbed for the whole day, and I reckon I'll get through it by the evening." What is ACOTAR? ACOTAR is a fantasy romance series, set in the fictional world of Prythian. There have been five books in the series so far, A Court of Thorns and Roses (2015), A Court of Mist and Fury (2016), A Court of Wings and Ruin (2017), A Court of Frost and Starlight (2018), and A Court of Silver Flames (2021). In 2015, ACOTAR was ranked a 'Most Read Book of the Year' on book recommendation site, Goodreads. The books have millions of fans, with the hashtag ACOTAR being used 2.1 million times on the social media app TikTok, and 1.8 million times on Instagram. Millions of fans have been posting on social media sharing their excitement ahead of the release - with some getting their hands on the book early. One posted on TikTok saying: "Why did I waste my annual leave on important life events, when there's a new acotar coming out". Another said: "I simply don't know if I'm ready for this". It has been five years since the last edition was released, something Fellows said has left fans "going crazy". "It's created this sense of community that - just from a book - is this massive magical world. "Where I work, there are women who are my age reading them, there's also women in their 40s, 50s that are picking them up. Online I'm seeing loads of men reading them. It's a universal craze to be honest." The author confirmed on her website that after the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony on 27 October, the seventh book in the series, A Court of Forgotten Melody, will be released on 12 January 2027. title: Fans prepare to say goodbye as anime series Bleach officially ends
description: Twenty two years after it first aired, one of the biggest animes of all time is coming to an end.
content: Fans praise 'perfect' ending as anime series Bleach officially ends Image source, Bandai Namco Image caption, Bleach follows the story of Ichigo Kurosaki, an orange-haired teenager with the unusual ability to see ghosts ByAbu Bakar Yasin and Naomi de Souza, BBC Newsbeat Published 26 October 2026 It's a finale fans have waited more than a decade to see. The epic conclusion to Bleach, the popular animated series based on the hit manga, or Japanese comic, has arrived - and early reactions have described it is as a "perfect" ending. Anticipation for the final episode of the climactic Thousand-Year Blood War storyline was especially high. The original comic book's "rushed" ending is widely considered disappointing but creator Tite Kubo has overseen some major changes to the new adaptation. As some mourned the "end of an era", many waited nervously to see if he could stick the landing second time around. BBC Newsbeat's spoke to fans as they said an "emotional" goodbye to Kubo's creation. Bleach is regarded as one of the "big three" manga in Japan alongside One Piece and Naruto, and animated adaptations of each are credited with helping to fuel the global popularity of anime. It follows the story of Ichigo Kurosaki, a teenager with distinctive orange hair who has the unusual ability to see ghosts. He navigates school and family life at the same time as defending humanity from evil spirits. "It is honestly my favourite series of all time, it has got me through a lot across my life," says fan Ruby. So how did it feel to say goodbye? "I honestly think I laughed more than I cried in this episode," she says. "I'm just really happy that Kubo finally got to show us his true vision for the story that he wasn't able to back in the early 2010s." The 27-year-old started reading Bleach aged nine and became friends with fellow fan Nicholas, 30, through their shared passion. "I've made so many friends through Bleach, it's been such a wonderful part of my life both in terms of what it teaches me and the kind of people I meet through it," says Ruby. For Nicholas, watching Bleach as teenager helped him get through school - and he even has a tattoo dedicated to the story. "It helped me make friends in school, talking to a few people who also knew Bleach and about our favourite characters," he says. Image source, Supplied Image caption, Nicholas (left) and Ruby became friends through their shared passion for Bleach The original Bleach anime ran from 2004 to 2012 across 16 seasons but never caught up to the manga source material - with fans left unsure if it would ever come back. But the first part of Bleach's animated final chapter eventually premiered 10 years later in 2022. The arc, Thousand-Year Blood War, has been split into four separate chapters, and the final run began this July. Bleach's original comic book ending was divisive and broadly unpopular with fans and was said to have been rushed due to creator Kubo experiencing health issues during its production. One of the reasons they've been so excited to see the new, animated finale is due to the fact Kubo and animation house Pierrot Films have made changes to the original storyline. And many had hoped the "final battle", external would "fix" the unpopular ending from 2016. Image source, Itanna Alakija Image caption, Itanna Alakija has praised the representation on the show Itanna Alakija describes himself as the "biggest Bleach fan there is" and says the revised finale was a "perfect conclusion to the entire arc of Bleach. The 28-year-old thinks some people will be disappointed by the lack of action in the episode, but thinks the anime succeeded in taking the original manga "a step further". And a tease at the end of the episode has given him hope that there might be more stories to come from the Bleach universe. Alakija says the series resonated with him because of its depiction of black characters, in contrast with other anime where creators can lean on stereotypes. "The way that Tite Kubo integrates all these cultures and represents them in a Japanese art form is really interesting and amazing," he says. Alakija was already a Naruto fan when he discovered Bleach as a teenager. "I remember stumbling upon Bleach and thought: 'This looks cool'," he says. And he praises the show for treating black characters as "normal people". "It's one of the few anime that has represented black characters in a non-stereotypical way." Bleach is available to stream via Disney+ globally and on Hulu in the US. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.
