title: Burnham leaves door open to referendum on EU free movement
description: The PM says he wants to start a conversation about potential options for the UK's future relationship with the EU.
content: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion Image source, Reuters ByBen Wright, Political correspondent, Jack Fenwick, Political correspondent and Becky Morton, Political reporter Published 26 October 2026 Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom of movement. Asked earlier by broadcasters if he could introduce freedom of movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no". But sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made and the prime minister's deputy spokesperson later said the government was not going to "get ahead" of how to consult the public. Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options. He told broadcasters that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit". Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK. Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union. And he has previously stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029. After lengthy questioning about the issue, Number 10 sought to clarify the prime minister's remarks, saying: "The prime minister isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement or any option." "He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said. "What he wants to do first is have a conversation with the public. The process will follow." She added: "The PM thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough." Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market. The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards. Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement Published 1 day ago Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham Published 30 September In an interview with the Sunday Times, external, Burnham said he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and the EU. The PM argued that the type of migration had changed since Brexit, with more foreigners moving permanently. In contrast, he suggested that when the UK was a member of the EU, migration was "generally younger people", who would spend a few years in the country before returning home. However, Burnham added: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen." The Schengen Agreement, which the UK was not part of when it was in the EU, allows passport-free travel across member countries. The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro. Burnham has argued that since Brexit, the UK has lost immigration control the country previously had. "For instance, the small boats crisis has arisen in the last 10 years because we lost that returns agreement when people came here that we could work with other countries to return them," he told broadcasters. The Conservatives and Reform UK both oppose a return to free movement with the EU. However, the Liberal Democrats have argued that allowing freedom of movement would help economic growth. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued most people who voted for Brexit did so because they did not want free movement, while Reform leader Nigel Farage has said such a move would be "a total betrayal of Brexit Britain". Farage told broadcasters he was "up for the fight again" on the EU and an "election is coming" to decide that. "Crucially, [Burnham] goes to Brussels on 20 November for a key summit - he must not sign up to anything there without at least putting those minor changes to a general election," he said. title: Borthwick's autumn questions as World Cup looms
description: The upcoming Nations Championship matches present a selection dilemma for Steve Borthwick's England with just nine matches to go until the World Cup.
content: Borthwick's autumn questions as World Cup looms Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Steve Borthwick's England have won three of their past eight matches By Chris Jones Rugby union correspondent Published 26 October 2026 With under a year to go until the 2027 Rugby World Cup, the countdown is on, with just nine competitive matches for the home nations until the tournament starts in Australia next October. But while the World Cup spectre looms large, there is plenty to play for between now and then, starting with the resumption of the inaugural Nations Championship in November. Steve Borthwick has named his 36-man training squad ahead of the Tests with Australia, Japan and New Zealand, and it gives a clear indication of the England head coach's thinking on both a long and short-term basis. England play Australia on 8 November before facing Japan on 14 November and New Zealand on 21 November. There is a recall for Joe Marchant, fellow centre Will Joseph is rewarded for his and Gloucester's excellent start to the season, while uncapped Archie McParland is the third scrum-half and uncapped Kepu Tuipulotu the third hooker. On the whole, though, it is a tried and tested group. "If we look at this training squad, it's not picked on form, is it?" former England wing Chris Ashton said on the Rugby Union Weekly podcast. "It is a squad to get to the World Cup. Will Joseph is picked on form, but the vast majority is not. It is based on the experience and relationships [Borthwick] has with the players, and that is why Marchant is in there." It is often the dilemma facing an England head coach. With 10 teams to pick from, there are always players playing well. How do you balance that with getting selection consistency from campaign to campaign? Fin Baxter, Luke Cowan-Dickie, Jamie George, Will Stuart, George Furbank and Ben Curry - among others - have all been short of minutes or form this season. But they are all Borthwick regulars with priceless Test match experience. "Part of the problem right now is that Steve feels he is under pressure to get results, so it is too late to make big changes," added Ashton. "There just aren't many lads that have played much rugby." Injury absences and a midfield conundrum The uncapped pair of McParland and Tuipulotu will both bring a freshness to camp. But will McParland get much gametime ahead of the established duo of Jack van Poortvliet and Alex Mitchell, and will Tuipulotu get any minutes when competing with the highly experienced George and Cowan-Dickie? "We know how talented Tuipulotu is, he is brilliant, but Nathan Jibulu at Sale has had two man-of-the-match performances and might feel slightly hard done by," said Ugo Monye, who also added that George Hendy at Northampton is another notable omission. "In my opinion, we need to have a look at Hendy," he continued. "He has been that good for that long. And if we are talking about form, where is [Bristol back rower] Fitz Harding? "But I am sure Steve had a rough idea of his squad a month ago." As ever, injuries will force Borthwick's hand. Benhard Janse van Rensburg is out - a big blow to Borthwick given how he was fast-tracked into the set-up - while incumbent number 12 Seb Atkinson is on the rehab list, as is Exeter flyer Immanuel Feyi-Waboso. Their fitness will be monitored forensically by the England medical staff. Meanwhile, the nailed-on starter at fly-half Fin Smith will also miss training this week with a calf niggle, although his injury is not thought to be serious. Charlie Atkinson was called up on Monday morning. In the forwards, the selection picture is reasonably clear. Ellis Genge, George, Cowan-Dickie, Joe Heyes, Will Stuart, Ollie Chessum, Alex Coles, Maro Itoje, George Martin, Ben Earl, Tom Curry and Henry Pollock all make the 23 if fit. Behind the scrum, especially at centre, it is more uncertain. "I would struggle to answer [who will play in the midfield]," said Ashton. Atkinson and Henry Slade started England's last Test, a crucial victory over Argentina in July, and could line up together again against the Wallabies on 8 November. But Marchant and Joseph are also battling for the number 13 shirt, and a possible World Cup place. "Marchant and Will Joseph are in a bit of a shoot-out," added Monye. "They can both do a job on the wing and when you look at a World Cup squad you look at versatility. "I would like to see bold decisions, but it is easy saying that when your job isn't on the line and you are trying to get selection right ahead of a World Cup. "Will Joseph has been excellent and there will loads of fans who watch the Prem and will say against Australia, Seb Atkinson and Will Joseph are your ready-made 12 and 13. "But I would be very surprised if that was to happen." The players will be in camp until Tuesday evening before returning to their clubs for one more round of league action, before re-joining England next Sunday, seven days before the Australia showdown. Borthwick has precious little time in camp with his squad before the Wallabies come to town, putting even more emphasis on established players, and established combinations. Twelve months ago, England were in the midst of a winning run and started the autumn series full of confidence. It is a different picture now after an underwhelming 2026, with just three wins from eight matches so far. As it stands, where the side will be come the World Cup in 12 months is anyone's guess. England and Borthwick need a big November. title: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again
description: The firebrand left-winger, who has at times been at odds with Trump, has won his fourth term as Brazil's president.
content: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Even for a veteran politician like Lula, uniting a divided nation will be a challenge ByPaulin Kola Published 26 October 2026 On the face of it, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has done the impossible one more time - within three weeks he overturned defeat in first-round voting to gain re-election as Brazil's president. It was no mean achievement for a man who before his first successful run at the post in 2002 had tried three times unsuccessfully. When he became president in 2003, he came to office as the first leftist leader of Brazil in nearly half a century. Now aged 80 and with plenty of experience at governing as large a democracy as Brazil, he has bucked the trend of electoral victory for right-wing leaders in Latin America whose policies mirror that of US President Donald Trump. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Who is Lula and what are his policies? Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty. The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old. He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near São Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s. Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism. Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement. In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history. The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform. Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system. He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation. Image source, Wojtek Laski/Getty Images Image caption, In this picture Lula is seen meeting fellow Polish trade unionist - and subsequently president - Lech Walesa in Rome, Italy, in 1981 In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities. By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor. However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education. He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - 83% - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades. Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012. Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback Published 15 hours ago Lula faces hostile congress and divided country after Brazil election win Published 1 day ago Why was Lula previously jailed? Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash. Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years. Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used. He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated. In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted. Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro. When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday. Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office. And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions. His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism. Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy. His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working. What is Lula's relationship with Trump? Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump. The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public. The Brazilian leader told the BBC in September 2025 that he had no relationship with Trump. Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year jail sentence and it was his son, Flávio, who Lula beat in Sunday's election run-off. Lula accused Trump of foreign interference and said "he's not emperor of the world". But their relationship improved after a White House in May this year, after which the two leaders exchanged public compliments - Trump called Lula "dynamic", while the Brazilian president said he left the meeting "very satisfied". In July of this year, the US imposed 25% tariffs on most goods, external from Brazil. The two governments still disagree on key issues such as crime, and Lula acknowledged they are especially far apart on trade. Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard". Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Trump and Lula had warm words when they met in Washington earlier this year Is Lula close to China and Russia? Lula has criticised the fact that five countries - the permanent members of the UN Security Council - have the power to veto decisions and argued that this tilted the balance in favour of those who won World War Two, excluding nations representing billions of people like Brazil, Germany, India, and Japan, as well as African countries. Brazil is an active member of the Brics - a grouping that unites Brazil with Russia, India, China and South Africa. Lula defends his continued alliances with Russia and China and sees the Brics as an emerging counterweight to the West. He has defended his choice to continue to purchase Russian oil while Russia wages war in Ukraine. title: Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US
description: This is how his signature policy has played out after returning to power promising a closed border and mass deportations.
content: Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US Image source, Getty Images ByBernd Debusmann Jr and Mike Hills Published 26 October 2026 Immigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message. When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since. Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts. But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress. Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency. He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both. But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far. His signature policy has played out in five key ways. 1. A border that is largely closed Crossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border. His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing. When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted. By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone. On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings. To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach. That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north. "President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October. "The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works." 2. Building of wall speeding up A vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign. Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill. According to government figures, external, about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US. Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction. Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated. Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate. "Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council. There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging. Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it. "I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history." Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning Published 4 days ago 3. Detentions and deportations rocketing Most of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country. During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first. Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project, external, a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA. But the same data, external shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%. Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office. But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 2026 that left two US citizens dead. A New York Times and Siena poll, external released on 21 October found that 50% of voters trust Democrats to handle the issue, compared with 46% for Republicans - despite the issue being a traditional Republican strength. A separate poll, from Politico and Public First, external in late September, found deep splits between Republicans on the issue, with 31% of non-MAGA Republicans, meaning those not aligned with Trump's movement, believing that campaign has become too aggressive. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midterms 4. Refugee intake down sharply After returning to the White House last year, Trump almost immediately suspended refugee admissions, saying at the time these could only restart if they were shown to be in US interests. In February, however, an executive order signed by Trump narrowly re-opened that process for Afrikaners from South Africa, who the White House has repeatedly said are being killed and "persecuted" - a claim that the government in Pretoria has denied. The cap for refugee admissions for the 2026 fiscal year was initially set at 7,500, which was raised to 17,500 in May this year because of what the administration described as an "unforeseen emergency refugee situation". Overall refugee admissions have slowed to a relative trickle. State Department data shows that 16,292 refugees were admitted into the US in the 2026 fiscal year - of whom 16,287 were South African. By comparison, in the final two fiscal years of the Biden administration - 2023 and 2024 - 60,000 and 100,000 entered the country, respectively. In the 2024 fiscal year, the highest numbers came from Democratic Republic of Congo, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela. Hundreds of thousands of people protected from deportation lost that protection when a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was also ended in Trump's second term. It gave vetted individuals the right to live and work in the US if their home countries were deemed to be unsafe to return to. One of those countries was Haiti. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US. Haitian migrants changed this US town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again Published 6 days ago 5. A squeeze on visas - and a $1m golden ticket Other legal pathways to come to live and work in the US have also been tightened up, through various policy changes. Dozens of countries the Trump administration has deemed a security risk have been subject to a full or partial freeze on visas and travel. Enhanced vetting and new rules that send people residing in the US back to their home countries to apply for green cards has slowed that process down. And in September 2025, a $100,000 fee on new H1-B visas for skilled workers, mostly held by Indians, stunned the US tech industry. In May this year, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services said on X, external that registrations for 2027 were down 40%. "The data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the program with mass, low-wage registrations are over, and that the program is better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers and protecting the wages, working conditions and job opportunities of American workers," the statement added. While a court has blocked the $100,000 fee - for now - the threat of it appears to have deterred employers. But some experts have cautioned the administration's aim of protecting American jobs, raising wages and stopping firms from outsourcing may prove elusive. One study, from the Wharton School of Business, external, found that the H1-B changes would have "no significant impact" on the wages of US-born workers, with any reduction in competition offset by reduced productivity growth. Other pathways to the US have been opened, however - if you have a spare million. The "Trump Gold Card" launched in 2025 sought to entice wealthy foreigners to come live in the US in exchange for a $1m "gift" to the US government, plus a non-refundable $15,000 application fee. At the time, Trump said that the programme would boost the US economy. Its uptake, however, appears to be minimal so far. By April, only one applicant had been accepted. title: Stunning photos capture October's Hunter's Moon around the world
description: October's full Moon, nicknamed the Hunter's Moon, lit up the night sky this weekend.
content: Stunning photos capture October's Hunter's Moon around the world Image source, Tayfun Coskun / Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, A good view for the passengers of this plane flying over San Francisco Bay in California, US ByJo Wade BBC Weather Published 26 October 2026 The October full Moon lit up skies around the world this weekend. Full Moons throughout the year have traditionally been given names that reflect what is going on in nature. This particular full moon is known by several names, including the Hunter's Moon, a name rooted in historical traditions in the Northern Hemisphere. The Hunter's Moon is known to sit in the sky for a particularly long time - similar to the preceding Harvest Moon - giving hunters extra light in the skies. Image source, BBC / BBC Weather Watcher Sam's House Image caption, The Hunter's Moon over Stoney Middleton in Derbyshire, UK Image source, Gary Hershorn / Getty Images Image caption, An autumn glow as the Hunter's Moon rises behind the skyline of midtown Manhattan in New York City, US Image source, Davide Pischettola / NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, The Moon can take on an orange or reddish hue when it is low in the sky due to the scattering of short wavelength blue light as it passes through a large depth of the atmosphere, as shown here as it rises behind the Basilica of the Madonna dei Martiri in Molfetta, Italy Image source, BBC / BBC Weather Watcher Moxley Image caption, A view of the moon from Kimmeridge in Dorset, UK Image source, Salih Zeki Fazlioglu / Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, The full moon glowing a beautiful burnt orange over the Galata Tower in Istanbul, Turkey Image source, BBC / BBC Weather Watcher Squiz Image caption, A clear view of the Moon in Felixstowe, Suffolk Image source, Ahmad al-Rubaye / AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Moonrise in Baghdad's Firdous Square, Iraq Image source, Tayfun Coskun / Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, The Hunter's Moon setting in San Francisco, California, US More on this story Northern Lights illuminate skies across the UK Published 11 October Your pictures as equinox marks the start of astronomical autumn Published 23 September Five night sky events to look out for this autumn Published 13 September

title: First Scotland call-up for Newcastle's Leatherbarrow
description: Uncapped Newcastle Falcons back-row Ollie Leatherbarrow is called up by Scotland for the first time for three home Nations Championship fixtures against New Zealand, Australia and Japan.
content: First Scotland call-up for Newcastle's Leatherbarrow Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Ollie Leatherbarrow has played for Scotland at youth level Published 26 October 2026 Uncapped Newcastle Red Bulls back row Ollie Leatherbarrow has been called up by Scotland for the first time for the three home Nations Championship fixtures against New Zealand, Australia and Japan. But in-form Edinburgh forwards Magnus Bradbury and Freddy Douglas are surprising omissions from the 37-strong squad. Macclesfield-born Leatherbarrow qualifies for Scotland because of his grandmother being from Perth and has already represented Scotland at under-16 and under-20 levels. The 24-year-old began his career at Exeter Chiefs before moving to Newcastle in 2023. Senior trio Jamie Ritchie, Darcy Graham and Duhan van der Merwe have all been included after returning recently from injuries. "This has been my goal for a long time," Leatherbarrow said. "When you feel like you are playing well for your club, you're obviously looking to get that national call-up. "It's just about showing what I can do. My strength is probably ball-carrying, so that lends itself to number eight a bit more, but I'm probably more the size of a seven. "I've played all three back row positions for Newcastle and I'm happy to play wherever really." Head coach Gregor Townsend acknowledged Bradbury's strong start to the season but said he was "looking for more" from the 31-year-old. "We know Magnus is hugely motivated for Scotland," he explained. "We know the qualities he brings. "We're also aware that Jack Dempsey [now based in Japan] is not going to be available in the Six Nations, so it's an opportunity for us to look at someone else in our environment. "We know Ollie can cover all three positions in the back row. He's an openside by trade, but he's played a lot of rugby at six and eight. "He'll be challenging for a place now and in the Six Nations, like Magnus will be as well." Glasgow Warriors' Seb Stephen, who made his debut in July's Nations Championship match against Fiji, is one of three hookers selected. Experienced Edinburgh lock Grant Gilchrist is not included after returning from injury, while club-mate Hector Patterson had been touted for potential involvement after a bright start to the season, but the scrum-half has not made the cut. Townsend said no decision has been made yet on New Zealand-born Josh McKay, the 29-year-old Glasgow full-back who will be eligible in time for the final Test against Japan. Scotland host the All Blacks on 7 November, the Wallabies on 15 November and the Brave Blossoms on 21 November at Murrayfield before the new Nations Championship concludes the following weekend at Twickenham, based around final hemisphere positions. The finals are on the weekend of 28-29 November, with fixtures determined by the placings of northern and southern hemisphere countries across these games and the ones played in July. Scotland squad Forwards: Ewan Ashman (Edinburgh), Josh Bayliss (Bath), Gregor Brown, Scott Cummings, Alex Craig, Rory Darge (all Glasgow Warriors), Jack Dempsey (Toshiba Brave Lupus), Matt Fagerson, Zander Fagerson (both Glasgow Warriors), Jonny Gray (Perpignan), Gregor Hiddleston (Glasgow Warriors), Will Hurd (Leicester Tigers), Ollie Leatherbarrow (Newcastle Red Bulls), Nathan McBeth (Glasgow Warriors), Liam McConnell (Edinburgh), Elliot Millar Mills (Newcastle Red Bulls), Jamie Ritchie (Glasgow Warriors), Pierre Schoeman (Edinburgh), Rory Sutherland, Seb Stephen, Max Williamson (all Glasgow Warriors). Backs: Fergus Burke (Saracens), Jamie Dobie (Glasgow Warriors), Darcy Graham (Edinburgh), George Horne (Glasgow Warriors), Rory Hutchinson (Northampton Saints), Huw Jones (Toulon), Tom Jordan (Bristol Bears), Blair Kinghorn (Toulouse), Stafford McDowall, Kyle Rowe (both Glasgow Warriors), Finn Russell (Bath), Ollie Smith, Kyle Steyn, Sione Tuipulotu, capt (all Glasgow Warriors), Duhan van der Merwe (Edinburgh), Ben White (Toulon). title: Baxter focuses on 'reality' of Exeter's early form
description: Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter says he is not fazed by the club's difficult start to the season.
content: Baxter focuses on 'reality' of Exeter's early form Image source, Shutterstock Image caption, Rob Baxter led Exeter to the Prem final last season Published 26 October 2026 Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter says he is not fazed by the club's difficult start to the season. The beaten Prem finalists from June lost 20-7 at Bristol on Saturday to slip to second from bottom in the Prem after four matches. Exeter's only win so far is a bonus point victory over Newcastle earlier this month, having lost at home to Gloucester on the opening weekend of the season and an away defeat at Bath. "The only odd result we've had in the league so far, if you compare it to the last season, was losing to Gloucester, and Gloucester clearly are going to beat people this season," Baxter told BBC Radio Devon. "We lost that first game of the season, but we picked up a point. We've been to Bath and picked up two points, which is what we did last season. "We beat Newcastle at home with five points, what we did last season [and] we didn't beat Bristol last season at Bristol. "The season's not hugely different, it just looks like it and feels like it." Bristol overcome Exeter to go third in Prem Published 2 days ago Exeter's final game before the break for the autumn international is at home against bottom of the table Harlequins. The London side got their first win of the season on Sunday to close the gap on Exeter to one point. "I've got to make sure I get the lads feeling some reality about where we are," added Baxter. "Despite [that] people can look and go, 'Ah this isn't right', a lot of things are right, we've just got to stick to it. "Harlequins becomes big because we beat Harlequins at home last season, so we've got to beat them at home this season, that's how we've got to do it." Related topics Exeter Chiefs Rugby Union

title: Court dismisses DOJ's request to force California to set aside ballots
description: A federal appeals court on Monday dismissed the DOJ's effort to force California election officials to set aside thousands of ballots that the Trump administration claims may have been cast by alleged noncitizens.
content: Politics Appeals court dismisses DOJ's request to force California to set aside ballots By Melissa Quinn Melissa Quinn Senior Reporter, Politics Melissa Quinn is a senior reporter for CBSNews.com, where she covers U.S. politics, with a focus on the Supreme Court and federal courts. Read Full Bio Melissa Quinn Updated on: October 26, 2026 / 7:37 PM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google Washington — A federal appeals court on Monday dismissed the Justice Department's effort to force California election officials to set aside thousands of ballots that the Trump administration claims may have been cast by alleged noncitizens. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit said in a 2-1 decision that it lacked jurisdiction over the appeal and granted a motion by the top elections official from Los Angeles County to dismiss the effort. The federal government, Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez said, failed to allow a federal district court "adequate opportunity" to consider its request for temporary relief. Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented. The two judges faulted the Justice Department for waiting until less than three weeks before the midterm elections on Nov. 3 to file its lawsuit and only seeking a temporary restraining order from the district court last week. They also pointed out that the department had sought a temporary restraining order as California was already processing ballots. "The United States's claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one," the 9th Circuit said in an unsigned opinion. "At least part of the delay here is attributable to the United States's own delay in filing suit, in realizing that existing California state law governs the issuance and processing of ballots, in recognizing that California has millions of registered voters and processes ballots on a schedule aligned with that scale, and in communicating to the court its desired relief." Both Bennett, appointed by President Trump, and Sanchez, tapped by former President Joe Biden, authored concurring opinions. Bennett said that even if the court had reached the legal merits of the Justice Department's effort, he would have rejected its bid to force California to set aside the ballots that may be cast by ineligible voters. Bumatay, who dissented, said the federal government has an interest in protecting the integrity of federal elections. "The question — does the federal government have the power to stop this potential attack on the integrity of our elections? Under both federal law and the Constitution, the answer must be 'yes,'" the judge, a Trump appointee, wrote. "Simply, the federal government has a sovereign interest in safeguarding federal elections and ensuring that the votes of noncitizens do not undermine our electoral results." California Gov. Gavin Newsom said the 9th Circuit's decision is a "positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump's disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country's democracy." "Trump is illegally trying to seize powers in the Constitution entrusted to others so he can stay in power. This lawsuit is just the latest step," he said in a statement. "Make no mistake: Trump's assault on democracy won't slow down." Dispute over list of voters The fast-moving dispute over California's mail ballots was filed earlier this month after Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to California's secretary of state and the top election official in Los Angeles County, Dean Logan, which gave them 48 hours to review a list of more than 20,000 registered voters who the Trump administration believes are "likely" noncitizens and were sent mail ballots. Los Angeles County told McCotter in a letter dated Oct. 15 that the list of suspected noncitizens contained addresses of registered voters throughout the state, and said his letter did not include information about how the list had been compiled. The county also told McCotter the letter did not provide any information as to how the county was to confirm citizenship status. A lawyer for Los Angeles County said the Justice Department was asking Logan, the registrar-recorder and county clerk, "to engage in an unlawful course of conduct." On the same day that the county sent McCotter its response, the Justice Department sued California, Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Logan, and claimed that state officials had failed to work collaboratively with the federal government to identify any noncitizens registered to vote in the state and protect the integrity of elections. The Justice Department asked a federal judge to order California to put aside mail ballots of people it has identified as suspected noncitizens and to independently verify their citizenship status before counting their ballots. The judge overseeing the case, David O. Carter, scheduled a hearing for Tuesday afternoon on the Trump administration's request for a temporary restraining order. But the following day, the Justice Department took the extraordinary step of filing an appeal with the 9th Circuit. Government lawyers argued that because Carter had not yet ruled on their request for emergency relief, his "silence" amounted to a "constructive denial" of their effort to require California to set aside the mail ballots returned by the voters on the Trump administration's list. The three-judge 9th Circuit panel then held a rare Sunday oral argument session, during which at least two of the judges appeared skeptical of the Justice Department's request for the court to step in. The 11th-hour lawsuit against California officials was filed less than three weeks before the November midterm elections, when voters across the country will decide which party controls the House and Senate. In California, elections officials began mailing ballots in early October. Los Angeles County has already processed an estimated 550,000 mail ballots, according to court filings. In the months leading up to the midterms, Mr. Trump has attempted to exert more federal control over elections and pushed Congress to enact a package of voting regulations, including requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote. The president has repeatedly claimed that hundreds of thousands of noncitizens are registered to vote in federal elections, including more than 190,000 in California. Both federal and California law prohibit noncitizens from voting. But the Department of Homeland Security has declined to provide California election officials with an explanation of how it identified those alleged ineligible voters. Instead, in its lawsuit, the Justice Department said the DHS compares information about voter rolls with internal data to identify potential matches between registered voters and possible noncitizens, and then uses "third-party software" to identify matches between voter information and data about that person compiled by the software program. The Trump administration also said it uses internal records and data from the Social Security Administration. But California officials have argued that the Justice Department's lawsuit does not contain any allegations that those suspected noncitizens will even vote unlawfully in the general election. Lawyers for Logan, the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder and county clerk, also said that the relief sought by the Trump administration exceeds the executive branch's constitutional authority. The Constitution's Elections Clause gives states the power to set the "times, places and manners" of congressional elections unless Congress steps in. Amid the ongoing litigation, lawyers for Logan and Los Angeles County said they attempted to analyze the data from the Trump administration's list of alleged noncitizens. The list includes 7,035 records with county addresses, they said. County officials reviewed a sample of 200 of those records and found 112 of them correspond to voter registrations that were canceled or inactive, so no ballot was mailed to that person. Most of the people in the sample had never voted, and more than one-quarter of them listed a birthplace in the U.S., according to a Los Angeles County election official. Federal prosecutors sent more letters to at least 18 other California county registrars on Friday with lists of alleged noncitizens registered to vote. The Justice Department demanded the elections officials set aside ballots cast by those it believes are ineligible to vote. The Justice Department could ask the full 9th Circuit to reconsider its appeal, and the panel gave the government until 7 p.m. local time to make such a request. 2026 Midterm Elections More John Thune's balancing act: Inside his push to save the GOP majority Bishops lament White House meeting that produced photo with Trump Gina Hinojosa says there's "deep disappointment" in both parties Blanche says DOJ is "doing our own research" with Alaska challenge Poll finds Democrats still boosted by voters' economic concerns Go deeper with The Free Press Why Voter ID Is Common Sense What Happens After Trump?: Why Tim Miller Thinks Politics Can’t Go Back In: Voting United States Department of Justice California 9th Circuit Court of Appeals © 2026 CBS Interactive Inc. title: DOJ takes steps to charge James Comey again
description: The DOJ took steps to charge James Comey with leaking information earlier this month, in its third attempt to bring criminal charges against the former FBI director and Trump foe.
content: Politics DOJ takes steps to charge James Comey again By Sarah N. Lynch, Sarah N. Lynch Senior Justice Department Reporter Sarah N. Lynch is the senior Justice Department reporter for CBS News, based in Washington, D.C. Read Full Bio Sarah N. Lynch, Joe Walsh Joe Walsh Senior Editor, Politics Joe Walsh is a senior editor for digital politics at CBS News. Joe previously covered breaking news for Forbes and local news in Boston. Read Full Bio Joe Walsh Updated on: October 27, 2026 / 12:38 AM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google The Justice Department took steps to charge James Comey with leaking classified information earlier this month, court records show, in its third attempt to bring criminal charges against the former FBI director and Trump foe. Prosecutors are seeking to charge Comey with two counts of violating the Espionage Act by transmitting national defense information to a person not entitled to receive it. He has not been indicted by a grand jury or charged by criminal complaint, and was instead targeted through a criminal information filing. In this case, the information was filed in order to preserve the statute of limitations before it expires, according to a Justice Department spokesperson. The official added that "this is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further." A criminal information does not require approval by a grand jury, or a finding by a magistrate judge of probable cause that there is evidence to establish that a crime was committed. Comey's attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said Comey "steadfastly maintains his innocence." The latest effort by the Justice Department stems from allegations that Comey gave national defense information to an unnamed individual for disclosure in a newspaper in October 2016. According to court filings in the case, The New York Times published an article on Oct. 5, 2016, titled, "Yahoo Said to Have Aided U.S. Email Surveillance By Adapting Spam Filter." The article cited two unnamed government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity. The Justice Department alleges that it has uncovered evidence that Comey sought to "correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before" and that Comey "directed staff" to speak with the Times reporter about the accuracy of the Reuters article. Fitzgerald said the information "purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit," adding that investigators looked into the matter twice during the first Trump administration and "determined that no charges should be brought against anyone." In a separate video statement, Comey said, "well, they're back again" — a reference to the two prior attempts to charge Comey, including a dismissed indictment accusing him of lying to Congress and a still-pending indictment accusing him of threatening President Trump via a social media post of a photo of seashells arranged to say "86 47." "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to," Comey said. "Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary." Asked about the case late Monday, Mr. Trump told reporters he'd "just heard about it." "I think he's a dirty cop, James Comey, but I know nothing about it," the president said. In a statement posted to social media, the Justice Department said: "Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals." Former prosecutors and defense attorneys told CBS News they had not seen a criminal information filed in a felony case in this manner before, and called the maneuver highly unusual. The practice had been approved in other federal appellate court districts in some cases, but is less common in Washington, D.C. Greg Rosen, a former federal prosecutor who helped lead Jan. 6 cases, told CBS News: "In years of practicing in D.C., I never saw one used this way, let alone in the third attempt by the same Department to charge the same man." Michael Bromwich, a former Justice Department inspector general who is now a defense attorney, told CBS News that he has never encountered a situation where a criminal information was filed to pause the statute of limitations. Normally, such charging documents are filed when a defendant plans to waive their right to have a grand jury weigh charges and opts to plead guilty. "I have never heard of proceeding by information to toll the statute of limitations. Most prosecutors you have ever dealt with have never heard of that. This seems to be a way to do an end-run around the statute of limitations and keep a case alive that deserved to die 9 years ago," Bromwich said. "This is just absolutely bizarro world stuff." DOJ and Comey fought in secret over charging efforts The criminal information were filed under seal in early October, and were unsealed by U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden on Monday at Comey's request. For much of this month, Comey's attorneys and federal prosecutors waged a behind-the-scenes fight over whether the Justice Department's effort to charge him should be dismissed. In an Oct. 9 court filing, Comey's legal team argued the government "filed a faulty information under seal … in an effort to toll the applicable statute of limitations." The crime that the government is seeking to charge Comey under has a 10-year statute of limitations, which would run out in October of this year — but the ex-FBI director's lawyers say the statute of limitations applies to indictments and can't be extended if the government files a criminal information. They also said Comey had "reason to believe that the government plans to use that information to seek an arrest warrant as soon as today, which could result in an after-hours arrest that would ensure Mr. Comey sits in jail over a holiday weekend." "Mr. Comey has reason to believe multiple federal law enforcement officers have surveilled his whereabouts while traveling to a family members' residence and around his own neighborhood throughout the week," Comey's lawyers wrote on Oct. 9, just before Columbus Day weekend. In an emergency court hearing, the government agreed to hold off on seeking an indictment for 30 days, attorneys for Comey later wrote. The Justice Department argued that Comey's efforts to dismiss the criminal information was premature because no indictment has been returned. "This is not the proper time for him to file pretrial motions or attempt to chip away at charging documents before he subjects himself to the Court's jurisdiction," the government said. Further, the department said the law allows the government to proceed because it permits prosecutors to meet the deadline if the "indictment is found or the information is instituted." In an unusual move, the criminal information filed by the department were signed by two senior officials — acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General Aakash Singh — as well as several special assistant U.S. attorneys who are not originally from the U.S. Attorney's office in Washington, D.C. McFadden, the Trump-nominated judge overseeing the case, ordered the court docket to be unsealed Monday, writing: "Criminal charges against a former FBI director for his conduct while in office are of significant public interest." He also said Comey "is aware of the criminal information and has offered to 'self-surrender,'" so there is no need to keep the case secret in order to help the government apprehend him. The judge did not rule on the merits of the case. Two prior investigations into FBI leaks This is not the first time that the Justice Department has sought to investigate the disclosure of classified information in connection with a 2016 Times article. Former U.S. Attorney John Durham of Connecticut, who was later appointed special counsel by Attorney General William Barr, investigated the matter in 2017, according to court filings in the case from Comey's defense team. At the time, he determined there were two sources for the article, including James Baker, the former FBI general counsel. As part of that investigation, Baker said the FBI's chief of staff instructed him to provide the information and he understood it was being conveyed at Comey's instruction. Durham ultimately did not recommend Baker or anyone else for prosecution. Baker could not be immediately reached for comment. The matter was later investigated a second time — in that case by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia under an investigation code-named Tropic Vortex. That was closed in February 2020, also without charges, according to court papers. Comey and Trump The Justice Department filed the criminal information in early October, about a month before the midterm elections. It marks the latest overt investigative step taken by the Justice Department in a politically charged case, a maneuver that runs counter to longstanding norms. Mr. Trump and Comey have had a contentious relationship for nearly a decade, dating back to when the president fired the former FBI chief early in his first term. His firing is what prompted then-Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein to appoint Special Counsel Robert Mueller, whose investigation dogged Mr. Trump for much of his first term. The two have exchanged barbs since then, with Mr. Trump calling Comey a "dirty cop" and repeatedly arguing he should be prosecuted, while Comey called Mr. Trump "morally unfit" to be president. In September 2025, the Justice Department obtained an indictment against Comey that charged him with lying to Congress, alleging he falsely told lawmakers in a 2020 hearing that he had never authorized an FBI employee to serve as an anonymous source. The indictment was personally signed by Lindsey Halligan, a former Trump White House aide who had been sworn in as interim U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia days earlier. Beforehand, staff in that office circulated a memo that argued charges should not be brought against Comey, CBS News has previously reported. A judge dismissed the charges on the grounds that Halligan was improperly appointed. Then, in April of this year, Comey was indicted in North Carolina on allegations that he threatened to kill Mr. Trump by posting to Instagram a photo of seashells arranged to form the numbers "86 47." (Mr. Trump is the 47th president.) Comey has long denied wrongdoing, and his attorneys have argued the charges against him are politically motivated. They are currently seeking to have the North Carolina charges dismissed on several grounds, including that his prosecution is vindictive and selective. That matter is currently pending. Comey isn't the only Trump foe to face criminal scrutiny. New York Attorney General Letitia James was also charged by Halligan's office with bank fraud last year. Her indictment was tossed out along with the first Comey indictment. Prosecutors presented her case to grand juries at least twice after that, but the grand jurors declined to re-indict her. Attorney General Todd Blanche has long denied that the charges against Comey and other Trump adversaries are driven by politics. In an interview with CBS News earlier this year, he said the "86 47" indictment was driven by "local prosecutors" and "local agents." Asked if Mr. Trump has called him up and ordered him to prosecute certain individuals, Blanche told CBS News he wouldn't discuss his conversations with the president, but "rest assured, he has much better, bigger and important things to do than to worry about me doing my job." title: Is the Federal Reserve likely to raise interest rates this week?
description: Fed officials will unveil their latest interest rate move this week, following the September rate hike, the first in three years.
content: MoneyWatch Federal Reserve to announce its latest interest rate move this week. Here's what economists expect. By Mary Cunningham Mary Cunningham Reporter, MoneyWatch Mary Cunningham is a reporter for CBS MoneyWatch. She previously worked at "60 Minutes," CBSNews.com and CBS News 24/7 as part of the CBS News Associate Program. Read Full Bio Mary Cunningham October 26, 2026 / 4:10 PM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google The Federal Reserve is scheduled to meet this week, when U.S. central bankers will decide whether to raise interest rates for the second time this year in a bid to subdue inflation. Most economists and Wall Street analysts expect the Fed to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4% when officials release the latest policy statement on Wednesday. Consumer prices have surged this year, with headline inflation across the U.S. rising at a 3.7% annual rate in September as energy costs jumped. Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and gas categories, rose 2.6% from a year ago amid signs inflation could be seeping into the broader economy. The Fed targets annual inflation of 2%. Gasoline prices, which have hovered above $4 a gallon for the last three months, accounted for more than half the September increase in consumer prices, according to the Labor Department. "Although the latest hot inflation readings and rise in inflation expectations will concern Fed officials, they still appear broadly intent on tightening policy at a measured pace," Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at investor advisory firm Capital Economics, said in a recent research note. In September, the Fed raised the federal funds rate — what banks charge each other for overnight loans — by a quarter of a percentage point — its first hike in three years, thereby raising borrowing costs across the U.S. economy. The Fed is scheduled to announce its latest interest rate decision at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday. The meeting comes at a crucial time, as Americans head to the polls to cast their ballots in the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Many Americans have expressed frustration with the state of the economy as they contend with rising costs of gas, food, utilities and other expenses. Most economists and investors expect the Fed to raise rates one more time before year-end, likely at its last meeting of the year on Dec. 8-9. According to CME Group's Fed Watch tool, which uses 30-day Fed funds futures prices to predict rate decisions, traders see an 88% probability that the Fed will hold rates steady in October and a 71% probability the Fed will raise rates in December (no meeting scheduled for November). In quarterly projections last month, the Fed signaled that its rate-setting committee expected to raise rates later this year. At the same time, some Fed policymakers have signaled that the central bank is in no rush to lift borrowing costs. "With the policy action we took at our September meeting, there is no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information," New York Fed President John Williams said in a speech at the University at Buffalo following the Fed's rate hike in September. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will give a press conference after this week's rate decision. Until then, investors are unlikely to get any clues from Warsh, who has argued against sharing forward guidance on rate decisions. title: Dollar General overcharged people at checkout for years, FTC says
description: The discount retailer routinely charges customers more at checkout than the prices it displays on shelves, price tags and ads, according to federal and state authorities.
content: MoneyWatch Dollar General overcharged millions at checkout for years, FTC and 20 states allege By Megan Cerullo Megan Cerullo Reporter, MoneyWatch Megan Cerullo is a New York-based reporter for CBS MoneyWatch covering small business, workplace, health care, consumer spending and personal finance topics. She regularly appears on CBS News 24/7 to discuss her reporting. Read Full Bio Megan Cerullo Updated on: October 26, 2026 / 9:53 PM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states on Monday sued Dollar General, accusing the budget retailer of charging customers more for products than it advertised. The chain, which operates 21,000 stores nationwide, allegedly mislabeled prices for years, "extracting millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges," the FTC alleged. "Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last," Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement. The FTC added that American consumers depend on Dollar General's advertised low prices to make ends meet on tight budgets, while prices that don't reflect advertised deals make it impossible for them to manage household finances. The agency filed its complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, Dollar General's home state. "Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store," Dollar General said in a statement. "As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement." Dollar General said it was made aware of the FTC's investigation in early February. "Inaccurate pricing" According to the suit, thousands of Dollar General stores unlawfully overcharged shoppers. Dollar General "has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve," the FTC and states allege in the suit. "Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags, and advertisements. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country." The company also faced thousands of consumer complaints claiming it failed to honor advertised prices at checkout, a sign Dollar General knowingly harmed customers, according to the FTC. The suit seeks a permanent injunction, along with monetary and other relief. Dollar General in its statement said, "FTC staff also demanded a monetary amount that was untethered to — and orders of magnitude larger than — any realistic assessment of amounts attributable to pricing discrepancies." The company said it "worked tirelessly and in good faith to resolve this matter without litigation," including an "alternative, and in our view, more reasonable, manner of calculating potential settlement ranges." "Although we respect the FTC's role in protecting American consumers and the State representatives' role in protecting the citizens of their respective states, we will defend this litigation vigorously," it said. title: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 workers as it invests more in AI
description: Roughly a quarter of Microsoft's workforce will be eligible for a "voluntary exit offer" as the company tries to shed workers.
content: MoneyWatch Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 workers as it pours money into AI By Megan Cerullo Megan Cerullo Reporter, MoneyWatch Megan Cerullo is a New York-based reporter for CBS MoneyWatch covering small business, workplace, health care, consumer spending and personal finance topics. She regularly appears on CBS News 24/7 to discuss her reporting. Read Full Bio Megan Cerullo Updated on: October 26, 2026 / 2:07 PM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, or roughly one-quarter of its global workforce, as the technology giant invests more in artificial intelligence. So-called voluntary exit offers are available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the U.S., Microsoft said in announcing the buyout program on Monday. Employees must be at the vice president level or below to qualify for a buyout. "This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's chief people officer, said in a memo to employees. Microsoft expects to spend $175 billion on AI infrastructure, including through investments in data centers, in 2026 alone, Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said in a July earnings call with Wall Street analysts. The exit program is the second voluntary buyout offer Microsoft has offered workers this year. In May, Microsoft planned to offer buyouts to about 8,750 people, or 7% of its U.S. workforce, the Associated Press reported, citing two people familiar with the plan who were not authorized to speak about it publicly. In July, the company said it was cutting 4,800 jobs, about 2% of its global workforce, including many workers in its Xbox video game business. Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings. Around 27% of Microsoft's workforce is eligible for the new buyout offer, according to Agence France-Presse. The offer is available to mid-level workers for what Microsoft said was a limited period of time. It's designed to let them leave the company with financial padding and career-planning resources, while allowing the company to save on labor costs. Eligible employees will be made aware of the offer by email on Monday, Coleman said. Workers in some business units are ineligible for the buyout, the company said. They include employees focused on data centers and those who work in sales and marketing, Bloomberg reported, citing a company spokesperson. Edited by Alain Sherter The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report. title: Walter Koenig, actor who played Chekov on "Star Trek," dies at 90
description: Walter Koenig played Pavel Chekov in the original "Star Trek" series and several movies.
content: Entertainment Walter Koenig, actor who played Chekov on original "Star Trek" series, dies at age 90 Updated on: October 26, 2026 / 3:44 PM EDT / CBS/AP Add CBS News on Google Walter Koenig, the actor who played Pavel Chekov in the original "Star Trek" television series and several movies, has died, his rep confirmed to CBS News. He was 90. Koenig died Sunday night at his home in the North Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles, talent rep Zachery McGinnis said in a statement. He died surrounded by his daughter and niece, McGinnis said. In "Star Trek," Ensign Chekov was the sole member of the spaceship Enterprise bridge staff from what was the Communist bloc. His friendly, supportive presence showed how the rival nations (in the far-off future in which the show was set) were capable of working together. Speaking heavily Russian-accented English, Chekov embodied stereotypical Russian personality traits, including fierce pride, love of poetry and blind loyalty. Walter Koenig is seen playing Pavel Chekov in the original "Star Trek" series. CBS via Getty Images "Star Trek" ran on NBC from 1966 to 1969 and has had an almost unprecedented afterlife as fans, or Trekkies, kept interest in the show alive. Koenig was born Sept. 14, 1936, in Chicago, the son of a businessman. He graduated from the University of California, Los Angeles, in 1958, then studied acting at New York's The Neighborhood Playhouse for two years. He began getting television roles in the early 1960s, appearing on "Mr. Novak" and "Ben Casey." "My heart is heavy," Koenig's castmate, George Takei, said on social media. "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend." Koenig was the best man at Takei's 2008 wedding to Brad Altman, his partner of more than two decades. McGinnis noted that Koenig's legacy extended far beyond the screen. "Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it," McGinnis said. "Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before." Walter Koenig attends the Creative Arts Emmy Awards at Microsoft Theater on Sept. 8, 2018, in Los Angeles. Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic Koenig played Chekov in seven "Star Trek" movies starting in 1979, as well as innumerable other spinoffs, including writing a "Star Trek" book, "Chekov's Enterprise," in 1980. The TV show has also inspired two spinoff TV series with new casts, and conventions that draw thousands of fans. After "Star Trek" ended, Koenig continued acting and wrote scripts for "Family," "The Incredible Hulk" and other shows. He also taught part time at UCLA and other schools. Koenig also worked in the burgeoning field of computer games, including some with a "Star Trek" theme. In 1995, he took a role in the CD-ROM game "Maximum Surge." "I'm at a point where I could opt in my life for complacency and a bit of predictability, or I could have one last holler — one last try for adventure," Koenig told The Associated Press in 1995. "I'm of the opinion that adventure is still a very enticing and exciting option." He returned to the science fiction genre with occasional appearances on the syndicated 1990s TV series "Babylon 5." title: Pope cleared for South America trip after lung cancer surgery
description: The trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, set for Nov. 6 to 17, is particularly grueling.
content: World Pope Leo cleared to make his trip to South America after successful lung cancer surgery By Anna Matranga October 26, 2026 / 1:19 PM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google Only two weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV has been given the medical green light to embark on an ambitious 12-day tour of South America next month. "Based on his current clinical status, as well as the instrumental and laboratory tests performed, there are no contraindications that would prevent him from undertaking his upcoming apostolic journey to Latin America as planned," the Vatican said in a statement on Monday. "The Pope is following medical recommendations with great care and diligence, and with a deep determination to continue serving the Church." The trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, set for Nov. 6 to 17, is particularly grueling. The 71-year-old pontiff plans to travel to 10 cities, board 14 flights, and attend many public appearances and religious ceremonies. The Vatican also confirmed that the trip would proceed "according to the program previously published," which means that a visit to the Peruvian city of Cuzco, Peru, situated at more than 11,000 feet above sea level, remains on the schedule. The thinner air there could pose difficulties for someone recovering from lung surgery. Pope Leo XIV addresses the crowd from the window of the Apostolic Palace overlooking St.Peter's Square during his Sunday Angelus prayer at the Vatican on Oct. 25, 2026. Alberto PIZZOLI /AFP via Getty Images Doubts about the pope's ability to undergo the South American trip surfaced again last week, when, on the advice of his doctors, Leo canceled a visit by helicopter to Assisi for an international peace gathering to take place Tuesday. Doctors said they advised him to do so preventively, because of the unpressurized air on the helicopter journey. The upcoming journey carries particular personal significance for the first American-born pope, who spent more than two decades working as a missionary and bishop in Peru. "I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," he said in a statement Monday. "May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy." Leo was operated on Oct. 13, when doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung after discovering a malignant tumor. The cancer, identified as a lung adenocarcinoma, was discovered accidentally during a routine abdominal examination, his doctors said. The operation was successful, without complications, and Leo was discharged from the hospital on Oct. 17. Since leaving the hospital, Leo has gradually resumed his public duties, including his weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square and meetings with visiting church leaders.
