title: These factors could decide Netanyahu's fate in Israel's election
description: Israelis are about to vote to choose their next government. The race is wide open, and Benjamin Netanyahu's political fate could hinge on a couple key factors.
content: World Israel's election is wide open. Here's what could decide Netanyahu's political fate. By Dov Lieber Dov Lieber Senior Reporter Dov Lieber is a senior reporter for CBS News based in Tel Aviv, covering political, diplomatic and security developments across Israel, the Palestinian Territories and the broader Middle East. Read Full Bio Dov Lieber Updated on: October 27, 2026 / 4:08 AM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google Tel Aviv — After three years with their country at war on multiple fronts, Israelis are casting ballots on Tuesday in a hotly contested election that will shape their next government. Polls show it is an incredibly tight race, and as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fights to hold onto his job, there's no guarantee of a quick, definitive outcome for him or his political opponents. Polls vary widely regarding the expected outcome. Right-leaning pollsters give an advantage to the right-wing and religious bloc led by Netanyahu, while left-leaning pollsters show an advantage for the so-called change bloc opposing the incumbent. Most polls show neither side is likely to win a decisive majority of the 120 seats in Israel's parliament, the Knesset, which would enable it to unilaterally form a new government. The tight margins mean the voting may end in a stalemate, which could lead to protracted negotiations across ideological lines, the formation of a minority government, or even an election do-over. "It looks like an indecisive outcome is the most likely outcome," said Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute. This is the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, which authorities have acknowledged as Israel's most catastrophic security failure since the country's founding in 1948. Israelis are heading to the polls with their country still fighting in the subsequent multi-front war in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and after two direct rounds of conflict with Iran and Netanyahu advocating for a third. Against that backdrop, there are a few key issues that could determine the election outcome, even if it does take days or weeks to shake out. But first, here's a look at the two main factions vying for the votes. The Netanyahu camp Netanyahu, Israel's longest serving prime minister and leader of the Likud party, is seeking to form another coalition similar to his current government, which relies on partnerships with ultranationalist and Jewish religious parties. He has two main pitches to voters: First, that only he can form a government without the support of Israel's Arab parties, which he argues would be a danger to the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Netanyahu's second argument to voters is that Israel's campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon, and especially Iran, are ongoing, and he needs more time to finish what his government started. President Trump offered a full-throated endorsement of Netanyahu last week. He reiterated his administration's firm support for the war the two men launched jointly against Iran almost eight months ago, and warned that he could be disinclined to continue with it if Netanyahu doesn't hold onto power. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Mr. Trump said. A campaign billboard depicting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Trump is seen in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Oct. 26, 2026. JACK GUEZ/AFP/Getty Images Since that endorsement, Netanyahu has argued that only he can work with Mr. Trump to ensure Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon, which many Israelis see as an existential threat. Netanyahu's campaign slogan, which rhymes in Hebrew, is: "Either right wing or Palestine, either right wing or a nuclear bomb." Over the weekend, Netanyahu posted an AI-generated photo of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv on social media, with a caption reiterating his insistence that Iran poses an existential threat to Israel. Netanyahu's supporters see him as a top-tier global leader. "Bibi can handle the whole world," restaurant owner Benny Abraham told CBS News, using Netanyahu's nickname. "Bibi is charismatic. He has a strong voice. The world loves him." "He's the king of Israel," Abraham added. The (anyone but Netanyahu) "change bloc" Running against Netanyahu is a diverse group of Arab, right, left and center parties that have one clear common denominator: They all want Netanyahu out of power. The front-runner to lead the "change bloc," should its various parties collectively win enough seats to build a coalition, is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the centrist Yashar party. Eisenkot lost his son and two nephews while they were serving in the military in Gaza. He was part of the Israeli war cabinet for much of the first year of the Gaza war, working alongside Netanyahu. About half of his party's candidates in Tuesday's election are women, in stark contrast to the male-dominated Netanyahu coalition. Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot waves to supporters at a campaign rally on Oct. 25, 2026, in Tel Aviv, Israel. Erik Marmor/picture alliance/Getty Images Eisenkot is framing himself as a humble veteran who wants to reunite Israel after years of division that he blames on Netanyahu. Eisenkot responded Monday to Netanyahu's rhetoric about Iran posing a nuclear threat by accusing him of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies, and threats — including images of nuclear bombs in the heart of Tel Aviv." "This time, it won't work for him," he said. Eisenkot's key campaign promises include launching a state inquiry into the intelligence and security failure to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas — something Netanyahu has thus far blocked. Uzi Aharoni, 73, an engineer from Tel Aviv, told CBS News he saw Eisenkot as the only real alternative to Netanyahu. "Eisenkot is not left, he's not right. He's straight and honest. He's the kind of leader who will take care of us, the people of Israel, and not himself or his corrupt family," Aharoni said. The Arab vote and the ultra-Orthodox draft There are a few factors analysts believe could hand a victory to either side. One thing polls can't predict well in Israel is voter turnout. Past elections have shown voters backing Netanyahu's Likud party, and Arab-Israeli voters, vary the greatest in their enthusiasm to come out on election days, so there could be room for turn-out surprises that significantly change the electoral math in favor of either side. Arab Israelis, also referred to as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up around 20% of Israel's population. "The higher the Arab turnout, the less likely that Mr. Netanyahu, within the current coalition, can form another government," said Plesner at the Israel Democracy Institute. More Arab voters will head to voting booths this year because of their strong desire to prevent Netanyahu from forming another government with far-right allies, who have made life difficult for them over the last four years, Jehad Abomoch, a cafe owner in the predominantly Arab city of Baqa al Gharbiya, told CBS News. "The last four years were a real catastrophe, both socially and in terms of wars," he said, adding that many Arab Israelis feel that under Netanyahu, they have "no hope, no future." There are also two new parties entering this election, and polls show each is hovering around the threshold of support required to gain seats in the Knesset. Whether either party ultimately crosses that threshold could also tip the scales — in either direction — toward a new coalition government. Both parties are focused on challenging Netanyahu's alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties by demanding that ultra-Orthodox Jewish citizens be formally included in Israel's mandatory military service. Ultra-Orthodox Jewish leaders of the Breslev Hasidic community take part in a rally against mandatory military conscription on Oct. 12, 2026, in Netanya, Israel. Amir Levy/Getty Images It's a key issue that cuts right through Netanyahu's traditional support base and coalition partners. Not all election outcomes are neat and tidy In the event that neither bloc wins a clear majority in parliament, there are several paths forward to a new Israeli government. One option is that parties or individual lawmakers could break election promises and switch sides, for which there is plenty of precedent in Israeli politics. There could be weeks of negotiating before a coalition is agreed on. Another possibility is that the change bloc, if it wins a significant share of the votes but not quite a majority, could seek to form a minority government. To do that, the parties just need to win more seats collectively than the other side, even if it's not more than 50% of the 120 available. Arab parties could give the change bloc that plurality by either voting in favor of a minority government, or just abstaining and not voting against its formation. If there's a stalemate and neither side can build a coalition government, the country will have to hold new elections. There is plenty of precedent for that scenario, too. Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections due to electoral deadlock. Plesner told CBS News that, if all the politicians running effectively stick to their campaign promises and refuse to swap sides in the event of a stalemate "we will roll into another election." "I'm sure that most politicians are not interested in that," he added. title: Maurene Comey, James Comey's daughter, was unlawfully fired, judge rules
description: Maurene Comey was abruptly fired in July 2025 from her job as a federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York. She sued the DOJ over her firing, claiming it was unlawful.
content: Politics Maurene Comey, James Comey's daughter, was unlawfully fired, judge rules By Jacob Rosen, Jacob Rosen Justice Department Reporter Jake Rosen is a reporter covering the Department of Justice. He was previously a campaign digital reporter covering President Trump's 2024 campaign and also served as an associate producer for "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan." Read Full Bio Jacob Rosen, Melissa Quinn Melissa Quinn Senior Reporter, Politics Melissa Quinn is a senior reporter for CBSNews.com, where she covers U.S. politics, with a focus on the Supreme Court and federal courts. Read Full Bio Melissa Quinn Updated on: October 26, 2026 / 12:55 PM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google Washington — A federal judge on Monday found that the Justice Department unlawfully fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, from her post as a federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York. U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman said in a 55-page decision that Comey's removal violated the constitutional separation of powers and federal law. The judge retroactively reinstated Comey to her role as a federal prosecutor and ordered the Trump administration to provide her back pay from the date of her firing in July 2025 through Dec. 20, when she accepted a different job. Comey's lawsuit was one of several filed by former government employees who were fired without cause that tested the limits of the president's power to fire federal officials. The Trump administration had argued that Article II of the Constitution gives the president unrestricted removal power, and said Congress could not limit the removal of federal prosecutors. But in his decision, Furman ruled that Comey's firing violated the Civil Service Reform Act, a landmark law enacted in 1978 that provides protections for federal workers. The Trump administration, he wrote, is attempting to "upend" long-settled case law allowing Congress to regulate the removal of so-called inferior officers. "Indeed, to accept Defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system," Furman wrote. Comey's legal team cheered the decision as a "hard-earned victory" for her and all civil servants. "As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system.' This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law," lawyers Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan said in a statement. A Justice Department spokesperson said it "disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course." Comey had served as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan since 2015, handling high-profile criminal cases against figures including Sean "Diddy" Combs, Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell and former Democratic Sen. Robert Menendez. In a letter to her former colleagues at the time of her dismissal, Comey said she was "summarily fired via memo" by the Justice Department's headquarters in Washington, and was not given a reason for her termination. The letter she received stated, "Pursuant to Article II of the United States Constitution and the laws of the United States, your employment with the Department of Justice is hereby terminated, and you are removed from federal service effective immediately." It was initially unclear who made the decision to oust Comey, but in May, the Trump administration said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi "directed" her removal, and her successor, Todd Blanche, "ratified" her termination. Comey sued the Justice Department over her firing last year, alleging she had probably been fired because President Trump dislikes her father, who has been indicted twice during the second Trump administration. One of the criminal cases was tossed out, and James Comey has denied wrongdoing in the second. "Ms. Comey's termination — without cause, without advance notice, and without any opportunity to contest it — was unlawful and unconstitutional," Comey's attorneys wrote in their complaint. The Trump administration attempted to dismiss the lawsuit on the grounds that Comey was required to bring her claims before the Merit Systems Protection Board, the agency tasked with adjudicating appeals from federal employees regarding adverse actions taken against them, but Furman denied the government's motion and allowed the case to continue. Furman found that because Comey's firing rested on Article II of the Constitution — not a federal law governing the civil service — the federal court had jurisdiction to hear the case. In court filings, the Justice Department admitted that Comey had received a rating of "outstanding" on her performance reviews from 2019 through 2024, but said that her firing had been carried out under legal authority Congress granted to the attorney general to fire assistant U.S. attorneys. In defending Comey's firing, the Trump administration relied, in part, on the Supreme Court's June decision allowing the president to fire members of certain independent agencies without cause. In that case, the high court overturned a more than 90-year-old decision that allowed Congress to restrict the president's ability to fire officials from multimember agencies at will. But Furman said the Justice Department's argument amounted to a "sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority." title: Consumers face scarier Halloween costs this year. Here's why.
description: Americans are forecast to spend a record $13.5 billion on Halloween this year, with the average consumer shelling out hundreds of dollars.
content: MoneyWatch Consumers face scarier Halloween costs this year. Here's why. By Maya Blackstone, Maya Blackstone Reporter Maya Blackstone is a consumer, business and technology reporter and producer for CBS News. Read Full Bio Maya Blackstone, Gelila Negesse October 26, 2026 / 10:52 AM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google Americans are on track to spend a record $13.5 billion on Halloween this year amid rising costs associated with the national scarefest, according to the National Retail Federation. Consumers are forecast to shell out $4.1 billion on candy alone. Cocoa costs remain elevated despite surging over the last two years, with shipping and other expenses also pushing up treat costs. Despite higher prices, the NRF expects consumers to spend $400 million more on Halloween this year than in 2025, and $1.9 billion more than in 2024. A poll from consulting firm PwC found that the average person expects to spend about $263; parents often spend the most because they're shopping for multiple Halloween events. Two-thirds of Americans think Halloween has gotten too expensive, according to a recent survey from personal finance site WalletHub. Why costumes cost more this year The general manager of Chicago Costume, Cortland Hickey, told CBS News higher transportation and fulfillment costs are driving up Halloween-related prices this year. "The tariff costs are pretty much baked into the products as opposed to being a surprise like they were last year," Hickey said. "But now it's the fuel surcharges and the cost of diesel and those kinds of things when you're receiving products on pallets and truckloads. " For shoppers ordering online, waiting until the last minute can mean paying more for rush shipping or risking a costume that arrives after Halloween. Online shopping is less popular for Halloween purchases this year, with 27% of consumers planning to shop online, slightly down from 31% in 2025, according to the National Retail Federation. Why candy is expensive Chocolate prices are expected to be 8% higher than last Halloween, according to the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute. FinanceBuzz found that a 100-piece bag of assorted Halloween candy costs an average of $16.96 in 2026, up 3.5% from last year and 71% higher than in 2021. Mondelez, the maker of Sour Patch Kids and Swedish Fish, raised prices on gummy candy packs 39%, while Ferrero, whose candy brands include Butterfinger, Crunch and Baby Ruth, raised chocolate pack prices nearly 19%. The higher prices are a lagging effect of the cocoa market. Cocoa prices have fallen from record highs in 2024 and 2025, but shoppers have yet to see the full benefit because candy makers are still using cocoa purchased during the 2025 price spikes, according to economists. Most of the world's cocoa supply comes from Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire in West Africa. In 2025, heat waves and heavy rains linked to climate change affected cocoa crops, contributing to shortages and price spikes. Higher U.S. tariffs on cocoa-producing countries also affected prices, although levies on cocoa and other commodities that can't be grown in the U.S. were removed last November. Some candy makers have cut production costs by replacing traditional ingredients in milk chocolate with cheaper alternatives such as vegetable oil. Products that no longer meet the official criteria for milk chocolate can instead be labeled "chocolate candy," "chocolatey" or "chocolate coating." According to federal rules, milk chocolate must contain at least 10% cocoa mass and solids, so candy products like Butterfinger, Rolo and Almond Joy that contain 2% or less of cocoa are labeled "Chocolate Candy." Earlier this year, Hershey's faced criticism for changing Reese's classic recipe in certain products, such as limited-edition or seasonal candies, to use less chocolate. Following the backlash, the company said it will revert to its original recipes in 2027. How to save Phil Lempert, editor of the Lempert Report and an analyst focused on consumer behavior, said shoppers should look online for better deals on candy, telling CBS News that ordering on Amazon "is going to be a lot less expensive." Comparing prices can also make a difference. Checking the price per piece or per pound on variety candy packs can reveal significant differences, with some chocolate assortments costing nearly twice as much as bags of gummy candy. For costumes, Hickey recommends ditching prepackaged costumes and instead prioritizing items shoppers are less likely to already own or make themselves, such as specific wigs, face paints, special makeup products and props. The higher costs are also changing when and how consumers shop. About half of shoppers said they started shopping in September or earlier, allowing them to spread out costs and search for deals, according to the NRF. Lempert also expects Halloween-related costs to continue rising in the years ahead, citing the impact of climate change on global cocoa prices and higher fuel prices, among other factors. "We're going to see these prices go up through 2027 and probably 2028," he said. Edited by Aimee Picchi More from CBS News Transcript: Rep. title: Violent crime victimization fell 25% in 2025, DOJ survey shows
description: A new preliminary survey finds that the rate of violent crime victimization in 2025 fell by about 25%, compared with 2024, which the DOJ claimed represents the largest decline since 1973.
content: Politics Violent crime victimization fell 25% in 2025 over prior year, survey released by DOJ shows By Sarah N. Lynch Sarah N. Lynch Senior Justice Department Reporter Sarah N. Lynch is the senior Justice Department reporter for CBS News, based in Washington, D.C. Read Full Bio Sarah N. Lynch October 26, 2026 / 9:51 AM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google A preliminary survey released on Monday found that the rate of violent crime victimization in 2025 fell by about 25% compared with the prior year, a significant drop that the Justice Department claimed represents the largest decline since 1973. The National Crime Victimization Survey, conducted by the Census Bureau and released by the Justice Department's Bureau of Justice Statistics, found that there were an estimated 669,000 fewer violent crimes, excluding simple assaults, committed in 2025 compared with 2024. Aggravated assault victimization dropped an estimated 31%, with about 390,000 fewer incidents in 2025, compared with the prior year. The data for the survey comes from a sample of interviews in U.S. households of people who are 12 or older. The interviewees were asked questions about the frequency, characteristics and consequences of criminal victimization. The survey for 2025 consisted of 101,980 household interviews. Overall, 53% of eligible households completed interviews, the Bureau of Justice Statistics said. Other findings from the preliminary results of the survey showed that robbery was down 27% in 2025, property crime victimization was down 19%, burglary and trespassing were down 25% and motor vehicle theft was down 29%. The preliminary results from the survey bolster findings from earlier this year in the FBI's Uniform Crime Report, which showed that violent crime rates plummeted in 2025 with the country's murder rate reaching a 20-year low. That report, which compiles crime data from most law enforcement agencies across the nation, also recorded significant year-over-year decreases in multiple categories. Aggravated assaults fell by 7.2%, rapes declined by 7.6% and robbery was down about 18.5%. President Trump and his allies have sought to capitalize on the decrease in violent crime rates as they have campaigned across the country ahead of the midterms to try to help Republicans retain control of the Senate and the House of Representatives. In a break from prior traditions, the White House unveiled the findings from the FBI's Uniform Crime Report ahead of a campaign event on Long Island, New York, that was also attended by Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel. title: Trump's oil and gas stocks gained millions during Iran war
description: A report from congressional Democrats found the president purchased millions in oil and gas stocks during the war.
content: First on CBS Politics As Trump brags about U.S. oil and gas company profits, his stocks gained millions during Iran war By Kathryn Watson Kathryn Watson Politics Reporter Kathryn Watson is a politics reporter for CBS News Digital, based in Washington, D.C. Read Full Bio Kathryn Watson Updated on: October 26, 2026 / 9:52 AM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google Washington — As President Trump boasts about how much money the U.S. oil and gas industry is making from the war with Iran, the president's personal holdings in oil and gas are now worth between $22.5 million and $81.6 million, compared with $12.6 million to $46 million at the end of 2025, according to a new report by Democrats on the Congressional Joint Economic Committee. The stocks the president holds have increased in value by an average of 43% since the end of 2025, the Democratic minority said, based on data from LSEG Data Analytics. The report also found the president purchased between $4.7 million and $17.5 million in oil and gas stocks between March, after the war began, and the end of August, which is the most recently available data. He also sold between $2 million and $5.4 million in oil and gas stocks in the same timeframe, the minority found. The report was obtained exclusively by CBS News and is based on the president's financial filings with the Office of Government Ethics. Filers are only required to report transaction ranges, not specific amounts. But as Americans are paying significantly higher gas prices due to downstream effects from the war, Mr. Trump on Saturday night in Georgia bragged that U.S. oil and gas companies are "making hundreds of billions of dollars." "And while oil prices are temporarily high and will be falling dramatically in a short period of time, as soon as that war's over, because there's so much oil," he told the crowd. "All in the Hormuz Strait, there are ships waiting to come, we're getting them out so fast. The United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars. … Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what's happened in the Middle East." The president added that his advisers told him not to mention how much money the oil and gas industry is making from the chaos in the Middle East. The wealthiest person to serve as president, Mr. Trump has a vast stock portfolio with holdings in all sectors of the economy. He has executed thousands of stock and securities trades this year, worth hundreds of millions of dollars, CBS News has previously reported. The White House says Mr. Trump doesn't make trading decisions himself, and his money managers try to replicate major stock indices. "President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly reelected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses," said White House spokesman Davis Ingle. Ingle said Mr. Trump's stock and bond portfolio is "independently managed by third-party financial institutions" and all his holdings are "maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes." "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold," Ingle added. "All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers. There are no conflicts of interest." In a July 2026 interview with CNBC, Mr. Trump said his son, Eric Trump, also handles his finances. Energy stocks have surged as the Iran war pushed oil and gasoline prices to their highest levels in years, driving profits for oil companies. The share prices of energy companies that are listed on the S&P 500 jumped more than 50% since the start of the year, easily outpacing the broader S&P 500's roughly 11% jump. In early February, before the Iran war began at the end of February, nationwide, the average cost of a gallon of regular gas was $2.87, and a gallon of diesel cost $3.68. Now, eight months later, it's $4.29, with diesel at $6.28 per gallon. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, is also hovering above $115 a barrel, compared to less than $75 the day before the war began. "Trump's Iran War has forced Americans to pay much more at the pump while Big Oil rakes in profits and the president's own stock wealth in the oil and gas industry continues to balloon," said Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee. "As Trump — the country's highest ranking public employee — continues to own and trade stocks in companies that stand to benefit from his decisions, his actions raise major concerns about conflicts of interest." Presidents, vice presidents and members of Congress are allowed to own, buy and sell stocks while in office, although insider trading laws still apply. The minority said the president's stock purchases or total value may be even higher, since he has not yet reported transactions for September or October. Among the nine stocks that make up the largest oil and gas holdings in Mr. Trump's portfolio, Chevron and ExxonMobil represent the most significant portion. He owns up to $23.1 million in Chevron stock and up to $18.4 million in ExxonMobil, which saw their stock prices grow nearly 25% and nearly 22% in value, respectively, since Feb. 20. Democrats on the committee estimated American families have spent an average of $856 more on gas since the war began. There are occasional reminders that pronouncements the president makes affect policies. In August, Mr. Trump called out ExxonMobil and Chevron by name for making "too much money" on fuel profits. "They're making too much money, okay?" he said in the Oval Office. "Based on a shortage, they're making too much money. I don't like it. And I should be the last one to say because I'm a big free enterprise guy, nobody bigger." Energy stock purchases and sales make up a small portion of the president's overall net worth, which Forbes estimated to be roughly $7 billion as of September. In August, CBS News reviewed the president's oil and gas trades. One notable large transaction was on April 7, the day the president declared a ceasefire in the war. His investment accounts sold between $500,000 and $1 million of ExxonMobil stock, according to a financial disclosure report Mr. Trump filed in late June. The company's share price closed at $163.91 on April 7, before Mr. Trump announced the ceasefire that evening, and it opened down over 6% at $153.52 on April 8. The cost of living continues to be a top issue for voters. Last week, Mr. Trump accused Iran of trying to drive up oil prices ahead of next week's U.S. elections. "Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election," he wrote on Truth Social. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict." Since Mr. Trump launched the war with Iran on Feb. 28, the conflict has stymied oil exports in the region, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil shipments from the Middle East have climbed since then as exporters look for alternate routes and some traffic in the strait is restored. But the disruptions, constricted supply and uncertainty have pushed up prices, even in the U.S., which is the world's largest exporter of total oil products. The president has made some efforts to bring down fuel prices, including by making a deal with Russia to purchase Russian diesel fuel and waiving sanctions he had just signed into law. But that fuel from Russia, a controversial move, is a drop in the bucket of the United States' massive demand, and does little to lower diesel prices. On Thursday, the president announced he would invoke the Defense Production Act to spend $150 million to boost gasoline and diesel production. Mr. Trump has said gas prices will "drop through the floor" once the war is over, but even if that's the case, it's not clear when the war will end. The president has not ruled out restarting strikes on Iran after the midterms. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told the Financial Times the war could last another year, although he said he hopes the Iranian leaders "come to the table" before that. This story published first on CBS News at 9:30 a.m. on Oct. 26, 2026. title: Duchess Meghan confronted dad over child abuse claims last year
description: Video has emerged of Thomas Markle receiving a letter from his daughter Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, in which she reportedly told him she "knew he had abused young girls."
content: World Duchess Meghan confronted dad over child sexual abuse allegations with 2025 letter delivered to hospital bed By Imtiaz Tyab, Imtiaz Tyab Senior foreign correspondent Imtiaz Tyab is a CBS News senior foreign correspondent based in London and reports for all platforms, including the "CBS Evening News," "CBS Mornings," "CBS Sunday Morning" and CBS News 24/7. He has extensive experience reporting from major global flashpoints, including the Middle East and the war on terror. Read Full Bio Imtiaz Tyab, Tucker Reals Tucker Reals Editor Tucker Reals is CBSNews.com's foreign editor, based in the CBS News London bureau. He has worked for CBS News since 2006, prior to which he worked for The Associated Press in Washington, D.C., and London. Read Full Bio Tucker Reals Updated on: October 26, 2026 / 9:20 AM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google London — Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, confronted her estranged father last year about child sexual abuse allegations leveled against him, about six years after she was first made aware of the claims, according to new information from CBS News' British partner BBC News. Last week, police in the Philippines confirmed they were investigating Thomas Markle Sr. over his alleged possession of a large stash of child sexual abuse photos and videos, which were handed in to authorities by his son, Thomas Markle Jr. Meghan, who is married to Britain's Prince Harry, said in a statement last week that she was "deeply distressed" by word of the investigation into her father, and that she had first learned of allegations against him in 2018, when London's Metropolitan Police shared a letter with her laying out related claims. She said it was based on that information that she and Harry decided to cut her father off from contact with their children. Video that the British tabloid the Daily Mail says it obtained exclusively shows Markle accepting a letter sent by his daughter in his hospital room in the U.S. in December 2025. According to the BBC, in that letter the duchess wrote that she and authorities "knew he had abused young girls," adding that he would never meet Meghan and Harry's children Archie and Lilibet. Thomas Markle Sr., 82, was quoted by the Mail in a Sunday article as saying he didn't remember what was written in the letter from his daughter, but "if Meghan says that's what she wrote, then she's probably right." Thomas Markle, Meghan Markle's father, is seen in a still taken from video as he gives an interview to ITV's Good Morning Britain program which is broadcast from London, June 18, 2018. REUTERS The Mail quoted her father on Friday as saying he had "never downloaded anything like that in my life," and dismissing the allegations against him as "sick lies." On Sunday, the tabloid ran a new article quoting him as saying he had paid for sex in the Philippines, but reiterating his denial of possessing child sexual abuse materials and insisting he never had sex with anyone under the age of 18. He vowed to cooperate with authorities, according to the Daily Mail. Another British tabloid, The Sun, reported over the weekend that the Metropolitan Police were made aware in 2019 of a number of claims against Markle, including alleged sexual abuse of a child, and that they had passed them on to the Duchess of Sussex's office at that time. In a statement last week, the duchess said it was because of these allegations that she had kept her family distanced from her father. "In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," Meghan said in her Friday statement. "I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, arrive at a youth and community charity during a visit to Nottingham, England, Oct. 15, 2026. Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty "We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met's Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018," a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said last week. "We are undertaking enquiries internally in an effort to confirm this." It is understood that the London police are not currently investigating Thomas Markle. It is unclear what allegations were in the letter about her father that Meghan says police shared with her in 2018, or what allegations she was referring to when she wrote to him last year. CBS News contributor Roya Nikkhah, royal editor for the Sunday Times newspaper, told CBS News on Monday that the revelations of the last week were very likely to garner new public sympathy for the duchess. "I don't think the wider public can not have sympathy for Meghan going through this," she said. "It's an ordeal, an extraordinary thing to learn about your own father." "I think a lot of the feeling by the British public around what has happened the last few years has been more about the way Harry and Meghan left the royal family and what we have heard from them since, which is completely separate to this — their grievances against the royal family, their feelings of not feeling comfortable here," said Nikkhah. "But they are now back, and they are back, we understand, for a considerable period of time. I'm sure the British public and wider public will have sympathy for what's happened regarding her father. I don't know whether this will change people's views about what's been said and done the last six or seven years since they've left." title: Anthropic files for IPO as it competes for AI dominance
description: Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot, is barreling ahead with its public offering despite mounting concerns about AI going rogue.
content: MoneyWatch Anthropic files for IPO, touting AI's ability to "improve how humans live" By Mary Cunningham Mary Cunningham Reporter, MoneyWatch Mary Cunningham is a reporter for CBS MoneyWatch. She previously worked at "60 Minutes," CBSNews.com and CBS News 24/7 as part of the CBS News Associate Program. Read Full Bio Mary Cunningham Updated on: October 26, 2026 / 12:43 PM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google Anthropic filed for an initial public offering on Monday, bringing the maker of artificial intelligence platform Claude a step closer to its highly anticipated public market debut and providing a key test for the rapidly emerging AI sector. In the filing, Anthropic outlined its vision for a future profoundly shaped by AI, touting the technology's potential to transform the global economy and improve lives worldwide. "We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning," the company said in its S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing highlights Anthropic's rapid growth, with the company generating $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. That staggering rate of expansion is likely to slow, with Anthropic noting that its revenue growth is expected to decline over time. The company has yet to turn a profit. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of the year, more than six times the net loss of nearly $13 billion for the first two quarters in 2025. Anthropic's founders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, pitched the IPO to investors in part as an opportunity to be part of a history-defining moment. "We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms," the company's seven co-founders said in a letter included in the S-1. "We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history." Referendum on AI The IPO, which market analysts expect as early as November, could instantly rank Anthropic among the world's largest publicly traded companies. The offering could raise as much as $100 billion, according to reports. That would slingshot it past Elon Musk-owned SpaceX, which raised a record-breaking $86 billion when it went public in June. Anthropic, which was valued at $965 billion in May, could see its value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. Anthropic shares will list on the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index, according to the company's filing. The AI company will trade under the ticker symbol "ANT." More broadly, the transaction will gauge the strength of investor demand not only for Anthropic shares, but also for the widening constellation of data center builders, chipmakers and other companies involved in developing the critical infrastructure powering AI services. "This IPO is a referendum on the entire AI trade," Nigel Green, CEO of investment firm deVere Group, said in an email. "If it soars, expect a queue of AI listings and even more capital piling into the theme. If it stumbles, valuations across tech could reset fast." The torrent of capital flowing into AI has helped propel the stock market to record highs. The question is whether AI can maintain its momentum amid signs that investors are fretting over when — and if — their money will eventually pay off and deliver the returns they are banking on. Anthropic's prospectus shows that the company has funneled massive amounts of money toward building the computing resources necessary to power its AI models. The company spent $8.9 billion in the first half of the year on chips and other infrastructure to run its platform, compared to $2.3 billion over the same period last year. "Anthropic could become the most valuable company in the world. It could also end up in bankruptcy," analysts with Lightshed, an investment advisory firm, said in a research note ahead of the IPO filing. Potential obstacles to growth Anthropic's IPO filing also outlines various risks that could hamper its growth or cause it to fall behind competitors. Much of the company's future growth hinges on whether it has access to sufficient capital, including debt financing, which more companies are using to finance the AI buildout. To maintain its competitive edge, Anthropic also said it will need to use its existing AI models to design and train next-generation platforms, a process known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI. "If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind. …" Anthropic said in the filing. AI experts warn that using AI to build ever more powerful frontier models raises the risk of people losing control of the technology, potentially leading to disasters such as deadly pandemics or cyberattacks that cut off internet, electricity or water. Barreling ahead despite safety concerns Anthropic filed a confidential IPO with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, beating out rival OpenAI, which filed just over a week later. Both companies are barreling ahead with plans to go public despite concerns about the potential threats AI poses to humanity. Reports of AI agents going rogue continue to pile up, stoking concern that the technology could escape human control and carry out cyberattacks. In September, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development after one of his company's former researchers said that there's a 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity in the next decade. In an interview with CBS News, Amodei said the pace of technological growth should serve as a warning sign, while making a case for continued development of AI. title: F-16 uses "headbutt maneuver" to intercept plane near Mar-a-Lago
description: A fighter jet intercepted a plane over Palm Beach, Florida, on Saturday afternoon, as President Trump cast an early ballot in Florida's midterm election.
content: U.S. Fighter jet uses "headbutt maneuver" to intercept plane near Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort By Emily Mae Czachor Emily Mae Czachor News Editor Emily Mae Czachor is a reporter and news editor at CBSNews.com. She typically covers breaking news, extreme weather and climate. Emily Mae previously wrote for outlets like the Los Angeles Times, BuzzFeed and Newsweek. Read Full Bio Emily Mae Czachor October 26, 2026 / 9:07 AM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google A fighter jet used a "headbutt maneuver" to intercept a civilian plane that had entered restricted airspace near President Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach, Florida, on Saturday, U.S. military officials said. Mr. Trump was in West Palm Beach that day to vote in Florida's midterm election. The interception took place at around 12:20 p.m. ET, when an F-16 deployed by the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, flew closely in front of the plane in order to gain the pilot's attention, NORAD said. That tactic, called the "headbutt maneuver," is considered standard, according to the command. In this case, the maneuver allowed the military jet to establish communication with the pilot, who proceeded to safely steer the plane out of restricted airspace, in compliance with flight instructions, NORAD said. The plane had violated a Temporary Flight Restriction, or TFR, enacted over the area, which means its pilot could "also be met by federal authorities upon landing and subject to enforcement action," the command said. The Federal Aviation Administration issues TFRs for a variety of reasons, often linked to large sporting events, extreme weather scenarios, political rallies or any number of other engagements attended by high-profile political figures, especially the president. The FAA transmits the latest information about such restrictions to pilots through Notices to Airmen, or NOTAMs. Pilots are encouraged to keep tabs on those regularly. Mr. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump were seen at a West Palm Beach polling station on Saturday afternoon, where the president cast an early ballot ahead of next week's midterm elections. Asked whether he voted along party lines, Mr. Trump said: "Very much so." He went on to travel to Georgia for a campaign rally. His appearances at midterm campaign rallies around the country have triggered various temporary flight restrictions in recent weeks. Earlier this month, NORAD reported that its F-16s intercepted a plane that had entered restricted airspace over Clemson, South Carolina, where Mr. Trump held a rally to support Darline Graham's Senate campaign. Just days before that, the command said a similar interception took place over Cincinnati, Ohio, near the site of another rally that the president attended. title: Betting companies cap winners while lavishing losers with rewards
description: As online sports betting companies offer extravagant perks to customers who are losing large sums of money, there are also questions about how they treat their biggest winners.
content: Investigation CBS Mornings Online betting companies lavish losers with rewards while capping winners By Jake Rosenwasser, Jake Rosenwasser Reporter and Producer Jake Rosenwasser is an investigative reporter and producer for CBS News, based in New York. Read Full Bio Jake Rosenwasser, Jim Axelrod Jim Axelrod Chief Correspondent Jim Axelrod is the chief correspondent and was the executive editor for CBS News' "Eye on America" franchise, part of the "CBS Evening News." He also reports for "CBS Mornings," "CBS News Sunday Morning," and CBS News 24/7. Read Full Bio Jim Axelrod October 26, 2026 / 8:41 AM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google As greater scrutiny is falling on online sports betting companies for the way they offer extravagant perks to customers who are losing large sums of money, there is another question emerging about this fast-growing industry: how the companies treat their biggest winners. States and state lawmakers have raised questions about a practice called "limiting" — a tactic sports betting platforms use to apply the brakes to gamblers who are having too much success. "They have to ensure that the house always wins," claims Brianne Doura-Schawohl, the director for the Campaign for Fairer Gambling. "I would argue it's not fair, and what makes it more unfair is all of the pervasive advertising tells us all that we can win." Last week, a group of U.S. lawmakers wrote to the major gambling platforms to express concerns about the exploitation of vulnerable bettors by granting frequent losers VIP status. "The dangling of perks — which include access to exclusive events, videos from celebrities and athletes, and tickets to the Super Bowl — distract bettors from their financial losses and encourage betting when they otherwise would not," the letter said. Big winners, however, sometimes get the opposite treatment — their bets are often capped at under $20, and even under 50 cents at times, effectively cutting them off. In a 2023 filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, sports gambling company DraftKings explained limiting in fine print: "We follow the industry practice of restricting and managing betting limits at the individual customer level based on individual customer profiles and risk level to the enterprise." The "sharp" bettor who can hardly bet When Massachusetts launched sports gambling in 2023, Mike Manning signed up with every sports gambling app available. Manning — a full-time professional bettor, or what they call a "sharp" bettor — doesn't bet on intuition. He uses a mathematical approach with analytical models. Manning says he was winning on nearly every app. Then, one by one, the platforms began limiting his bets. On DraftKings, he said he was limited to $25 per bet. On BetMGM, he started betting $1,000-$5,000 per game, but soon, he said, he was only able to bet $5. Mike Manning is a full-time professional bettor. CBS News Limiting caught the attention of the Massachusetts Gaming Commission in 2024. The regulator required gambling companies to answer questions and provide data on how they limit their bettors. After an investigation last year, the Commission found a trend: Winning gamblers have their betting limit decreased while gamblers who lose have their limit increased. "It's that whole 'ban or bankrupt' model," said Gadoon Kyrollos, a professional sports bettor whose bets are often limited. Manning called the disparity in treatment predatory and unfair. "You're exploiting the losing bettor, you're taking advantage of them, and guys like me get shown the door," Manning told CBS News. BetMGM declined to comment. The number of accounts the companies limit is small. Massachusetts Gaming Commission found that 0.64% of Massachusetts betting accounts had been restricted. Matthew Litt, a New Jersey attorney who works on gambling cases, says the practice is legal as long as gambling companies are not discriminating against customers based on protected characteristics such as race or religion. Massachusetts became the first state to require gambling companies to notify gamblers who had been limited and to stipulate why they were being limited. FanDuel wrote to Manning that he was restricted because of "an assessment of your overall wagering patterns and their impact on our long-term risk position…" DraftKings told Manning it took action "for internal risk management purposes." Another bettor, Michael Trevithick of Ann Arbor, Michigan, shared a betting ticket with CBS News that showed the maximum DraftKings would allow him to wager on the NBA Cup was 49 cents. A DraftKings spokesperson said the company "applies customer-specific wagering limits to less than 0.15% of accounts as an enterprise risk control, generally in response to activity that appears designed to exploit errors or target discrepancies in odds. These decisions are based on customer behaviors, irrespective of whether a customer is winning or losing." The VIP who was incentivized to bet more Chris Swett was once a highly paid South Carolina attorney, but these days he is awaiting sentencing after pleading guilty to four counts of wire fraud and four counts of money laundering in federal court. Swett stole about $2 million from his law firm to fund his gambling addiction. "Every bit of it went into FanDuel," Swett said A young, successful lawyer with a growing family, Swett discovered Daily Fantasy Sports, a game in which contestants could set lineups of athletes and compete against other contestants for money on FanDuel. Chris Swett admits he stole from his employer to keep gambling. CBS News By 2019, he was wagering $5,000 to $10,000 a month Then, he says, a FanDuel employee emailed him saying anyone who spent $25,000 a month was eligible to be paired with a VIP host. The host would provide him free tickets to sporting events and complimentary entries to fantasy contests, if Swett wagered enough. "When they sent me to the first NFL game, I felt like a high roller," he said. Swett says he was in over his head, but his VIP host kept incentivizing him to bet more. In one email from 2020, Swett wrote to his VIP host: "I think I'm tapped out this month..." Two days later, the host offered him a 4% bonus on any new bets. In one two-year span, Swett says he wagered $11 million and lost about $1 million on the site. When he ran out of money, he says he set up a complex illegal scheme, defrauding his law firm and the firm's clients by submitting fake invoices for legal work. He now faces a maximum of 20 years in federal prison. "I take personal responsibility for everything I did, but it just seems like their system was designed to keep me playing," Swett said. FanDuel said in a statement: "Every day, millions of customers use FanDuel responsibly as a form of entertainment and every customer has a robust and easy-to-use suite of tools that support informed and controlled play, including deposit limits, timeouts and the ability to easily self-exclude with a few clicks. "Since the time [Mr. Swett] was in our VIP program — and as part of our broader effort to foster a culture of responsible gaming and strengthen our customer protection tools — FanDuel has made significant changes to how we operate that program, including additional training for our employees, and new technologies to identify and stop problem gambling. "FanDuel is an entertainment company — it is not a tool for professional bettors to gain an edge in play or earn a living. In the very rare instances where an individual attempts to deploy sophisticated income generation strategies, it is common for casinos and online sports betting platforms, including FanDuel, to use tools to protect our financial risk. These measures have been reviewed by multiple state regulatory bodies." If you or a loved one needs help, the National Problem Gambling Helpline offers resources. Call or text 1-800-MY-RESET or get more information on their website. Gamblers Anonymous also has a national hotline at 1-855-222-5542. title: "Maxxing" is Dictionary.com's 2026 Word of the Year
description: The viral social media trend "maxxing" has earned its stripes as Dictionary.com's 2026 Word of the Year.
content: U.S. "Maxxing" is Dictionary.com's 2026 Word of the Year By Emily Mae Czachor Emily Mae Czachor News Editor Emily Mae Czachor is a reporter and news editor at CBSNews.com. She typically covers breaking news, extreme weather and climate. Emily Mae previously wrote for outlets like the Los Angeles Times, BuzzFeed and Newsweek. Read Full Bio Emily Mae Czachor October 26, 2026 / 8:17 AM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google From AI chatbots to lifestyle trends, the concept of optimizing one's life came sharply into focus in 2026. That's why Dictionary.com picked "maxxing," a reflection of our increasingly online society, as its latest Word of the Year. "Maxxing (sometimes -maxxing) is short for 'maximizing,'" says Dictionary.com. "This trendy term can be used on its own or added to the end of any word to convey you're doing something to the fullest or optimizing it as much as possible." The word was chosen following an analysis of search data, social media trends and news stories "to capture a society that's deeply online and focused on optimization in all forms," Dictionary.com says. "Maxxing" rose through the cultural lexicons of Gen Z and Gen Alpha quickly, and now works as a noun, verb, adjective and adverb all at once. Leveling up your workout routine? "Gymmaxxing." Your personal care practices? "Healthmaxxing," an umbrella term that covers numerous subgenres, including "proteinmaxxing" and "fibermaxxing." "Maxxing really stood out this year because not only was it everywhere, in all types of articles, but it crossed a lot of different domains," said Steve Johnson, the director of lexicography for Dictionary Media Group, which runs Dictionary.com. At work, people talked about "tokenmaxxing," meaning leaning ever harder on AI. In wellness circles, there was "sleepmaxxing." Even leisure received the "maxxing" treatment, with "cozymaxxing," as did politics, when the federal government used "homelandmaxxing" in some of its messaging. "That's not something that we often get with a lot of slang terms," Johnson told CBS News. How Dictionary.com picks a Word of the Year Johnson keeps a running list of words to watch throughout the year, some of which have been rolled over from years prior and tracked for growing usage. To choose an annual winner, Dictionary's lexicographers look at how often a word appears in news articles, on social media and in online searches. They also weigh a word's cultural significance during selection. "We not only look at the data behind the word usage, but we also are really looking to see what's capturing something distinctive that describes the year," Johnson said. The latest word choice marks a turn from last year's winner, "67," a term that, despite its virality, left many bewildered over its meaning. "Maxxing" has had the opposite effect, Johnson said. "'Maxxing' is so accessible," he said. "People do understand it because it's tied to something that people instrinsically get." What is "maxxing"? The word itself isn't new. "Maxing out" a credit card, or 100 miles an hour on the highway, are well-established uses that go back decades. But the newer, optimization-focused definition comes from game theory, Johnson said. In the 1940s, academics used "mini-max" to describe a strategy for minimizing their maximum possible losses, an idea that later moved into contemporary games like Dungeons & Dragons. In that context, "min-maxing" referred to building up a character's strengths in one particular area, to the point that its weaknesses no longer mattered. According to Johnson, words like "looksmaxxing" gave the term its extra "x" and, ultimately, turned it into the trend it has become today. He said "maxxing" started standing out on its own, too, this year, in phrases like, "What are you maxxing?" or "Everyone's maxxing something." "Looksmaxxing" remains the most popular version of the word by far. Johnson said its use rose more than 1,000% since the start of the year in the media that Dictionary.com analyzed, while "tokenmaxxing" also grew with the proliferation of AI tools. What "maxxing" says about us Johnson said the word captures a pressure many people feel, especially online, to constantly do, or be, more. "Whether it's at work and your career, whether it's in school, in so many aspects of your life, just kind of being more is something that is a pressure that I think a lot of people can feel," he said. The pressure has also produced its own pushback, as playful versions of the word like "normalmaxxing" reject the drive to optimize everything while still using the same language. "One of my favorite 'maxxings' is 'nothingmaxxing,' which is just completely paradoxical, right?" Johnson said. "It's going all in an optimizing doing nothing, which also requires a lot of effort." The flexibility helps explain why the word spread so widely, he said, adding: "It resonates with people." 2026 Word of the Year finalists Dictionary.com pulled from different corners of internet culture, politics, technology and media to compile a list of finalists. Here are the others that were considered: Affordability: the quality of being inexpensive, which is an issue at the center of American life and, now, the upcoming midterm elections, as people face increasing costs of housing, groceries, childcare and more. Data center: a building or facility used for processing, storing or transmitting large amounts of computer data, which are cropping up more often around the U.S. with the rise of artificial intelligence. Unc: short for "uncle," Gen Z and Gen Alpha popularized this humorous and lightly pejorative slang term for an older person who's uncool, trying too hard, or just doesn't get it. Odyssey: a long and eventful journey, such as that of Homer's protagonist in his epic poem of the same name, which this summer was adapted into an ensemble blockbuster by director Christopher Nolan. title: Bishops lament White House meeting that produced photo with Trump
description: Two Catholic bishops have expressed regret about agreeing to a White House meeting that produced a publicly distributed photo of them praying with President Trump.
content: Politics Bishops lament White House meeting that produced photo with Trump, say session was "manipulated" and "exploited" Updated on: October 26, 2026 / 3:57 PM EDT / CBS/AP Add CBS News on Google Two Catholic bishops have expressed regret about agreeing to a White House meeting that produced a publicly distributed photo of them praying with President Trump. Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, in a statement titled "A Public Apology," said Sunday that he had received many questions and comments — some of them distraught — about the meeting on Thursday that he and 11 other bishops attended. He said the meeting was speedily publicized by the White House with photos and a video without consent of the participants, less than two weeks away from the midterm elections. "I feel a heavy sadness, not only over the pain I caused, but also for the fact that something so sacred to a group of religious leaders, prayer to our Heavenly Father, would be manipulated in that way," Grob said. Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob in an undated photo. Milwaukee Archdiocese The bishop of Des Moines, Iowa, William Joensen, also issued a statement making clear he felt the White House had taken advantage of the bishops. "I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purpose," he wrote. "I pray I am more prudent and wise going forward, even as I remain resolute in my openness to engaging and praying for political leaders at all levels." Asked whether the White House had received the bishops' consent for releasing the photos and video, the press office declined to answer. Instead, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers replied, "There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it." The White House invitation to the bishops, extended in September, offered discussion about such issues as immigration enforcement, religious worker visas, abortion and the use of federal tax credits to support private education, according to Joensen and Grob. "The meeting was in no way an endorsement of the president, his policies, or his party," wrote Grob. "We were told the meeting was to be a private discussion, that several Catholic members of the Cabinet might make an appearance, and that there could be an opportunity to pray privately with the president." "It did not take long thereafter for the White House to post a video and photos of the prayer," Grob said. "I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he added. "I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family had been harmed by the president's policies. " ... We came in good faith to try to work for the betterment of our fellow human beings, to ease their suffering, to build up the common good, and to pray with a president, not to pose for a political photo opportunity to benefit the few. We should never have been put in that position by the White House. "I did not go without reservations. I wish I had heeded them," Grob concluded. "Please know that I have heard these concerns, understand how I caused them, and I apologize for any damage my actions have done." Collectively, members of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops have diverse views on Mr. Trump and his administration's policies. Minnesota-based Bishop Robert Barron, for example, agreed to serve on his Religious Liberty Commission, which was filled almost entirely with conservative Christians. Some other bishops vehemently denounced aspects of Mr. Trump's tough stance on immigration enforcement, saying it runs counter to Catholic teaching. 2026 Midterm Elections More John Thune's balancing act: Inside his push to save the GOP majority Court dismisses DOJ's request to force California to set aside ballots Gina Hinojosa says there's "deep disappointment" in both parties Blanche says DOJ is "doing our own research" with Alaska challenge Poll finds Democrats still boosted by voters' economic concerns Go deeper with The Free Press What Happens After Trump?: Why Tim Miller Thinks Politics Can’t Go Back ‘Pretend I’m on the Ballot’ Is Trump’s Midterm Strategy © 2026 CBS Interactive Inc. title: Iran shrugs off Trump's attack threats, says diplomacy ongoing
description: Iran says indirect negotiations with the U.S. continue but rules out bending to Trump's demands, even if he orders new strikes.
content: Live Live Updates: 8-month Iran war looms over Israeli election as Egypt wades into Saudi's fight with the Houthis By Frank Andrews Frank Andrews Frank Andrews is a CBS News journalist based in London. Read Full Bio Frank Andrews Updated on: October 27, 2026 / 7:39 AM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google What to know about the Iran war: Israelis were voting Tuesday in a national election set to shape the country's next government, with the Iran war looming large over their decisions. Israel's defense minister called on voters to back Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration so it can "finish the job" started in Iran almost eight months ago. Oil prices held more or less steady early Tuesday, with international benchmark Brent crude hovering around $116 a barrel, little changed from the previous day when senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting. Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen said Tuesday that Egypt's decision to send troops to Saudi Arabia to defend against the rebels' attacks on the kingdom was a "declaration of war," as the interwoven conflicts in the Middle East threatened to escalate. New Updates 28m ago Experts warn of effects of slick as oil seen on UAE beach An oil slick in the Gulf has reached a beach in the United Arab Emirates, video from the AFP news agency showed on Tuesday, with experts warning it could threaten desalination plants as it spreads. UAE authorities said Friday that they had "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," referring to an emirate north of Dubai. By Tuesday morning, footage shot by AFP showed workers cleaning up oil on the emirate's beaches, which had been shut earlier by authorities along with other beaches in the country. Satellite images taken on Oct. 21 and analyzed by AFP show what appears to be a slick of about 70 square miles in that area. Three days later, images showed it had quadrupled in size to around 290 square miles. Experts from NGOs including Dutch peace group PAX said oil came from the tanker GEM NO.2 after it was attacked on Oct. 9. They warned the slick could affect operations at UAE desalination plants, crucial for supplying water to the Gulf country. "Satellite imagery from October 26 shows oil slicks a few hundred metres away from the intake of the Naqaa desalination plant. It remains unclear to what extent this will affect the process at the plant itself," said Wim Zwijnenburg from PAX. The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on Oct. 9 that a vessel had been hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control. CBS/AFP https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-diplomacy-oil-prices-strait-of-hormuz/#post-update-7c761096 link copied 7:01 AM Iranian official says Middle Eastern countries must stop relying on the U.S. for security Mohsen Rezaee, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said regional countries should not rely on the United States for security, arguing that Washington has failed to provide credible security guarantees. In a post on X Tuesday, Rezaee wrote: "America has not brought security to any country in the region, and Washington's inability to provide security guarantees has become clear. Security in West Asia must originate from within the region, and any foreign intervention must be prevented." The U.S. has military bases in several Gulf countries that repeatedly were targeted at the height of the war. By Khaled Wassef, Frank Andrews https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-diplomacy-oil-prices-strait-of-hormuz/#post-update-b4bbdce6 link copied 6:14 AM Houthi official calls Egypt's military support for Saudi Arabia a declaration of war A Houthi official said Tuesday that the Egyptian parliament's decision to authorize President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to deploy forces to Saudi Arabia to help the kingdom defend against the Iran-backed group's attacks was a declaration of war. "Egypt and its parliament declared support for what is called the defense of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and in doing so, it declares war against the Republic of Yemen," said Mohammed Ali al-Houthi, a member of the Houthi political bureau, in a Telegram post. El-Sisi stressed last week that the Egyptian deployment would be entirely defensive, "and does not include an attack on Yemen." CBS/AFP https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-diplomacy-oil-prices-strait-of-hormuz/#post-update-905ff338 link copied 4:49 AM Oil prices stick around $116 a barrel despite Iran lauding talks with Saudis and others aimed at averting new fighting Oil prices held more or less steady early Tuesday, with international benchmark Brent crude hovering around $116 a barrel, little changed from the previous day when senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting. Tehran said the discussions were "very good." Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis," a Saudi foreign ministry statement said. The talks followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war, with some observers suggesting the period between next Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections and the new Congress taking office could be particularly fraught. Also in view are elections in Israel, where voters began delivering their verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who told President Trump a week ago that they have "a job to finish" in Iran. CBS/AFP https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-diplomacy-oil-prices-strait-of-hormuz/#post-update-ac1a09a4 link copied 3:58 AM As Israeli election begins, defense chief calls on voters to let Netanyahu "finish the job" in Iran Israelis started casting votes Tuesday morning in a national election set to shape the country's next government, with the Iran war looming large over their decisions. Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, echoing warnings issued repeatedly by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for weeks leading up to the vote, told voters that they were facing a decision "between two security paradigms: an approach based on offense, initiative, and decisive victory — or a return to a policy of containment and restraint." "We have struck Iran twice and eliminated existential threats; we have expanded Israel's security perimeter in Lebanon, Syria, and Gaza to protect Israeli communities; and we are currently strengthening and fortifying our eastern border and the Jordan Valley," he said, calling on Israeli voters to "support this path in order to finish the job." Israeli voters pass campaign booths and posters after voting at a polling station, Oct. 27, 2026, in Hod Hasharon, Israel. David Silverman/Getty Netanyahu has called for Israel and the U.S. to resume attacks on Iran, telling President Trump, who has endorsed him enthusiastically, last week, "we have a job to finish." The Iranian regime has dismissed the importance of the Israeli election, with foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei telling reporters Monday that the outcome will have no bearing on Iran's preparedness to face a resumption of hostilities, or to negotiate a deal to end the war based on its longstanding demands. By Tucker Reals https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-diplomacy-oil-prices-strait-of-hormuz/#post-update-6ab75a1a link copied 1:43 AM Saudi coalition says it intercepted 3 Houthi ballistic missiles The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthi rebels said on Tuesday that it had shot down three missiles fired by the group toward the kingdom's eastern region. "Air defenses intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Eastern Province," coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki wrote on X. By AFP https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-diplomacy-oil-prices-strait-of-hormuz/#post-update-7dacba0a link copied 4:28 PM / October 26, 2026 Iran's talks with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan on Middle East security were "very good," officials say Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran on Monday in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting, with Tehran saying the discussions were "very good." Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis," a Saudi foreign ministry statement said. It was the first joint visit to Tehran by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey since they formed a defense alliance in Mecca, the holy city in western Saudi Arabia, in August. The talks, which included heavyweight Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war. The delegations met Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. The meeting ended without concrete announcements, with the various parties saying they "agreed to continue discussions" according to Iranian state media.
